events.title: Nike lays out financial goals ahead of first investor day in 9 years
events.summary: Nike is hosting its first investor day in nine years at its Oregon headquarters as the company tries to prove to investors that its turnaround strategy is working. The footwear company has been enduring a yearslong slump, including significant sustained declines in the China market. Nike said Tuesday ahead of its first investor day in nine years that it was reaffirming its 2027 financial guidance. The retailer also laid out a financial framework and said that by the end of fiscal 2031 it's targeting approximately $5 billion in incremental revenue growth from fiscal year 2027, operating margins of 12% to 14% and adjusted earnings per share of $3.00 to $3.50. The company also introduced a strategy it's calling Full Stride Ahead, which the company said aims "to get closer to athletes and focus resources on the greatest opportunities for long-term growth." Nike is holding an investor day at its Oregon headquarters Tuesday as the company aims to prove to investors that its turnaround strategy is yielding success after a yearslong slump. Last month, the company reported mixed fiscal first-quarter results as it announced a restructuring plan, including layoffs that it said would start next year. It's the company's third round of layoffs to be announced this year. Nike's net income and revenue both fell during the most recent period compared with a year ago, and the company said it expects revenue to decline by a high single-digit percentage in fiscal 2027. The new strategy, dubbed Pace, focuses on the company's supply chain and reorganizing into three geographies. Nike said the turnaround plan is expected to deliver roughly $2.5 billion in savings through fiscal 2031. Nike has been seeing significant sustained declines in its China market, where revenue last quarter dropped 26%. Experts have said the company is losing relevance in the country, while Nike has said it's actively working to win over younger consumers. At the same time, Nike announced last quarter that it's creating a new global campus in India as part of its new growth strategy, hoping the country will help boost its performance. The company said it was remaining focused on China even as it begins to build out its India presence. CEO Elliott Hill's turnaround strategy includes improving different parts of the business at different rates based on priority. While it's seen some signs of progress in the North America business, Hill has said that performance isn't enough to offset the pressures on the company elsewhere, including internationally. The Nike consumer has also been under increased macroeconomic pressure as geopolitical tensions mount and inflation rises.

events.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia exit is now X official
events.summary: Jensen Huang's X page no longer lists him as CEO. X screenshots Jensen Huang's X profile got a post-Nvidia departure makeover. It's the latest sign that he may not be returning as Nvidia's CEO, despite some calling for it. Elon Musk said Huang's blue check is coming back "on the house." Shortly after, it returned. Jensen Huang's Nvidia exit just got a little more real on X. The former CEO's X account now identifies him only as the "Founder of NVIDIA." Before the late Monday profile overhaul, it also said "CEO." The makeover did not stop at three missing letters. Huang's once-green Nvidia banner has been replaced with a plain gray one. His Nvidia affiliation badge also vanished, as has a link to his Nvidia biography. Huang also lost his blue check verification badge — but it didn't last too long. "Blue check coming back for free on the house," wrote Elon Musk , the CEO of X owner SpaceX, in a reply to a post about Huang's disappearing verified badge. By Tuesday morning, Huang's blue check was back. 📝 Bio change detected: @jensenhuang pic.twitter.com/CJG1dfOglV — Big Tech Alert (@BigTechAlert) November 17, 2026 A blue check on X costs $8 a month, but Nvidia's green affiliation badge would require the company to pay $1,000 a month for X Premium Business's Full Access tier, plus $50 a month for each affiliated account. Huang is worth $136.2 billion, according to Forbes, a figure that has dropped significantly since he stepped down after an extramarital affair scandal and a board investigation into whether he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Huang's LinkedIn profile, however, remains unchanged: it still lists him as "founder and CEO" of Nvidia. It doesn't look like Huang has got round to updating his LinkedIn profile yet. LinkedIn screenshot A Huang comeback? The X profile changes come as a growing number of Huang's supporters call for him to be reinstated. More than 191,000 people had signed the "Stand With Jensen" petition as of Tuesday morning, according to the campaign's website. The drive has attracted support from Musk, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, as well as other business leaders, investors, and Nvidia employees. But Silicon Valley is hardly united behind a Huang comeback. While some supporters argue that the board should complete its investigation before permanently replacing the founder, others say the push to restore him reflects the industry's tendency to excuse powerful men. Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told Business Insider on Monday, as it investigates whether Huang had been the target of a foreign-intelligence effort. Dan Ives, a senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, said Sunday that he saw "no chance" Huang would return as Nvidia CEO, while leadership experts told Business Insider on Monday that a comeback was unlikely in the near term . The uncertainty is also weighing on Nvidia's stock ahead of its closely watched earnings on Monday afternoon. Shares closed down 4.1% at $156.14 on Monday. Huang resigned last Thursday after a fast-moving series of revelations . He acknowledged in a memo to employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife. The New York Times reported that he had relationships with Alice Huang, a former Singapore-based Megaspeed executive who US officials suspected of passing information to Beijing, and Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him. Whether the changes to Huang's X profile are a message or merely housekeeping, Nvidia has begun planning for a future without him at the helm. "There is a world after Jensen, and there is still so much progress to be made," Lior Susan, the founder and CEO of venture firm Eclipse, told Business Insider on Monday. events.title: Silicon Valley leaders forge a 'save Jensen' faction
events.summary: Huang’s Silicon Valley compatriots continue to rally around him. “This narrative of the Chinese spy is falling apart,” said David Sacks, President Donald Trump’s former AI and crypto czar, at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, joining a chorus of (admittedly geographically and ideologically cloistered) allies casting doubt on the crux of the scandal that bounced the Nvidia CEO from his job last week. Sacks said that the public has been too quick to judge, a sentiment echoed by Bill Ackman: “If it’s a personal foible … I think there’s a very powerful case for putting him back in place.” (The longtime activist investor, who has lately hung up his sword, laid out a tactical playbook for reinstating Huang, while saying he was unlikely to get involved.) Replit CEO Amjad Masad, who signed an online petition to bring Huang back, called Huang’s ouster “ an attack on open models, ” feeding a theory that frontier AI labs threatened by Nvidia’s Nemotron model contributed to his downfall. Huang’s absence from Nvidia “would be a huge loss and it would potentially bring about a world where there’s only the frontier model labs that exist,” Masad said. Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner urged the Nvidia board to reconsider Huang’s ouster , saying the company needs to find all the information in order to “get this right.” Trump, for his part, put it more directly, telling reporters on Monday that he “wouldn’t mind” if Huang was reinstated. — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: Nvidia’s first big move after Jensen Huang’s exit targets national security
events.summary: Nvidia has formed a committee to oversee national security policies and export control compliance following the abrupt resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who had links to one of the company’s customers. Nvidia said Tuesday that the new standing committee will give board-level oversight of national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risks. The move comes amid increased scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Huang’s alleged ties to the suspected spy and his advocacy for easing restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China. The Commerce Department said Monday it was planning to introduce new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside of the U.S. in an effort to prevent companies in China and elsewhere from circumventing existing rules by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries. The interim rule was made in direct response to the unfolding chip smuggling scandal at Nvidia. The announcement comes just a few hours before Nvidia’s highly anticipated third-quarter earnings call. Analysts, the media, and shareholders expect the company to address the controversy and outline how it might affect operations. This is the first major action by the company under the leadership of Collette Kress, the company’s CFO who took over as interim CEO after Huang stepped down last week. The committee, which will meet at least quarterly, will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and include fellow directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members. Nvidia already has a national security team and global trade compliance team. Those teams will now report to this board committee and Kress on day-to-day operations. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress later this month. events.title: China vows to take ‘necessary measures’ against US AI chip restrictions, as investors brace for Nvidia’s results – business live
events.summary: China slams new US chip curbs and pledges 'necessary measures' China has threatened to retaliate against the US after Washington tightened restrictions on remote access to AI chips and servers. At a press conference on Tuesday, China’s foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Beijing would take “necessary measures” to safeguard its own interests, saying: “The US has repeatedly overstretched the concept of national security, abused export controls and even interfered in China’s normal trade and technological cooperation with other countries, unjustifiably suppressing the development of China’s high-tech industries.” Guo also called the US move a typical example of economic coercion that deviates from the consensus reached by both countries, Reuters reports . As we blogged yesterday , the US Commerce Department has issued a new rule which limits remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips by companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil. The new measure closes a loophole which allowed Chinese companies to access cutting-edge US tech by using data centres based in other countries in Asia. Awkwardly for Beijing, the new “interim final rule” is being imposed just as Donald Trump prepares to meet China’s president Xi Jinping later this week in Shenzhen, which is hosting this week’s APEC summit. Dexter Roberts , a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Global China Hub, says ( via Bloomberg ): “This is the worst situation possible for China because the last thing they want to see is any new restrictions on their access to chips.” “Export controls are what upset them practically more than anything else right now other than maybe Taiwan.” 6m ago US retail sales growth slows 1h ago US government confirms investigation into Megaspeed over Nvidia chip exports 2h ago Nvidia establishes National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee 3h ago EU charges Temu with illegal items failings 5h ago Tension rises ahead of Nvidia's results tonoight 5h ago China slams new US chip curbs and pledges 'necessary measures' 6h ago Deutsche Bank shares drop after leak 6h ago UK interest rate rise in December a 90% chance 6h ago Imperial Brands cutting another 2,500 jobs 7h ago Youth unemployment down to 15.1% 7h ago Introduction: UK wage growth slows as payrolls fall Over in the US, retail sales growth has slowed – possibly a worrying sign ahead of the festive spending season. US retail sales growth slowed to 0.2% in October, driven by a drop in demand for motor vehicles and parts, clothing and sports equipment. That’s down on the 0.8% sales growth recorded in September, when spending on gasoline jumped due to higher prices at the pumps. Here’s a great chart from Jim Reid at Deutsche Bank , showing how Nvidia’s earnings have soared since the AI boom began, and how they are expected to keep accelerating: Forget the macro, the biggest event of the next few weeks is probably tonight’s Nvidia earnings. It’s a good moment to remember that the company’s transformation is arguably one of the most extraordinary in corporate history. When ChatGPT launched in November 2022, Nvidia was earning around $5bn a year. That was a respectable number for a company still best known to gamers and crypto miners. Today, on a rolling four-quarter basis, it’s likely to be nearer $240bn, and consensus has it reaching around $625bn by 2031. If that happens, Nvidia will have gone from $5bn of net income to over $600bn in under a decade. I can’t think of anything that comes close. The biggest annual profit ever reported is generally thought to be Saudi Aramco’s roughly $160bn in 2022, when oil was last above $100 and Europe was scrambling for energy. Nvidia is now ahead of this. Its 2031 forecast would be about the size of the current annual GDP of Thailand, the UAE or Austria. Those countries have populations of around 72m, 11.5m and 9.2m respectively. Nvidia, at its last filing, employed around 42,000 people. Yes, it’s apples and oranges, or perhaps chips, but it shows the sheer scale of what’s going on. The Chinese online-shopping retailer Temu has rejected EU charges of failing to tackle the sale of illegal products on its website. Responding to the European Commission’s charge sheet announced earlier ( 12.08 ) a Temu spokesperson said they “respectfully disagreed” with the findings. Temu invests significantly in compliance infrastructure and human expertise and implements a suite of control measures that effectively mitigate illegal product risks with a consistently low incidence of problematic products. Promising to respond to the findings carefully, the company added: We are confident that we will reach an amicable resolution of the matter that fully addresses the Commission’s remaining concerns. Options traders are pricing in a roughly $335bn swing in Nvidia ’s market value after the company reports third-quarter earnings tonight.

events.title: Shoppers slowed spending in October with high prices leading to caution
events.summary: Shoppers increased spending more slowly in October as economic uncertainty and high prices led more Americans to become cautious with their moneyRetail sales rose 0.2% in October, down from a revised 0.8% gain in September, according to the Commerce De... NEW YORK -- Shoppers increased spending more slowly in October as economic uncertainty and high prices led more Americans to become cautious with their money. Retail sales rose 0.2% in October, down from a revised 0.8% gain in September, according to the Commerce Department's report released Tuesday. Excluding business at gas stations, retail sales were up 0.1%. Oil prices have been volatile with the flow of exports from the Middle East rising. Sales at gas stations rose 1.5% last month; in September, that figure spiked 30.3% compared with the previous month, according to the Commerce Department's report. The average price for a gallon of regular gasoline fell again to $3.78 per gallon Tuesday, according to motor club AAA, down 12% from last month at this time. That is still well above the price Americans were paying at this time last year, when a gallon was closer to $3. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Spending was mixed across different merchandising areas, according to the Commerce Department report. Business at furniture and home furnishings stores fell 2.3%, while clothing and accessories stores had a 0.7% decline. Business at online retailers rose 1.2%, according to the report. The data offers only a snapshot of consumer spending and doesn’t include activities like travel and hotel stays. But the lone services category – restaurants registered a 0.2% increase. The retail sales report followed new evidence that inflation put more pressure on Americans last month. events.title: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
events.summary: Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all. The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user's knowledge. It’s “worse than a bug” Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent's reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.” Read full article Comments

events.title: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot
events.summary: The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years. The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward. “Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon , associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade. Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing. Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator. Optalysys “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright , assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.” Optics to inference’s rescue? Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication. Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N . N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors. VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N 2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N 2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N 2 . In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N , not N 2 . So the energy used will scale as N , not N 2 , as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied. Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10 -19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10 -14 and 10 -12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000. But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements. McMahon says this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.” It’s also important to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law . “Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.” With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data. Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. events.title: Spotify’s new tool aims to stop deepfakes from being attributed to real artists
events.summary: As AI-generated slop continues to flood music streaming platforms, Spotify is rolling out an “Artist Profile Protection” tool to all artists, giving them control over the music appearing under their name. The official launch comes eight months after the company began beta testing the feature with select artists. Spotify says the tool is designed to address a longstanding issue across streaming services, where music can end up on the wrong artist profile due to deliberate impersonation, metadata errors, or shared artist names. The update comes as Billboard reported last month that Sony Music had requested the removal of more than 260,000 deepfake songs from digital platforms, nearly double the number the label disclosed in March. With this new feature, Spotify is aiming to give artists more control over their digital identities as the volume of music uploaded to streaming services continues to grow. Artists can enable the feature through Spotify for Artists to receive alerts when new music is submitted under their name. If a release doesn’t belong to them, they can remove their association with it to stop it from appearing on their profile. By default, releases go live as scheduled unless an artist intervenes. If artists want greater control, they can choose to switch on an advanced setting that requires them to manually approve or reject releases before they appear on their profile. “Artists should never have to find someone else’s music under their name, said Sam Duboff. Spotify’s Global Head of Marketing and Policy, in an email, stated to TechCrunch. “Their artist profile should be in their control. Starting today, every artist on Spotify can use Artist Profile Protection to review what shows up on their profile and prevent spammy and incorrect releases from ever reaching their page or their fans. We’re the first and only streaming service with a solution to the industry-wide problem of content mismatch, and we hope it sets a new standard for streaming platforms.” The company says it worked with thousands of artists during the beta testing phase to refine the tool and make it easier to protect their profiles without disrupting release schedules. events.title: Genesis AI raises $500 million to deploy glove-wearing robots
events.summary: Genesis AI has “cracked dexterous manipulation,” CEO and co-founder Zhou Xian says. To make his case, Xian hosted TechCrunch at Genesis AI’s Silicon Valley facility, where its physical AI model operated a pair of off-the-shelf robotic arms. In one demo, the arms picked up two small cardboard boxes, scanned them, placed them in a larger cardboard box, folded it closed, taped it shut, and then plucked a label off a strip of printer tape and applied it to the box. It’s an impressive demo, exactly the kind of complex workflow that today’s robots struggle to complete. And while Genesis wouldn’t let your reporter mess with the robot’s mise en place to test its wiles, the company did agree to re-run the presentation. During the second go-round, the robot fumbled a box and had a heck of a time peeling the tiny adhesive label off the printer tape. A mistake, but also the kind of edge case that can be used to improve a model—”hiccup data,” a Genesis executive suggests. This is the exact gap —between a lab demo and reliable automation—that Genesis , and the rest of the humanoid physical AI ecosystem, need to bridge if they want to avoid another robot winter. To do so, Xian’s company is announcing a $500 million Series A round led by Khosla Ventures, Premji Invest, and Eclipse. Xian and Genesis president Théophile Gervet, who met as graduate students in a Carnegie Mellon University lab, cofounded the company in 2024. Genesis announced its $105 million seed round in July 2025. The company’s strategy is vertical integration: generating the bulk of its own training data, developing its own generative AI model, and doing both in concert with the design and construction of a humanoid robot. “We wanted to ship the best robot, end-to-end product,” Xian said. The startup’s focus on dexterity — the robot’s ability to do stuff with its hands — and gathering the right data to achieve it sets it apart from competitors like Figure or Agility. Genesis gathers force data (apparently the unlock for effective manipulation) using a sensor-enabled glove. The gloves, and accompanying headset cameras, are worn by more than 100 real workers around the world, whose activities contribute to a training dataset that feeds into the company’s model. The company’s robots wear the same sensor-equipped gloves, and their “hands” are designed to mimic the proportions of human hands. That fidelity, Xian says, enables the robots’ capabilities in sorting and wire manipulation. The other big investment the company has made is in simulation. One of its advisers, Minchen Li, is a co-author of an influential physics algorithm used by the startup to create millions of high-fidelity models of the robot’s experience. Still, about that robot: Xian said that the company’s model was more capable when operating Eno, the company’s flagship humanoid robot. But Eno wasn’t ready to demonstrate its abilities for TechCrunch. A handsome machine bearing more than a hint of the late Steve Jobs’ influence on tech gadgets and their marketing, Eno reflects “the feeling” the company wants to deliver to its customers. That means less of a Terminator -styled metal skeleton and more of an iMac on wheels. Genesis said it has built 30 to 40 Enos, but wasn’t ready to share how many it would make in the year ahead. The company would only say that a mass-manufacturing contractor had been chosen to start work next year in the U.S. and that the design of the mass-produced version had been finalized. The company is piloting the machine with a handful of undisclosed customers. To realize the company’s vision, Xian says the key bottleneck is hardware capability, both in mechanical design and in the supply chains needed to produce industrial-grade machines. Right now, the company’s dexterous hands can only operate for a few weeks of regular work before they need to be replaced. For truly generalized robotic intelligence, Genesis needs more data. Xian pooh-poohs the finer distinctions between architectures like Vision-Language-Action models and World-Action models . In his view, the software is ultimately transformers and attention, so “what really matters is is the whole infra — the training infrastructure, the data infrastructure, and the quality of the data.” He estimates that “the model architecture contributes to maybe 10% of of the final [result].” “I don’t think we expect or we need another fundamental scientific leap,” he told TechCrunch. “No, we have all the recipes. It’s just about execution.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. events.title: Upside Foods can now make a million pounds of chicken a year without killing any animals
events.summary: Upside Foods didn’t even have to try to garner interest from MrBeast, the most-followed creator on the internet. The YouTuber showed up at the company’s facility with his video crew. The eleven-year-old company had undergone a 10,000-fold scale-up that it hopes could revolutionize the nascent cultivated meat industry. Upside says it can now make over one million pounds of edible, cultivated chicken each year without killing a single animal in the process. Such an achievement challenges the long-held industry skepticism over whether lab-grown meat will ever be affordable enough to meaningfully scale. So MrBeast, whose real name is Jimmy Donaldson, came to see for himself, taste-testing two chicken sandwiches on camera, one made with meat from a chicken killed that day, and one using Upside Foods chicken. He was unable to identify which sandwich was which — they tasted exactly the same to him. “I mean, you see me in the video – I was like, ‘Oh my gosh, what is he going to say?’” Upside Foods CEO Dr. Uma Valeti told TechCrunch. “I thought he would maybe say a nice thing here and there, but he would get it right. But he didn’t.” If there was any reason to doubt Donaldson’s assessment, now you can taste the chicken yourself, if you live in California. Upside Foods announced on Tuesday that it will now be available at several restaurants in the state, marking a major milestone for the cultivated meat industry. “This has been a decade of foundation building,” Valeti said, adding that Upside Foods has secured its next set of regulatory approvals from the FDA and USDA. “With that comes the whole excitement and ice-breaking for the field … There’s brilliant ideas in science, but science only makes an impact when you get to scale.” Solving this scale problem has been the biggest obstacle for the cultivated meat industry. The first ever lab-grown hamburger, produced in 2013, cost $300,000 to make. Now, Valeti says that Upside Foods can match the price range of “really high quality organic chicken.” “The whole industry was going through this really difficult scale-up period… We had to go through that grinder to come out on the other side,” Valeti said. The cultivated meat movement isn’t just about animal welfare (though for many, that’s a plus). According to the Good Food Institute, a nonprofit think tank for alternative proteins, it would take 5.5 Earths to feed the world with conventional meat production in 2050, when the United Nations predicts that the global population will approach 10 billion . “We use less water, less land, less energy,” Valeti said. “The power of this technology is you protect the choice of eating what we love, but we can also protect everything else we love about protecting life, and the environment, and animal welfare.” The process of cultivating meat also cuts the risk of E. coli, Salmonella, and antibiotic resistance while lowering cholesterol and saturated fat, the company promises. Upside Foods’ chicken is also augmented with soy protein isolate, pea fiber, and olive oil, making it more nutritionally dense. Valeti says that this doesn’t affect the flavor, which is something he agonized over. He even brought in Michelin-starred and James Beard Award-winning chefs, Thomas Keller and Nancy Silverton, to weigh in on the taste. “We got a lot of confidence after we worked with [these chefs],” Valeti said. “They said, ‘Uma, you and your team are obsessing too much about it. The majority of people, when you put this in your chicken dishes, will not be able to tell.’” Upside Foods’ milestone of producing one million pounds of chicken per year is meaningful, but the industry still has a long way to go. In 2021, it was estimated that Americans consume about 8 billion chickens annually. But aside from sheer capital, Valeti believes the company has been able to scale the amount it has because of how much it has learned by experimenting with the process over the years. He thinks more growth is possible. “Unless we show it at the largest scale possible that anybody has done, no one is going to believe us,” he said. events.title: Hank Green is self-funding ClockwiseTV, a curated educational video platform for kids
events.summary: “I was recently on a podcast and the host asked me what my lowest part of my career was,” Hank Green mused on a recent episode of his own podcast, Dear Hank & John. That’s a tough question for anyone to answer, let alone someone who has spent about two decades regularly posting videos online for an increasingly broad audience. “Really the low — the long low — was just watching as [the internet] went from being this lovely thing that a bunch of creatives were goofing around [on] to it being freaking everything, and mattering so much, and getting taken over by all tons of terrible vibes and algorithms selecting for outrage, and it being a huge degradation to the social order,” Green said. That’s bleak, but Green is at least trying to lead by example in showing that we don’t have to accept that the good parts of the internet are gone forever. The notoriously entrepreneurial vlogbrother has spun up a new company with Leslie Morgan : ClockwiseTV, a curated, ad-free educational video platform for children ages 8 to 12. “[Hank] came to me last September like, ‘I have had this idea for a really long time, and it stems from the fact that my child, who’s nine, always is asking me for five more minutes on whatever device he’s on,” Morgan, who has spent twenty years working on the business side of the creator economy, told TechCrunch. “I was like, I have that same problem… How do you contain time, but also give the child agency?’” Clockwise’ answer to that question seems to be this: At the start of each viewing session, the parent and child decide how long they can watch for, and the platform will recommend videos that will adhere to that time frame. If a kid is in the midst of a 30-minute session and has already watched two ten-minute videos, they’re not going to be suggested a 20-minute video when they only have 10 minutes left. The startup is addressing a pretty widespread concern among parents, who are worried about more than simply negotiating with their children about how long they can use the iPad. According to a 2025 study by the Pew Research Center, about 51% of parents of children 12 or younger say their kid watches YouTube every day, among other video apps. YouTube has a dedicated app for children under 13, YouTube Kids, which offers a wide range of parental controls, but the app can reportedly still serve children a wealth of low-quality AI slop. Other apps that don’t have a kids’ version can be even worse. Clockwise says it is also solving that problem by hand-curating a library of educational videos from creators like Odd Animal Specimens , Draw with Jazza , and Nerdforge , as well as channels Green had a hand in creating, like Crash Course Kids and Sci Show Kids . “When you go into the app, there’s a dozen choices [of videos] that you can choose from to start,” Morgan, the startup’s CEO, said. “There’s search functionality as well, so you can say, ‘Hey, I’m really interested in math today,’ so you can look up Stand-up Maths and look at what’s available in that time frame.” Some of these creators cater to people of all ages, but Clockwise says its team manually reviews each video it uploads and edits it so that it’s ready for younger eyes. The team might remove anything from embedded product placement to what Morgan calls “spectacle power tool use.” “ Simone Giertz , who’s a maker creator, tends to curse a lot. But a lot of that content is great for kids,” Morgan explains. “She makes a skateboard for her three-legged dog, and if she drops an f-bomb, we’re going to cut it out so that it’s suitable for children.” Clockwise pays these creators an upfront fee to use their videos, then shares 25% of revenue based on watch time. Clockwise charges parents $6.99 per month or $69.99 per year to access the platform, which it promises will remain free of ads. “Humans are checking [the videos] four times at least before it’s ever published into our app […] That will always stay,” Morgan said. “We’re not interested in using AI to wash down our content.” So far, a few hundred parents have tested Clockwise with their children in beta. On Tuesday, the platform is opening to the public with apps made for iOS and Android smartphones and tablets. The platform has not taken on any outside funding, and is funded by Green himself. “It was really important that he had full control,” Morgan said. “He wanted to invest his own wealth into this. That was also really important because it is something he just believes in so wholeheartedly, as do I.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters BBC, Zoom, HSBC, and GitLab among those caught up in supply chain attack targeting visitors' crypto wallets, credit cards, and iPhones Hospital gave very sick doctor a special PC for his very personal use 11 days ago Pokémon bakeoff reveals best JavaScript frameworks for AI 13 days ago Topcoat enables Rust to render server-side web apps 18 days ago How Google fumbled the frontend with Angular 2 19 days ago UK pentester 'killa' claims $2K Bitcoin prize in PHP2Shell capture-the-flag contest 21 days ago Some of the world's most popular websites spent Monday serving malware to visitors after crooks found a way into a piece of software used to A/B test web pages. Scott Helme, a security researcher at Report URI, identified malicious JavaScript being served by websites belonging to at least 178 organizations, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom, IKEA, Salesforce, HSB, and TalkTalk. All have one thing in common: they use Optimizely's Web Experimentation software. Optimizely allows businesses to tweak the content and layout of their websites without changing the underlying site code. Unfortunately, someone other than its paying customers figured out how to do just that. The attackers abused a feature that allows Optimizely customers to add their own JavaScript to web pages. The malicious code was distributed alongside the legitimate stuff from Optimizely's own content delivery network, giving customers little reason to suspect anything was amiss. Optimizely has since confirmed that the criminals exploited a vulnerability, dubbed "OPTIMJACK" by researchers, in the sign-up process for its experimentation software, adding that it had patched the hole, removed the offending code, revoked tokens, and notified affected customers. "Earlier today, Optimizely identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects,” the company said. “We've fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects. We've also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorized code from being delivered." Of the 1,611 Optimizely scripts examined by Helme and his team, 188 contained malicious code, including those used by Optimizely's own website and login portal. Given the researchers examined only a subset of the scripts, the number of affected businesses could be higher. The malware underwent several revisions over the course of Monday, with cryptocurrency theft among the crooks' money-making schemes. Copy a wallet address to your clipboard and the malware could quietly swap it out for one belonging to the attackers, diverting any funds sent to that address. A card skimmer added later in the day grabbed card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes from payment forms. However, according to a separate analysis by StepSecurity , card details entered into an iframe hosted by a third-party payment processor were beyond the malware's reach. There was something nasty in store for Apple users, too. The malware attempted to deploy the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits on iPhones and iPads running older versions of iOS, though how many devices the criminals managed to compromise is anyone's guess. Helme traced roughly $7,000 in cryptocurrency to the attackers' wallets on Monday, though there’s no telling how much more the crooks stand to make from stolen payment card details. By 2152 UTC on Monday, TalkTalk was the only organization remaining on Report URI's list whose Optimizely code still contained the malware. All that money spent securing corporate websites, and the attackers found their way onto them via a bit of software the marketing department uses to tinker with web pages.

events.summary: Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook's attorney on Tuesday gave the strongest signal yet that his client will not attend a hearing at the White House with a committee investigating mortgage fraud allegations against Cook. events.title: Investor Steve Eisman says the AI neocloud stocks are in 'big trouble' from Nvidia fallout
events.summary: Investor Steve Eisman said the so-called AI neocloud stocks will be the biggest losers from the unfolding Nvidia scandal. Nvidia was essentially a "virtual vertical holding company and it's unwinding," said Eisman of "Big Short" fame on CNBC's "Squawk Box ." "I think neoclouds are all in big trouble though because they are part of that vertical holding company and I think they're about to get ejected." Neoclouds, which used borrowed funds to build data centers, have been among the hardest hit stocks during the recent pullback in the AI trade. CoreWeave and Nebius are each down more than 50% the last three months. All eyes on Wall Street are on chipmaker Nvidia as it reports earnings on Tuesday after the bell while grappling with a potential Chinese espionage scandal. Founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Monday under a cloud of controversary revolving around his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The Commerce Department has subsequently moved to close a loophole on China's remote use of data centers. Investors are worried as scrutiny increases on Nvidia's China revenue, it may pullback on its extensive financing that supported the AI industry. Frontier algorithm company Anthropic is expected to make its public debut on Thursday as concerns about the company's profitability potential linger amid the rapid and ongoing commodification of AI. Eisman said he doesn't think the much-ballyhooed offering is very important anymore to the AI trade because expectations have come down. "I don't think anybody really cares," the investor said. Instead, the investor is focusing on how much Democrats will restrict data center building when they take control of Congress and various governorships in January. "I think the biggest issues by far are how much are, how much are local and state governments going to slow AI data center construction? Is it going to be 100% moratorium? That would obviously be -- that would put the country into recession overnight. Or is it something like 10% to 30%?" he said. In the event of a 10% to 30% slowdown in data center construction, Eisman said the group of companies within the AI trade that he favors the most are the hyperscalers. "The group that makes out the best are the hyperscalers because they go cash flow positive again," he said.

events.title: Disney beats fourth-quarter estimates, targets $3 billion in savings through cost-cutting efforts
events.summary: Disney topped Wall Street estimates for revenue and earnings per share for its fiscal fourth quarter. It's targeting $3 billion in cost savings by fiscal 2029 via measures that include layoffs, CFO Hugh Johnston told CNBC. The company's results were once again boosted by strength in its streaming and parks divisions. Disney on Tuesday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that exceeded analysts' expectations and announced it's targeting $3 billion in cost savings by fiscal 2029. Those cost-cutting efforts include several rounds of layoffs announced in recent months, Disney's chief financial officer, Hugh Johnston, told CNBC. The most recent round, which seeks to reduce costs by up to 20%, was reported earlier this month . Future cost-saving measures will include reductions in administrative and other general expenses, Johnston said, while adding, "We do expect more layoffs." Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro told investors on the company's earning call that the job cuts are "not easy." "They affect people who care deeply about Disney and have contributed so much to this company," he said. "At the same time, these steps are important if we want to be a company that moves faster, adapts to a rapidly changing environment, and keeps investing in the content and technology that will drive our growth." The cuts will help Disney fund its $26 billion in projected content spend for fiscal 2027, a 9% increase from fiscal 2026. The entertainment giant is also forecasting double-digit growth in earnings per share in the next fiscal year, as well as segment operating income growth of around 8%. Disney noted that the majority of that growth will be concentrated in the first half of the year due to the theatrical debut of "Avengers: Doomsday" and a boost from the Super Bowl, which will air on Disney's ESPN and ABC networks. "The growth is really going to come in the first half of this year," Johnston said. "That's the opposite of what we saw in '26, where the growth was backloaded." The company will also increase its annual dividend to $2 a share, a 33% increase from the previously declared dividend. It will be payable in two installments of $1 per share, one in January and one in July. Here's how Disney performed in its fiscal fourth quarter ended Oct. 3 , compared with what Wall Street expected, according to LSEG: Earnings per share: $1.77 adjusted vs. $1.67 expected Revenue : $25.95 billion vs. $25.18 billion expected Disney reported net income for the fiscal fourth quarter of $2.61 billion, or $1.51 per share, compared with $1.31 billion, or 73 cents per share, during the same period the year prior. Adjusting for one-time items, including severance and other restructuring charges as well as the value of intangible assets, Disney reported earnings per share of $1.77. The company's revenue for the quarter was 16% higher year over year, and results were once again lifted by its parks and streaming divisions. Disney's experiences segment, which includes its theme parks and cruises, reported nearly $10.11 billion in revenue, up 15% year over year. Operating income for the unit increased 20% to $2.25 billion. The division is already a top performer for the company, but it benefited in the fiscal fourth quarter because of an extra calendar week compared with the previous fiscal year. While international attendance continues to lag at Disney's domestic parks, it is being offset by domestic attendance, especially at the Walt Disney World resort in Orlando, Florida, Johnston said. Growth at Disneyland Paris was driven by recent investments including an expansion area called World of Frozen. Attendance at the Hong Kong and Shanghai parks remained soft because of broad economic challenges in those regions, according to Disney. The company expects operating income for the experiences segment to grow in the high-single digits in fiscal 2027. Growth is expected to be front-loaded as the company laps the launch of the Disney Adventure cruise ship, which set sail in March. Sports, streaming and entertainment Over at its entertainment division, Disney saw revenue increase 17% to $11.89 billion. Operating income nearly doubled to $1.33 billion. Revenue from streaming, specifically, rose 19% to $6.1 billion, Disney said. The segment benefited from the extra week on the fiscal calendar as well as from growth in subscription and affiliate fees. Additionally, the company saw higher theatrical distribution revenue from titles like "Toy Story 5." Disney said Tuesday it expects operating income for the entertainment division to grow in the high-single digits in the coming fiscal year. The company's sports division saw revenue increase 16% in the fiscal fourth quarter, reaching $4.61 billion. Operating income for the segment surged more than 50% to $1.39 billion. Subscription and affiliate fees fueled this growth alongside an increase in advertising revenue.

events.title: Jensen Huang was building Anthropic's worst nightmare. Then he was ousted.
events.summary: Nvidia cofounder Jensen Huang, left, and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. Fortune/NurPhoto Pictures via Reuters Connect Jensen Huang was building an open AI ecosystem that threatened Anthropic. He also pushed for Chinese access to US AI technology, clashing with Anthropic's CEO. Now Huang is gone from Nvidia. It's a huge win for Anthropic ahead of its record IPO. Jensen Huang 's dramatic departure from Nvidia may be the best thing to happen to Anthropic just as the AI startup prepares to go public this week. Under Huang, Nvidia was investing heavily in cheaper, more open AI models that compete with Anthropic's offerings. The chip giant was also backing startups developing these alternative models and helping make them widely available. That threatened Anthropic's business model, which involves spending heavily to develop closed AI models and charges customers to use them, often at higher prices than open alternatives. "People really need to understand that the 'Cold War' going on here is that Nvidia was on a titanic collision course with the labs," the CEO of a leading AI startup told Business Insider. This person asked not to be identified while discussing sensitive topics. The executive, who supports the open-source AI community and is sympathetic to Huang, described an ambitious Nvidia strategy to develop its own AI models, invest in rival startups, and build an ecosystem that could challenge not just Anthropic, but OpenAI too. This strategy was just beginning to come together. But with Huang gone, the threat has diminished considerably. The timing is extraordinary. Anthropic is preparing for a stock market debut this week that could value it at $1.4 trillion. Investors are being asked to make an enormous bet on the future profitability of its AI services. Huang was helping build a world in which companies wouldn't necessarily have to pay Anthropic for that intelligence. Nvidia's open AI push Amjad Masad, chief executive officer of Replit David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images The strategy centered on " open-weight " AI models. Unlike Anthropic's Fable and Opus offerings and OpenAI's top GPT models, these alternative systems can be downloaded, modified, and operated independently. That makes them attractive to businesses that want greater control over their AI systems without paying a leading AI lab every time someone uses the technology. Nvidia was pursuing this aggressively. It developed its own family of open models, called Nemotron. It also backed startups including Reflection AI, Thinking Machines Lab, and Poolside, while moving to acquire Hugging Face, a major platform for sharing open-weight AI models. Replit CEO Amjad Masad called Jensen Huang's ouster "an attack on open models" at a Silicon Valley conference on Monday. "Jensen is the premier champion of open models," Masad said. "If it wasn't for Jensen, there wouldn't be a lot of funding going into US open model companies." Fireworks Fireworks AI CEO Lin Qiao (left) interviewing Jensen Huang at the startup's conference in San Francisco on Nov. 3, 2026. Alistair Barr/Business Insider On November 3, I watched Huang evangelize this strategy at a Fireworks AI conference in San Francisco. He acknowledged the value of closed AI models from companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI, but argued that businesses shouldn't have to rely on them. Instead, they could take open-weight models and adapt them to their specific needs, creating AI systems that could be even more powerful. "By taking an open frontier model, adapting it and providing it with your domain knowledge, your access, your specialized tools, and the proper evaluation, you should be able to create essentially a super intelligence," Huang told Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao on stage. "And I think those times are here," he added. Nvidia's worst nightmare This strategy made business sense for Nvidia. More open models running on its chips meant more potential customers. It was becoming increasingly important as Anthropic and OpenAI sought alternatives to Nvidia's expensive hardware. In fact, Anthropic has developed a system that could be Nvidia's worst nightmare, as Business Insider reported in October . Anthropic disclosed in its IPO filing that it has spent years developing software that allows it to shift AI work between different types of chips from Nvidia, Google, Amazon, and AMD. That gives Anthropic more flexibility to choose the cheapest or most effective chips for a particular task, reducing its dependence on Nvidia and potentially weakening Nvidia's ability to charge premium prices. The shift is already significant. A November 14 analysis by Michael Cembalest of JPMorgan Asset Management estimated that Nvidia accounted for just 39% of future computing commitments by leading AI labs, down from more than 80% of AI chip revenue in recent years. The China battle There was another key area of AI where Nvidia and Anthropic clashed. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has advocated for very strict limits on advanced US chip sales to China, arguing these restrictions are essential to maintaining America's technological lead. Huang fought against those restrictions, warning that shutting China out would encourage Chinese companies to develop competing technology. Now he's gone, Anthropic's worldview is prevailing. On Monday, the US government rolled out new restrictions that close a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to use Nvidia GPUs by renting them from data centers outside China. It's a win for China hawks within the administration and a huge victory for Amodei, arguably the biggest China hawk of them all. There are caveats. For instance, Nvidia's interim CEO could continue Huang's strategies. Still, the immediate strategic implications are striking. Anthropic is about to ask investors to bet on its future dominance of AI. Just days before that moment, one of the industry's most powerful figures pushing an alternative vision has been forced out. events.title: Altimeter’s Gerstner says Nvidia’s board should keep door open to Huang’s return: ‘Get this right’
events.summary: Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner urged Nvidia’s board on Monday to reconsider Jensen Huang’s ouster, saying the board needs “to get this right.” Gerstner said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that he wasn’t calling for Huang’s immediate reinstatement as Nvidia CEO but that “everyone is rushing to judgment…and I simply don’t know the facts.” Gerstner acknowledged that Huang “engaged in personal behavior that was pretty bad,” but that he’s messaged the former CEO to express his support. He told Semafor Editor-in-Chief Ben Smith that Nvidia’s success is “too critical to the future security of our country” for the board to make a wrong decision. People familiar with the matter have told Semafor that Huang is mulling a comeback as CEO but that the board isn’t considering a return. Huang resigned last week following reports that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with two subordinates and a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. Gerstner co-authored a letter with Atreides Management CEO Gavin Baker sent to the Nvidia board on Friday calling for “a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding future leadership of Nvidia that leaves all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Gerstner said Monday people are misinterpreting his letter as a call for Huang’s immediate reinstatement, rather than a call for a thorough investigation. “We don’t want to take shortcuts,” Gerstner said. An August SEC filing showed that Nvidia is Altimeter Capital’s largest disclosed equity holding, worth almost $1.9 billion as of June, according to CNBC . On ‘Trump accounts’ Gerstner, who was one of the architects behind the Trump Accounts, founded Boston-based Altimeter Capital in 2008. He said he expects the accounts to survive future Democratic administrations, saying they are universally popular across ideologies. He said he expected Elon Musk to personally contribute to the accounts. “Elon’s always told me he wants to do something big here,” Gerstner said. — Ben Kesslen

events.title: Trump's former AI czar criticizes rush to judgment on ex-Nvidia CEO
events.summary: President Donald Trump’s former AI and crypto czar, David Sacks, argued on Monday the public was too quick to judge former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on reports that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, though he stopped short of saying whether the board should reinstate Huang as CEO. “You have the right to have allegations against you adjudicated in a proper court of law,” Sacks, a longtime venture capitalist and co-founder of Craft Ventures, said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World on Monday. Sacks went on to say that the public “should wait until there’s a proper determination by a legal authority” on the allegations against Huang. The Trump administration and Congress have launched investigations related to the controversy. Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO last week following revelations that he had affairs with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset as well as an Nvidia employee who had reported directly to him, sending shockwaves throughout Silicon Valley. Huang acted as a linchpin of the AI trade, deploying nearly $99 billion across the tech ecosystem to fuel the AI infrastructure buildout. Sacks cast doubt on the allegations that Alice Huang, the woman with whom Huang admitted to having an affair, was spying on Nvidia, citing reports that US intelligence hasn’t arrived at a definitive conclusion. “This narrative of the Chinese spy is falling apart,” he claimed. Sacks is a staunch proponent of the AI buildout, and has argued that any guardrails on the technology’s development would hamstring the US in its competition with China. The venture capitalist played a decisive role on US policy while in the White House, pushing for softer AI regulation. Sacks drafted parts of Trump’s “AI Action Plan,” a comprehensive blueprint that involves cutting red tape and prioritizing private-sector growth over federal oversight. — Jake Angelo

events.title: Elon Musk’s policy difficulty prevents Starlink’s South Africa entry
events.summary: Elon Musk’s “difficulty in understanding” a key South African policy is the main issue preventing his Starlink satellite internet service launching in Africa’s biggest economy, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told Semafor on Monday. Under the country’s Black Economic Empowerment policy, introduced nearly 30 years ago to redress apartheid-era inequality, at least 30% of the South African operation of any company must be sold to Black locals. Musk, who was raised in South Africa, has called the policy “openly racist” and cited it as the reason Starlink does not operate in the country. “All countries have policies in terms of how they admit companies to operate,” Ramaphosa told Jonathan Karl, chief Washington correspondent at ABC News, at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “You’ve got to subscribe to the policies of the country.” Ramaphosa said the Tesla and SpaceX boss “doesn’t fully understand the extent” of the impact apartheid policies had on Black South Africans. Ramaphosa also said Musk should be “loyal” to the country in which the billionaire spent his early years. An ‘ambush’ Musk has been a powerful figure in American politics as well business since the start of US President Donald Trump’s second term in January 2025. The Trump administration shuttered the US Agency for International Development, its main overseas aid agency, under Musk’s guidance as a government adviser. And his influence is widely seen to have played a role in Washington’s increasingly fractious relationship with Pretoria. South Africa has refused to meet US demands for reforms of BEE, and has previously provoked the Trump administration’s ire over Pretoria’s criticism of Israel. Ramaphosa said their highest-profile flashpoint since Trump took office — an Oval Office meeting in which the US president accused him of presiding over a white genocide — was an “ambush.” He said Trump was “seriously misinformed.” Ramaphosa said he and Trump had not spoken since that meeting, having previously held conversations. He added that it was a pity that the US president’s belief in a white genocide — a widely discredited allegation — underpinned Washington’s approach to South Africa. The South African president said he was in California this week for meetings with tech executives, and will hold talks with a number of companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, and Google. Asked about the opposition to the data center buildout in some parts of the world, he said South Africa welcomed them. — Alexis Akwagyiram

events.title: Americans worry capitalism won’t work for them in the AI era. Here are 3 ways for companies to show that it can
events.summary: According to Just Capital’s 2026 Americans’ Views on Business survey , three in four Americans believe the nation’s best days of innovation are happening now or are still to come. Yet only half say our current form of capitalism gives people like them a fair shot at getting ahead financially. The percentage of people who believe they will be financially worse off this time next year is at its highest since 1960. In other words, Americans believe that—in the age of AI and related innovation—our economic system is working for someone else, not them. Bridging this divide is the defining leadership challenge of our time. And as the recent midterm elections showed, when people feel strongly enough about something they are apt to seek change. Americans haven’t given up on business as a driver of solutions—78% say large companies have a role to play in solving important societal issues. The key is to show Americans they have a place in the AI-powered economy. Our assessment of the 500 largest American employers shows that so far approximately 180 companies have publicly reported AI-related actions affecting their own employees or the broader workforce since December 2025. 161 of those companies announced actions that specifically aim to support their workers and the American workforce at large. These companies are primarily in industries with large frontline workforces like Personal Care, Drug, & Grocery; and Telecommunications. Companies in industries with close ties to the AI buildout such as Energy; Construction & Materials; and Utilities were less likely to have announced an action in our analysis. Of the twenty industries we examined, six had a higher percentage of companies taking action than the Technology industry, which sits at the center of the AI transition. However, the Tech companies that did announce an action took roughly twice as many as peers in other industries. The first movers can offer lessons for leaders in every industry: redefine roles rather than eliminate them, open pathways into skilled trades, and equip the next generation of innovators. Redefine rather than eliminate Many experts now predict AI will reshape jobs rather than lead to a wholesale disruption of the workforce. Our data reflects the same trend. In the Fall 2026 edition of Just Capital’s quarterly survey of the American public, investors, and corporate leaders, 52% of corporate leaders say they have redefined or transitioned existing roles over the past 12 months compared to 15% who say they have conducted layoffs. Several companies show how this could work in practice. At General Dynamics Information Technology (GDIT) , 12,000 employees have moved into new roles inside the company since 2023, and more than 9,000 have earned certifications in AI, cyber and other technologies. Kimberly-Clark takes a similar approach to training. Its “IT Digital University” covers 17 skill areas, and employees are assessed before and after, with completers averaging 60% skill growth. ServiceNow put AI agents to work on its own operations, and they now resolve 90% of IT service desk tickets. Instead of laying off the service desk team, the company assessed everyone’s skills, provided role-based training and held one-on-one career conversations before moving anyone. As a result, 85% of the service desk moved into new roles in security, AI operations and executive briefing, and the other 15% now supervise the AI agents. While the dominant narrative has focused on the negative impacts AI may have on the American workforce or on communities across the country, the real story may be a revolution of reskilling and internal mobility. Offer pathways to prosperity through skilled trades Our polling shows 47% of Americans aged 18 to 25 worry AI will make it harder to land an entry-level job in their field, yet only 20% of recent grads are considering a trade or licensed profession despite the U.S. facing a historic skilled trades labor shortage . Several companies are tackling the issue head on. Caterpillar is investing $100 million over five years in manufacturing and industry technician jobs in Illinois and Indiana, building a pipeline in the communities where it operates. Lowe’s has gone further by convening the nation’s largest skilled trades coalition, with NVIDIA, AT&T, Bank of America , Carrier, General Motors, DEWALT and Duke Energy , and a goal of training 1 million people. Beyond the founding corporate partners, Lowe’s also brought on over 75 educators, businesses, workforce organizations, industry vendors and stakeholders, including the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), The National Center for Construction Education and Research (NCCER), SkillsUSA and Carhartt. The message here is that workforce readiness is not a problem to be owned by any one company, and the firms with the most to gain from solving it are well placed to lead. Power the next generation of innovation 24% of Americans in the Americans’ Views on Business survey say that individual entrepreneurs and innovators are the primary driver of American innovation, more than large companies R&D investments (23%), venture capital and private investment (14%), government funding (13%), and universities and academic research (13%). Several companies stand out for cultivating entrepreneurial capacity. Boeing put $250,000 behind Technovation, pairing its engineers as mentors with 25,000 girls building AI-powered solutions worldwide. DoorDash offers a one-day Local Business Workshop that gives small business owners training, tools, local connections and advertising credits. Duke Energy sponsored the third annual high school AI design contest at the University of Florida, where student teams used AI tools to design a smart power grid for their own communities. Investments like these, aimed at people early in their careers or businesses, can widen who gets to participate in what comes next. Investing early in entrepreneurs is also an investment in the customers, suppliers and talent pools companies will depend on later. Trust is built on opportunity Just Capital’s monthly National AI Monitor asks 1,000 Americans how they are experiencing AI as workers, customers, community members, investors and stewards of the environment. Americans are net positive about AI today (+37 overall, +44 at work). But their outlook for the next few years falls to +13, with job loss among the main concerns for the future. The examples of corporate action outlined here illustrate the path forward for leadership to address these concerns in a new era. By redefining roles, creating internal mobility, and fostering the skills of the future, including a focus on entrepreneurship, these companies are showing how to broaden access to opportunity rather than narrow it. events.title: Bill Ackman says it’s ‘unlikely’ he’ll get involved to bring Huang back
events.summary: Billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman said Monday it was “unlikely” that he would get directly involved in an effort to reinstate former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Ackman, an outspoken activist investor who runs Pershing Square Capital Management, has come to Huang’s defense following the revelations that Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. At Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, Ackman acknowledged that the situation presents “a pretty interesting activist setup.” There’s still legal uncertainty about what exactly happened, Ackman told Semafor’s Liz Hoffman, but if Huang’s missteps were a “personal foible as opposed to a corporate defense conspiracy, there’s a very powerful case for putting him back in place.” While “truth is pretty darn important,” he said a board should treat a CEO lying about a personal matter differently from lying about something that could endanger the company’s business. If he were running a comeback campaign, Ackman said he would “present the facts, and you call a special meeting.” Huang would have heft: Having co-founded the company, he still owns more than 3% of Nvidia. — J.D. events.title: UK unemployment unexpectedly eases to 4.6% as government releases Milburn report
events.summary: Wage growth falls to 3.5% in September, as ministers examine how best to get young people into work Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on young people Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts The UK unemployment rate has unexpectedly fallen as the government released an important report on the youth jobs crisis . The unemployment rate was 4.6% in September, dipping from 4.7% in August and down from 5% earlier in the year, according to the Office for National Statistics . However, the number of vacancies fell as employers delayed hiring in response to global economic uncertainty and the use of artificial intelligence, which many analysts expect will lead to widespread job losses. Business groups said the slump in vacancies posed a problem for the government as responded to Alan Milburn’s report on young people not in employment, education or training (Neets) . Milburn, a former health secretary, unveiled his long-awaited report into youth unemployment on Tuesday morning in London, urging ministers to cut disability and sickness payments for under-25s and invest the money in back-to-work schemes. The British Chambers of Commerce said it was “alarming” that the number of vacancies had tumbled to its lowest level since 2014 and unemployment for 18- to 24-year-olds was nearly triple the average for UK adults, at 13%. “This will put further pressure on today’s Milburn review to deliver a sea change in the government’s approach to tackling youth joblessness,” it said. The number of vacancies dropped to 690,000 in October after soaring to more than 1.3m after the pandemic. Wage growth also fell to 3.5%, excluding bonuses, in the latest official figures for the three months to the end of September, down from 3.7% in the three months to August. City economists had expected unemployment to remain steady and wages, excluding bonuses, to fall slightly to 3.6%. With inflation also at 3.5% and expected to rise for a fourth consecutive month to 3.7% when figures are released on Wednesday, the average worker faces a fall in real wage growth to zero or even negative figures. Martin Beck, the chief economist at the consultants WPI Strategy, said: “The UK labour market remained relatively resilient in late autumn, but beneath the surface, there were more signs that the economy is struggling to generate jobs. The jobs market isn’t falling off a cliff, but is going nowhere fast.” The jobs market has proved difficult for analysts and politicians to assess in recent years. It has been called weak after a dramatic slide in the number of vacancies, which illustrates the reticence of companies to hire new staff. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Ministers are known to be concerned that some large employers, including several banks, have said they intend to use AI to reduce their staffing levels. Economists are divided over whether AI will enhance productivity across all the big sectors of the economy – after signs it has boosted GDP – or lead to improvements in certain industries such as healthcare. Employer groups have complained that Labour’s increase in employer national insurance contributions, a higher minimum wage and changes to employee rights have increased costs, leading to a fall in the number of advertised vacancies. The Bank of England increased interest rates earlier this month after a rise in the consumer prices index to 3.5% in September. It has said that its own surveys showed employers did not expect to increase pay beyond 3.5% to 4% next year, despite the higher level of inflation, and also reported little change looking ahead in their own prices. However, a growing number of the Bank’s policymakers believe the prospect of high oil and energy prices next year as the Iran war drags on will push inflation towards 5% and force employers to offer higher pay, which will be passed on in higher retail prices. A spokesperson for the Department for Work and Pensions said the Milburn review would “shape our next steps for young people”. “Despite the difficult global backdrop, the unemployment rate is falling, and the number of people in work is rising,” the spokesperson added. “We are determined to go further. Our £2.5bn youth employment support will give almost 1 million young people opportunities to earn and learn, while wider reforms including improving jobcentres, will create a more personalised work and skills advice service for all.” UK unemployment and employment statistics
