events.title: Trump has arrived in Asia. Here’s what he said about Iran and Deutsche Bank
events.summary: Trump has arrived in Manila ahead of meetings with regional leaders and a trip to China for talks with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. He threatened Iran after CNN reported a possible dirty bomb or chemical weapon plot in Washington, D.C. Trump said Deutsche Bank “shouldn’t have” leaked his tax details, after the FT reported the bank mistakenly disclosed them in 2017 and didn't tell the White House. U.S. President Donald Trump has arrived for his high-stakes trip to Asia, and took a range of questions on subjects from Iran to Deutsche Bank leaking details about his tax. The president landed in Manila, Philippines, for the initial leg of his trip on Tuesday and answered rapid-fire questions from the press while meeting with other leaders. Asked about a possible Iranian threat to Washington, D.C., he said that, if there were an attack, Iran would "pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before." The question was about CNN reporting that U.S. intelligence suggested the country was planning to target senior members of Trump's administration with a dirty bomb or chemical weapon in the U.S. capital. "We take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," Trump said. CNBC has not independently verified CNN's report. But the president also said he believed his administration was "very close to getting it done" when it came to the Iran war. While Trump was airborne, the Financial Times reported Deutsche Bank had mistakenly leaked details of his taxes in March 2017, during his first presidential term. The mistake was kept from the White House at the time, per the FT. Asked about this in Manila, the president said: "I paid a lot of tax." "They shouldn't have done it. It's illegal for them to do it," he added. Trump was also asked about Nvidia's announcement on Tuesday of a new National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. The company, which reports earnings later on Tuesday, is reeling from the sudden departure of CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week after having an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a Chinese spy. "It's a great company. It's a great idea," Trump said. Trump is due to fly to Shenzhen, China, where he is scheduled to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a three-way meeting on Thursday, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. He is also due to hold a separate bilateral meeting with Xi. Asked by a reporter if he would have a separate meeting with only Putin, Trump said: "I don't know, but I would, if it's available, I would do that. He's coming. I mean, it's really with the guests. I am the guest of President Xi." Trump met the leaders of Australia, India and Japan as part of the Quad grouping in the Philippines and the prime minister of Thailand. He is due to China on Wednesday. Speaking at a dinner with Southeast Asian leaders as the event wrapped up for the day, Trump touted his record during his second term, citing investment into the U.S., trade deals made with countries represented by attendees at the dinner, energy infrastructure buildouts and America's AI industry. Trump, who has led a campaign to rename artificial intelligence "super intelligence," or "SI," told leaders around the table that the U.S. is "leading the world" in the technology. "We have the world's most powerful SI ecosystem," he said. "We're leading everybody by a lot, and we hope to keep it that way, and we will keep it that way." He added that the U.S. has "the strongest and most capable military on the planet," pointing to investments in the armed forces and the country's defense sector. "We make the greatest equipment. You saw that in Venezuela. You see it in Iran. You see it everywhere," Trump said.

events.title: St. Louis Fed's Musalem says four more rate hikes may be needed in coming months
events.summary: St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem suggested Tuesday that the central bank may need to hike its benchmark rate as many as four times by early next year. In a speech delivered in Argentina, the policymaker said there is "an unlikely but still plausible scenario" in which no further increases will be needed. St. Louis Federal Reserve President Alberto Musalem indicated Tuesday that the central bank may need as many as four rate hikes in coming months, offering one of the most hawkish views yet by a Fed policymaker about the steps needed to quell inflation. During a speech delivered in Argentina, Musalem made the case that current policy is not significantly restricting economic activity. "The economy will likely require several interest rate increases before the spring of 2027 to achieve 2% inflation in a timely manner," he said. Musalem said the real policy rate, which subtracts the inflation rate from the Fed's target rate, needs to be between 2%-2.5% by next spring, and estimated that the current rate is about a full point below that range. That position suggests the Fed may need to hike at each of the upcoming Fed meetings in December, January, March and April. Musalem does not get a vote on the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee over the period where he says that the rate increases will be needed, though he does get to present views and provide input on the "dot plot" of individual members' expectations. He will next vote in 2028. To be sure, Musalem noted "an unlikely but still plausible scenario" in which no further hikes would be needed. "Falling energy prices and lower shipping costs, or an increase in potential output growth driven by higher productivity growth, might ease inflation pressures such that inflation moves toward target in 18 months," he said. Another possibility is that demand might decelerate as spending on artificial intelligence slows. However, he said the more likely scenario is that "persistent strong demand and ongoing supply pressures" combine to keep inflation above the Fed's 2% target , thus requiring further increases in the fed funds rate from its current range of 3.75%-4%. "It would be preferable for a higher real policy rate to happen in a balanced way, driven both by lower inflation and a higher nominal policy rate," he said. "However, the nominal policy rate may need to do most of the work."

events.title: Deutsche Bank dismissed warnings about dealings with risky clients, reports claim
events.summary: International investigation using trove of leaked internal data allegedly shows German bank overlooked compliance concerns to safeguard profits Deutsche Bank reportedly dismissed warnings about its dealings with risky clients, including high-profile Russian oligarchs, to protect profits, the findings of an investigation into a trove of leaked bank documents indicate. A leak of 15m internal files is reported to show that the troubled German bank repeatedly ignored concerns by its compliance officers about its risk-taking, despite having already been caught being used to launder billions of dollars for Russian criminals, spies and oligarchs between 2010 and 2015. The investigations, which were published by media outlets including Der Spiegel, the Financial Times, the New York Times and Le Monde, will represent a fresh blow for Deutsche Bank, which has struggled to repair its reputation after a number of scandals and dealings with controversial clients including US president Donald Trump and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Deutsche Bank said on Tuesday that the issues raised in the investigations “date back many years, in some cases as much as two decades” and had been addressed by its leadership. “Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators.” However, the reports suggested Deutsche Bank prioritised profit ahead of internal controls, and continued to expand its Russian business until 2021, despite warnings from internal compliance officers and growing geopolitical tensions between Nato allies and Moscow. Deutsche Bank allegedly resisted pulling out of Russia even after the Kremlin sanctioned a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, before launching a U-turn and exiting the country in March that year. The investigations suggested Deutsche Bank was driven by competitive pressure, including from American banks, and that its chief executive, Christian Sewing, pursued a growth strategy that involved doing business with a list of customers known as its “most sensitive clients”. That covered roughly 50 corporate clients ranked by how close they were to the Kremlin, and other potential risks including financial crime, according to the Financial Times. Some names allegedly on that list included: Russia’s state-owned gas company Gazprom; petrochemicals group Sibur; and oligarchs including aluminium magnate Oleg Deripaska, the report said. Outside its Russian dealings, the German lender is facing fresh scrutiny for allegedly processing almost $600m (£454m) of suspicious payments linked to Epstein, much higher than previously known. Deutsche said it “regrets [its] historical relationship” with Epstein and that it had made “considerable investments in strengthening controls”. The lender is also accused of accidentally leaking Trump’s tax documents to another client during his first term in office, which Deutsche Bank allegedly kept secret from the White House. Deutsche Bank said it did not comment on former or existing client relationships. Deutsche Bank cut ties with Trump in 2021. The reports prompted a 4% drop in Deutsche Bank’s German-listed shares on Tuesday. Deutsche Bank issued a public statement in response to the investigation on Tuesday, saying it had “gone through a fundamental transformation” under Sewing. “We made substantial investments in our control environment while restoring sustainable profitability, as evidenced by record profits in 2025 as well as in recent quarters. This involved €7bn of direct investments in our control environment between 2019 and 2025.” The bank added: “We remain committed to ensuring continuous enhancements of our control environment and a culture of integrity and completing any outstanding remediation.” “Regardless of how the information was obtained, it includes confidential information about clients, employees and other third parties, which remains legally protected. We have acted, and will continue to act, decisively to protect this,” the bank said.

events.title: Anthropic IPO: For hundreds of billions of dollars flowing into AI startups, a big debut is a must
events.summary: Anthropic's IPO will be a key moment in the valuation of an AI startup ecosystem that captured 86% of U.S. venture capital dollars in the first half of 2026, and for infrastructure funds that boomed on the data center buildout. The VC industry has rebounded from a five-year period of underperformance, buoyed by big gains in the largest AI companies. Other alternative assets, including private credit and private equity buyout funds, have lagged. Artificial intelligence has propelled big gains in venture capital funds this year, and a flood of money — over $350 billion — into AI startups. Venture funds were up close to 18% through the first half of 2026, with 86% of U.S.-based VC investor money going into AI companies. With Anthropic set to make its public market debut this week at a reported valuation of $1.4 trillion , the market's reception to the deal and early trading in its shares may set the tone for the next leg in the private market AI boom. It has been a period of increased volatility for tech stocks and the public market AI trade. In addition to concerns about balance sheet strength and valuation, midterm elections showed widespread public opposition to data centers , and the CEO scandal rocking Nvidia, the "central bank" of AI financing , has compounded risks in the sector. But on the private side of tech investing, firms are closely watching how investors react to Anthropic's IPO. "I think that will end up guiding further intentions for the VC space," said Mike McLelland, managing director of investments within private markets at Cleveland, Ohio-based Clearstead. "Once you have a couple of good exits, it gives people a little more confidence in the realization story." Anthropic is getting some deep-pocketed support for the deal. Altimeter Capital is aiming to invest $5 billion , according to its founder and CEO Brad Gerstner, who noted that was five times as much as he has ever invested in an IPO. "I think this is a cornerstone compounder for a long time," Gerstner told CNBC's "Halftime Report" on Monday. "It's where the trade is going." Chip giants Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Nvidia, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and Micron are all investing, as are Google and Microsoft. The direction of the IPO market is important given that companies have been staying private longer than they did in the past and strategic exits have been relatively muted, McLelland said. A notable exception is Google's $32 billion acquisition of cloud security firm Wiz. That 2025 deal was Google's largest ever, overtaking its $12.5 billion purchase of Motorola in 2012. A very concentrated private bet on AI VC gains have been concentrated in a small number of large funds that hold the biggest AI-linked companies. MSCI reports that the 10 largest holdings make up 22% of the value of its venture index. That concentration comes amid improved performance. Venture capital funds returned 17.8% in the first six months of 2026, according to Opto Investments, using proprietary and MSCI Private Capital Solutions data. Venture fund portfolio data is reported by fund general partners on a delayed basis. The six-month gains would equate to a full year return as high as 38% if the pace is maintained. It comes on the heels of a recent period of underperformance for the asset class, with a 6.19% return over five years, according to Juan Mier, lead analyst of fund strategies at PitchBook. Venture's 10-year average return is 13% annually, according to PitchBook. For the year ended March 2026, venture capital delivered a nearly 22% return, driven in large part by AI valuations, Mier said. It is not just the largest AI companies that are venture-backed and tied to the IPO performance of the giants. Thousands of smaller companies that supply AI giants with infrastructure, component manufacturing, and data services, for example, have also seen their valuations rise quickly, said Jake Miller, co-founder of New York-based Opto Investments, which helps investment advisors design private investment programs. Notably, AI captured $355.9 billion, or 86% of U.S. venture dollars in the first half of 2026, according to Clearstead analysis of PitchBook data. Globally, AI deal value reached $521.4 billion over the trailing twelve months. That's more than double the prior year, even as AI deal count fell 21.6% from the previous quarter. Mier said venture capital returns are expected to moderate in the third quarter as valuations in the AI space in public markets have adjusted, and that flows to private markets eventually. "That may moderate returns for the second half of the year," he said. Anthropic's deal, reported to be on target for a $1.4 trillion valuation, is well below the $2 trillion deal value originally floated by bankers. But amid the AI proliferation, industry participants expect VC to continue piquing investors' interest in the coming years.

events.title: 'Not rocket surgery' claims researcher who found six Danfoss fridge controller zero-days in under an hour
events.summary: A Dutch cybersecurity researcher claims he found six zero-days in Danfoss refrigeration controller firmware in under an hour, then delivered a withering assessment of the vendor's defenses against memory corruption. The Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium (CCB) warns that the flaws could let attackers take control without credentials, potentially retain access after resets, or disable controllers altogether. Carlo Meijer of cyber consultancy Midnight Blue examined the latest AK-SM800A firmware, version 5.3.2, manually – no AI required. He said that he went looking in random places where strcpy() is invoked, given the vendor's "extremely liberal use" of the function (which doesn't check whether the destination buffer is large enough), and swiftly found five cases in which he said he could trigger a segfault with a one-line cURL command. "Of course, remotely triggering a crash is bad in itself, but being able to leverage the buffer overflow to obtain remote code execution is much worse," he wrote . Meijer added: "Any reasonably experienced exploit developer will agree exploiting straightforward stack-based buffer overflows on ARM Linux without exploit mitigations is very straightforward. And if they don't, there's probably a frontier or open-weight model out there willing to help them agree." He noted that before achieving RCE, an attacker would need to overcome the limitation of strcpy() where it stops copying bytes after hitting a null byte, but said "it's not exactly rocket surgery." He went on to claim: "Also, the exploited application runs as root (because of course it does)." Later firmware adds "session control," an authentication mechanism whose strict setting blocks unauthenticated access to most web interfaces. But Meijer found a memory corruption flaw in that protective layer too. He described the final zero-day as a "trivial" pre-auth memory corruption bug which again starts with a segfault but can be wangled into an RCE "with some additional effort." Meijer also considered whether attackers could maintain access after a reset, as seen with implants such as Saltwater and Firestarter . He considered this feasible because the controllers do not use their processor's secure boot features. "In such a scenario, an attacker could either retain remote access or leave a time-triggered payload for a 2nd (or 3rd...) strike – increasing damage by spoiling new batches of food," said Meijer. "Alternatively, attackers could simply wipe flash memory and/or push a malformed firmware update to brick the controllers and render them permanently inoperable – requiring costly and time-consuming replacement similar to the TTPs deployed during the December 2025 attack on the Polish electric grid ." Meijer's priority for operators was to remove the controllers' direct internet exposure, rather than spend scarce resources on piecemeal patching. He said the vendor's advice following the attacks on European supermarkets and blood banks in recent weeks – rotating creds, applying patches, enabling strict session control – was insufficient given the flaws in the controllers' codebase. "This is insufficient and asset owners need to remove internet exposure as soon as possible," said Meijer. "We recommend against allocating scarce security resources to patching efforts and instead focus on reducing exposure." The CCB likewise urged operators to remove direct internet exposure immediately, but also recommended applying patches when they become available. Beyond the liberal use of strcpy(), Meijer criticized the absence of standard exploit mitigations, including stack canaries and position-independent executables. "These mechanisms have been staples of memory corruption defenses for decades and enabling these features... requires no engineering work at all," he said. "It is simply a matter of setting the right compiler flag. Enabling these features became the default in Ubuntu 17.10 and there is simply no excuse for a network-facing application that was last updated a few months ago to not have them enabled." The Register asked Danfoss to respond to the findings, but it did not reply. Danfoss has consistently blanked our requests for information since being implicated in at least some of the attacks that affected European supermarkets recently, alongside rival controller vendors Copeland and Dixell. It also did not respond when we asked about its involvement in the attacks on US commissary appliances over the summer, after some alleged that its controllers were targeted. ®

events.title: Current price of oil as of November 17, 2026
events.summary: As of 8:15 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil is trading at $94.94 per barrel, based on the Brent benchmark we’ll explain in a bit. That’s $1.74 below yesterday morning’s level and about $30.70 higher than where it stood a year ago. Oil price per barrel % Change Price of oil yesterday $96.68 -1.79% Price of oil 1 month ago $111.71 -15.01% Price of oil 1 year ago $64.25 +47.76% Will oil prices go up? No one can say for sure where oil prices will go next. Many forces shape the market—but at the core, it’s still about supply and demand. When risks like a potential recession or war ramp up, oil prices can change direction quickly. How oil prices translate to gas pump prices When you buy gas at the pump, you’re covering more than the cost of crude oil. You’re also paying for every step in the process, including refineries, wholesalers, taxes, and the markup your local gas station adds. Even so, crude oil has the biggest influence on what you pay, often making up more than half the cost per gallon. When oil prices jump, gas prices usually climb right along with them. But when oil falls, gas prices often slip much more slowly—a pattern sometimes called “rockets and feathers.” The role of the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve If an emergency hits, the U.S. keeps a backup supply of crude oil called the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. It’s mainly there to protect energy security during crises, such as sanctions, catastrophic storm damage, even war. It can also help cushion the blow when supply shocks send prices soaring. It’s not meant to solve long-term problems. Instead, it provides quick relief for consumers and helps keep vital parts of the economy moving, like essential industries, emergency services, and public transit. How oil and natural gas prices are linked Oil and natural gas are two of the world’s primary energy sources. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by extension. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, which which increases demand for natural gas. Historical performance of oil When looking at how oil performs, two main benchmarks stand out: Brent crude oil is the main global oil benchmark. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) is the main benchmark of North America. Of the two, Brent gives a better picture of global oil performance because it prices a large share of the world’s traded crude. It’s also the go-to for tracking oil’s historical trends. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now relies on Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook. If you look at the Brent benchmark over several decades, oil has been far from stable. It has experienced sharp rises tied to wars and supply cuts, along with steep drops linked to global recessions and oversupply (called a “glut”). For example: The early 1970s delivered the first major oil shock when the Middle East slashed exports and placed an embargo on the U.S. and others during the Yom Kippur War. Prices fell in the mid-1980s due to lower demand and an influx of non-OPEC oil producers joining the market. Prices surged again in 2008 as global demand grew, but then crashed alongside the global financial crisis. During the 2020 COVID lockdown, oil demand plummeted like never before—pushing prices below $20 per barrel. To sum up, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s heavily influenced by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, shifting energy policies, and much more. Energy coverage from  Fortune Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage: Son of ex-Alamo Rent a Car owner went from hip hop label founder to lithium leader Future of U.S. renewable energy rests on Nextpower—the backbone of the growing solar sector Standard Chartered profit jumps 46% as CEO bets on a fragmenting global economy Frequently asked questions How is the current price of oil per barrel actually determined? The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic. How often does the price of oil change during the day? The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing. How does U.S. shale oil production affect the current price of oil? In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply. How does the current price of oil impact inflation and the broader economy? When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf. events.title: 'Heroes have flaws': Sam Altman says he has personal empathy for Jensen Huang
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said Monday he has “personal strong empathy” for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, though he declined to say whether Huang should return to the chip giant. Altman — who about three years ago was ousted from his own post, only to return shortly thereafter — said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that Huang has “long been a hero of mine. Heroes have flaws.” Huang is reportedly considering trying to make a comeback as CEO, and some tech leaders are pushing for him to return. Asked whether Huang should return, Altman told Semafor’s Reed Albergotti: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.” Altman said it’s hard to imagine Nvidia without Huang at the helm, but Nvidia is “a behemoth of a company,” and people still trust its guarantees as an investor. In an expansive 30-minute interview, Altman struck an honest tone about the challenges he and the rest of the AI industry are facing, including the Nvidia fallout, the backlash against data centers, and increasing pressures on the cost of capital to fund the AI buildout. On public sentiment toward AI Following the US midterm elections that were broadly seen as a rebuke of AI, Altman said the industry should take a “strong stance” on how it approaches the long-term vision of AI. He said much of the backlash to data centers is about people latching onto a physical thing to fight back against, but that the real issue stems from people wanting to stay “in control of the future.” “We should not want to have a ‘handover’ … either gradual or sudden, to AI making decisions about our future,” he said. The public should understand, he argued, that the people building AI are “team human.” He thinks data centers will still get built, but added that “the engagement with communities is not working for people. And the ecosystem will adapt.” Public sentiment is likely to change over time, Altman said, recalling a period where communities wanted data centers in their areas because they created jobs and industry in underinvested areas. Now, perhaps, developers have to listen to the pushback and build them further away from where people live. “We have a giant country, we have a lot of space we can do this.” On going public Some investors have grown concerned with the massive amounts of capital required for the AI infrastructure buildout, and the buildup of debt. With an OpenAI IPO still looming, Altman said he wasn’t concerned. OpenAI “will go public at some point,” even if there are “real downsides to being public,” including intense volatility. Altman said he isn’t concerned with there being enough dollars to go around, even if Anthropic is the first to the IPO party later this week. “That is not a worry,” he said. “There’s been way too much investor demand and not enough supply.” On espionage OpenAI recently faced its own spy drama when an employee put a recording device in a company conference room. It’s clear that “people are looking for an edge in all sorts of ways,” Altman said, adding that the company’s operational security has not been perfect, but it has had time to address it. “We have been living in a reality that everybody else is now very publicly and suddenly coming to grips with.” On memory and RAM Altman clarified his recent comments suggesting that it’s a bad thing for people to have RAM memory units sitting on their personal devices at home, amid a global memory supply shortage. His comment, he said, got “misinterpreted,” and that he wants people to have RAM at home: “I think the home tinkering is great.” Only in an optimal world, he said, would personal tinkerers be able to “share this memory” with people who need it. On the next generation of tech Altman said the world is “underpricing or underweighting what can happen with the next generation of products.” “We had the chatbots, then we had the coding agents. I think in the last few months we started to see the beginning of AI for science,” he said. “I think we’re going to see what a lot of compute can do to a lot of the kind of rote work inside of an organization.” OpenAI on Monday announced a new program to boost scientists’ access to frontier AI. “The world can get so much better,” Altman said. On AI safety Altman said OpenAI could push more forcefully toward recursive self-improvement — the idea that an AI model can train its own successor to improve — but added, “I don’t think we could safely do that right now.” Still, he said, the company is able to develop new models faster than it would without AI. OpenAI is now working with embedded evaluators from AI safety watchdog METR: The principle of getting outside experts to evaluate AI labs’ safety work “is going to be increasingly important and valuable,” he said. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: Data center policy dominated the midterms. The 'Virginia of Europe' is the latest battleground
events.summary: Spain’s government is seeking to approve tighter data center rules ahead of its Nov. 29 election. The revised decree would require large data centers to meet strict renewable-energy conditions, prompting industry warnings that investment could be delayed or reconsidered. Aragón, one of Europe’s fastest-growing data center hubs, is at the center of the debate over investment, grid capacity, water use and regulation. Spain's government is seeking to tighten restrictions on one of Europe's fastest-growing data center booms, as the country's Socialist prime minister prepares to fight an election. Investors like Amazon, Microsoft and Blackstone-backed QTS are on tenterhooks. The measure, which doesn't need parliamentary approval, could be approved by Pedro Sánchez's cabinet by next week, and is widely expected to pass ahead of the Nov. 29 elections. It could potentially cost one of Europe's fastest-growing tech regions billions of dollars in investment. The government first introduced the decree in August, partly in response to concerns over energy demand and prices. After fierce opposition, it put forward a revised version on Oct. 26, but the proposal still includes strict renewable-energy requirements. "These requirements could pose insurmountable barriers and act as an effective moratorium," S&P said in an October report. The proposed rules would require 80% of electricity used by data centers to come from renewable sources matched hour by hour, with projects potentially losing grid access if they fail to comply. Projects already in development or awaiting grid connections would also be subject to the rules, with a five-year transition period to comply. Data center buildout faces public backlash Data center build-out has quickly become a prominent political issue around the world. In the U.S. midterm elections, CBS exit polls found data centers were a major influence for more than half of voters. In Spain, concerns over the water and energy demands of data centers are increasingly part of the election debate as the country faces mounting pressure to expand its electricity grid to meet the demand. CBRE estimates that while developers have announced 10.5 GW of data center capacity across Spain and Portugal, only about 4.5 GW is currently considered realistically deliverable because of grid, permitting and infrastructure constraints. Alberto Nadal, the opposition center-right Popular Party's deputy secretary for the economy, has said a conservative government would repeal the decree. Recent polling shows the Popular Party leading, with several seat projections putting the PP and far-right Vox together above a parliamentary majority. Aragón, a landlocked region in the country's northeast, governed by the Popular Party, has emerged as one of Europe's fastest-growing digital infrastructure hubs and is at the center of opposition to the draft rules. The region has attracted investors with fast-track permits, abundant renewable energy and land, and international cable connections. Aragón president, Jorge Azcón, wants to turn it into the "Virginia of Europe," referring to the U.S. state with the world's highest density of data center sites. Aragón is set to receive more than 60 billion euros ($66 billion) in data center and digital infrastructure investment over the next decade. But concerns are growing among residents over noise, water use and pressure on the electricity grid. Pilar Alegría, leader of the Socialist Party in Aragón, told a Nov. 15 rally that the election would be decisive for the region's future and for protecting its natural resources. She highlighted the Ebro River, which runs through Aragón, and raised concerns about the resources used by data centers in a region vulnerable to drought. Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, speaking the same day, sought to reassure investors. "It would be a mistake to squander that advantage through poor planning or regulation that creates uncertainty for investors," Feijóo said. Eva Valle, Aragón's economy minister, has also called for the decree to be scrapped. "It is necessary to halt the approval of this decree, which abounds in harmful conditions placed on the sector," she said at an AWS-organized event on Oct. 27, accusing the government of pursuing "a political agenda." Amazon Web Services and Microsoft have said their investment plans in Aragón remain unchanged, while urging Spain to provide long-term legal certainty and regulatory predictability. Google has already put a multibillion-euro data center project on hold pending greater regulatory certainty, according to a report in Spanish newspaper El Mundo , which cited anonymous sources. Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC. SpainDC, which represents the data-center industry in the country, said the decree would give the group's members the most restrictive data center framework in the European Union and could put 80% to 90% of investment at risk.

events.title: Mars CFO: $1.4 billion U.S. manufacturing investment aims to deliver ‘durable growth’
events.summary: Good morning. Mars Inc., maker of M&M’s, Snickers and Pedigree, plans to invest an estimated $1.4 billion in U.S. manufacturing and operations in 2027, its largest single-year investment. “It is fundamentally a growth investment,” Mars Inc. CFO Claus Aagaard told me. “In the near term, we are putting capital behind high-demand, high-growth brands and businesses where additional capacity can unlock growth.” Longer term, Mars is modernizing its network with automation, high-speed lines and standardized systems “so we can scale efficiently and build a stronger, more resilient supply chain,” Aagaard explained. Following its combination with Kellanova , Mars is now a more than $65 billion family-owned business, based on combined 2025 net sales, according to the company. In the Q&A below, Aagaard discusses the rationale for the investment in manufacturing, how Mars will measure its return and what it means for the communities where it operates. Why is 2027 the right time for Mars’s largest single-year investment?  We have invested more than $9 billion in U.S. manufacturing and operations over the last decade, and while this $1.4 billion commitment is the largest we’ve invested in a single year, it is part of our long-term approach. Demand across our business is high, and American manufacturing is very strong.  Advances in smart factory automation, energy-efficiency technology and digital tools mean that retrofitting or building facilities today can deliver a higher return than it did a decade ago. Right now, we’re seeing a compelling opportunity to not only invest in meeting growing demand, but to unlock capabilities and ensure operational excellence for generations to come.    How is the $1.4 billion divided, and how do you measure the return?  The $1.4 billion investment in 2027 and the $9 billion that has been committed over the past decade, supports manufacturing and operations across our snacking, food and pet businesses, with capital allocated where we see clear opportunities to expand capacity, modernize facilities and strengthen resilience.  For example, we’ll spend more than $34 million to open four new Mars Veterinary Health hospitals in 2027, expand access to emergency and specialty veterinary care, bring innovative medical capabilities to growing communities, and support the development of highly skilled veterinary professionals.  We have invested $60 million in Salt Lake City to add two Trü Frü production lines to our recently opened Nature’s Bakery facility, unlocking capacity for 17 million frozen products annually. And, we have spent $49 million in Columbus, Ohio, to bring Temptations Lickable Treats manufacturing to the U.S., with a target of 400 million pouches annually. We measure return across several dimensions, including our ability to meet consumer demand, improve efficiency and productivity, strengthen supply chain resilience, support profitable growth, and expand access to high-quality veterinary care.  Why does keeping 94% of U.S. products made domestically matter to Mars?  Mars has operated in the U.S. for 115 years—it’s our largest market, and we’re globally headquartered here. The U.S. is critical for Mars. Making 94% of the products we sell in the U.S. domestically gives us an important foundation for long-term growth. A strong local manufacturing footprint puts production closer to consumers, creates greater supply-chain resilience, and allows us to expand capacity as demand grows. It also means that when we invest in growth, those investments can translate directly into facilities, capabilities, and jobs in the communities where we operate.  What does this investment mean for the communities where Mars operates?  We have operated in many U.S. communities for generations, so these investments are about more than adding capacity. They modernize and strengthen facilities, support skilled jobs, and create additional economic activity locally.   This month, our facility in Waco, Texas is celebrating 50 years of operations. Mars has steadily expanded and modernized the Waco site, which produces Snickers, Starburst, and Skittles, to meet growing consumer demand while advancing environmental sustainability. Mars has invested $165 million in the facility since 2024, with recent capital projects heavily focused on enhancing energy efficiency and operational excellence. Today, the site is powered by nearly 900 dedicated associates, but the milestone speaks to the dedication of generations of associates and longstanding partnerships we share with the Central Texas community.  What would success look like for this investment a few years from now?  Success means we have converted this capital into durable growth and a stronger operating network. We should be able to serve more consumers and pet owners, scale high-growth brands, operate more efficiently, and have greater resilience across our supply chain.  Sheryl   Estrada Sheryl.Estrada@fortune.com This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: My husband and I were serious gamers before having a baby. GTA 6 will be our biggest parenting challenge yet.
events.summary: The author now has a toddler and has to plan her playing hours around her. Courtesy of the author My husband and I met playing Halo and spent more than 30 hours a week gaming before becoming parents. Since having our daughter, we've struggled to find time to play and worry about violent video games. We're determined to play GTA 6 together even if it means waiting until our toddler is asleep. My husband and I already know we want to play Grand Theft Auto 6 together. What we don't know is when. The game comes out November 19. Right now, our controllers are under a pile of burp cloths, and every time our daughter toddles past the TV, someone hits pause so she doesn't see what we're playing. We met in a game, and for years gaming was how we spent our time together, 20-plus hours a week. Then, last year, we became first-time parents. Now we have two problems we never expected: finding time to play and figuring out what's OK to play when a 15-month-old is watching. For years gaming was our date night Before I met my husband, gaming was something I did alone. It was how I unwound after work. The author now needs to plan when to play GTA 6 when her toddler is not around. M-ART Production/Getty Images Then a random Halo Infinite lobby put us on the same team. I'd like to say it was love at first sight, but it was really love at first aim-down-sights. One match turned into two, and then our after-work matches became a regular nightly duo, and a duo turned into a relationship. For years, gaming was our date night, our downtime, and our shared language : 30-plus hours a week, side by side. We gamed through the Braxton Hicks and baby kicks When I got pregnant, we didn't stop playing. We just changed how we played. We still logged about 20 hours a week, often passing one controller back and forth through open-world single-player titles while the baby kicked to remind us she was on her way. After our daughter was born, we gamed for exactly zero hours. As she got older, we started finding our way back. First came quick multiplayer matches in Halo Infinite that we could drop at a moment's notice. Then we started playing the campaign of the recently remastered Halo: Combat Evolved together, very slowly, with long breaks between sessions because one of us always got pulled away by a suspiciously quiet toddler all of a sudden. Those big open-world games we love didn't survive that schedule. My husband played all of Starfield while I slept. Or "slept," since most nights I was half-awake in a haze of revenge bedtime procrastination, doomscrolling long past when I should have closed my eyes. Cyberpunk 2077 is still sitting in our backlog. Now GTA 6 is looming, bigger than all of them, and that's the part that worries me, but we're more determined than ever to try. She's almost a year and a half now, and we want back the pastime that brought us together in the first place. What better way to celebrate our original duo than by playing as a couple in the biggest game of the year? I'd never thought about how graphic my games were until now The first time it hit me, I was sneaking in some Fallout 4 next to my husband on the couch. I was clearing out a raider camp, with gunfire cracking and limbs flying, when I landed a shot that took a raider's head clean off. Out of the corner of my eye, I saw my daughter's little head snap toward the TV. The sound had pulled her in, and she was staring right at the screen as the body hit the ground. I froze. I'd played violent games for years without a second thought, and I'd even started gaming again when she was barely mobile and hardly noticed anything, and somewhere along the way she'd started to watch. Keeping up with how fast she was changing and rethinking my habits with every new leap she made had already had my head spinning. Now here was one more thing I'd missed. Now we feel pulled in two directions. We want to protect her from anything overly graphic, and we still love the games we've always played, which aren't exactly gentle. So we've started treating game settings like childproofing. We look for options that reduce or turn off blood and gore, or change the color of blood. We turn the volume down so gunfire doesn't startle her, and we play with subtitles, or one of us wears headphones. We look for settings that tone down bright flashes to protect her eyes. I'll be checking GTA 6 's menu for every one of these on day one. And honestly, a lot of these accessibility settings make the game better for me, too. Our plan for GTA 6 We don't have it all figured out, but we have a plan. Violent missions wait until she's asleep. Naps are now prime gaming time. And when we can't both have a controller, we'll go back to what got us through pregnancy: passing one back and forth. It feels right that GTA 6 stars Jason and Lucia, a couple who do everything as a team. They just have fewer diapers to change. We may not reach the end credits on launch week, or even launch month, but we'll get there together, one nap at a time. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Nasdaq-listed HomesToLife lands SGX dual-listing amid rising global demand for custom furniture
events.summary: HomesToLife CEO Phua Mei Ming said 95% of the company’s revenue is derived from its export business, which includes white-labelled furniture sold by retail partners around the globe. HomesToLife, a Singapore furniture maker, secured a dual listing on SGX after placing 7.5 million shares at $1.15, raising about $8.6 million. It is only the second company with SGX and Nasdaq listings. The company says rising demand for custom, premium and mid-price furniture in Asia-Pacific, especially South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and Japan, supports growth. It plans to use about 80% of net proceeds for expansion. HomesToLife makes most of its revenue from exports, with 95% from business outside retail. It controls its supply chain end to end and faces low-cost online rivals like Taobao, but says quality, customisation and service set it apart. SINGAPORE – When it comes to furniture shopping, online e-commerce platforms such as Taobao are hugely popular for their easy access to a wide range of mass-market products at affordable prices. But increasingly, homeowners who have more particular tastes are on the hunt for premium quality furniture that can also be customised to their needs, and local company HomesToLife is bullish this demand will continue to grow as it secured its secondary listing on the Singapore Exchange. The Nasdaq-listed company completed a placement of 7.5 million shares on the SGX Mainboard on Nov 17 at $1.15 per share, raising some $8.6 million in gross proceeds. The placement attracted more than 50 accredited and institutional investors, including funds under the Equity Market Development Programme. Institutional investors, including Amova Asset Management Asia and Lion Global Investors, collectively subscribed for about 4.6 million shares worth around $5.3 million. UOB Kay Hian acted as the placement agent, while Maybank Securities was the sub-placement agent. This is the second company to achieve a dual listing on both the SGX and Nasdaq, with the first being cybersecurity firm Avepoint in September 2025. About 80% of t he $7 million in net proceeds will be used for business expans ion , and 20% will be reserved for general working capital. Chief executive Phua Mei Ming told The Straits Times that the company is seeking to expand its presence in the Asia Pacific, where it already has a sizeable presence but still has room to grow its distribution. A burgeoning middle class in markets such as South Korea, Taiwan and Thailand presents good opportunities for HomesToLife’s business, she said. “We see huge potential in growing not just our premium offering but also a mid-price range of products, as the emerging middle-class appreciates well-made products.” HomesToLife was started by Phua’s father and his two brothers in 1976 as Hwa Tat Lee, one of Singapore’s first sofa makers, with local retailer Courts as one of its major clients. By 1994, it had started its own leather tannery operations here. In 2014, the current iteration of the brand was launched as a retail business, with six stores in Singapore at its peak. Today, it operates four stores here, with three more in South Korea. In addition to HomesToLife’s range, the company also owns German luxury brand Domicil, which it acquired in 2005. Phua said retail comprises only a small percentage of HomesToLife’s business, as 95% of its revenue comes from its export business. Its furniture is sold by major leading retailers around the world, including DFS in the UK and Cuir Center in France. For its 2025 financial year ended Dec 31, Europe accounted for almost 60% of its revenue at $377.9 million, while 26.9% stemmed from Asia-Pacific, and the rest from North America. HomesToLife reported $19.4 million in operating profit for FY2025, a 103.7% increase from the previous year. But it also faced cost pressures due to disruptions in the Suez Canal, which raised freight rates by 22%. Most of the company’s products are made to order, allowing both retail customers and retailers to customise their furniture before they are shipped from factories in China, Vietnam and India. A number of retailers also carry the brand’s white-labelled products, which are developed and designed exclusively for the retailers’ territories. HomesToLife's outlet at Marina Square. Phua said the company is one of the few furniture brands that controls its own supply chain end to end, from design all the way to distribution, where the company would deliver its products to retailers’ warehouses while other customers may pick up directly from the port. The advantage of HomesToLife’s made-to-order model is lower inventory risk for its distributors – if demand for a particular product has waned, for instance, they can flexibly move on to selling new products. “This is what we call our ‘easy buy, easy sell’ approach to business. We just make it easy for our partners to do their business, which is selling furniture,” she said.

events.title: Nvidia has lost $2 trillion in value. Here's what options traders expect from earnings
events.summary: Options traders expect a bigger than usual move on Tuesday's earnings. Nvidia has lost $2 trillion from its all time highs. Open put interest below $150 is drying up. Jensen Huang's forced exit from Nvidia shocked Wall Street and Washington, wiped $2 trillion off its market value, and raised serious questions about national security and regulation of the AI complex. Traders, for the moment, must content themselves with the comparatively mundane business of Tuesday's earnings, and options traders are expecting big moves. With volatility in the stock near the highest since April 2025, options traders are now pricing a 7% reaction in the stock after its report, the biggest implied move going into an Nvidia report since February 2025, and well above the median move of 3.2% over the last eight quarters. Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia's third-quarter 2027 earnings Pro: Nvidia earnings: Three things investors are watching Exclusive: How Trump traded Nvidia stock as he championed the chipmaker Nvidia warns chip buyers of legal risks tied to China access: Sources Implied volatility reached 68 Monday, compared to under 40 in early October, according to ThinkOrSwim data. Nvidia vol reached a multi-year high above 92 in the aftermath of President Trump's tariff Liberation day in April '25. In other words, the company that for much of the AI boom was the most reliable winner in the market, is now more volatile than all but 35 companies in the S&P 500. "Longer term, I see significant downside risk unless Nvidia can attract an exceptional leader, someone like Tim Cook or AMD's Lisa Su," Nigam Arora, founder of the Arora report, said in a text ahead of the company's after-market report on Tuesday. Since hitting all-time highs in October, Nvidia shares have fallen 35%, shedding $2 trillion in market capitalization along the way. Including Nvidia, there are only five companies in the S&P 500 worth more than $2 trillion. However, there is evidence that bulls have been holding out hope while bears snatch up profits: the ratio of open puts to call contracts has actually widened towards calls, according to Barchart data. The ratio is currently 0.87, down from a one-year high of 1.02 two weeks ago and the lowest since the first week of October. The most popular contract by volume on Monday was the 155-strike put expiring at the bell Monday, but the most popular trade for later expiry was the 160-strike call expiring Thursday, and the second-most-common purchase was the 190-strike call expiring Friday, SpotGamma data show. One catch is that most call contracts traded Monday looked like neutral to bearish positions opened by traders selling calls. Of the 5 million options traded on Monday, 3 million were calls, but more were likely opened by sellers than buyers. Of the $2.3 billion in options premium traded on Nvidia Monday, $1.2 billion was tied to puts, SpotGamma data show. With bears taking profits in puts the past month, there's another potential snag on open interest. There are very few open put contracts at or below the $157 level at which the stock closed Monday. That suggests any bad surprise would find many traders with little downside protection. By the same token, there's notable open interest in call contracts from the 175-strike and above, suggesting profit-taking on a bounce could limit Nvidia's recovery past levels it breached over the past week. Either way, Tuesday's earnings could provide fireworks.

events.title: Roth 401(k) matches are 'surging,' report finds. What workers should know
events.summary: More employers are offering workers the option of a Roth 401(k) match, according to a new report by the Plan Sponsor Council of America. A Roth employer contribution is made after income taxes. Workers don't pay income tax upon withdrawal in retirement. By contrast, a worker defers taxes on traditional pretax contributions. They get an up-front tax break, but not upon withdrawal in older age. There are pros and cons to pretax and Roth savings. Many more workers can now or will soon be able to accept a 401(k) match as a Roth contribution — giving them a new avenue to build a bucket of tax-free savings for retirement . Historically, workers could only accept 401(k) match money from an employer as pretax, meaning they had to defer income taxes on those funds until they withdrew them in retirement. Until a recent rule change, workers generally couldn't elect to receive a match as a Roth contribution. With Roth savings , investors don't get an up-front tax break — they pay income tax on the funds now but can take out the contributions and growth tax-free in retirement. A law known as Secure 2.0, which former President Joe Biden signed into law in 2022, gave employers the option to add a Roth match as a feature of their 401(k) plans. If a plan offers a Roth match, it's not automatic; workers must opt in. The number of employers that now let workers accept a 401(k) match or other employer contribution as Roth savings has "surged," according to a new report from the Plan Sponsor Council of America, a trade group representing employers. About 42% of surveyed businesses that sponsored a 401(k) plan in 2025 have added or will add an option to accept employer contributions as Roth savings, according to an annual PSCA report published Nov. 10. That's more than double the share — about 20% — that did so in 2024, the report found. Another 11% are still considering the option, according to the report. The PSCA report is based on data from 753 employers that sponsor 401(k) plans of various sizes. "My guess is we will continue to see [the share] increase," said Hattie Greenan, the group's research director. "Roth is becoming mainstream," she said. But just because employees have the Roth match option available to them doesn't mean it will be their best option. There are pros and cons to pretax and Roth savings, and the right choice can vary from person to person, financial advisors said. "[Roth] is not a bad idea if you're not so worried about your taxes today," said Philip Chao, a certified financial planner and chief investment officer at Experiential Wealth, based in Cabin John, Maryland. "It's personal preference." Roth vs. pretax: How to weigh the tax trade-offs While there are ample benefits to saving at least some money as Roth funds in a 401(k), most investors opt against it. In fact, while almost all 401(k) plans already allow workers to save part of their paychecks as a Roth contribution, only a quarter of workers actually do so, according to the PSCA report. "The list of cons may be short for Roth 401(k)s, but missing tax deferral is a big one," according to a May article written by Fidelity, a retirement plan administrator. "When faced with a choice of paying more tax now or later, most people choose to pay later, hence the low participation rates for Roth 401(k)s." IRS announces 2027 401(k) contribution limits, raises savings cap Why Nvidia stock drop isn't a big deal for many ETF, mutual fund investors Social Security could pay benefits until 2059 if payroll kept pace with GDP: AARP CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 Tax deferral has long been a "key driver" of retirement savings, Fidelity said. Saving on a pretax basis effectively increases a worker's take-home pay. It also reduces their adjusted gross income today, and may therefore positively impact the calculation of eligibility for child tax credits, financial aid for college or federal aid, according to Fidelity. A Fidelity example shows the financial benefit of an up-front tax break: Let's say a saver with a $75,000 annual income in the 22% federal income tax bracket makes a $400 monthly 401(k) contribution. Making the full contribution as Roth would reduce their paycheck by $400. Making the contribution into a traditional — i.e., pretax — 401(k) would reduce their paycheck by just $312. For those who can stomach the up-front tax hit, Roth provides for powerful tax-planning opportunities in future years, according to financial advisors. "Roth gives you a lot more flexibility at retirement," Chao said. "But you have to be OK with paying years of tax on it first. It's never something for nothing. There's always a trade-off." For example, the government doesn't require investors to withdraw a minimum amount from Roth accounts in retirement, as it does with pretax savings.

events.title: At the origin of France’s education protests, students refuse to give up
events.summary: Blockades continue at some schools in the Parisian suburbs, as students and teachers say little has improved in their classrooms. Paris, France – On a cold, rainy morning in early November, students and teachers met outside the locked gates of Paul Eluard, a high school in Saint-Denis north of Paris. Some were wearing costumes. For 17-year-old Kamelia, dressing as a dinosaur helped her to maintain the joy and hope that coexisted with the anger driving the student movement in mid-September. “Costumes are the fun part. They show that it’s not all about violence. There’s also good cheer and fun in all of this,” Kamelia told Al Jazeera. “Today there are huge protests all over France, and it’s very important. I got up early, and even though I’m a little tired, I came anyway.” list 1 of 4 Radical or hero?: France debates leftist candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon list 2 of 4 ‘Nobody can stop them’: Who are Europe’s Black Bloc protesters? list 3 of 4 Mapping how France’s protest wave spread across Europe list 4 of 4 France accelerates minimum wage hike in bid to quell protest Four days after students at Paul Eluard returned from a mid-term break, they joined a national strike on November 5. Nearby, students from the trade school Bartholdi had blockaded the gates of their school. Although the size of the student protests peaked in early October, many young people, especially in the suburbs, are refusing to return to the classroom until some of their demands are met. “Sometimes, we see rats in the courtyard and in the restrooms. The restrooms are a mess. We don’t have enough water; it flows very slowly. We don’t have enough to drink, and the restrooms are dirty. The hallways are dirty, the classrooms are dirty, and there are cockroaches,” 17-year-old Nohlan, a student at Bartholdi, told Al Jazeera outside the school’s blockade. The movement started at a high school in Creteil, a suburb southeast of Paris in the Val-de-Marne region, on September 17, and rapidly spread to Saint-Denis, then the rest of France. Students blocked the entrances to their schools to protest poor classroom conditions and took to the streets. “The movement started in the suburbs, then Paris followed suit. Now the whole world is watching us,” Kamelia said. “[In Saint-Denis], we’re basically ignored, even though we’re part of this country. But we’re here, and we are the future of this country.” By the end of September, an estimated 400 schools across France, including some universities, had joined the student movement. Protests on October 17 in Paris saw an estimated 550,000 participants, according to the interior minister, while organisers put the number at 800,000. Although this is not the first time in recent years that students in working-class suburbs have protested against school conditions, the scale of this year’s movement has been remarkable. “It really started to gain momentum, and when everyone started to get involved, it was incredible. It really moved me because last year, we set up a few blockades, but no one heard about them,” Kamelia said. Although students are at the heart of the movement, many teachers have since joined, expressing solidarity with their students and deploring the conditions under which they have to teach. High school students are setting the pace for the movement, said Lucie Sabze, an English teacher at Paul Eluard. “I’m impressed by the students, their demands and their political discourse, which is very lucid and very clear,” she told Al Jazeera. “I think the scale of the movement can be explained by a growing frustration.” Teachers at Eluard are celebrating one “victory”. They had been calling for the resignation of the head teacher, who they accused of letting an officer from France’s notoriously violent motorised antiterrorism brigade into the school to arrest a student. On Sunday, a government agency announced Xavier Artaud had stepped down “as a safety precaution”. “Given the unacceptable public accusations made against the high school principal by name, he requested protective measures requiring his removal from the Saint-Denis area,” said the Academic Director of National Education Services. Bruno Gbalou, an English teacher at neighbouring Bartholdi, noted that conditions have only deteriorated in recent years. “It’s been about 15 years since I came back from England and started teaching here, and things have only gotten worse. So there are more students, but we have fewer resources,” Bruno Gbalou told Al Jazeera. “It’s not fair to the students, and it’s not fair to us, and that’s one of the reasons why we’re going on strike.” In a statement to the media in early October, President Emmanuel Macron said the government planned to respond to students’ demands “in the most concrete way possible”. “I understand the anxieties, sometimes the anger, that our youth can have, whether about the climate, technological changes or geopolitical situations,” Macron said.

events.title: This legendary quant fund sold virtually all of its Nvidia stock before its recent plunge
events.summary: Nvidia stock has tanked by as much as 36% in the past six weeks. Haven Daley/AP Renaissance Technologies sold virtually all of its Nvidia stock last quarter, before it slumped. RenTech shrank its stake in the AI chipmaker from about $1.4 billion to just over $5 million. Nvidia stock has tanked a third in the past six weeks due to AI jitters and the Jensen Huang scandal. A leading hedge fund sold almost its entire Nvidia stake last quarter, before the AI chipmaker's stock crashed. Renaissance Technologies slashed its Nvidia position by about 99.7% in the three months to September 30, per its third-quarter US stock portfolio disclosure, also known as a 13F. RenTech — founded by the late Jim Simons , who also worked as an NSA codebreaker and MIT math professor — cut its Nvidia holding from 7.1 million shares to only around 23,000 shares. The value of the position dropped from about $1.4 billion to just over $5 million as a result. Nvidia had been RenTech's No. 1 holding at the end of June, making up about 2% of its portfolio. The hedge fund also took a knife to its second-largest holding, Meta, cutting its position from 2 million shares worth over $1.1 billion on June 30, to only around 1,600 shares worth about $1.2 million three months later. The quant fund, which relies on algorithms to decide most of its trades, ranks among the biggest and best-performing hedge funds in history . It's worth underscoring that quant funds frequently overhaul their portfolios, and 13F filings provide only a snapshot of an investment firm's holdings on a single trading day. They also exclude shares sold short, private investments, overseas stocks, and other assets such as gold or crypto, so they don't always paint a full picture of a fund's investing strategy. It's unclear whether RenTech escaped the worst of the current Nvidia fallout by cashing in its shares, or reinvested in October and got caught up in it. The firm has made big changes to its Nvidia position in the past. It cut the holding from about 5.6 million shares at the end of September last year, to fewer than 900,000 shares on December 30. It then rebuilt it to 2.5 million shares by the end of March, then to about 7.1 million going into last quarter. RenTech was one of several well-known funds to make big changes to their Nvidia bets last quarter, regulatory filings revealed late on Monday. Bridgewater Associates, founded by Ray Dalio , cut its stake by 30%. Soros Fund Management, founded by George Soros, pared its position by 19%. On the other hand, Cathie Wood 's Ark Investment Management boosted its Nvidia holdings by 85% last quarter. The tech investor's flagship Ark Innovation ETF held nearly 2 million shares worth about $310 million at Monday's close. Nvidia's central role in the AI boom catapulted its stock price from under $15 at the start of 2023 to over $240 at its peak this October, a 16-fold increase. But it has plunged 36% to a 16-month low over the past six weeks, wiping roughly $2 trillion from Nvidia's market capitalization — more than SpaceX or Meta are worth. The stock initially slipped due to mounting worries about the sustainability of the debt-fueled AI buildout. It plunged further after its founder, Jensen Huang, resigned as CEO following reports that he had extramarital affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a direct report. CFO Colette Kress has stepped in as interim CEO while the board searches for a successor. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Ukraine’s Magura drone boats have downed Russian helicopters and taken out air defenses. The maker didn’t see that coming.
events.summary: Ukraine's Magura naval drones have used missiles and drones to hit targets in the air and on land. AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky Ukraine's naval drones now hit Russia away from the water, downing aircraft and taking out defenses. "I didn't expect it," one major ground robot maker told Business Insider. Ukraine's soldiers often surprise arms makers with how they use their gear, and that drives updates. Ukraine's Magura naval drones have taken out Russian targets at sea. They've also taken out helicopters in the air and air defense systems on land, proving to be a versatile platform. That came as a surprise to their primary manufacturer. "I didn't expect it," Oleg Rogynskyy, the founder and CEO of UFORCE, told Business Insider. "It's the ingenuity of Ukrainian engineers and Ukrainian soldiers that really drives this," he said. "Where this gets more interesting is I keep on being surprised." UFORCE, founded in Ukraine and headquartered in London, makes the Magura drone, which has been central in combating Russia's Black Sea Fleet . Without warships but equipped with an unconventional uncrewed navy, Ukraine has damaged and destroyed Russian ships and driven them away from a key port in occupied Crimea. Ukraine says Magura drones armed with missiles have also shot down Russian helicopters as well as Russian fighter jets , while other mothership designs have been used to launch FPV drones against air defense targets. After a strike in August, a GUR commander said this "marks a fundamental shift in the nature of the conflict." Ukraine's Main Intelligence Directorate, the GUR, said Magura naval drones have destroyed Russian helicopters. YouTube/Defence Intelligence of Ukraine "That's the definition of asymmetric warfare right there," Rogynskyy said, "when a $40,000 drone can take out a $400 million" Russian air defense system." Ukraine has reported that FPV drones launched from Magura naval drones have taken out S-400 launchers and other expensive equipment. "The more use there is," he predicted, "the more creative outcomes we're going to see." Ukraine's soldiers are encouraged to experiment with, find new uses for, and modify their weaponry. Units often have R&D elements near the front lines , and companies work closely with combat units to design systems toward those ends. Soldiers surprise makers Makers have repeatedly told Business Insider they've been caught off guard by how soldiers used their products. Achi, the CEO of Ukrainian defense firm Ark Robotics, said that when it comes to soldiers using his robots and technology, "there are some really crazy ideas I would never imagine in my life." Oleg Fedoryshyn, director of R&D at Ukrainian ground-robot and weapons maker DevDroid, shared that  the company was surprised  to see Russian soldiers surrender to one of its robots. Meanwhile, an executive at Ukrainian drone maker TechEx, said that the company was surprised by how much explosive weight Ukrainian soldiers can pack on its drones. Kuldar Väärsi, the founder and CEO of Estonian ground robot maker Milrem Robotics, another company surprised by the ways that Ukrainian soldiers use the company's robots , said previously that "Ukrainian troops are really creative, and they really find very simple ways how to get even more out of the equipment." Milrem Robotics is among the companies that have been surprised at how Ukrainian soldiers use their gear. Mykhaylo Palinchak/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Soldiers often come up with modifications that manufacturers then help develop and scale. Fedoryshyn said Ukrainian troops first proposed mounting RPGs on robots , and then the company helped make it happen. Western firms with products in Ukraine are seeing it, too. Germany's ARX Robotics supplies Ukraine with ground robots. David Roberts, CEO of ARX Robotics UK, told Business Insider that "the Ukrainian armed forces are the absolute consumer innovators." "As soon as they get a system," he said of the Ukrainians, "the first thing they'll do is they'll think about whether they can mash it together with another system they have to create something that's bigger and better than the sum of parts." Naval drones have been a key area of innovation helping Ukraine win at sea without a conventional naval force. Drone boats can still execute one-way explosive attacks, but they do so much more now. They launch missiles and drones, they've been used to deploy uncrewed ground vehicles for amphibious assaults, and they are also engaging Russian naval drones in maritime gun battles. Sea drones are not new, but Ukraine is advancing the technology and using it at scale and with a coordination not seen before, while also demonstrating new uses regularly. Global navies have long recognized the potential of naval drones and invested in their development, but the war in Ukraine has spurred new urgency to build this capability. Military officials have signaled that crewed fleets may not be enough on their own. Gen. Sir Gwyn Jenkins, the UK's first sea lord and chief of the naval staff, said in September that "it is that it is no longer possible to defend a vast, contested ocean with crewed warships alone." The UK is currently pursuing a hybrid fleet in which traditional warships command maritime drones and other naval assets. Other militaries are also building similar capabilities. Rogynskyy predicts that "pretty much every navy on the planet is going to be scaling itself using cheap, attritable, unmanned assets that are AI-controlled." Time will tell. events.title: Investors look to Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's IPO to refresh the tech rally
events.summary: Defensive stocks like Big Pharma have taken the lead from imploding chip stocks, but these stocks lack the heft to carry a bull market. Can Nvidia’s results on Tuesday and Anthropic’s IPO refresh the tech bid? Twenty years ago this week, my "Death of the Floor" cover story for Barron's antagonized plenty of friends in the stock-trading profession. How the market setup is more favorable for the Anthropic IPO than the lead-up to SpaceX's debut. Get Mike Santoli's Market Memo in your inbox first. SUBSCRIBE HERE I've spent the past 20 years pushing back against the periodically popular notion that markets are replaying the late-1990s and early-2000s tech bubble and bust. We've simply never matched the levels of gross overvaluation, pervasive public greed, fevered IPO issuance, corporate malinvestment and Wall Street malfeasance that set up a generational market peak, a halving of the S&P 500 over two-and-a-half years and a lost decade for stocks. We still haven't. Even if June was the peak in AI speculative fervor, as seems possible, and if Oct. 6 proves to have been a consequential broad-market top, the major indexes simply never stretched far enough into the thin air to make a potential retrenchment nearly as damaging as the early 2000s were. Still, in a more muted fashion, markets have been behaving in ways that generate uncomfortable comparisons to past buying climaxes accompanying a technology revolution. There is still room and time for the market to prove that the messy sell-down in AI-reliant growth stocks is simply a painful adjustment phase and the S&P 500's six-month purgatorial range a mid-cycle refresh. But it will need to start getting on with it. Everyone wants to celebrate the way the market has absorbed the damage to semiconductors and other AI-buildout plays, rendering it a controlled demolition rather than indiscriminate destruction. The Financial Times Unhedged newsletter on Monday called it "The perfect sell-off," the same day the Wall Street Journal cheered, "When Nvidia Stumbled, Equal-Weight Funds Delivered." This is true, as far as it goes. A rush into defensive and "quality" stocks has largely offset the drag from Nvidia's $2 trillion market-cap loss from its October peak. But recent defensive leadership, especially from low-growth consumer staples and Big Pharma, sends a less-reassuring macro message, and those groups lack the earnings momentum, narrative appeal or market-cap heft to carry a bull market to new heights. BTIG technical strategist Jonathan Krinsky has noted echoes of the 2000 period when "boring" defensive stocks ripped as tech rolled over, supporting the tape for a while. Barclays equity desk noted Monday that the "quality factor" basket of stocks just had one of the best 100-day runs ever of the past 20 years. And JP Morgan here plots the stampede into "low-volatility" stocks, mirroring the hasty retreat from "high-momentum" areas. There's room here for defensives to get even more popular before tripping multi-year extremes, but is that what an index investor should root for? As for the ascendance of everyone's favorite, the equal-weighted S&P 500 , Ned Davis Research analyst London Stockton this month noted that just over 50% of S&P 500 stocks were outperforming the index itself in 2026. Sounds healthy, right? Only to a point. He explains: "Levels [of stocks outperforming the index] above 58% have most often occurred in and around years where there has been a large bear market." The current phase follows a period when leadership was extremely narrow, producing a "resemblance of the prior three years (2023-2025) to the two years prior to the last Tech bubble (1998-1999) with a very small percentage of companies outperforming the overall S&P 500. "It is not likely that we are in a situation like in 2000," Stockton concludes, "but this highlights the importance that these large tech stocks at the very least do not decline substantially for the S&P 500 to continue rallying higher." There are other straws in the wind that harken to prior tech busts: The Federal Reserve is trying to restrain the corporate sector from overheating in the latter part of a cycle, same as in 1999. Retail traders have maniacally bought the cascading decline in Nvidia shares the past week or so, invoking the voracious dip-buying made famous in the late-'90s which worked until it failed spectacularly. The market's refusal to pay up for sizzling earnings growth raises alarms about whether they are pulled forward, unsustainable or overstated; profits from 2000 were later revised down radically. And Nvidia's alleged breach of chip-export rules and the forced departure of CEO Jensen Huang are a reminder that major corporate scandals were a key feature of the Tech Bubble's prolonged reckoning, though nothing resembling the multiple accounting frauds of that era are implied here.
