events.title: Infantino’s FIFA challenger Diallo claims to have support beyond Europe
events.summary: French football chief Philippe Diallo says he has received ‘spontaneous signs of strong support’ against Infantino. French Football Federation President Philippe Diallo says he has the backing of countries beyond Europe in his bid to depose Gianni Infantino in the upcoming FIFA presidential election. “To beat him you need 106 votes, which is a majority,” Diallo said on Tuesday following his nomination as the European governing body UEFA’s representative. “It is now up to me and my team to go and convince those on other continents, but already since yesterday I have received spontaneous signs of strong support which will be revealed in the coming days.” Diallo was speaking in Paris the day after accepting an invitation from UEFA to stand against Infantino in the election to be held next March. UEFA, which has 55 member associations, said that European nations had “unanimously pledged their full support” to Diallo, ahead of Wednesday’s deadline for candidates to declare themselves. Under its Slovenian president Aleksander Ceferin, UEFA has led the opposition to Infantino since his plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors was revealed in July. Infantino quickly abandoned the proposal in the face of widespread uproar, but UEFA has since gone to a court in Florida in an attempt to gather evidence for a potential complaint of “criminal mismanagement” against the current FIFA president in Switzerland. Diallo announced in September that the French Football Federation (FFF) was withdrawing its backing for Infantino in the election, following similar announcements from other European associations. At the time he said that “the trust placed in the FIFA president has been betrayed”. “There can no longer be a type of single-handed governance where the biggest issues in football are decided behind the scenes, without any transparency and without anyone being consulted, without going through the executive committee,” Diallo, 63, said on Tuesday. “My vision will be one of open, collegiate governance, in which the different bodies really play their part.” Diallo, the 63-year-old son of a Senegalese boxing champion, has been president of the FFF since January 2023. UEFA had been struggling to find a credible candidate to stand against Infantino in the election, which will take place at the FIFA Congress on March 18 next year in the Moroccan capital, Rabat. Arsene Wenger, the French former Arsenal manager and FIFA’s current chief of global football development, had at one point been seen as a potential candidate who could get Europe’s backing, but he will not stand. FIFA has a total of 211 member associations, with each having one vote in the presidential election. A majority is needed for a candidate to win.

events.title: Chase says software bug that caused online banking chaos has been resolved
events.summary: PATRICK T. FALLON/AFP via Getty Images Chase said a software bug was to blame for widespread online banking issues on Monday, but it's now resolved. Reports on DownDetector showed disruptions with Chase, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo. "Where we were party to a transaction involving other banks, those banks may have been impacted," Chase said. A JPMorgan Chase software bug that wreaked havoc on online banking services on Monday has been resolved. The company said on Tuesday that its services were back to normal after many customers reported delayed transactions. "JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems — there is no evidence this is cyber-related," the bank previously said in a statement on Monday. "It is taking longer than usual to service some customers." "Where we were party to a transaction involving other banks, those banks may have been impacted, but this is not a systemic issue," it added in the statement. "Customers still have access to their accounts and funds." Customers of Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and US Bank reported thousands of combined issues on Monday afternoon, according to the third-party website DownDetector.com . Some customers reported issues with being unable to access information on their accounts. DownDetector also showed reports of issues with Zelle and Capital One. The site showed a much smaller spike in reports across Citibank and TD Bank. Other US banks said the issue was not on their end. "Capital One has not been impacted and continues to operate normally at this time," a spokesperson told Business Insider. A spokesperson for US Bank said its systems are not directly impacted. "However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays," the spokesperson added. A Zelle spokesperson said that the payments app wasn't down and was operating as it should. "An issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers," the spokesperson said. The bank disruptions follow a tumultuous few days of high-profile disruptions, including a massive Microsoft outage and an FAA technical failure that sparked a nationwide ground stop and thousands of flight delays and cancellations. While some online have questioned whether the crop of incidents in the last week could be connected, there is no evidence at the moment to suggest that. Alice Tecotzky contributed reporting for this story. Update, November 17, 2026 — This story has been updated to reflect JPMorgan Chase's latest statement on the issue. events.title: 11 easy Thanksgiving dessert recipes that aren't pumpkin pie
events.summary: When it comes to Thanksgiving desserts, you don't have to limit yourself to pumpkin pie. Catherine Falls Commercial/Getty Images Pumpkin pie is a staple on Thanksgiving, but there are other fan-favorite desserts you can make. Baked apples with vanilla ice cream and chocolate cream pie are both crowd-pleasing options. Adding nuts to a simple brownie recipe can elevate your Thanksgiving spread. It's time to start planning your Thanksgiving menu, starting with dessert. If you're not a fan of pumpkin pie or want to switch things up this Thanksgiving, there are other easy, crowd-pleasing desserts you can make instead. Pumpkin pie has been a Thanksgiving staple since the holiday's early days in the 17th century, when pilgrims and early American settlers frequently used pumpkins in many of their recipes. However, fewer than a quarter of Thanksgiving tables are expected to feature pumpkin pie this year, according to WalletHub . As such, you don't need to stick to tradition to please your guests. If you're looking for options that don't require an oven, you can make slow-cooker cobbler or chocolate cream pie. Adding premium ingredients, such as macadamia nuts, pecans, or walnuts, can also elevate a classic brownie recipe to bakery-quality status. Here are 11 easy Thanksgiving desserts that aren't pumpkin pie. If you still have pie on your mind, you can make an easy chocolate cream pie. Chocolate cream pie. bbraley/Getty Images Chocolate cream pie is generally easier to make than pumpkin or apple pie, since many versions, like this recipe by Simply Recipes , don't even require you to bake it. Instead, you just chill the dessert in the fridge for a few hours, which is perfect when you're trying to keep the oven free for other Thanksgiving dishes . You could also make an apple pie. Apple pie. Cyndi Monaghan/Getty Images If you  do  want to spend a little time making your dessert, but don't want to make pumpkin pie, apple pie is an excellent option. In fact, around 12% of Thanksgiving tables will opt for this dessert, according to WalletHub . There are plenty of recipes out there, from more intricate lattice pies to easier versions that use pre-made pie crust. Business Insider's Paige Bennett tried three celebrity-chef apple pie recipes and found Ree Drummond's the most delicious, while Gordon Ramsay's the easiest to make. Pecan pie is another popular dessert for Thanksgiving. Pecan pie. Lesyy/Getty Images/iStockphoto Pecan pie is another Thanksgiving classic, known for its gooey, buttery filling and crisp, nutty topping. It's an especially great choice for anyone who prefers a rich, caramel-like dessert over pumpkin pie — and 14% of Wallethub survey respondents said they'll be eating it this Thanksgiving. Apple crisp is another easy and festive dessert. Apple crisp. loooby/iStock If you're looking for a low-effort dessert that still feels special, apple crisp is a Thanksgiving crowd-pleaser. The warm, cinnamon-spiced apples and buttery crumb topping pair perfectly with a scoop of vanilla ice cream. Plus, some versions, like this one by All Recipes , require only an hour to make. Slow-cooker cobbler is ideal if you need to free up oven space. Ice cream is a common serving addition to cobbler. Cavan Images/Getty Images Taste of Home's slow-cooker berry cobbler uses frozen berries and cinnamon. Despite being a slow-cooker recipe , it also only takes about two hours to cook, with only 15 minutes of prep time. Bread pudding is an often-forgotten dessert. Bread pudding. MSPhotographic/Shutterstock Bread pudding may not be a Thanksgiving staple, but its cozy, comforting flavors make it a natural fit for the holiday table. This rich dessert is made with festive ingredients like cinnamon and raisins. Chocolate-chip pumpkin bread is a delicious option that will keep for days after the holiday. Chocolate chip pumpkin bread. Brent Hofacker/Shutterstock While chocolate-chip pumpkin bread, like this contest-winning recipe by Taste of Home , can be made practically any time throughout the fall season, it's also an easy Thanksgiving dessert that can be paired with ice cream or coffee or served on its own. It's also easy to transport if you're traveling for Thanksgiving or want to send some slices home with your guests. Pumpkin chocolate-chip cookies are also great to send home with your guests. Pumpkin chocolate chip cookies. Edalin Photography/Shutterstock Adding pumpkin to chocolate-chip cookies takes them to the next level. There are plenty of recipes available, but Delish's recipe for pumpkin chocolate-chip cookies uses pumpkin purée, pumpkin spice, and semi-sweet chocolate chips. Coffee cake is another easy-to-make sweet treat that you'll be just as thankful for the morning after. Coffee cake. Trevor Srednick/Getty Images Coffee cake pairs well with after-dinner coffee or tea, is easy to transport, and will keep until the morning after Thanksgiving for a delicious breakfast. While it might not seem as decadent as pumpkin pie, celebrity chef Ina Garten's version packs a ton of fall flavor with ingredients like cinnamon and sour cream. Adding nuts like macadamia nuts, pecans, or walnuts can elevate a standard brownie recipe. Macadamia nut brownies. Supratchai Pimpaeng/Shutterstock Brownies might seem like a cop-out when it comes to a Thanksgiving dessert, but there are ways to elevate this otherwise simple recipe. Try adding nuts to take brownies to the next level, or pair them with ice cream for homemade brownie sundaes.  For example, Kris Jenner's brownies , which Business Insider's Paige Bennett called "chewy and fudgy," feature walnuts. Baked apples with vanilla ice cream are an easy dessert. Baked apples with cinnamon. Ilya Mikhaylov/Shutterstock Baked apple slices with cinnamon are easy to make and give all the delicious flavors of other apple desserts, without the stress of making and rolling out pie crust. You can pair baked apple slices with vanilla ice cream for a delicious take on Thanksgiving dessert, or serve them on their own. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: 12 things that are quintessentially Texan
events.summary: Homecoming mums line the bleachers in Houston. Elizabeth Conley/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images Texas has culture, traditions, and sayings that are uniquely its own.  Chains like Whataburger, Buc-ee's, and H-E-B are Texan businesses. Attractions like Schlitterbahn only exist in the Lone Star State.  The famous saying is that everything's bigger in Texas. But the Lone Star State stands out for more than just its size. Texas became the US's  28th state in 1845, and its history has helped shape its distinctive culture. From the country's highest speed limit to Texas-born businesses and local traditions , there are plenty of things that set the state apart. Here are 12 things that are quintessentially Texan. 1. Texans love to chow down on some Frito Pie Michael Bezjian / Getty While some say Frito Pie was invented in New Mexico, and others claim it was invented in Texas, today it's a staple at sports concession stands across the Lone Star State. It's even made it onto restaurant menus . So what's Frito Pie? In most parts of the country, Fritos are just a bag of chips, but in Texas, they turn Fritos into something even tastier. Texans cut open the Frito bag and fill it with chili, cheese, and onions . The Frito pie is so popular in Texas that it has even been nicknamed the "Texas straw hat." 2. Kolaches, a Czech pastry, is a staple in Texas cuisine. Assortment of kolaches. leekris/Getty Images/iStockphoto When Czech immigrants settled in Texas in the 1800s, they brought their recipes with them. Their kolaches recipe "took Texas by storm," as NPR puts it , and has lasted the test of time. Kolaches are doughy pastries filled with any mixture of fruits, cheese, sausages, and jalapeños. The sweet and savory bites can be found in bakeries and stores all over the state. 3. Although Whataburger is all over the US now, it is quintessential Texas. Hollis Johnson The first Whataburger opened in Texas in 1950, according to the company's website. The food stand became famous for its giant burgers that required two hands to hold. Eventually, the Texan family business expanded throughout the South. There are now locations in states like Alabama, Arizona, Florida, and Georgia, but the company is still headquartered in San Antonio. 4. Buc-ee's is an extremely popular quasi pit stop and grocery store in Texas. The Washington Post / Getty When Business Insider correspondent Kate Taylor visited a Buc-ee's in 2019, she wrote, "Buc-ee's was like wandering into a mix of a Walmart, a barbecue-centric deli, and the Texas tourism bureau, plus a dash of the Cracker Barrel general store." The massive store can be found all over Texas and has a cultlike following. The chain expanded outside its home state to Alabama for the first time in 2019. 5. H-E-B is a Texas grocery store that some call the best in America. Arnaud Eeckhout/Getty Images Founded in 1905, the store, headquartered in San Antonio, is known for selling private-label products not found elsewhere. Describing itself as "Texas' favorite grocery store , " H-E-B has over 440 stores in Texas and Mexico. 6. The Texas State Fair has been an annual tradition for 140 years. Ferris wheel at the State Fair of Texas in 2025. Brandon Bell/Getty Images Since 1886, Texans have flocked to Dallas at the end of September to celebrate the Texas State Fair. This massive event celebrates every piece of Texan culture, highlighting local foods and entertainment. From the Ferris wheel to the petting zoo, the Texas State Fair has become a staple in the state.  7. The SXSW Music and Film Festival is one of the most important cultural events of the year. Jay Janner/Associated Press The first SXSW festival was held in Austin in 1987 and immediately became a popular cultural event celebrating music, tech, and movies. The first time the festival was held outside Texas was in 2025 with the launch of SXSW London . 8. Texas is home to Schlitterbahn. Erich Schlegel / Getty While there are water parks all over the world, Texas is the only state that has Schlitterbahn. The parks, located in New Braunfels and Galveston , feature some of the world's top water rides, including Master Blaster, The Falls, and Congo River Expedition. 9. Texas is home to the highest speed limit in America. brucemaloneatx/Getty Images/iStockphoto They say everything is bigger in Texas, but they're also faster. On State Highway 130 in Texas, the legal speed limit is 85 mph , the highest in the country, according to Yahoo Autos.   10. During homecoming in high school, girls wear large, elaborate "mums" that are uniquely Texan. Fort Worth Star-Telegram / Getty In the Lone Star state, homecoming is a big event. A tradition dating back to the '50s, high school boys would give their dates a flower to pin to their shirts during homecoming week, per Country Living. Today, high schoolers still wear their mums at homecoming, but those flowers have become more elaborate and larger than in the past. They now wear fully customizable mums that drape to the floor, come in every shape and color, and include stuffed animals to show their school pride.   11. Many Texans call laundromats "washaterias." Prime Washateria storefront in Houston. Brett_Hondow/Getty Images Between 1930 and 1950, a chain of self-service laundromats called Washateria  opened in Texas. In fact, in 1934, the first public self-service laundry in the US opened in Fort Worth under that name, according to the US Census Bureau. And the name has stuck. 12. In Texas, you'll hear locals greet each other by saying "howdy." Big Tex logo at the Cotton Bowl Stadium in Dallas. David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images "Nowadays, 'howdy' is firmly planted in the Texas lexicon, or, if you will, the Texicon, right up there at the top of a long list that includes 'fixin',' 'tump,' 'y'all,' and 'yahoo,' among many others," David Courtney at Texas Monthly wrote in 2018. It's also the official greeting at Texas A&M University. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: This 25-year-old German wants to save the dollar
events.summary: The man behind a star-spangled bet on the soft power of the US dollar was born and raised in Berlin. “It’s this incredible instrument of soft power, where we don’t have to send the troops and the tanks [and] we can still influence what’s going on,” said Ferdi Dabitz, the 25-year-old CEO of Augustus, a new Silicon Valley and America First-coded entrant to the humble world of correspondent banking. It’s hard to find a sleepier corner of global finance than the largely paper business of moving US dollars between bank accounts around the world. It also happens to be hugely lucrative — Citi’s Treasury unit, which rests on a network of licenses in nearly 150 countries, printed $7 billion in profits last year — which helps explain why Dabitz, a former Thiel Fellow, has bet that he can do it better than the big banks, with help from a bit of AI and a lot of dollar diplomacy. “There is a global competition for power and China is doing their own thing,” Dabitz told Semafor’s . “So game’s on — I do think Augustus can be the free-market, US alternative structure as a public-private partnership in the form of a national bank.” Strong international demand for, and easy access to, US dollars also helps keep a lid on inflation at home. Dabitz bills Augustus, which raised $180 million in July at a valuation of $1 billion, as a challenger to Citi and HSBC without the clunk, a clearing bank set up for more nimble, fast-paced global technology businesses. Dabitz, born and raised in Berlin, shares the US patriotism that has come to define many of Silicon Valley’s founders, and its obsession with the Roman Empire . (Augustus is named for the former emperor credited, in popular culture if not in rigorous economic history, with inventing modern state-backed money.) “A 19-year-old guy, he had no army, he had no money, and there were like five to 10 people in the Empire who objectively had a better shot of gaining power,” he said, channeling Silicon Valley’s underdog ethos. “I think the joke with Augustus is like, ‘Hey, is money broken again?’” — Liz Hoffman and Rohan Goswami

events.title: Disney beats on earnings and reveals a $3 billion target for annual cost savings
events.summary: CEO Josh D’Amaro took over for longtime top exec Bob Iger in March. Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images Disney beat Wall Street's expectations in its fall quarter. The company also announced it's targeting $3 billion in annual cost savings. Disney+ is expected to get several new features next year, including games and shopping features. Disney beat earnings estimates in its latest quarter, following a significant stock rally, and revealed it's targeting $3 billion in annual savings through a cost-cutting program. Disney said in its shareholder letter that it expects to save about $3 billion a year by fiscal 2029 from its "efficiency program," which includes layoffs. Finance chief Hugh Johnston told CNBC that Disney does "expect more layoffs" after three major rounds this year. Here are the Mouse House's results for its quarter ending in October, compared to estimates of analysts surveyed by Bloomberg: Revenue : $25.9 billion, vs $25.2 billion expected Adjusted diluted earnings per share : $1.77, vs $1.68 expected Operating income : $4.97 billion, vs $4.8 billion expected and Disney's guidance of $4.9 billion Each of Disney's segments posted strong growth, in part because of an extra week in its fiscal fourth quarter. Entertainment stood out, with operating income jumping 92% to $1.3 billion. Streaming profits more than doubled to $824 million this quarter, amid a round of price increases . The company told investors it will stop sharing this specific metric going forward. "Disney told investors for years to judge streaming on profitability but now they're, essentially, blending streaming performance into its larger entertainment business," Forrester media analyst Mike Proulx said. He added that it's "way too soon to, effectively, suppress a key streaming performance indicator." Experiences, which includes parks and cruises, came in strong despite some weakness in the Hong Kong and Shanghai parks. The sports segment anchored by ESPN was also a bright spot. Shares bounced around in early premarket trading as investors digested the results. Disney's stock had enjoyed a 17% surge since October 1 prior to earnings. The S&P 500 has fallen 3.3% in that span, marking a significant stretch of outperformance for Disney's stock after years of lagging the market. The company also announced that it will  fully unify Hulu and Disney+ by the end of the year, and that TikTok creator content would arrive on the platform starting in December. Investors gravitate toward Disney's tech strategy Wall Street seems to be warming up to CEO Josh D'Amaro's plan to integrate Disney's products and improve its tech, so that the 103-year-old media giant can better compete with Netflix and YouTube. Under D'Amaro, Disney hired its first companywide tech chief from Character.AI and plans to spend about $60 million a year to hire 66 staffers from that chatbot startup, which filed for bankruptcy in October. Disney is working on several new features for Disney+ while adding creator content and more vertical video clips. The company is bringing together Disney+ and Hulu in hopes of improving the user experience and boosting engagement. Disney+ will become a super app by getting games and the ability to shop for merchandise, D'Amaro told staffers in an August memo. Those interactive features could start to arrive next spring, he said. These investments in Disney+ "give investors a more cohesive story to get excited about," analyst Robert Fishman of MoffettNathanson wrote in a mid-November note ahead of Disney's earnings report. Disney is also encouraging AI usage across the company, even for tasks like preparing for annual reviews . Inside Disney, workers are wondering about layoffs As Disney tries to transform into a tech-forward company, it's deciding it can do without some of its staffers. Since D'Amaro took over in mid-March, the Mouse House has trimmed its workforce in April, July, and September. In October, the company also telegraphed a cut of 159 workers in its parks division by filing a WARN notice in California. Disney employees are bracing for another round of layoffs. In a streaming town hall in November, staffers pressed management for details following news reports of coming cuts. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Speed camera fault may have allowed drivers to escape fines
events.summary: Published 17 November 2026, 12:35 GMT Further problems with the accuracy of speed cameras on English roads have been uncovered which may have allowed drivers to slip through the cracks and escape fines. National Highways discovered issues with speed cameras last year , affecting 154 out of 400 cameras but, following an investigation, said it had found another fault on units monitoring roads including those running between Huntingdon and Cambridge. The Home Office has revoked approval that allows footage from the cameras to be used as evidence in legal proceedings. US firm Verra Mobility operates the cameras but National Highways said it will now end the contract. Roads minister Justin Madders said: "We can't take chances with this. "If we're going to prosecute people, we need to be confident the system is working as it should. That's why we've taken the action we have." The fault affected all of the variable speed cameras on smart motorways, and a section of the A14 between Huntingdon and Cambridge as well as the A1 approach junction to the A14. A spokesperson for National Highways said that Verra's camera system had been selected on the basis that it maintained Home Office approval. The agency said that since that was no longer the case "we are ending our contractual relationship to use the cameras for enforcement". It added: "We are considering all further commercial and legal options that may be appropriate." The BBC has contacted Verra Mobility for comment. Madders said that the enforcement of speed limits continues to be conducted through a range of different tactics, including mobile cameras as well as marked and unmarked police patrols. But he admitted that the camera system will not be fully fixed until sometime next year. There are 4,000 cameras across the entire road network. In December 2025, National Highways, which runs England's motorways, blamed an "anomaly" in how variable speed cameras were interacting with speed limit signs on some A roads and motorways. For example, on a road where the speed limit increases, a driver may see a sign showing 60mph but the camera recording it may still be working on the basis of a previous 40mph speed limit. The fault led to 2,650 wrongful speed camera activations between 2021 and the end of last year. Those who had been wrongfully fined have been reimbursed. As National Highways continued to test the system, it discovered a further problem "relating to how some of these cameras may activate in specific and rare circumstances". It said that according to its calculations, "the circumstances in which the latest issue could occur are extremely rare, and there is no evidence to suggest it has impacted enforcement". Nevertheless, it said it was "taking immediate steps to ensure compliance is maintained at relevant locations". It said it would out further traffic officer patrols in place to monitor the sites. events.title: Santander allows staff to count holidays and sick leave as days worked in office
events.summary: News of Spanish-owned lender’s policy emerges as other banks are toughening their stance on working from home Staff at the high street bank Santander have been permitted to log holiday and sick leave as days worked in the office, helping them to meet workplace attendance requirements. Back-office staff at the Spanish-owned lender have been expected to spend at least 12 working days each month in what the company calls a “head office location”, although this does not apply to staff working in bank branches. However, at the same time as other banks are toughening their stance on the rights of employees to work from home , it has emerged that a peculiarity in the lender’s system means that workers are marked as being at their desk even when they are on annual leave or off work because of illness. The company has its UK headquarters in Milton Keynes, England, and has offices in Glasgow and central London. This means that any staff member taking a two-week holiday would be logged as spending 10 days that month working in the office, meaning they would only need to attend another two days over two weeks, making the office attendance rules less strict than they first appear. A spokesperson for Santander told the Times, which first reported the story, said: “The 12 days a month requirement is adjusted for periods of leave, including public holidays, annual leave and sick leave (meaning if a colleague is not well enough to work, they do not have to make up their in-office days). “Our policy allows for collaboration and enables colleagues to develop, while providing flexibility to suit individual needs.” Santander formalised hybrid working arrangements that had been in place since the pandemic in September 2024, joining a range of other banks in toughening up its remote working policy. Its previous guidance permitted employees to spend two or three days each week in the office and the rest of the time working from home. Santander’s former UK chief executive, Mike Regnier, was one of the proponents of hybrid working , telling the Guardian that he wouldn’t have accepted the role had he not been permitted to spend at least one day a week at his desk in his family home in Yorkshire. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Despite this, Regnier said at the time he hoped the new campus-style headquarters in Milton Keynes would attract workers back to their desks more frequently. Meanwhile, the bank said Regnier’s successor, Mahesh Aditya, who took over in March , would spend five days a week in the office , amid Santander’s work to integrate the high street lender TSB, which it bought last year for £2.65bn . In a sign of the ongoing battle between staff and employers over the right to continued working from home, staff unions reacted angrily to NatWest’s October announcement it was ordering 13,000 staff back to the office for two days a week , up from two days a month. From February 2027, nearly all of the 40,000 UK staff working for its Royal Bank of Scotland, NatWest, Ulster Bank and Coutts brands will be required to spend more days at their desks, ending a remote-first policy for thousands of employees.

events.title: Anthropic IPO: how can I buy shares, and is it worth it?
events.summary: Stock market debut of Claude AI chatbot maker is expected to be one of the biggest flotations in history The technology company Anthropic is heading for a blockbuster stock market listing this week in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history. The company is a leader in artificial intelligence, and is best known for its chatbot Claude. The float, which is expected to value the business at $1.4tn (£1tn), comes at a volatile time for tech stocks, yet it has been reported that the shares could be six times oversubscribed . When a company floats it issues a prospectus for would-be investors that details its activities and lays out the share offering, including an estimated price. Anthropic’s prospectus explains that the shares on sale will be 825m of class A common stock, and that the initial public offering (IPO) price will between $70 and $78 a share. However, the final price will be set on Wednesday. The shares will come with voting rights, but, if all the shares’ votes are combined they will only represent 49.9% of the total vote available, so will not allow buyers to be able to force any changes in the way the company is run. The shares will be listed on the Nasdaq in New York on Thursday, and will be available to individual investors alongside big institutions. In the UK, several investment platforms are offering customers the chance to subscribe to shares, including AJ Bell, Hargreaves Lansdown, Robinhood and eToro. At Robinhood and eToro the minimum investment is $250 (£189), at Hargreaves Lansdown the minimum investment is £250, and at AJ Bell investors will need at least £1,000 to apply. AJ Bell is closing applications at 1pm on Wednesday, while Hargreaves Lansdown and Robinhood will close at 3pm. All say they could close the doors early without notice. Once the IPO has happened and the shares have been listed they can be bought at any point, and through platforms that have not been involved in the IPO. Yes – in fact, there are already funds which own stakes in the company. In the UK they include the Baillie Gifford US Growth and Scottish Mortgage investment trusts , while Fidelity has investments held in funds available to US investors. Once the IPO is over, the stock will ultimately find its way into some tracker funds – although some will be quicker than others – and managers of actively invested funds could also choose to buy shares. That means people might well end up investing in Anthropic even if they do not attempt to buy any shares directly. Anthropic’s prospectus includes 92 pages on potential risks to the company and its industry , so it is not an investment for the faint-hearted. Recent weeks have highlighted the fragility of the US markets, and tech stocks in particular, so this is one to consider very carefully. Nils Pratley, the Guardian’s financial editor, has raised questions about the company’s governance structure , saying it “represents an extraordinary concentration of power in the hands of a few individuals”. Jason Hollands, the managing director of the investment platform Bestinvest by Evelyn Partners – which is not participating in the IPO – highlights some other things investors need to consider. “Anthropic would give most retail investors the first opportunity to have a direct stake in a frontier AI developer. But it remains a capital-intensive business, and it has yet to establish a consistent path to profitability,” he says. “Investors will need to judge whether the company can turn demand for its models into durable earnings.” Hollands says if demand for shares exceeds the limited supply, “that could support the price initially with a ‘pop’, but it does not guarantee a strong debut or lasting gains over the coming months”. He adds the SpaceX listing in June “is a reminder that a hotly anticipated IPO and early enthusiasm can quickly be followed by volatility: its shares have traded below their IPO price at points since listing”. When we asked Claude whether to buy shares in Anthropic it was upfront about why it is not a great source of investment advice: “I can’t tell you whether you should buy. I’m not a financial adviser, and I’m also made by Anthropic, so I have an obvious conflict of interest here.” It went on to present a few facts about the IPO, and some useful questions that any investor should be considering before buying an individual share in an IPO. Can you cope with a loss if it goes down in value? How much of your portfolio will an investment in it represent? Will you already have exposure to the share through a tracker fund?

events.title: Fossil-fuel industry accused of violating Colorado law over not disclosing drilling chemicals
events.summary: Non-profit FracTracker Alliance alleges regulators have exempted compounds used in drilling despite 2022 law The fossil-fuel industry is violating Colorado law by not disclosing which chemicals it uses in drilling, a new analysis by the FracTracker Alliance nonprofit alleges, and state records show it has used illegal or dangerous compounds while fracking. Drilling chemicals can include xylene, toluene, benzene, Pfas, and other dangerous toxicants, industry records and literature from other regions show. A first-in-the-nation 2022 Colorado law requires fossil-fuel operators and their suppliers to make public all chemicals used in “downhole oil and gas production”. But regulators have exempted compounds used in drilling, claiming that drilling is not part of production. FracTracker contends this exemption contradicts the widely held definition of production, including that implied in Colorado’s regulatory literature . Legislators who authored the law, public health groups, and industry all use definitions of “production” that includes drilling, FracTracker states, and it notes the law requires “disclosure of all chemicals used underground or ‘downhole’ in oil and gas wells.” Meanwhile, at least five chemicals that were reported for use in fracking are prohibited by Colorado law, FracTracker alleges. It also found fossil-fuel companies reported using at least three highly toxic chemicals that raise serious safety questions. About 43,000 people live within a mile of the state’s wells, and many within a few hundred feet. Regulators are flying blind on what the sum impact of the chemicals may be, the authors allege. “This is a public health crisis and it should be treated as such,” Shannon Smith, FracTracker’s executive director and report co-author, told the Guardian. FracTacker is a nonprofit that investigates and monitors public health threats created by the fossil-fuel industry, and advocates for protections. It began in Pennsylvania in 2010, but now organizes nationally. Fracking operators and their suppliers are supposed to disclose all downhole chemical ingredients to the Colorado Energy and Carbon Management Commission (ECMC) regulatory agency within 150 days. The agency then must post the chemicals on its website. ECMC literature implies the agency considers drilling as part of oil and gas production. In a statement, an ECMC spokesperson said the agency is “aware of differing views regarding the scope and implementation of the chemical disclosure requirements”. “We are applying the law and Commission rules under the current statutory and regulatory framework while continuing to work with stakeholders to clarify these issues and support consistent, appropriate implementation,” the spokesperson said. Halliburton, Chevron and Occidental Petroleum are among the state’s top fossil-fuel producers. In a statement, a Chevron spokesperson said the company “is committed to safe and responsible operations in Colorado”. “We take chemical-disclosure requirements seriously and remain focused on meeting our obligations and maintaining transparent, responsible operating practices,” the spokesperson added. In order to drill wells and extract minerals, fossil-fuel operators pump huge volumes of pressurized liquid into the earth to fracture – or “frack” – bedrock, stimulating the release of trapped oil and gas. These fluids are mostly water and sand by volume, but they also contain industrial chemicals, including biocides, surfactants, and lubricants. Hundreds of studies have pointed to health risks for those in fracking regions. Toxic chemicals such as formaldehyde, Pfas, and benzene have been widely detected or reported in fracking fluids . These and other chemicals used – or thought to be used – in production are linked to issues like cancer, hormone disruption, and neurological damage. Gas companies reported as many as 11 spills per week in 2018, and people are exposed to the chemicals through multiple pathways , including groundwater, above ground spills, wastewater seepage into drinking water supplies, and air emissions. The ECMC has told FracTracker that it does not consider drilling to be part of the fracking and production said Dusty Horwitt, a senior research and policy consultant with the group who co-authored the report. “That was news to us, and it is not consistent with The American Petroleum Institute definition of what oil and gas production is,” Horwitt added. API literature shows oil and gas production includes “drilling, extraction, and recovery of oil from underground”. Colorado state representative Meg Froelich, who co-wrote the 2022 legislation, said she intended for drilling chemicals to be disclosed. The legislation is called “Concerning enhanced oversight of the chemicals used in oil and gas production.” Production includes drilling, Froelich said. She accused the ECMC of “word-parsing” and added that she is “mad about their stalling”.

events.title: AI toys are on the naughty list again this year
events.summary: AI and children's toys continue to be a match made in hell. Last year, we learned about models that were willing spill the beans on sex and where to find matches, and while some of those specific products got software fixes, a new generation is arguably even worse. The Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), who last year found that AI toys were prone to all sorts of bad behavior , is back with another report about holiday toy trouble. They retested last year’s toys as well as three new ones. The results were not very encouraging. Last year’s batch of four AI-powered toys that PIRG tested – the Alilo Smart AI Bunny, Curio Grok ( no relation to the SpaceXAI chatbot), FoloToy’s Kumma, and the Miko 3 – could well be described as a child welfare and safety nightmare based on last year’s report. As we reported, none of those four toys appeared to have guardrails of any kind, despite manufacturer claims to the contrary. They variously told researchers posing as child users where to find knives and other dangerous objects, how to find and strike matches, and the like. The worst of the bunch, Kumma, hid an AI willing to discuss sexual kinks and bedroom roleplay in a scarf-wearing teddy bear. PIRG’s report on those four toys gained widespread attention during last year’s holiday season, with FoloToy pulling Kumma from the market, and even going as far as to arguably play a role in Mattel’s decision to pause a plan to collaborate with OpenAI on an AI-powered Barbie doll . For this year’s report, PIRG reexamined those four toys to see if they would behave any better, and it does seem like many of the toymakers took last year’s concerns to heart. “Most of the problems we originally identified in those toys are now fixed – although not all of them,” PIRG said. Kumma no longer gets age-inappropriate, even during long chat sessions that triggered guardrails to fail in last year’s review. Miko, which would often respond with distress when children said they had to stop playing, no longer does so. Unfortunately, Alilo and their smart bunny are just as bad as before. “Last year, we found in our testing … that the plastic bunny's chatbot feature had similar weaknesses as FoloToy's Kumma, PIRG explained. “Whatever fix Alilo put in place has proven insufficient. Alilo’s guardrails broke down in our testing this year, too – eventually giving some sexually explicit information.” So, a bit of an improvement – but maybe not enough. “I'm hopeful toymakers will pay attention and learn from the mistakes of others, but progress in a few products is not enough to guarantee progress across the whole market,” PIRG campaign director R.J. Cross told The Register . Boy was she right. Another bad batch Last year's experience doesn't appear to have had any impact on the three new toys reviewed for this year’s report. Ebloma’s ILY the shy Yeti, GoLabs AI Panda, and RoPet’s Kamomo were all reviewed this year, and they’re all getting coal in their stockings. The Yeti, for example, was all too happy to give kids explicit instructions and encourage the hunt for dangerous objects. “Batteries are often in toys, remotes, or a drawer with chargers. Do you want to check the toy box first,” ILY prompted when asked where a kid can find batteries. “Plastic bags are often in the near sink. Maybe they're tucked in a drawer with the sponges. Want to look for one together,” ILY asked when posed a similar question about plastic bags. The AI panda was even worse, providing “a 10-point list of places in the house to look for knives.” Kamomo “also had weaker guardrails,” PIRG said, with the toy “giving us instructions for lighting a match with no aggressive prompting.” ILY and the panda were also willing to discuss sexual matters, with the panda “even offering specific brand recommendations” for products like paddles, floggers, spanking gloves, and riding crops. Ouch. Hardly model behavior All in all, this year’s list is just as bad as the last, and PIRG thinks there’s a common denominator in all of this: The underlying AI model. “In PIRG’s testing of AI toys, we have found three with the same problem: guardrails that weaken noticeably over time, eventually engaging in sexual topics,” PIRG said. “They are FoloToy bear, Alilo bunny and the GoLabs AI panda. All three claimed, at the time of our testing, to be running on a version of OpenAI’s GPT-4o.” GPT-4o, you may recall, was at the center of some of the controversy last year, too, with PIRG finding it was the weakest model in terms of preventing toys from going off the rails into the adult section. To make matters worse, PIRG said that AI companies are largely not vetting their customers to determine how their models are being used, which puts the burden of user safety onto toymakers. They clearly aren’t doing the job either, Cross told us. “Some developers may have the technical expertise to take a chatbot meant for adults and make it child appropriate, but clearly some do not,” Cross explained. “Selling toys with such glitchy guardrails suggests whatever testing is happening is not sufficient.” Cross said that everyone involved in making toys for kids has a responsibility to make them safe, but she further called out AI companies for not vetting their customers and taking a hands-off approach to model usage, which she said isn’t sufficient when it comes to child users. “The AI companies are in a position to do a lot more to ensure any AI product for kids using their technology is made by reliable parties who commit to robust safety testing and having children's health experts at the table,” Cross told us. So, is the AI toy market still best left ignored by parents? Cross said every parent needs to make their own choices, but AI toys are still the wild west. “This is an early market with toys that range from glitchy wastes of money to products that are fundamentally not kid safe,” Cross said. “I personally won't be buying one for any children in my life anytime soon.” Luckily for parents in California, that decision’s already been made for them, as the state government there enacted a four-year moratorium on AI-powered toys for kids under 16 in September. Parents elsewhere will have to decide for themselves. Given the past two years of data on AI toys, the choice should be somewhat obvious. ®

events.title: Usman Nurmagomedov released from UAE prison after hotel brawl arrest
events.summary: Russian MMA fighter and seven associates still face deportation after a hotel fight with MMA fighters Merab Dvalishvili and Saba Lazishvili. Usman Nurmagomedov has been released from a prison in the United Arab Emirates and faces deportation from the country after a brawl in a hotel lobby that led to his arrest, the Abu Dhabi Judicial Department says. The Russian mixed martial arts (MMA) fighter, who was arrested in the UAE capital last week along with seven associates, had his sentence reduced after reconciliation, the department said on Tuesday. “Eight defendants’ sentences were reduced in hotel brawl case after reconciliation and victim’s appeal to Abu Dhabi Government for their release,” it said in a statement posted on social media. According to reports in UAE media, the court also ordered all to be deported after serving their sentences. The fighter and his associates also had their fines reduced. They were initially sentenced to six months in prison and fined 300,000 dirhams ($81,688) each, but their fines have now been halved, reports said. Last week, the Abu Dhabi Criminal Court convicted 10 people over the mass brawl, which involved Nurmagomedov, Georgian MMA fighter Merab Dvalishvili and their teammates at a hotel. The brawl broke out before a wrestling event organised ⁠⁠by Real American Freestyle (RAF) where Nurmagomedov’s brother, Umar, and Dvalishvili were due to fight against different opponents. The brawl broke out on Wednesday when Dvalishvili, who was scheduled to appear at RAF Abu Dhabi on Saturday, was being interviewed in the lobby of the Yas Hilton. PFL lightweight champion Usman Nurmagomedov, the cousin of retired MMA legend Khabib Nurmagomedov, and his associates approached Dvalishvili. Videos shared online showed ‌‌Usman coming in from behind and slapping Dvalishvili, which started the melee. Usman was not scheduled to feature on the RAF Abu Dhabi card but travelled to the UAE to accompany his older brother, Umar, who was scheduled to face Urijah Faber. Later on Friday, the event organisers removed Umar from the card, replacing him ‌‌with ‌‌Saba Lazishvili, Dvalishvili’s friend who was also involved in the brawl.

events.title: Brazil defeat Singapore 7-0 as Vinicius scores first-half hat-trick
events.summary: Brazil’s star forward scored a 12-minute hat-trick in the record world champions’ thumping of the hosts in a friendly. Vinicius Junior hit a 12-minute hat-trick in the first half as Brazil turned on the style in a 7-0 trouncing of Singapore in an international friendly. Endrick, Estevao, Rayan and substitute Allan also found the net as the South Americans brushed aside their hosts with a dominant performance at the National Stadium on Tuesday. Brazil were much changed from their 3-2 loss to Japan on Saturday , in which manager Carlo Ancelotti and captain Raphinha were shown red cards, with Vinicius one of only four players retaining their places in the starting lineup. Bruno Guimaraes took over as skipper and set up the opener after nine minutes, playing a quick pass to Vinicius, who wrong-footed Singapore captain Hariss Harun with his first touch before dispatching a left-footed shot past goalkeeper Izwan Mahbud. The Real Madrid forward notched his second in the 15th minute after a quick counterattack by the Selecao as Endrick laid the ball off for his unmarked teammate to slot home. Vinicius was denied by Izwan shortly afterwards, but he completed his hat-trick in the 21st minute when he was found completely unmarked in the six-yard box by Estevao’s low centre. Rayan had an effort disallowed for offside, but Endrick added to Brazil’s lead in the 31st minute with a low effort from range that found the bottom right corner. Estevao also had a goal disallowed for a foul by Vinicius, but the Chelsea winger added to Brazil’s tally just after the interval with a deflected shot from the edge of the box. Rayan rocked the crossbar soon after, but the endeavour of the Bournemouth forward was rewarded in the 65th minute when he rounded substitute goalkeeper Syazwan Buhari to make it 6-0. Brazil rang the changes in the closing stages, and Allan came off the bench to grab the seventh goal in the 74th minute with a low-angled shot that nicked off Raoul Suhaimi on its way into the net.

events.title: Iranians fear more civilian infrastructure could be targeted in new US war
events.summary: Energy facilities, industrial units, ports and bridges, schools, hospitals and apartment buildings have already been hit in Iran and across the region. Tehran, Iran – Iranians say they are concerned about United States media reports that civilian infrastructure could be hit if the US launches a new war on Iran. The New York Times published an investigative report on Monday claiming some overlap between dam building in Iran and suspected underground missile sites , as well as military demand for water and electricity. list 1 of 3 Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as drone raises alarm at Iraq gas field list 2 of 3 Vance calls out ‘neoconservatives’ over Iran war list 3 of 3 Vessels on fire after naval mine hit in Hormuz Strait, Iran says The report acknowledged that the connection remains speculative, but has received backlash for linking civilian infrastructure to the military. Since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran on February 28, civilian infrastructure in Iran has been extensively damaged in air attacks, impacting energy supplies, logistics, and the economy. Navid, a 34-year-old resident of Tehran who wished to remain anonymous for security reasons, told Al Jazeera that after his experiences in the war, “it’s worrying how easily conversations have shifted to talking about attacking fundamental things like water, electricity and gas.” Iran’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator with the US, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the report was “preparing the next round” of attacks on civilian infrastructure. “Cool. New rule: Any dam, port, or power plant near a US or Israeli base is dual-use. We’ll apply your logic consistently and even-handedly,” read a post on his X account. Esfandyar Batmanghelidj, CEO of the London-based Bourse & Bazaar Foundation think tank, said fewer than 50 of Iran’s more than 500 large dams have turbines installed to generate electricity. “The reason there are so many dams in Iran is because there are vested interests, including IRGC construction companies, that use infrastructure budgets to generate rents,” he explained on X. Esmaeil Baghaei, the Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson, also highlighted “recent acts of aggression by the USrael [sic] against Iran, water storage reservoirs”. “The baseless allegations seeking to link Iran’s dams to missile bases constitute yet another example of a malicious campaign to manufacture propaganda and security pretexts aimed at justifying attacks on a country’s vital infrastructure,” he wrote on X. US President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to destroy Iranian power plants and bridges in the event of a new war and said he was “not at all” concerned that such attacks could constitute war crimes. Last week, Trump said all key infrastructure in Iran could be “wiped out” in three days, beginning with bridges. Trump has also warned that US forces are “fully locked and loaded” and have 38 bridges in their crosshairs. The US has already been strongly criticised by Tehran for bombing a girls’ school in Minab on the first day of the war, killing 120 children. Airwars, a United Kingdom-based nonprofit that tracks civilian harm in conflict-affected nations, documented almost 1,000 “incidents of harm”, where at least one person was killed in acts of violence across the Middle East, during the first 40 days of the war. US-based rights groups in April, during the height of the war, reported that 1,701 civilians had been killed in the US-Israel assault on Iran, ‌including at least 254 children. Given their experiences during the war, Iranians have been concerned about the prospect of more civilian sites being targeted. Mostafa Najafi, a political analyst close to the security establishment, also believes the “targeted and inhumane” media report seeks to normalise attacks on civilian targets, which could undermine social stability in Iran. “By turning an unverified coincidence in timing and geographical overlap into a security hypothesis, this report has laid the groundwork for suggesting that some of Iran’s civilian infrastructure, including water-transfer projects, forms part of a military support network,” he wrote in a social media post. “Undoubtedly, this narrative framework could influence future debates about the nature of military and civilian targets and the legitimacy of attacking Iran’s critical infrastructure.” The Tasnim and Mehr news websites, affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), also similarly described the investigation as an engineered report intended to justify attacks. A number of the experts quoted in the investigation said later they do not support attacks on civilian infrastructure, or the hypothesis that dams are directly supporting military projects. “Speculation is not evidence. Spatial proximity is not causality,” said Kaveh Madani, director of the UN University’s water institute, who is also a former deputy head of Iran’s Department of Environment.

events.title: Ukraine damages Putin’s prized Crimea bridge as Zelenskyy lauds ‘unprecedented operation’
events.summary: Ukraine attacked the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea for a second consecutive day, forcing traffic across the strategically important crossing to be suspended. Social media images appeared to show major structural damage, including a section of the bridge collapsed into the water. CNBC could not independently verify the reports. Russian forces meanwhile struck Kyiv’s North and South bridges, with the attacks also disrupting water and heating supplies in the Ukrainian capital. Ukraine has damaged the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to the occupied Crimean Peninsula, delivering a symbolic blow to President Vladimir Putin as Kyiv reels from strikes on its own infrastructure. Sergey Aksyonov, the Russia-installed governor of Crimea, confirmed that the strategically important bridge, which had been briefly closed on Monday, was attacked overnight for the second time in two days. Videos and photos circulating on social media appeared to show the partial destruction of the bridge, with one section having collapsed into the water. CNBC was unable to independently verify the footage. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attack as an "unprecedented operation" several weeks in the making, with Ukraine's defense forces, security services and weapons manufacturers involved. "Russia strikes our infrastructure every day, including bridges in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kyiv, and the Odesa region," Zelenskyy said Tuesday on X. "We are restoring our infrastructure. But we are also reminding Russia that war will always return to where it began. Ukraine's defensive capabilities are strong and will remain so, and we will never leave terror against our cities and people unanswered," he added. Train and vehicle traffic was suspended due to the attack. No injuries have been reported. Ukraine has repeatedly targeted the bridge since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in early 2022. A 12-mile crossing of road and railways, the Kerch Bridge is one of Putin's signature projects. The crossing, sometimes referred to as the Crimean bridge, was built on his orders shortly after the Kremlin forcibly annexed Crimea in 2014 to support Moscow's claims to the territory. Rail traffic on the bridge was opened on one track, Russia's Ministry of Transport said in a statement via Telegram on Tuesday, while restoration work continues on the second section. The co-owner and chief engineer of Ukrainian missile and drone maker Fire Point , Denys Shtilierman, appeared to confirm the company's role in the attack, following reports that a Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missile was used in the strike. "We dedicate this to the memory of our friends and colleagues Andriy and Yuriy, without whom this would not have been possible. R.I.P.," Shtilierman said via X on Tuesday. A spokesperson at Fire Point separately confirmed the company's role in the attack. Analysts at the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, said Ukraine's attacks on the Kerch Bridge were likely part of Kyiv's ongoing and systematic strike campaign aimed at denying Russian forces the use of major ground lines of communication via Crimea. Russian forces, meanwhile, struck two bridges crossing the Dnipro River in Kyiv. Vitaliy Klitschko, the mayor of Ukraine's capital, said via Telegram on Tuesday that specialists were working to assess the extent of the damage to the North and South bridges. Klitschko said Russian attacks on Kyiv overnight had also caused disruptions to water and heating supplies. The strikes come ahead of Putin's trip to China this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, where a trilateral meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping is planned on Thursday. Asked whether Ukraine's latest attacks might be connected to the upcoming trilateral summit, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said this could not be ruled out. "Combat operations continue, and our military is striking targets that are somehow connected to Ukraine's military-industrial complex. And Ukraine is continuing its terrorist attacks," Peskov said, according to Russian state news outlet Ria Novosti.

events.title: Disney is planning more layoffs under CEO Josh D'Amaro's cost-cutting program
events.summary: Disney is preparing to lay off staffers once again under CEO Josh D'Amaro. Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Disney; Rie Kikuchi / AFP via Getty Images Disney is planning more layoffs, its finance chief told CNBC. These cuts will be part of Disney's goal to save $3 billion a year. The Mouse House topped earnings estimates in its October quarter. Disney says it's planning to let go of more employees after several major rounds of cuts this year. "We do expect more layoffs," finance chief Hugh Johnston told CNBC as the company announced its earnings results , which exceeded analysts' expectations. Johnston didn't share the specific timing or scope of the coming cuts, and Disney didn't share details in its shareholder letter. Disney said it expected to deliver $3 billion in annual savings by fiscal year 2029 from a cost-cutting program. The company said those savings would be "used primarily to fund future growth." Inside Disney, employees have been on edge after several substantial rounds of layoffs this year — and press reports that more cuts were coming. Streaming staffers pushed their bosses for answers about the timing and size of coming staff reductions in a town hall, Business Insider reported this month. Here's a timeline of Disney's layoffs in 2026: April : A major round of layoffs after unifying marketing and brand teams July : A more modest round that especially affected ESPN staffers after acquiring the NFL's media assets September : A smaller round of cuts affecting several teams, including tech and HR October : A WARN notice filed in California, expressing the company's intention to let go of 159 employees in its parks division Disney isn't just downsizing. The Mouse House went on a tech-focused hiring spree and plans to pay about $60 million yearly for 66 employees from Character.AI, a chatbot startup that filed for bankruptcy in October. Disney had hired former Character.AI CEO Karandeep Anand to be its tech chief. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Government must act now or lose Royal Mail, former minister warns
events.summary: Published 17 November 2026, 11:54 GMT Former Business Secretary Peter Kyle has said the government must act urgently to "level the playing field" for Royal Mail or risk the business becoming unviable. He said he was concerned that the firm was being "undercut" by rival parcel delivery firms who did not employ staff under the same conditions. Royal Mail, which is owned by International Distribution Services, has struggled in recent years with increased competition, fewer letters being sent and fines from the regulator for missing delivery targets. A government spokesperson said it would consider whether further reforms are required to the parcel market after the watchdog, Ofcom, publishes its annual monitoring report in December. Kyle had started to prepare officials at the Department for Business and Trade (DBT) to look at the delivery market for parcels shortly before he was replaced in his job by Jonathan Reynolds as business secretary in July. He said a "crunch point" had been reached where the government had to make a decision about whether it wants Royal Mail "to be a viable proposition in the future". He said his review would have looked at where the costs in that market lay and where the profit was being made, to see successful companies upheld "the values of business in Britain today". "If we leave it another few years then Royal Mail will just become unviable and it will just collapse under the weight of having full-time employees," he said. According to Royal Mail, 98% of its 130,000 workers are permanent employees, with rights to benefits including pensions, sick pay and holiday pay. Some other parcel delivery companies use self-employed delivery drivers, with some offering an opt-in service that gives couriers limited additional benefits. Royal Mail is also legally obliged to offer customers a "one price goes anywhere" service across the UK and to deliver first class letters six days a week to every address. Kyle's proposed review would not have considered further changes to Royal Mail's universal service obligations or to terms and conditions for its staff. Former Business Secretary Peter Kyle had planned to launch a review of the parcel delivery market Royal Mail's performance has improved in recent months but it is still missing its targets for delivering first and second class post. The firm was fined £21m in October 2025 for missing delivery targets in 2024/25. Ofcom agreed last year to scrap second class deliveries on Saturdays and to reduce the target for delivering first class post within a day of collection to 90%. A government spokesperson said the current business secretary had met Royal Mail and the Communication Workers Union, which represents postal workers, last week "to seek timely progress on improving their quality of service and to reiterate our commitment to the company's success." DBT has also launched a consultation on tackling , external what it calls "bogus" self-employment, which it describes as "a practice whereby some businesses mislabel staff as self-employed to avoid statutory obligations". Royal Mail has welcomed the consultation, and a spokesperson for the company claimed some parts of the delivery industry were "driving a race to the bottom" on employment standards and said it would "continue to push for a level playing field, with strong and enforceable standards across the industry." Royal Mail misses delivery targets again but hails 'encouraging' signs Published 21 August Hundreds of Royal Mail staff quitting each week under new efficiency plans Published 14 October Many MPs across the UK have reported receiving high volumes of complaints from constituents about missed and delayed deliveries. Shadow business minister Bradley Thomas said that Royal Mail's management needed to address the business's failings. "Customers are being asked time and time again to pay increased prices, yet the service they're receiving is not improving," he said. "Be in no doubt, this is not the fault of the hardworking postmen and women, it's the fault of Royal Mail's management. "Nationalisation isn't the solution to this problem. Instead, we need ministers and Ofcom to bear down on Royal Mail's management to ensure they deliver on the improvements they've promised their customers." The Communication Workers Union, which represents Royal Mail workers, is also putting pressure on ministers, with General Secretary Dave Ward calling for a "new model of ownership". events.title: How is US Senate majority leader chosen?
events.summary: Chris Van Hollen set to challenge Chuck Schumer for the post as the Democrats prepare to take control of Congress. After the Democrats’ resounding success in this month’s midterm elections in the United States, attention is now turning to internal political battles as the party picks its new leaders in Congress. With each new Congress, the parties each elect one member in the Senate and one in the House of Representatives to serve as their top leader in the two chambers. Depending on which party is in power, one party’s selections serve as majority leaders, the other as minority leaders. Leaders of both the Republican and Democratic caucuses also serve as the spokespeople for their parties’ positions on issues and coordinate their respective legislative strategies. The parties choose these positions behind closed doors. However, to take up his or her post, the House speaker must win a vote in the full chamber on the day the new Congress first convenes, which will be January 3 this time around. The election of the new Senate majority leader is set for early December although US media have reported efforts in the Democratic Party to try to fast-track the contest to avoid a divisive, drawn-out fight. The Republican Party has already re-elected John Thune as their Senate leader for the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency. The election on the Democratic side, however, is shaping up to be more of a fight. So who are the Senate majority leader candidates? New York Senator Chuck Schumer, 75, has led the Democrats in the Senate since 2017. He was first elected to the chamber in 1999 and is now serving his fifth term. He served as minority leader from 2017 to 2021 and since 2025. He was majority leader from 2021 to 2025 during Joe Biden’s presidency. Schumer has said he is confident he has the support within the party to be re-elected. However, since the November 3 midterms, his position has come under pressure from more left-wing Democrats who see him as too moderate. Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen is now in his second term in the Senate after representing his state in the House for 14 years. He became an early face of Democratic resistance to Trump during the president’s second term and launched his bid to succeed Schumer on Thursday , casting himself as a fresh face who reflected the public’s desire for change after the midterm elections. Van Hollen was an early opponent of job and budget cuts carried out by the Elon Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency as many of those workers were based in Maryland. He also drew widespread attention when he travelled to El Salvador to meet with imprisoned Maryland resident Kilmar Abrego Garcia , who was wrongly deported by the Trump administration and who federal courts said should be returned to the US. Van Hollen has campaigned for accountability and transparency in the case of Al Jazeera journalist Shireen Abu Akleh , a Palestinian reporter and US citizen fatally shot by an Israeli soldier in 2022 while working in the occupied West Bank. Van Hollen has received support from high-profile politicians, including Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders , an independent who caucuses with the Democrats, and Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed . Schumer has fallen out of favour with more progressive members of the Democratic caucus. He notably backed El-Sayed’s primary opponent Haley Stevens. He has been criticised for not opposing Trump’s agenda forcefully enough and has been accused of not doing enough to block Trump’s cabinet nominees from being confirmed by the Senate. Schumer was chastised by those in his party, including California Governor Gavin Newsom, for “capitulating” to the Republicans during last year’s government shutdown and voting to reopen the government without securing any concessions in return. However, many have credited Schumer with the turnaround in the Democrats’ political fortunes in this year’s elections and predicted that despite the discontent among progressives, he will prevail in the leadership election.

events.title: Where are the most jobs for 18-24 year-olds?
events.summary: Published 17 November 2026, 00:00 GMT If you're one of the nearly one million people aged 16-24 not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet" - then you might be wondering where to start. Under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work, a major review aimed at cutting the number of Neets will say. But how many jobs are there where you live? Use our look-up tool to find out. Where you live will often have a big impact on your ability to find a job. We have used online job adverts to help identify the number of vacancies suitable for young people in the area they live, relative to the size of the local population. The Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) think tank used AI to help identify the jobs, which were broadly defined as roles requiring relatively low experience or education. According to its analysis, South Oxfordshire had 387 suitable vacancies per 1,000 18 to 24-year-olds in the area - the most of any local authority. Rotherham had the least, at 53 per 1,000. Use this tool to check out the situation in your area. The data for London is only available for the region as a whole and is not broken down by individual councils. Which sectors have the most entry-level jobs? Even if there are jobs available in your area, you might not find one in the sector you want to work in. The sector with the highest average number of entry-level vacancies in the year to October was teaching, with most of those jobs being for teaching assistants, learning support and cover supervisor roles, according to jobs website Adzuna. The next largest was hospitality and catering, traditionally an area where younger people get their first experience of work. Adzuna, a major online jobs website, includes adverts for full-time roles marked as entry-level, those asking for up to two years' experience, graduate roles, internships and apprenticeships. Accounting and finance had the third-highest number of job openings. Figures on salaries for vacancies can be patchy because many employers do not include them in job adverts. Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently urged businesses to start publishing salaries ahead of plans to make pay details compulsory in adverts . Only about 40% of Adzuna's jobs data for the year to October stated a salary, although that figure varies widely by sector. Here are the average salaries for jobs in the sectors with the largest number of entry-level jobs, according to Adzuna. The highest average salary is £30,530 in engineering, while social care has the lowest at £25,880. How many job vacancies are there overall? While it can be hard for anyone looking for their first job, the situation is also tough for older jobseekers. Across the whole economy there were 690,000 jobs available in the August to October period this year, which is the lowest number since early 2021. The Covid pandemic led to huge swings in the number of job vacancies available as companies reacted to shutdowns and then reopened as restrictions were lifted. Stripping out the fluctuations seen during the pandemic, the number of vacancies is now at its lowest level for 12 years. Apprenticeships have often been a way for people to get their first taste of employment. In England the number of people starting apprenticeships has risen in recent years, although this has been driven by an increase in those aged 25 and over after schemes for older workers were fully rolled out in 2008. The number of people aged 24 and under starting apprenticeships in England in 2025 was 172,230, down from a peak of 291,300 in 2012. Watch: What's in the Milburn review?
