events.title: Is the US-Israel war on Iran turning into a ‘frozen conflict’?
events.summary: Trump says Washington doesn’t need a deal with Tehran, while Iran rejects the state of ‘no war, no peace’. Is the war at an impasse? United States President Donald Trump has signalled that Washington is in no hurry to end its war with Iran. “We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform late last week. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”, referring to the Strait of Hormuz, which joins the Gulf to the open ocean. list 1 of 3 How does Iran view Trump sidelining Vance from talks? list 2 of 3 Iran targets US military radar in Bahrain in ‘retaliatory’ drone strikes list 3 of 3 Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as drone raises alarm at Iraq gas field In the same post, Trump told Vice President JD Vance to give his “complete and total attention” to what Trump described as “corruption and crime” in Democratic-run cities. Vance led the talks with Iran, which produced a short-lived truce in June. But Trump has given mixed signals in recent days. Earlier last week, he said the war was “militarily … effectively over”, though he added that he “would not hesitate” to resume strikes if diplomacy failed. Trump’s mixed messaging came as his Republican Party suffered heavy losses in the November 3 midterm elections, which Vance blamed on the deeply unpopular US-Israel war on Iran and its economic fallout, in particular soaring fuel prices. Here’s what we know about where this war may be heading now and what history tells us about where frozen wars end. Observers say Trump’s mixed messages – and Vance’s comments criticising the war – indicate a disagreement within the party, with at least some members of the administration more comfortable with leaving the conflict unresolved. That could mean leaving the US naval blockade of Iranian ports in place and sanctions against Iran ongoing – both red lines for Iran, which has consistently stated that it will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz or resume peace talks until these are lifted, among other demands. On November 9, President Masoud Pezeshkian said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had ordered officials to end the state of “neither war nor peace”. Pezeshkian added that Iran was ready to negotiate but would not yield to coercion. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator, told Al Jazeera that “the ball is now in the American court” – to accept its terms for talks or continue the war. The term has no strict legal definition. It generally describes a conflict in which large-scale fighting has stopped or sharply declined, but no peace agreement or political settlement has been reached. The issues which caused the war remain unresolved. The front lines or the balance of control then harden into a de facto reality – in this case, with the US blockading Iranian ports and Iran targeting ships in the Strait of Hormuz that it says have not been authorised to pass, or firing missiles at US assets in neighbouring countries. Both sides keep their forces in place, often separated by a ceasefire line or a buffer zone. They may agree to an armistice or a series of truces without formally ending hostilities, such as the memorandum of understanding signed in Islamabad, Pakistan, in June, which fell apart within weeks. The phrase “frozen war” became common in the 1990s and 2000s as a way to describe conflicts in the former Soviet Union. These included conflicts in Transnistria in Moldova , Abkhazia and South Ossetia in Georgia, and Nagorno-Karabakh . A frozen conflict is not necessarily a peaceful one. Skirmishes, blockades, economic warfare and periodic flare-ups are common. The defining feature is that neither side can impose a decisive outcome, and neither is willing to make the concessions a lasting peace would require. Could the US-Israel war on Iran become a ‘frozen war’? The war began in February, when the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran. Talks in Pakistan in April produced a memorandum of understanding in June which paused the fighting and briefly lifted the US blockade. The truce collapsed soon after – primarily over disagreements about control of the Strait of Hormuz – and Washington reimposed its naval blockade on July 14. “Diplomatically, we are already there and have been since July, when the June memorandum fell apart,” said Muhanad Seloom, an assistant professor in critical security studies at the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies. However, he added that the word “frozen” “flatters” a conflict with a US blockade, attacks on shipping around Hormuz running at more than one a day and strikes in both directions. The US has carried out limited strikes, including on Iranian air defence systems on Qeshm Island . Iran has attacked tankers using what it calls unauthorised routes in the Strait of Hormuz.

Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust (BXDC) says the definitive agreement will see it acquire a 75 percent majority interest in two joint ventures with AWS, in a transaction valued at approximately $5 billion. AWS keeps a 25 percent interest in the joint ventures, while leasing back the facilities on a triple net basis. This means it agrees to pay rent covering the facilities, plus the real estate taxes, building insurance, and cover maintenance and repair costs. A Form 8-K filed by Blackstone with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) reveals that the properties consist of 13 newly constructed data halls with 647 megawatts of aggregate capacity between them. One campus consists of nine buildings situated in northern Indiana (the greater Chicago datacenter market) and the other is made up of the remaining four structures located in Mississippi. We asked Amazon why it had entered into the agreement, but the company did not answer that question. Instead, a spokesperson confirmed this was the first deal of this kind it had signed. In a supplied remark, VP of AWS Infrastructure Prasad Kalyanaraman said that "Partnering with Blackstone allows us to continue expanding responsibly while keeping communities at the center of how we build." AWS does lease capacity from other datacenter operators, of course, and has existing agreements with partners like STACK Infrastructure to develop $12 billion worth of campus sites across northwest Louisiana, signed earlier this year. Sale-leaseback transactions are not unheard of in the datacenter industry. QTS Realty Trust (also backed by Blackstone) developed facilities for lease by Microsoft , for example. BXDC is a real estate investment trust (REIT), launched by Blackstone on the New York Stock Exchange earlier this year. The AWS deal is its first since then. "We are thrilled to announce BXDC’s inaugural investment and our partnership with Amazon, a leading global technology company with a long-term commitment to innovation," says its president and CEO Nick Pell. "The quality, basis and tenant profile of these assets make this an attractive match for the deployment of our IPO proceeds. Given the deep expertise across our platform, we believe BXDC is well positioned to capitalize on a highly compelling opportunity and deliver value for our shareholders." Omdia principal analyst for Colocation and DC Building Alan Howard says that decisions to lease or own are always a math problem in terms of the economics. "I'm not sure those datacenter assets bring much benefit to their financials sitting on their balance sheet and it's possible a sale/leaseback is more economical. Keep in mind that all this has nothing to do with all the IT equipment inside, rather just the building and its infrastructure," he told The Register . "It's also clear that the massive capex spending by hyperscalers is putting pressure on their financials and they are leaning on debt markets to fund some of the buildout. Of course, using debt is not out of the ordinary, but I imagine the debt for AI buildout is significantly more now than in the past.

events.title: Nvidia's earnings mark start of post-Jensen era
events.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios Nvidia's post-Jensen Huang era begins in earnest with the release of its third-quarter results after the close of trading Tuesday. Why it matters: Investors and analysts will be reading tea leaves and listening for hints about near-term changes the company is making (or expecting the government to make) as a result of Huang's resignation last week and the circumstances that led to it. The big picture: Besides selling the world's most sought-after AI processors, Nvidia is a giant source of financial backing to the AI ecosystem — buying equity, making co-investments and backstopping debt in companies ranging from neoclouds like CoreWeave to fiber-optic cable providers like Lumentum. Nvidia is also a major partner of the two AI labs at the heart of the boom, striking a deal to provide a backstop for an OpenAI data center in Ohio and planning to invest about $10 billion into Anthropic following its IPO later this week, according to its prospectus. Huang could make these unorthodox deals — some call them circular finance — because of his position as a co-founder and sole CEO of Nvidia. Now that he's gone, investors will be listening closely for any indication that Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress, plans to step back from Huang's strategy of using Nvidia's resources to bolster the AI sector. What they're saying: Analysts will also be tuning in to Nvidia's conference call for hints about how the circumstances of Huang's ejection from the corner office — after reports of multiple affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset — could shift global sales patterns over time. "Our biggest concern now is new scrutiny that may restrict some of its sales into certain geographies such as Singapore/Malaysia. In a worst case, we estimate this could cut up to ~10% out of revenue," wrote UBS analysts. "Greater scrutiny of NVDA Asia shipments that indirectly (via cloud) service China customers, or more conservative funding/product allocation to US emerging/neocloud customers could also impact market share," wrote analysts with BofA Securities. "While the findings of the independent probe by NVIDIA and Congressional scrutiny remain to be seen, one possible outcome could be enhanced export restrictions," wrote analysts at HSBC, in a note downgrading the stock to "hold" from "buy" last week, adding that "during the past six quarters, 11% of total revenue was from countries excluding the U.S. and Taiwan, which we believe could be the focus of restrictions." By the numbers: Few expect anything other than another giant jump in sales and profits in the report itself. (If there's a significant miss, the already wobbly AI trade would likely get another clubbing.) Zoom in: That said, we'll be watching data center sales, which are expected to nearly double to about $101.87 billion. Also, given the weakness in the market, Nvidia's guidance for overall revenue in the current quarter will be of interest. Wall Street analysts expect it to be $125.2 billion. The company offered full-year sales guidance for the first time ever last quarter, and any tweak to the approximately 70% Nvidia previously said it expected for fiscal year 2028 sales growth will be huge. The bottom line: This will be a very delicate earnings report for the interim CEO and the rest of Nvidia's team to handle.

events.title: Mozambique’s opposition leader stands trial over deadly 2024 protests
events.summary: Venancio Mondlane faces five charges, the most serious being instigating ‘terrorism’. Mozambique’s opposition leader has arrived at the country’s Supreme Court to stand trial over his alleged role in deadly protests that followed 2024’s disputed election results . Venancio Mondlane addressed reporters outside the court in Maputo on Tuesday. He faces five charges, the most serious of which is instigating “terrorism”. If found guilty, he could be jailed for up to 24 years. list 1 of 3 Mapping Africa’s energy wealth and 560 million who remain without power list 2 of 3 Exiled critic of Rwandan president found beheaded in Uganda list 3 of 3 Foreign national beaten to death by a mob in South Africa “I arrive calm and confident in my legal team,” Mondlane said. Months of antigovernment protests broke out in Mozambique in 2024 after Mondlane came second in national elections. President Daniel Chapo and his Frelimo party beat Mondlane, extending Frelimo’s time in power to more than 50 years. Mondlane disputes the results, and his allegations of harassment of the opposition have been echoed by rights groups, including Human Rights Watch. Following the elections in 2024, the organisation said the vote had been marred by political killings, widespread irregularities, and restrictions on freedom of expression and assembly. Frelimo denies any wrongdoing. Amnesty International says more than 300 people were killed during protests against the election results. It accused authorities of waging a crackdown against demonstrators, with police allegedly using unlawful force, mass arbitrary arrests and suppression of information. Mondlane has also been charged with inciting “terrorism”, advocacy of crime, public incitement to a crime, and incitement of civil disobedience. Thousands of people gathered for protests in response to calls by Mondlane to organise against the results. While preparing to challenge the vote, Mondlane’s lawyer and aide were shot dead. Before Tuesday’s trial, Mondlane accused the government of attempting to silence him during a livestream on Facebook. “The message being sent is that you must remain silent. You must remain in captivity, in prison, in darkness,” he said. “In truth, Venancio is being used as an example to an entire generation: A warning that nobody should dare to rise up against the regime, against an empire of kleptocracy, or against the system of oppression that we have lived under for 50 years.” Mondlane denies all charges against him.

events.title: I founded a cancer biotech company. Then, my mom, dad, and I were all diagnosed with cancer.
events.summary: Dr. Ryan Beal founded a cancer-focused biotech company. Then, he got cancer himself. Courtesy of Dr. Ryan Beal Dr. Ryan Beal founded a bioscience company focused on cancer treatment in 2014. Years later, he was diagnosed with a rare cancer, and his approach to the business shifted. Being in the oncologist's office helped him understand the human impact of his innovations. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Dr. Ryan Beal , CEO of Dyve Biosciences . It has been edited for length and clarity . My brother and I were about 60 miles into a 120-mile race in Colorado when chest pain made me stop. I thought I was having a cardiac emergency , but doctors diagnosed me with thymoma — a rare cancer of the thymus gland, which sits in the middle of the chest. To say it was a shock is an understatement. I was only 49 and healthy enough to run for six days through the Rockies. Months earlier, my mother had died of cancer ; her celebration of life was just days before the race. My brother and I had considered canceling, but decided to run together to reflect on her life. Instead, I found myself in an emergency room in Vail, facing a terrible diagnosis. But I had something few cancer patients do: I'm the CEO of a cancer-focused biotech company. I immediately sent my results to three doctor friends, and they got to work. His mom survived breast cancer, then received a pancreatic cancer diagnosis. Courtesy of Dr. Ryan Beal I'm an MD, but went into business, rather than medicine I've always been a science nerd, and grew up wanting to be a physician. While I was in medical school at UPenn, I developed an interest in business. Med school felt like a lot of memorization and regurgitation of facts; in business classes, there were no rote answers, but more nuance and decision-making. Then, while assisting with a surgery, I overheard two well-respected surgeons saying they wouldn't want their kids going into medicine. That stuck with me. I got my MD, but rather than doing a residency, I started working for McKinsey, the large consulting firm. I left that position because I wanted more time with my kids . I had another startup initially, and co-founded Dyve in 2014. Our technology delivers therapeutic agents through the skin in a noninvasive way, to target the acidic environment that cancer tumors thrive in. He and his brother ran an ultramarathon together, during which he was experiencing chest pains that led to his own diagnosis. Courtesy of Dr. Ryan Beal I didn't fully understand the emotional side until I was a patient As I led Dyve, I was very much a scientist, focused on solving scientific problems. I knew our work would impact real people, but I very much came at the work through an empirical lens. That changed when my mom was diagnosed with cancer. She survived breast cancer , but eight years later, was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer that killed her within weeks. Then, I was diagnosed. I had sat in boardrooms discussing cancer infusions many, many times. Yet, I'd never sat in an infusion center or the waiting room at the oncologist's office. Being in these spaces as a patient was incredibly emotional. It was eye-opening about not only the reality of cancer, but also the work I was doing. I'm entirely focused on patients now In some ways, my expertise helped me through treatment. I was familiar with the chemotherapy drugs I was taking, for example. I thought navigating insurance would be easy, given my background, but it was a nightmare, even for someone who knows the system well. I took a two-year sabbatical during treatment. It took me that long to feel like I was back to myself. My team was kind enough to say they didn't notice my brain fog, but I did. When I returned, the way I thought about my company had dramatically shifted. Now, I'm entirely focused on the patient experience. I understand more acutely that long trials and timelines mean less hope for patients who have been told they have no more options to explore. I'm driven by emotion and my own experience now, more than science. It takes capital to drive innovation, and I want to build a successful business where investors do well. But what drives me is patient outcomes. I want people like me, my mom, and my dad — who died of cancer more recently — to have access to better treatments. Even if that's all that happens with my business, I would be thrilled. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Disney beats earnings forecasts, plans to increase content spending
events.summary: Disney reported adjusted earnings per share of US$1.77 for the fiscal fourth quarter ended Oct 3. Disney beat quarterly earnings forecasts, with revenue up 16% to US$25.9 billion. Higher theme park attendance and strong NFL viewership helped results. The company will raise content spending 9% to US$26 billion in 2027. It will also invest more in international programming and sports rights. Disney plans to cut operating costs by about US$3 billion by 2029. Its board also raised the annual dividend by 33% to US$2 per share. LOS ANGELES – Walt Disney on Nov 17 reported quarterly revenue and earnings that beat Wall Street expectations, helped by higher theme park attendance and strong NFL viewership, and said it would increase content spending by 9% in the next fiscal year. Disney reported adjusted earnings per share of US$1.77 for the fiscal fourth quarter ended Oct 3. Analysts had forecast US$1.67 on average, according to LSEG. The owner of the Disney+ streaming service and ESPN cable network said it would boost cash content spending to US$26 billion (S$33.5 billion) in 2027, including by investing more in international programming and sports rights. The company plans to cut operating expenses by about US$3 billion by fiscal 2029, executives said in a letter to shareholders. Disney said its board agreed to raise the annual shareholder dividend by 33% to US$2 per share, paid in US$1 installments in January and July. New chief executive officer Josh D’Amaro, who took the helm of Disney in March, is steering the company through a consumer shift to streaming and competition from social media platforms such as YouTube and TikTok. D’Amaro has said he wants to strengthen Disney’s streaming business and continue to invest in theme parks and cruise lines. Revenue rose 16% to US$25.9 billion in the latest quarter. At the entertainment division, which includes streaming, ABC and other networks, revenue rose 17% to US$11.9 billion, helped by higher subscription revenue. Operating income at the segment rose 92% to US$1.3 billion. The experiences division, home to theme parks and cruise ships, reported record revenue and profit. The unit’s revenue rose 15% to US$10.1 billion and operating income increased 20% to nearly US$2.3 billion. At sports, revenue rose 16% to US$4.6 billion as ESPN viewership for the start of the NFL and college football seasons reached record highs. The segment’s operating income increased by 53% to nearly US$1.4 billion. Looking ahead, Disney reiterated that it expected double-digit growth in adjusted earnings per share in fiscal 2027. It said total segment operating income would grow about 8% for the year. The company plans capital expenditures of about US$9 billion, similar to the current fiscal year. REUTERS

events.title: Latham & Watkins partners: Corporate leaders should prepare for a new era of congressional scrutiny
events.summary: Within hours of Democrats winning control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, Representative Robert Garcia, the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, delivered a two-word warning to potential investigative targets: “Lawyer up.” Corporate leaders would be wise to heed that warning too. Seasoned oversight members in the House and Senate are already telegraphing their investigative priorities and targets. And when Democrats take control of Congress in January, their ability to legislate will be constrained by a Republican President with veto power. Instead, investigations will offer lawmakers a way to pursue their policy priorities, demonstrate accountability, respond to the economic frustrations that helped propel them to victory, and provide a message testing ground for the 2028 presidential election. The implications for CEOs and boards extend well beyond partisan politics. Companies often face questions not only about whether they have complied with the law, but also about their business decisions, political relationships, and internal communications. Congressional investigations create reputational harm and resource drain—and they can spur state-level enforcement and regulatory activity—even without any proof of misconduct. What companies should do now While Democrats will not officially take control for another six weeks, lawmakers are re-issuing letters from months ago with a renewed verve. Past history on an issue is the best indicator of where committees will start in January: staff have already done the legwork on these issues and received member sign-off, where necessary. And paying close attention to issue areas (e.g., donations to Administration priorities) or sector-wide issues affecting an industry (e.g., hyperscalers and data centers) can provide an early warning of scrutiny to come. Government affairs teams and trade associations should be providing ground truth into how lawmakers view a company or industry. Another priority is understanding what records exist and where, with congressional investigators increasingly seeking emails, text messages, encrypted messaging application chats, and other communications involving senior executives and board members. Companies should review their document retention policies, ensure employees understand their preservation obligations, and consider whether sensitive business decisions are discussed over informal messaging channels. A casual exchange between executives can take on an entirely different meaning when displayed during a congressional hearing. Companies also need to get their response team in place now. Internal legal, government affairs, and communications teams too often approach these situations in silos, despite the interdisciplinary nature of congressional investigations. A legal strategy designed to limit disclosure may prolong a damaging public fight, while an effort to quickly resolve a political controversy can create problems with regulators or in subsequent litigation. These tradeoffs are easier to navigate when the right people are at the same table from the outset. And companies should consider whether they need to add key external resources to support their response strategy and retain those resources. Congressional oversight does not have to be inherently adversarial, but preparation is key to ensuring that companies can navigate the reputational, legal, and potential enforcement risks that can accompany investigative activity. The Democratic oversight agenda is broad and cross-jurisdictional Because the Administration has signaled its intent to stonewall congressional investigators, Congress will go after the private sector actors who can act as proxies for their policy priorities and may have the non-governmental end of important communications. Private sector entities and individuals who aren’t the target of investigations can still find themselves as important third-party sources of information, or even as “friendly” witnesses in hearings: all of these interactions create resource drain and pull attention from running a business. While companies with financial relationships to President Trump, his family, or his administration are obvious investigative targets, the coming wave of investigations will not stop there. Affordability, a defining issue of the midterms, will likely drive scrutiny across industries. For example, data centers could face questions about their impact on household electricity bills and their relationships with utilities and municipalities. Artificial intelligence companies and social media platforms may face pressure over safety and protecting kids online, while financial institutions should anticipate questions about market fairness and financial regulation, including private credit, cryptocurrency, and prediction markets. Interestingly, several of these issues have bipartisan appeal. Children’s online safety, financial market practices, and consumer costs are not just Democratic concerns. Companies that have avoided taking controversial political positions may nevertheless find themselves at the center of investigations driven by broader economic frustrations. Because several of the oversight themes cross traditional committee jurisdictional lanes, House Democratic leadership has signaled its intent to distribute investigative responsibilities across more committees. In both the House and the Senate, committees will draw on existing teams of experienced investigators, and may try to recruit additional staff to help drive an ambitious agenda, including former federal prosecutors and law firm attorneys. The House and Senate operate under different rules and possess distinct investigative authorities, so responding to one inquiry won’t necessarily satisfy another. Companies could find themselves navigating competing demands for documents, testimony, and executive attention from multiple committees and from both Houses of Congress. The consequences won’t end with Congress Congressional investigations are driven in many ways by public optics and media attention. Policymakers who cannot legislate are using hearings, subpoenas, and document disclosures to draw attention to their priorities. Consequences can quickly extend beyond the headlines: regulators and enforcement authorities closely follow congressional proceedings, and information that emerges during an investigation can trigger additional scrutiny, shareholder litigation, or other private lawsuits. And the ecosystem also works in the reverse, with congressional investigators often pulling issues from ongoing litigation or state regulatory activity. The new Congress will be sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027, starting a two-year clock for Democrats to highlight and execute on their accountability and affordability agendas; this will happen mostly through oversight investigations, as Democrats deal with a lame-duck Administration. events.title: US-China rivalry is structural, countries must invest in strategic resilience: Ex-US Treasury official
events.summary: The comments come as the US announced new export controls on advanced AI semiconductor shipments to overseas data centres. US and China are decoupling in strategic industries, not all trade, because both see each other as rivals. Justin Muzinich said this is a lasting structural shift. He said the split has already hit rare earths, and will impact AI, quantum and biotech, while goods like clothing may still be traded to keep costs down. Businesses are unlikely to separate on their own. Muzinich warned governments will need to pay for secure supply chains and data centres, which could raise prices and lower returns. He advised investors to diversify and stay humble. SINGAPORE – The United States and China are set to pull further apart in industries critical to national security, as their strategic rivalry drives a lasting effort to reduce dependence on each other, said Justin Muzinich. Muzinich, who served as the US Deputy Secretary of the Treasury from 2018 to 2021, said the separation is unlikely to extend equally across the economy, with both powers retaining an interest in trade that keeps costs down. The shift is structural rather than a passing feature of the American political cycle, he said on Nov 17 at a panel discussion on investing in a fragmented world at the inaugural HSBC Singapore Wealth Investment Summit 2026. Muzinich, who is chief executive of Muzinich & Co, a global credit investment firm founded by his father George Muzinich in 1988, said there is strong bipartisan consensus in Washington that China is a strategic rival, and a similar view of the US in Beijing. “You have two countries which see each other as strategic rivals, and I think it’s rational for both countries to want to pull apart when it comes to strategic dependencies,” he said. That process was already evident in rare earths, he said, and would continue in artificial intelligence, quantum technology and biotechnology. The more consequential dividing line for businesses and investors would therefore be between strategic and non-strategic industries, rather than a wholesale severing of economic ties. Trade in products such as clothing remained in both countries’ interests because it helped contain costs. “But when it comes to strategic industries, I don’t think we’re going back to where we were before,” he said. Muzinich added that US President Donald Trump appeared, in some ways, more willing to extend a hand to China than either the Republican or Democratic foreign policy establishment – a distinction that would be important to watch as relations evolve. His comments come as the US announced new export controls on advanced AI semiconductor shipments to overseas data centres, following reports of these chips being illegally diverted to China through other countries, including Singapore. Muzinich said the push to reduce strategic dependencies would increasingly come from governments, as companies focus on their bottom lines. Left to themselves, companies would adjust investment decisions at the margins but would be unlikely to undertake a substantial separation in strategic industries. He also noted that there were growing expectations in Washington that governments would have to intervene – drawing a parallel to military spending, where a country pays for its defence – and should be prepared to bear the cost of secure supply chains in critical sectors. “Private companies aren’t going to do that on their own,” he said. “So I think more and more will be forced from the top down.” Justin Muzinich, chief executive of private-debt specialist Muzinich & Co, said the more consequential dividing line for businesses and investors would therefore be between strategic and non-strategic industries. For investors in Asia, the emergence of parallel industrial and technological systems could create new financing needs, even as fragmentation raises costs. Muzinich cited the prospect of data centres financed by the Asia-Pacific region for the region’s own use. As the structure of the global economy changes, so too would the investments needed to support it, he said. But those opportunities would come with a broader economic trade-off. “A s the world is focused more on geopolitics, I think for the whole world, economic returns come down because prices go up,” he said, describing the shift as inflationary. On a global scale, countries were trading economic efficiency for geopolitical resilience. Financing the infrastructure required for that resilience offered opportunities for investors, he added. For Muzinich, the uncertainty reinforced the importance of diversification rather than confidence in any single geopolitical forecast. “There is wisdom in a little bit of humility because it is very difficult to predict how geopolitics will develop,” he said.

events.title: Rebeca Grynspan could be the UN’s first woman boss, if she can sway Trump
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? Swaying the US could be Grynspan’s biggest test but she likes taking risks – and wants the UN to take more, she tells Al Jazeera. In straw poll after straw poll among members of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) to choose the organisation’s next leader, one name keeps emerging ahead of all others: Costa Rican diplomat Rebeca Grynspan. If Grynspan, 70, beats out the other candidates, the current head of the UN’s top trade body would become the world’s first woman and the first Jewish person to hold the post of UN secretary-general. list 1 of 3 UN says Israeli policies worsened deadly impact of Gaza winter storm list 2 of 3 US and rivals spar over next UN boss as race lurches towards deadline list 3 of 3 Secret votes and vetoes: How will the next UN chief be picked? But as the December 31 deadline to pick UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres ‘ successor rapidly approaches, Grynspan continues to struggle to convert her frontrunner status into a win, because of at least one veto against her candidature. With secret ballots , geopolitical rivalries and multiple – eight in all – candidates vying for the world’s top diplomatic job, there is no public confirmation of just which of the five permanent members of the UNSC are opposed to Grynspan’s election. Yet her background as a UN insider, and her work on Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory and Russia’s war on Ukraine, mean that Grynspan carries baggage that she will need to overcome in order to win the support of the world’s most powerful nations, say analysts. And she’ll need to win over one leader above all, who has demonstrated his desire to dismantle the very UN Grynspan hopes to lead: United States President Donald Trump. What she has going for her, though, she says, is a track record of diplomacy – and a willingness to take risks, herself, and for the organisation. “The UN must become less risk-averse. Its biggest risk today is the risk of not trying,” she told Al Jazeera. “I have listened to people who need the UN but increasingly doubt it can act. They want leadership willing to take risks for peace.” The current chief of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) and the former vice president of Costa Rica acknowledged that diplomatic negotiations don’t always work – at least at first. But that, she argued, only makes the UN chief’s job that much more important. “Any mediator knows that 10 ideas may fail before the 11th succeeds,” she said. “Few governments can afford the political cost of so many rejections. The secretary-general can.” A past spanning Costa Rica, Latin America and beyond Grynspan is no stranger to the “first” label – she became UNCTAD’s first woman secretary-general when she was appointed to the role in 2021. She took on its reins, promising post-COVID economic recovery, supporting digital transitions, and aligning with UN goals on climate change. But before this post, Grynspan held a long career in Latin American politics and international diplomacy, including as second vice president of Costa Rica from 1994 to 1998. An economist by trade, her various government ministerial positions included at one time being deputy finance minister, where she played a key role in the country’s debt crisis in the eighties. After years of government experience, she took on roles beyond Costa Rica. In 2014, she was appointed as the secretary-general of the Ibero-American Conference by the bloc’s 22 nations spanning Latin America, the Caribbean, and Europe. She has also held leading roles within the UN Development Programme (UNDP), as well as the UN Commission for the Reconstruction of Haiti. In her bid for UN secretary-general, Grynspan has laid out her vision of reform of the international body, and says she would push for the UN to take a more active role in negotiations to end wars. “To defend the United Nations today is to have the courage to change it. No organisation after 80 years can say, we don’t have to change anything,” the frontrunner said to Al Jazeera. “The UN has to embrace reform, not be defensive about reform.” As head of UNCTAD, Grynspan has spearheaded the organisation’s work on global trade, debt, and economic inequality. She is widely credited with having played an important role in the UN’s Black Sea Grain Initiative, which facilitated Ukrainian agricultural exports through the Black Sea during the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war. She negotiated that deal between the warring parties while undergoing breast cancer treatment. “Making the agreements work meant bringing others to the table,” Grynspan recalled. “Banks would not clear payments, insurers would not cover vessels and shipping companies hesitated. We brought them into the effort.” According to UNCTAD, the UN and Turkiye-brokered initiative in 2022 exported 32 million tonnes of grain and lowered global food prices by 22 percent, before Russia withdrew from the deal a year later.

events.title: As outages persist, Puerto Rico finds a way to help keep the lights on with 'virtual power plant'
events.summary: Hector Ríos is part of Puerto Rico's innovative “virtual power plant” system, which uses household batteries to support the island's electric grid SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- On nearly 20 days in October, an electric utility took energy from a battery attached to Hector Ríos’ house in Cabo Rojo, on the southwest corner of Puerto Rico, and used it to support the power grid. With the U.S. territory's frequent power outages that disrupt daily life and restrain its economy, he likes the idea of helping prevent blackouts for other people. He's also compensated for the energy. “It just seems like a good deal, to contribute to the community and make money at the same time,” Ríos said. Ríos, 75, is part of what has become one of Puerto Rico's most effective tools for energy resilience amid nearly a decade of electricity woes : a “virtual power plant,” or VPP, that harnesses batteries from nearly 115,000 households to bolster the grid when its aging and fickle power plants can't meet demand . Nine years after Puerto Rico's public power utility filed for bankruptcy and Hurricane Maria ravaged its already dilapidated energy grid, residents still face unpredictable blackouts and electricity rates higher than in almost any state . Few new utility-scale power sources have been built since Maria, and most of the federal dollars promised for grid recovery have not yet reached the territory. But the VPP — the first of its kind in Latin America and the Caribbean, and the U.S.' second largest in terms of capacity — showed its potential this summer, preventing or mitigating outages more than 60 times since June 1, according to Luma Energy, its transmission and distribution utility. “There’s nothing virtual about it,” said Javier Rúa Jovet, chief policy officer at the Solar and Energy Storage Association of Puerto Rico. “It’s real, and it’s better than a power plant.” Dozens of states now operate similar networks of distributed energy sources like battery storage systems , electric vehicles and smart thermostats to help manage the grid. Experts expect their role to grow in the U.S. amid energy constraints, rising utility prices, and tech companies’ push to build power-hungry data centers . As President Donald Trump’s administration promotes fossil fuel expansion and redirects dollars away from solar adoption in Puerto Rico , proponents of the territory's system say it highlights the value of distributed solar and storage, and shows how these systems can bolster resilience for other energy-vulnerable communities. “There’s a way for this technology to benefit not just the individual buildings that they’re on,” but instead be “in service to the community all the time,” said Nathalie Jordi, community solar lead at Together New Orleans, a nonprofit that championed an upcoming $23 million city program to provide and network over 1,000 batteries on homes and businesses across New Orleans. The opportunity to harness a vast network of residential batteries arose after Hurricane Maria in 2017 , which left some communities without electricity for nearly a year. Experts linked the infrastructure failure to thousands of post-hurricane deaths . “We had to procure resiliency in some other way,” said Rúa Jovet, “not a centralized system that will completely fail for a whole year.” There are now over 207,000 rooftop solar systems on an archipelago of fewer than 3.2 million people, a 20-fold increase from before Maria that was propelled by households who could afford installations, philanthropy, and some federal dollars. Because of the territory's unique need for resiliency, nearly every installation includes at least one battery, a necessary add-on to keep the system running in a blackout. “The mindset was, get yourself ready for everything,” recalled Ríos, who after Maria bought a diesel generator for his house, then installed panels and a Tesla Powerwall battery in 2023. The system also cut his utility bill in half, from about $400 to $200 in the summer. Solar panels create an energy boon during the day, charging batteries and sending excess power to the grid. But when the sun sets and demand rises, Puerto Rico barely has enough power to meet the need. Any power plant malfunction can prompt an outage. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech In late 2023, Luma launched a small pilot program that would leverage residential battery capacity to offset the shortages. Ríos was among the first to enroll; now over half of solar customers participate. If Luma predicts an energy deficit, customers are digitally notified that a battery sharing event is coming. They can opt out via app, or adjust how much of their battery — enrollees typically offer 30% — they make available. The experiment has faced challenges.

events.title: A dovish détente gives way to geopolitical gravity
events.summary: To be a China “hawk,” Jensen Huang declared last year, is a “badge of shame.” The former Nvidia CEO was a proud dove, one who found a dovish partner in US President Donald Trump — quite literally, in a business sense. Together, they formed an enterprise that aimed to sell high-end Nvidia chips to China, with the US government taking a cut of the profits. Their alliance represented the high-water mark of a Sino-US détente — peak dovishness, where a prime consideration in the White House was expanding Nvidia’s market share, not blocking China’s AI ambitions. Asked on CNN if it mattered who won the AI superpower race, Huang replied “I don’t think it does.” That moment has come and gone. A trade that not only sent powerful chips into China via legal channels, but also billions of dollars of hardware illicitly through Chinese-funded companies in Southeast Asia — one of the most active, Megaspeed, set up by a suspected Chinese intelligence asset with whom Huang was having an affair — has run headlong into the hard realities of US-China strategic competition. Their superpower rivalry is structural. Its main focus is technology and, whatever Huang says, AI has made the struggle existential. At times, Trump has seemed confused about the geostrategic stakes. In arguing for a let-it-rip approach to frontier AI model development, he has several times invoked the China bogeyman by insisting that “Whoever wins AI, wins.” Yet he pushed Huang and chip sales to China into the forefront of his diplomacy with Beijing. In May, Trump scrambled Huang onto Air Force One at the last minute to join his business entourage in Beijing at a Sino-US summit, reportedly despite knowing that his intelligence services were aware of the Nvidia CEO’s potential links to a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Then in September, Huang was at the head table with Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a state banquet in Washington. Huang would likely be with Trump in Shenzhen this week at a meeting of Asia-Pacific leaders if he hadn’t been forced to resign. Instead, the prospect of the US Congress ratcheting up tech sanctions against China will hang over Trump’s third meeting this year with Xi, and could endanger their fragile trade truce. Beijing, at least, is clear-eyed about the nature of its competition with Washington. Although over the longer term Huang’s spectacular fall may hold back US innovation and economic dynamism — a plus for China — the short-term consequences of a tightening embargo on semiconductors and chipmaking equipment would be immensely damaging. For all its advances in critical industries, China remains heavily dependent on American IP. In retrospect, as my colleague Reed Albergotti argued, Huang’s mistake was to get mixed up in politics in Washington, where he had a target on his back. His defenders see a conspiracy involving the US intelligence services to bring down America’s foremost business supporter of engagement with China. Elon Musk posted on X that he would sign a petition reinstating Huang. Epic Games founder Tim Sweeney said his exit showed an “Apple firing Steve Jobs level of idiocy.” The broader question is the appropriate role for US business leaders in forging a relationship between rival superpowers whose economies are nevertheless deeply entwined through innovation networks, finance channels, and human talent. US strategy, writes Julian Gewirtz , a scholar at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs, “has come to depend, to an extraordinary degree, on powerful private-sector actors whose incentives the government cannot simply assume will align with the national interest.” In Trump’s lame-duck presidency, that issue will be taken up by an incensed Congress pushing bipartisan bills aimed at China. The doves have had their time to shape the US-China agenda. Now, geopolitical gravity takes over.

events.title: Alan Milburn says his plan to get young people into work will save only £200m a year
events.summary: Author of long-awaited report says money saved in benefit cuts will mostly be used to fund new job support system Neet ideas: what’s in Milburn’s report? Alan Milburn has said his plan to get more young people into work will save the government only £200m a year as the cost of job support swallows up almost all of the anticipated cuts to benefits. The former health secretary unveiled his long-awaited report into youth unemployment on Tuesday morning, urging ministers to cut disability and sickness payments for under-25s and invest the money in back-to-work schemes. Figures contained in the report show that his plan will not deliver significant overall savings. The figures are likely to be seized on by the Conservatives as evidence that Labour is not serious about reducing the welfare bill – something the opposition party has put at the heart of its economic policy. But they will bolster the arguments of Milburn and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, that the year-long review has not been motivated by cuts. “The system I propose will spend less on compensating for economic inactivity, more on creating routes out of it; less on the consequences of failure and more on avoiding it,” Milburn said in the report. He told Labour MPs at a meeting on Monday night: “The Tories will say it’s too expensive, you can cut faster. But you can’t – or you’d drive young people into destitution with poor housing and ill health.” Milburn’s report, the outlines of which have been widely trailed over the past few weeks, sets out in detail what he thinks should be done to reduce the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet). The plan would involve the government spending nearly £2bn a year on a new youth opportunity service, which would provide support and advice to give every young person a guaranteed route into education, training or work. It would involve spending just over £2bn to create more vocational training courses and apprenticeships, and a further £1bn in direct payments and tax breaks for companies that hire young people. The new system would be paid for largely by taking disability and sickness benefits away from young people and replacing them with a single youth allowance, which would be considerably below what some people can claim currently. People aged 18-24 would no longer be able to claim personal independence payments, which would be replaced by a new allowance available only to those whose conditions are “well established, significant and ongoing”. The benefits cuts would be expected to save £3.6bn by 2036-37, with an additional £2.4bn being generated by higher tax receipts. That money would be almost entirely swallowed by the £5.8bn cost of the new system, Milburn said. Milburn began his review last year amid concern at the top of government over the rising numbers of young Neets. That figure reached 1m earlier this year, equating to 13% of young people – a higher rate than in any European country except Romania. In his report, he argues: “Our country is at a fork in the road. Go on as we are and see the Neet crisis grow. Or change course and make the difficult changes that can shift the trajectory.” He says his proposals constitute a wholesale rethinking of how the benefits and education system works for young people, and should not be cherrypicked by ministers looking to impose only the ones they like. He has received public backing from the governments of Burnham and his predecessor, Keir Starmer. When he addressed Labour MPs on Monday he was accompanied by the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden. McFadden and Burnham will speak to the parliamentary party about the plans again on Tuesday morning. Ministers are hoping they can avoid a repeat of last year’s bruising welfare rebellion, when Labour MPs forced Starmer to drop his plan to cut benefits by about £5bn a year. That humiliation arguably spelled the beginning of the end of Starmer’s time in office. Several of the architects of the rebellion now have government jobs, including the de facto deputy prime minister, Louise Haigh, and the chief whip, Anneliese Midgley.

events.title: Neet ideas: what’s in Alan Milburn’s report on young people not in education, employment or training?
events.summary: Former minister’s 278-page report calls for changes to employment regulations, education, healthcare and benefits Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on young people Five months on from a first report detailing the growing crisis of young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet), Alan Milburn has produced his recommendations on how to tackle it. Set out over 278 pages, they amount to, as he readily accepts, a major rethink of everything from employment regulations to education, healthcare and benefits. 1. The context While this was in part covered by the first report, Milburn is at pains to begin the new volume with his belief that the issue of Neets is not a failure of the younger generation but a case of them being let down by a series of structural factors. “The young people I have met over the last year are not asking for an easier life. They are asking for a fair chance to build one,” he writes. The answer must be radical, he says. “This cannot be fixed by tweaking the edges of the existing system. The response now has to be full throttle: not another initiative or another round of incremental reform, but transformational change.” At the centre of the proposed new system is a youth opportunity service (YOS), which would offer young people support in areas such as training and health – and would in return expect participation. 2. The goals Currently, about 13.5% of people aged 16-24 in the UK are classified as Neet, the highest proportion in Europe outside Romania. This is not a new problem, the report notes, pointing out that the Neet rate has stayed above 10% for most of the past 25 years. The aim over a decade-long transformational plan would be to match the records of the best-performing European nations on this metric, such as the Netherlands and Denmark. While Milburn talks playfully of aiming for “Neet zero”, he says this means an eventual consistent rate of about 5%. He says the policies in his plan would get the Neet rate to about 6.8% by 2036. 3. Employers and the labour market Noting that youth employment has declined even as overall employment rose, Milburn says opportunities are limited by issues affecting young people – for example, a lack of connections to secure work experience or first jobs – and also employers, including the costs of taking on staff and regulatory complexities. The report says this is worsened by a lack of government help. While Denmark spends about 1% of GDP on all-age hiring incentives and subsidies, in the UK it is about 0.1%. Milburn’s historic report on Britain’s lost generation says one key thing: finally, young lives will really matter | Polly Toynbee Read more The report sets out a series of recommendations, including: Doubling the salary threshold for employer national insurance for entry-level jobs for young people in retail and hospitality, possibly then expanded to other sectors. Extending the existing youth jobs grant, which gives up to £3,000 to employers who takes on a staff member on universal credit for at least six months, so it also applies to people not on benefits, with extra incentives for small employers and people facing barriers, such as those with disabilities or care leavers. Avoid minimum pay rates being a barrier – for example, any moves to put young people’s minimum wages closer the adult rate should be judged “ against the critical goal of protecting youth employment”. This should be matched with increased simplicity for companies, with a single digital gateway leading to all the schemes set up to help young workers, and more clarity on help for workers with disabilities. All this would be united in a so-called youth opportunity test, under which any future tax or regulatory policy changes would look at their effect on young workers, set out in a law. 4. Education and training The report notes that this is a long-term issue, with many of the indicators of future Neet status, such as low attainment and poor attendance, being clear during childhood. Milburn also says that while countries with low Neet rates take vocational skills seriously, in England “technical education has too often been regarded as for somebody else’s child”. Among changes the report recommends are: More investment in early years provision, such as family hubs, and individual support in school if a student is seen as being at “material risk of disengagement”. Less use of school exclusion where possible. The report notes that the Netherlands has a permanent exclusion rate 73% lower than England’s. More focus in school on preparedness for work, as well as passing exams. More investment in further education and in apprenticeships, with greater financial incentives for employers who hire apprentices. University courses “must be able to demonstrate clear value for learners, employers and the wider economy,” with funding withdrawn for poorly performing examples. 5.

events.title: Chalmers proposes rules to allow super to invest in housing, energy, startups
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Jim Chalmers announces plan to let super funds place riskier investments in housing, energy, startups Treasurer Jim Chalmers will announce long-awaited changes to super investment rules. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) Super funds will be allowed to invest 5 per cent of their portfolio in longer-term assets such as housing projects and venture capital, under a new proposal. Funds would remain obligated to prioritise their members' best interests and will not be required to use the new option, or be directed towards any particular asset class. It is unclear how many funds will use the new category. Super funds will be able to take riskier, longer-term bets with their members' money, in an overhaul of fund rules which Treasurer Jim Chalmers hopes will promote investment in housing, energy and startups. Under changes to the performance test, a benchmarking exercise introduced by former treasurer Josh Frydenberg, Mr Chalmers will propose to let super funds invest 5 per cent in so-called "emerging assets" with a lower minimum return. The intention is to allow funds to choose investments which may have low or uncertain returns today but higher returns tomorrow, such as early-stage housing developments or renewable projects or venture capital funds. Funds will not be required to invest in housing, energy or any sector, or to use the new option at all, and their obligation to invest in members' best interest would not change. But the move hands a win to some industry super funds who have argued the current benchmarks, measured relative to average stock market returns year by year, have prevented them from making long-term investments with irregular return patterns. It also fulfils a longstanding ambition of Mr Chalmers to leverage the vast pool of funds tied up in super — nearly $5 trillion — to support national priorities, first articulated in a 2022 speech on whether "workers' capital" could help "to solve our biggest challenges". New class of investments would not need to be Australian The Coalition and One Nation have positioned against any such move, described by Shadow Assistant Treasurer Kevin Hogan on Tuesday in advance of this announcement as "treating your super like a piggy bank for its pet projects". But not only does the measure not direct super funds towards any particular sector, the proposal will not require the "emerging assets" to be Australian assets. That would have required a specific rule, since super funds face no general requirement to invest in Australia or any particular jurisdiction. While the move was welcomed by ASFA in a statement, and some super funds had wanted there to be no cap on their use of emerging assets, it is also unclear how many funds will use the new category. Super funds have already sought to get involved in some housing projects in Australia, such as the super-backed Assemble build-to-rent housing project in Kensington. ( Supplied: Assemble Communities ) In a submission to Treasury's consultation process, industry fund Australian Super said it did not believe the current super performance test was "constraining [its] investment in the types of assets canvassed", such as housing, energy or venture capital. One area where possible investment has been envisaged is in investor-owned housing projects (such as so-called "build-to-rent" developments), which are common in the US but less so in Australia, and which the government has tried to encourage. Venture capital funds are prime candidates because they often group together several startups, some of which will fail and others of which may have large pay-offs after a few years. Those investments would risk failing the existing benchmarks. Rather than the average returns of a benchmark portfolio, the new benchmark for emerging assets would be equal to inflation plus some additional return premium, which would be set under advice from the independent Australian Government Actuary. Treasury says performance test has improved outcomes The performance test was introduced after a Productivity Commission inquiry found some super products were failing their members, who were often too disengaged to shop around for a better fund. It compares a fund's returns over a ten-year window with a comparable portfolio, such as the S&P/ASX300 for Australian equity investments. The test also assesses whether the product fees are comparable to other similar super products. Are the super wars another Mediscare? A political war over superannuation has been inflamed in the past fortnight.

events.title: Where every US governor and governor-elect stands on AI and the data-center boom
events.summary: Some state governors are bigger advocates for AI and data centers than others. Getty Images This year's midterm elections saw a blue wave sweep over the US and an artificial intelligence and data center backlash. The outcome of several gubernatorial races depended on the candidates' views on AI and data centers. Both current and incoming US governors' views range from exploring an AI "kill switch" to welcoming data centers. It was up to voters whether artificial intelligence and data centers would play a role in the outcome of the coming midterm elections , and the jury is out: It did . The AI boom — and the infrastructure needed to power it — has slowly become a flash point in US politics. The debate ranges from AI safety, regulation, and deepfakes to the rapid expansion of data centers . Many Big Tech firms advocate for faster expansion, while local residents have pushed back against data-center projects over their potential environmental and energy-cost impacts. That has left voters with big questions: What roles should state and federal governments play in regulating AI? And how much power should local communities have over the data centers increasingly being built in their backyards? Governors across the political spectrum — 17 of whom were up for reelection this year — and their opposing gubernatorial candidates have taken varied approaches to the AI boom. Some governors, including outgoing California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) and New York's Kathy Hochul (D), are exploring an AI " kill switch " to disable advanced AI systems in the event of an out-of-control situation. Republican Utah Gov. Spencer Cox has also called for federal AI safety rules. Others, including the Republican governors of Nevada and North Dakota and the Democratic governors of Michigan and New Mexico — whose states have major AI-computing projects under construction — see data centers as an economic opportunity. Following this year's blue wave, Goldman Sachs economists predict that the Democratic wins at the state and local levels will likely lead to "short-term data center moratoria, potentially affecting about 45% of planned US data center capacity expansion." Here's what every sitting and incoming US governor has said so far about AI, data centers, or both. Alabama Kay Ivey is the governor of Alabama. Tommy Tuberville is the governor-elect. Getty Images During his campaign, Alabama governor-elect Tommy Tuberville (R) campaigned for data center developers to pay their own electricity, infrastructure, and water costs. He has also pushed for locals' ability to reject data center projects. He has not, however, laid out his opinions on AI as publicly. Outgoing Gov. Kay Ivey (R) has approached AI as an opportunity to improve government, but one that needs guardrails. In 2024, she created a statewide generative AI task force to examine how it could be used within the state government, emphasizing AI use while prioritizing transparency, privacy, and public safety. "GenAI represents a monumental step forward in the potential for our state government to serve the public," Ivey said in a 2024 statement . "However, its capabilities must first be studied carefully to ensure it is implemented in the most responsible and efficient manner possible." She is one of the few governors across the US who have taken a harder line on Chinese AI tools. In 2025, Ivey issued a ban on Chinese-affiliated artificial intelligence platforms DeepSeek and Manus from all state-owned devices and networks. Alaska Michael Dunleavy is the governor of Alaska. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is the governor-elect. Getty Images During his campaign , Alaska's incoming Democratic governor, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, ran against current governor Mike Dunleavy's idea that Alaska's cold weather could make it an AI and data center destination. Kreiss-Tomkins has said that he supports a temporary moratorium on new facilities until the state legislature creates rules requiring developers to cover energy and infrastructure costs. He has also called for guardrails around AI surveillance, deepfakes, and fraud. Outgoing, term-limited Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) has pitched the state as a potential hub for the AI boom and the computing infrastructure it requires, arguing that Alaska has an "arctic advantage." Dunleavy has said he believes Alaska's colder climate can significantly reduce the cost of cooling AI server racks, saying in late 2025 that an Alaskan 1-gigawatt campus could save operators up to $150 million annually in cooling costs compared to a warmer state. Dunleavy has also said that data centers could be an economic driver for Alaska, particularly by creating more construction jobs across the state. He frequently uses AI, too , incorporating certain tools into his work as governor, including using the technology during meetings. Arizona Katie Hobbs is the governor of Arizona. Mario Tama/Getty Images Katie Hobbs (D), Arizona's governor up for reelection, has largely framed AI as an economic opportunity that the state needs to prepare for, rather than turn away from. Hobbs has said she does not support a moratorium , which is a temporary pause, on new data-center development. At the same time, she has pushed for more structure around AI. Her administration created the state's first AI steering committee in 2025 and launched an AI government tool in 2026, and she has described the goal as ensuring AI strengthens rather than undermines the state's economy. "Arizona has built one of the strongest AI ecosystems in the country, and our community colleges help power it," Hobbs wrote in a January 22 post on X. Arkansas Sarah Huckabee Sanders is the governor of Arkansas. USDA Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders (R), who is up for reelection, has said she believes AI has the potential to strengthen government efficiency, but it requires proper policies and regulations. "AI is changing how we work, interact, and find information — and Arkansas can't afford to be left behind," she wrote in a statement in February following a new state AI effectiveness and safety report . The report, which was completed by an AI working group that Sanders launched in 2024, found that AI could help the state improve Medicaid and SNAP programs and expand other digital services. Earlier this year, she also joined RAISE US, a national artificial intelligence initiative launched by former Indiana governor Eric Holcomb and former US Secretary of Commerce Gina Raimondo. The initiative intends to partner with governors, employers, workers and training organizations to help the workforce transition to an AI economy. events.title: Iran escalates threats as third U.S. carrier arrives in Middle East, tanker struck in Hormuz
events.summary: Iran has ratcheted up threats against U.S. forces and commercial shipping. A third U.S. aircraft carrier has arrived in the Gulf, adding to American firepower. Washington may have "misread" Iranians' capacity to resist as Tehran intensifies efforts to disrupt the critical shipping chokepoint: analyst. Iran has ratcheted up threats against U.S. forces and commercial shipping as a third American aircraft carrier arrived in the Gulf, stoking fears of renewed escalation in the nine-month conflict . Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy warned shipping companies against using the U.S.-backed southern route through the Strait of Hormuz, describing it as fully closed and a "minefield of fire," according to regional media outlets citing a statement from the force. Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akrami-Nia, a spokesperson for the Iranian Army, said the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen until "the enemy accepts Iran's conditions." Separately, CNN reported Monday that new U.S. intelligence indicated Iran was developing plans that could target senior Trump administration officials with a so-called dirty bomb, or a chemical weapon in Washington, D.C. CNBC cannot immediately verify the report. The intelligence was characterized as an effort by Iran to develop options rather than evidence of an imminent attack, CNN reported. U.S. officials have held several meetings over the past week to consider how to respond to the potential threat. The heightened security concerns come after Iranian threats prompted Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to relocate to military housing last week. "We remain vigilant, monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland," a White House spokesperson said in a statement to CNBC. Oil prices inched lower in Asian trading Tuesday, with international benchmark Brent crude futures dropping 0.7% to $91.8 a barrel and U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures falling 0.7% to $85.1 a barrel. On Tuesday, the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations said a tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile in the Strait of Hormuz and subsequently caught fire. The agency did not say who was responsible and urged vessels to transit with caution and report suspicious activity. Separately, the Iranian navy said four oil tankers had struck mines and caught fire in the eastern Strait of Hormuz over the previous 24 hours. The escalation in Tehran's rhetoric came as the USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived in the Gulf region on Sunday, joining the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington. That added to U.S. firepower near Iran even as President Donald Trump said the war was winding down. Trump has sent mixed signals regarding the conflict in recent weeks, alternating between declaring it could soon end and warning of renewed large-scale strikes if efforts to reach a deal fail. After meeting Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani last week, Trump said the war with Iran could end "fairly soon," adding that it "militarily is effectively over." Tehran said Sunday that it launched six drones at a U.S. air-defense radar at Bahrain's Riffa air base, the second attack Iran claimed against the kingdom in three days. Bahrain's military said it intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks. Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks in a call Monday with Bahraini Foreign Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani and reaffirmed Washington's commitment to the security of Bahrain and other Gulf partners. The conflict began in late February when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran, prompting Tehran to retaliate with strikes on Israel and Gulf states hosting American military bases. Indirect talks between Washington and Tehran through Qatar have since appeared to run into a stalemate as warring powers disagreed over terms to reach a lasting peace deal. Washington appears unwilling to accept several of Iran's demands to end the war, including lifting the U.S. naval blockade on its southern ports and lifting sanctions, while stressing that Iran cannot possess a nuclear weapon. Iran is likely to continue escalating attacks on tankers and container ships, along with occasional strikes on U.S. military targets, in an effort to pressure Washington into offering concessions, said Ian Bremmer, president and founder of Eurasia Group. In response, Washington will likely expand its blockade on Iran's maritime and inland trade routes, he said. "The presumption is that eventually Iran can't handle the economic pressure and will accept better terms," Bremmer said, calling that view a "misread of the Iranian leadership and their capacity to resist." Over the coming year, Iran is likely to intensify efforts to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, Bremmer said.

events.title: Tim Cook's advice for handling disagreements — and how you can use it at work
events.summary: Former Apple CEO Tim Cook said it's even more important to engage with people when you disagree with them. David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Ana Altchek; Alyssa Powell/BI Former Apple CEO Tim Cook has a longtime practice of engaging with people he disagrees with. Picking up the phone has paid off in securing Apple's exemption from various tariffs. If you ignore disagreements and let tension build, you're avoiding fixing the problem. Get better at: Handling conflict Today's move When you disagree with a coworker, your first instinct may be to avoid them — but former Apple CEO Tim Cook has another suggestion: have a conversation. In a 2023 interview with GQ, Cook described his philosophy as "engagement." He said that it's even more important to speak with people when you disagree with them. Why it works While Cook wasn't known for meddling in politics or controversy, he had a record of talking things out with people when disagreements came up. That has paid off on several occasions. For example, in 2019, President Donald Trump said Cook was the only tech leader to call him personally, rather than hiring someone else to do it. That had a direct impact on Apple. Cook's discussions with Trump helped secure  some of Apple's products  from various tariffs. The former Apple CEO also managed to get Elon Musk from criticizing Apple on X to touring its campus in under a week. Try it today Instead of letting the tension build with a coworker you disagree with, ask to speak with them. Go into that conversation with the goal of understanding their perspective before you try to change it. The bottom line You can't fix problems that you're not willing to speak about. By listening to the other person's perspective, you might walk away with a better understanding of their opinion and more information. Plus, having a conversation creates an opportunity to solve the problem, rather than putting it off or pretending it doesn't exist. Source This insight is drawn from Business Insider's reporting about Tim Cook meeting with Elon Musk and Donald Trump during disagreements. Read the full story about it from Sindhu Sundar here . It also references a 2023 interview with Tim Cook, published in GQ . How have you approached disagreements at work? Tell us what you think of Cook's leadership advice in the comments below. events.title: US government confirms investigation into tech firm Megaspeed
events.summary: The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China. In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024. It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions. Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair , allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies. Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs. Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business. The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation. Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations". In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list. Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time. Alice Huang and Jensen Huang pictured together in Taiwan in June 2024 Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed. The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed. On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips. Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips. While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls. Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair. The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia. The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance. Trump downplays warnings of AI risks, citing rivalry with China In the statement, the US government said it would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred". They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge."
