events.title: Is Pakistan about to carve out new provinces? Inside the controversial plan
events.summary: Talk of new provinces has gathered pace, but there is no formal proposal or agreement among governing parties. Islamabad, Pakistan – Pakistan’s defence minister has said the country could have multiple new provinces as early as the New Year. “My own view is that New Year will see this, the new system also, God willing,” Khwaja Asif told a private news channel programme this week. list 1 of 4 How would Pakistan’s 27th Amendment reshape its military and courts? list 2 of 4 Pakistan’s Punjab allows ‘secret’ terrorism trials: Why it’s controversial list 3 of 4 Pakistan passes amendment empowering parliament to pick top judge list 4 of 4 Will Pakistan’s defence overhaul strengthen or upset its military balance? Asif, a senior leader of the governing Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) party, was discussing proposals to carve new provinces out of the existing four: Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) and Balochistan. But Asif stressed that he was offering his own assessment. “I have no inside information at this time, and even if I did, obviously I cannot spill it over on a show,” he said. Nearly four months after Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi first pitched the idea publicly, the proposal appears to be gaining steam. Yet no draft constitutional amendment, agreed number of provinces or timetable have been made public. Here is what we know about the proposal, the constitutional process, the referendum being discussed to implement it and the concerns raised by political parties: What is being proposed and why now? At an economic summit in Islamabad on July 30, Naqvi, considered a close confidant of military chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, said Pakistan needed new administrative units to improve governance. “Unless units are made and they take ownership and a new leadership comes, this will not happen,” he said. Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal has spoken of 12 to 15 provinces to be created through consensus. Supporters argue that the four provinces are too large to deliver services effectively to a population of about 250 million and a constitutional amendment in 2010 aimed at decentralising powers and resources to districts and cities has not been effective. “Powers and resources were taken in the name of the people and parked in the chief minister’s house. That is exactly why there is talk of smaller administrative units,” Mustafa Kamal, the federal health minister and a leader of the Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P), Sindh’s second-largest party, said in television interviews this week. But Kamal said the federal cabinet had not formally discussed the matter. Asked how many new units were planned, he said he did not know. “I am also hearing all these things, watching everything, but officially I do not know at all,” he said. Malik Ahmad Khan, the Punjab Assembly speaker and a PML-N leader, told Al Jazeera that Asif had not explained his timeline. Kamal, however, pointed to the political calendar: Elections for the Senate, the upper chamber of Pakistan’s Parliament, are due early next year, followed by the federal budget. “December is a very important month. There are Senate elections ahead. After that, the budget will come in June, so whatever has to happen has to happen before that,” he said. How can Pakistan create new provinces? Pakistan’s Constitution recognises four provinces but has no separate procedure for creating new ones. The debate, therefore, centres on Article 239, which governs constitutional amendments. An amendment requires two-thirds of the total membership of each house of parliament: 224 of the 336 National Assembly members and 64 of the 96 senators. Under Article 239(4), an amendment changing a province’s boundaries must also win two-thirds support in that province’s assembly before it goes to the president for assent. That would require, for example, 248 of the 371 members in the Punjab Assembly and 112 of the 168 in the Provincial Assembly of Sindh. “With this specific system in place in the constitution”, no other “route can be used” to try to carve out provinces, Abdul Moiz Jaferii, a Karachi-based constitutional lawyer, told Al Jazeera. There has been an earlier attempt. In May 2012, the Punjab Assembly unanimously adopted two resolutions moved by Rana Sanaullah, the then-provincial law minister and now an adviser to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, calling for a South Punjab province and the restoration of Bahawalpur province. In March 2013, the Senate passed a constitutional amendment bill to create a Bahawalpur Janoobi Punjab province. But it lapsed days later when the National Assembly’s term ended without the lower house taking it up. Jaferii also questioned whether creating new provinces would necessarily improve governance. “New provinces would not in and of themselves make government work better. They would allow for smaller administrative units, which in theory are easier to manage.

events.title: Ikea ditches plans for new UK stores, blaming high business taxes
events.summary: Retailer’s British boss says John Healey ‘missed opportunity to back retailers’ in October’s budget Ikea has ditched some planned store openings in the UK blaming the cost of business taxes , which it said were the highest in Europe. As its annual UK sales little more than flatlined at the Swedish flatpack furniture retailer, its UK boss, David McCabe, said: “There are locations where we were planning to open a new unit, and those plans have been abandoned due to the cost that we experience and the complexity within the market. “I would hope that we’re able to bring those projects back to life,” he added. “But it’s a very real impact here in the UK, when those investments will go to other countries in Europe.” The planned investments were smaller UK stores, but the retailer declined to comment on exact locations. Ikea has been pushing further into smaller high street shops , rather than its traditional out-of-town outlets. Ikea’s UK arm pays the most business taxes of its operations in Europe, and the third highest in the world, after the US and China, he said. The retailer’s UK sales edged 0.5% higher to £2.26bn in the year to the end of August. Sales rose 4.7% in the first four months of the year but fell in the second half as weak confidence and “sustained pressure” on household budgets led consumers to pull back on big purchases. McCabe said he had talked to customers in stores in recent weeks who were planning to replace an entire bedroom, but then decided to just buy one or two smaller pieces of furniture and a refresh with new textiles to save money. “We are seeing a change in the way that customers shop and we do anticipate a difficult period going forward,” he said. “We don’t think that there’s going to be a sudden, miraculous turnaround in confidence.” McCabe described John Healey’s recent budget as a “missed opportunity to back retailers under real pressure”, but said Ikea continued to talk to the government. The company has spent £54m on reducing prices by an average of 20% on 425 products, including its popular Billy bookcase , Hemnes daybed and the cantilever Poäng armchair. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Ikea is using seasonal offers to pull in customers, for example discounts on extendable dining tables, folding chairs and soft toys in the run-up to Christmas. McCabe said smaller stores, between 1,000 and 2,000 sq metres, had been popular with customers, in sites such as Oxford Street in London and retail parks. As well as the Oxford Street shop which opened within the former Topshop flagship site, Ikea opened stores in Brighton, Norwich and York last year, followed by a small store in Chester. It also opened a “plan and order” site – dedicated to kitchen, bedroom, and living room planning – in Dundee, and one in Aberdeen last month.

events.title: UK music industry hits record high of £8.4bn – but are working musicians being left behind?
events.summary: Major tours by the likes of Oasis helped make 2025 a lucrative year, with music export revenue reaching £4.8bn Major tours by Oasis, Robbie Williams and Dua Lipa, as well as hit albums by the likes of Olivia Dean, have helped to push the UK music industry to record revenues. But there are concerns over a widening gulf in income between A-listers such as these, and the less well-known artists that form the bulk of the UK’s music community. The annual report by UK Music, an umbrella organisation featuring various industry bodies, finds that music added £8.4bn to the UK economy in 2025, a record figure and an inflation-outpacing rise of 5.7% from the previous year. Export revenue rose 3.6%, to £4.8bn, encompassing money made outside the UK by British artists – including via international touring and royalties and revenues raised from sales and streaming of music abroad. There was also a slight rise in employment in the sector in the UK: 730 jobs were added, to take total recorded employment to 220,500. The success is powered in part by a live music sector in which stadium performances – once the preserve of only the very top artists – are becoming increasingly commonplace, with consumers willing to spend three-figure sums on tickets. However, the This Is Music report cautioned that “many emerging and grassroots artists experienced rising costs which reduced net incomes, and even well-known artists have found it hard to make money”. The report highlights a number of hit albums by UK artists that have helped boost recorded music revenues – including No 1s by Sleep Token, Yungblud, Sam Fender, Wet Leg, and Biffy Clyro – but also highlighted a troubling trend. In terms of album consumption figures, UK artists had historically been more popular than US ones in the domestic marketplace, but US artists overtook UK ones in 2018 and their popularity has continued to diverge, levelling out somewhat in 2025 thanks in part to blockbuster hits by Dean, Fender and others. AI also threatens to divert listeners’ attention away from human artists, with the report warning: “AI generated ‘slop’ and deepfakes are an increasing problem, which is reflected in a dramatic increase in takedown notices for AI deepfakes issued by labels,” referring to songs taken down from streaming services for imitating existing artists. There was a marked difference between two sets of data the study used to monitor the income of artists. A survey of the accounts for “top and mid-level” artists found that these musicians were flush, their earnings rising more than 14% year on year. But the Music Creators’ Survey, which asks musicians (including artists, songwriters, producers, composers and more) to self-report their income, found growth of just 0.2% in the same period. “It has never been easier to record and release music, but given the intense level of competition that has ensued, it has never been more difficult to establish a profile and build a scalable career,” reads the report. “This makes life especially tough for many music creators with average earnings. “Once artists and music creators break through beyond a certain level, more options and better terms of business can enhance their careers very significantly, but the challenge remains developing more artists and creators to that level.” UK Music is made up of industry bodies, including royalty agencies PRS for Music and PPL; the BPI, the collective body for the UK’s record labels; AIM, which represents the independent label sector; plus the Musicians’ Union and more. Tom Kiehl, UK Music’s chief executive, used the report’s launch to lobby the government on a range of issues. “The government must use the upcoming UK EU summit on 20 November to work to remove barriers to EU exports,” he said. “It must not give AI a free pass and should support a sustainably funded BBC – and deliver economic growth for music in every postcode. He added: “We are not simply asking government to act. We stand ready to be part of the solution too. The UK music industry has never lacked talent, ambition or creativity. The challenge now is ensuring the right environment exists for those strengths to flourish. If we get that right, the opportunities ahead are enormous.” Ian Murray, creative industries minister, highlighted government funding schemes such as the Music Growth Package and said: “We are investing in the grassroots infrastructure, talent pipeline and independent businesses that keep the sector competitive.” Some of the UK’s most successful acts are already eyeing a potentially lucrative 2027. Oasis will head back out on tour after the blockbuster success of their 2025 reunion, playing 11 different locations across the UK, Europe and North America; Dua Lipa has been announced as a headliner of Coachella festival and is expected to release a fourth studio album; and Sam Fender has announced the Proper Massive tour, with 12 UK and Ireland stadium dates plus major venues in North America.

events.title: Up to 99% of UK civil servants rely on Microsoft for comms, minister admits
events.summary: As many as 99 percent of Britain's civil servants rely on Microsoft to communicate, a government minister has admitted, days after Redmond demonstrated the perils of putting quite so many eggs in one basket. Ian Murray, minister for creative industries, media and online safety, laid bare the extent of Whitehall's Microsoft habit in the House of Commons on Monday, where MPs were also told that the public sector shelled out £1.9 billion on Microsoft licenses in 2024-25 alone . "We know that 98% to 99% of civil servants use Microsoft as their platform for communications, which is incredibly high," Murray told MPs . The admission followed last week's 18-hour Microsoft 365 outage , which left businesses unable to carry out transactions, public sector workers struggling to do their jobs, and even MPs unable to access their usual means of communication. Rebecca Paul, shadow technology secretary, said at least 47 NHS trusts experienced problems, with some services having to fall back on pen and paper. The Conservative MP, who cited the £1.9 billion licensing bill, pressed Murray on whether the government would seek contractual remedies from Microsoft. Murray said the government was unaware of any delays to NHS treatment or instances in which patients had been put at risk. Emergency departments remained open, and 999 services continued to operate. Only two NHS trusts activated incident response units, the minister said. The outage, which affected 74 countries, has since been blamed on a software update Microsoft rolled out in July . A surge in Teams traffic hit infrastructure already short of server capacity, exposing the months-old bug. More than 80 percent of the servers in the affected gateway stopped responding, leaving Redmond's engineers scrambling to fix their previous fix. Much of Monday's discussion centered on how the UK had allowed itself to become so dependent on a handful of American technology companies in the first place. Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of Parliament's Science and Technology Committee, pointed out that the government had been unable to tell her committee how much it spends on IT and which suppliers it uses. She also challenged ministers over their reluctance to embrace open source software, something both France and Germany have pursued to loosen Big Tech's grip on their public sectors. “Germany has 500,000 civil servants using open source products and services, but the government told my Committee that though open source could address vendor lock-in, they would not include open source targets because of a lack of what was called ‘commercial accountability’,” she said. Paul, meanwhile, reminded Murray that just last month the government had rejected the committee's recommendation to introduce supplier diversification targets. Murray conceded that the government's extensive dealings with Microsoft probably result in "vendor lock-in," but defended the arrangement, saying it gives Whitehall access to the latest technology at scale. The admission comes less than a week after research from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) revealed just how little of the British public sector's IT budget ends up in British hands . Of the £19.2 billion spent with the public sector's 150 biggest technology suppliers in 2024-25, just 15 percent went to businesses headquartered and owned in the UK, with a predominantly British workforce and which weren't reselling overseas technology. American companies took home almost twice as much as suppliers from all other foreign countries combined. Murray said the government intends to use its considerable purchasing power to give British businesses a leg up. Its national cloud infrastructure program will see departments procure cloud services collectively rather than individually, with the intention of giving more suppliers a crack at lucrative government contracts. Whitehall has also set up a technology risk group and a central IT operations function to scrutinize outages and work out what needs fixing across the public sector. Ministers intend to press Microsoft on how it plans to prevent a repeat of last week's cock-up and whether it can get services back online more quickly next time. The government, however, offered no timetable for weaning civil servants off Microsoft's software, nor did Murray commit to targets for adopting open-source alternatives. Redmond's days as Whitehall's IT supplier of choice hardly look numbered. ®

events.title: Bangladesh police clash with garment workers amid protests over wages
events.summary: Protesters hurl bricks, torch vehicles and block the main highway between the capital, Dhaka, and the key financial district, Mymensingh. Bangladeshi police have fired tear gas and stun grenades at thousands of garment workers protesting after a key wage board meeting was postponed. Protesters on Tuesday hurled bricks, torched vehicles and blocked the main highway between the capital, Dhaka, and the key financial district of Mymensingh. list 1 of 3 Ten killed in fire at beach resort in Bangladesh list 2 of 3 Bangladesh prosecutor warns Hasina faces execution if she returns list 3 of 3 Sheikh Hasina must return to Bangladesh to face her sentence Bangladesh is the world’s second-biggest garment exporter behind China, producing clothes for big international brands, including Fruit of the Loom and Levi Strauss. But growing worker unrest over wages, which began last month, has disrupted the industry that generates $38bn annually and employs more than four million people. Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($240) – a 140-percent increase on the current 12,500 taka, as they struggle to cope with rising food, housing, transport and healthcare costs. About 500 of the country’s 4,500 garment factories are shut, sources told the AFP news agency, further stoking unrest among workers. A “no work, no pay” provision in the country’s labour laws allows factory owners to suspend operations and withhold wages when production is disrupted. “The owners seem unwilling to meet our salary demands. They are already dragging their feet,” one worker, Khanom, 24, told AFP. Tensions were also running high in the garment hubs of Savar and Ashulia on Dhaka’s outskirts. The wage board , comprising representatives of employers and workers, was set up by the government earlier this month to negotiate a pay rise. The new minimum wage would be announced in December and take effect in January next year. “We want to return to our machines,” garment worker Rakib, 28, told AFP. “We are not sure if the wage board members are aware of our demands,” he said, adding that workers feared their concerns might not be reflected in the revised wage proposal. Most factories had opened on Tuesday morning, but were shut down as protests spread to the highway, Rakib said. In a joint statement, the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) called for a resumption of wage negotiations as soon as possible. A wage board meeting scheduled for Monday was postponed after a member representing the garment workers said he was unwell, a BGMEA source told AFP. The next meeting would be held on November 23, the board said. In the wake of Tuesday’s protest, Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) stepped up patrols across the industrial zone, deploying hundreds of personnel. “BGB headquarters has been closely observing the situation from a monitoring cell,” it said in a statement. The force said it was also using drones, body-worn cameras and other devices to keep a close watch on demonstrations.

events.title: U.S. gets another D+ on premature births
events.summary: Data: National Center for Health Statistics via March of Dimes; Map: Carly Mallenbaum/Axios The U.S. earned a D+ for its preterm birth rate yet again , according to the latest March of Dimes report card . Why it matters: Babies born before 37 weeks of pregnancy face greater risks of serious health complications, hospitalization and death in their first year of life. By the numbers: The national preterm birth rate remained at 10.4% in 2025 for the fourth year in a row. It marked the fifth consecutive year at D+ (which March of Dimes considers 10.4% to 10.7%). Zoom in: Mississippi had the highest rate at 14.9%. Vermont had the lowest at 8%. Rates improved in 23 states and jurisdictions, including D.C. and Puerto Rico, per the report that relies on CDC data. But only Idaho, South Dakota and Puerto Rico recorded statistically significant declines. Between the lines: Rising rates of chronic health conditions before pregnancy are one reason the nation's preterm birth rate remains stubbornly high, Michael Warren, chief medical and health officer of March of Dimes, tells Axios. High blood pressure and diabetes became more common among women giving birth in 2025. Both conditions increase the risk of pregnancy complications and premature birth. What they're saying: "It's not just about improving care during labor and delivery," Warren says. "It's really about improving their health across the life course." That means addressing chronic conditions even before pregnancy. What we're watching: Whether strategies including expanding access to doula care and encouraging low-dose aspirin use among pregnant women at risk for preeclampsia can help bring down preterm birth rates.

events.title: Satya Nadella has one piece of career advice for software engineers in the AI era: Do more, talk less
events.summary: Satya Nadella said Microsoft launched a "preceptorship" program to help early-career engineers learn to work with AI. Dimitar DILKOFF / AFP via Getty Images Satya Nadella says software engineers should get hands-on experience building with AI. Microsoft launched a "preceptorship" program to help early-career engineers learn to work with AI. Nadella said that a "new software engineering" is emerging. Satya Nadella has tips for software engineers who are anxious about AI. Speaking on an episode of "The Pragmatic Engineer" podcast released on Monday, the Microsoft CEO said that one of the best ways for early-career software engineers to learn in the AI era is to get on a team building with the technology. "It's just not about the hype cycle, and that constant need to talk," Nadella told podcast host Gergely Orosz. "But it's do more, learn more, and hands-on experience — experience it firsthand." "If one piece of advice, whether you're mid-career or even a CEO like me or a fresh college grad, the more you can take the time to sort of learn to do, be in teams that are doing, the better it is versus, I think, anything else," Nadella added. Nadella's advice comes as software engineering hiring shows signs of rebounding, but opportunities remain uneven. Nearly 69.3% of US software development job postings in the first quarter of 2026 were for senior-level positions, up from 54.5% in early 2019, according to Indeed data. Nadella said that companies need to create more opportunities for junior workers to learn these new ways of building software. "I care a lot about, hey, can you have an early-career person come in, join one of these teams, go up the learning curve," Nadella said. "So what's the new form of that is what I think we have to really discover." Nadella said Microsoft recently launched PRAISE, or Preceptorship for AI-accelerated Software Engineering, with Carnegie Mellon University. The program pairs early-career engineers with senior mentors to build AI-assisted development skills. "In a world where code generation has become cheap, what has become hard is verification," Nadella said. "There's just so much, I would say, new type of tribal knowledge people are building up in managing complex software projects." "There's an entire new way to build that is emerging, and it's new software engineering," Nadella added, "And it requires software engineers." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The $200,000 woman: How donors' tissue is turned into boob jobs and butt lifts
events.summary: Getty Images; Alyssa Powell/BI Sometime before May, somewhere near St. Louis, Missouri, a 45-year-old woman died. By the end of July, nearly 8 pounds of fat had been cut off her body, frozen, shipped to Texas, run through a meat grinder, processed with chemicals to remove her genetic material, centrifuged several times, and packed into more than 70 syringe-like tubes. The containers were blasted with gamma radiation, packed into dozens of yellow boxes, and shipped to plastic surgeons' offices. Her fat had been turned into alloClae, a hot, new injectable product being used to lift butts, augment breasts, and fill in hip dips for deep-pocketed patients across the country. It was enough to supply procedures that would cost around $200,000, a Business Insider investigation found. Human tissue can generate enormous revenue. Documents reviewed by Business Insider offer the first detailed look at the economics of alloClae, and reveal how its for-profit producer, Tiger Biosciences, turns a few pounds of donated tissue into a product used for procedures that can cost tens of thousands of dollars. The reporting sheds new light on the commercial value of a human body after death, and includes never-before-reported details on the money being made from processing human tissue into cosmetic products. Under US law, donors and their families can't be paid. The recovery and processing of tissue is a multibillion-dollar industry in the US. Tissue recovered from a single donor — most commonly skin, bone, and corneas, but sometimes also tendons and ligaments, veins, or heart valves — can be worth tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars to companies like Tiger, depending on the cost to recover and process them. Donated tissue is used in skin grafts for burn victims, reconstructive surgery for breast cancer survivors, and replacement valves for heart patients. For decades, it has also been used in cosmetic surgery, including cartilage for nose jobs and skin for breast augmentations. Now, a new family of injectable cosmetic products made from human tissue can be administered in under an hour. AlloClae is not alone. At least two other US companies make injectable cosmetic products from cadaver fat. And in South Korea, at least 10 companies are making or planning beauty injections made from ground-up skin, largely from US donors. Tiger Biosciences co-CEO Oliver Burckhardt told staff earlier this year that the company was betting big on alloClae and other products made from cadaver fat. "I mean, in 30 years I've been doing this right now, I never had a more amazing technology," he said. Tiger's chief legal officer, Larry Wood Jr., told Business Insider its reporting was "neither accurate nor fair." He declined to specify what was inaccurate. He also said Business Insider had obtained confidential information. Wounded Tiger Since hitting the market in 2024, alloClae has been a hot commodity at the offices of exclusive plastic surgeons, whose patients are willing to spend six figures on some alloClae procedures. It is partly about convenience. No longer do patients wanting a boob job or a butt lift have to undergo general anesthesia. The rise in GLP-1 weight-loss drugs has fueled demand for alloClae. Patients come in not only for Ozempic face — but also for deflated breasts, hips, and butts. Some doctors have had to queue up on wait lists to obtain alloClae. The product has become a minor plot point in two Real Housewives franchises. Plastic surgeons have called it "liquid gold," "pure gold on demand," and "revolutionary." For its manufacturer, Tiger Biosciences, alloClae could be a life preserver. Heading into 2026, Tiger's top revenue stream was from wound-care products made from donated birth tissue. Then Tiger and several other businesses were sent reeling by the federal government's decision to slash Medicare spending on skin substitutes. Tiger conducted layoffs and projected in April that its sales would fall 75% this year compared to last year, according to an internal company presentation. In the April staff meeting, Burckhardt outlined a new strategy, according to a recording of the meeting reviewed by Business Insider. To get back to profitability, he said, the company would focus on alloClae and other products derived from cadaver fat, also known as adipose tissue. A slide in Burckhardt's presentation described alloClae as "high-growth," "high-margin" and "high-demand." Burckhardt described it as a cornerstone of the company's revenue moving forward. First, the company needs more tissue. "Without tissue, we don't have a sales strategy," Burckhardt said in the April staff meeting. Tiger Biosciences co-CEO Oliver Burckhardt presented at a staff meeting in April. Obtained by Business Insider Tiger was working on securing more supply, Burckhardt said. He outlined a strategy to win over additional suppliers — the largely nonprofit organ procurement organizations and tissue banks that recover tissue from donors. "We need to drive awareness for natural beauty products so that the overall tissue recovery community understands what we do with the tissue that we are collecting and what our values are," he said. events.title: Rogue Agents Hacked His Company. Why Is Clément Delangue So Optimistic About AI?
events.summary: Clément Delangue, CEO of the open-source AI company Hugging Face , may go down in history as one of the first people ever attacked by a rogue AI agent. His company, which hosts millions of AI models and datasets, was breached in July when hundreds of agents being tested by OpenAI broke free from their sandbox and went on a hacking spree. As the agents worked at superhuman speed to probe and exploit systems, Hugging Face confronted a bewildering deluge of data. The company’s engineers were only able to analyze the attack by using an open-weight model called GLM 5.2 from a Chinese company called Z.ai . Delangue moved to the US more than a decade ago, “barely speaking English,” and built Hugging Face into a platform that supports tens of millions of AI developers. The fresh-faced Frenchman, who dresses even more like a skater than most AI execs, says the summer attack highlighted the value of open-weight models, which unlike ChatGPT or Claude can be downloaded and run by anyone. Despite championing the democratization of AI, however, Hugging Face was acquired by one of the industry’s biggest players, Nvidia, for $12.93 billion in September. When I caught up with Delangue recently, that was the subject of my first question. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. CLÉMENT DELANGUE: We need more resources to give open-source AI a chance. It has grown really well in the past few years and has become a really credible alternative to closed-source APIs. But the field is still dominated by closed-source. We’re gonna have the Anthropic IPO in a few weeks. They basically went from zero to a top five or top 10 most valuable company in the world in a few years. I don't think that's ever happened before. The people, inventions, and viral moments that made 2026 a little more bearable . Something we missed? Let us know in the comments. Does Anthropic's IPO suggest the closed approach is winning? It’s hard to say. I've always said that there is a very strong natural tendency for AI to concentrate capabilities and wealth. People haven't internalized how much of the future compute capacity has already been reserved by a few companies. Talent, compute, resources—these all fuel the natural tendency for AI to be dominated by a few closed-source labs. Let’s talk about the attack. When did you first realize Hugging Face was being hacked by a group of AI agents? At the beginning, it didn't go to the top of our priority list. It just wasn't bad enough to really trigger that. The goal was pretty narrow and wasn’t deemed to be very dangerous or damaging. But it was raising questions. Especially the number of actions taken compared to the narrowness of the goal. It was surprising to us, and we couldn't really fit it into a familiar pattern. That's why we started investigating. And you used the Chinese model called GLM to investigate. I actually think that 95 percent of the risks are being created by a few companies that are pushing the frontier behind closed doors. And 95 percent of the protection or defense is going to be done by the open-source ecosystem. Does the US need its own open-weight models—ones as powerful as GLM, DeepSeek, Kimi, or Qwen ? Yeah, I think it's very, very important for sovereignty, for understanding AI, and for academia. It’s kind of weird that most academic labs have to use Chinese models because they’re the ones that are open. If you go to Stanford or MIT, you have no choice but to use the Chinese open-weight models. There is some momentum, but I don't think it's enough. I think there's a lot more to do. A lot more investment is needed. The best open-source non-Chinese models are actually coming from outside of the US. Right from France, Mistral; Cohere from Canada; South Korea is starting to do more and more. But it’s still pretty far from what the US could do. Perhaps we don’t need to panic about AI agents, but what about the idea of AI escaping human control due to recursive self-improvement? You use a computer to write code. There's already some form of self-improvement in using the tools to build more tools. Now the question is how fast it accelerates. One thing that a lot of people realized this summer is that keeping AI behind closed doors in a few labs isn't actually safer. For recursive self-improvement, I think openness is a way to understand, follow, and regulate if we need to regulate. Can we talk about the Microduck ? I’m a bit obsessed. Oh yeah, it's so fun, no? We're probably gonna sell over 50,000 of them this year. It's probably the most popular robot of the year. We haven't talked about this much, but AI was really the unlock for the robot. We had the design for two years, but the problem was that when it fell, it couldn’t get up. And then at some point with reinforcement learning, one of our software engineers managed to get the Microduck to get itself back up. At the end of the day, how do you convince people to take an interest in open-source AI?

events.title: A Federal Women’s Prison Became a “Rape Club.” After Officials Shut It Down, Rampant Abuse Continued Elsewhere.
events.summary: Officer Felix Wilder sauntered around the women’s prison like he owned the place.  Prone to showing up to work in gold chains and stylish jeans instead of his concrete gray government uniform, the slender 35-year-old moved, one woman said, “like he had just gotten off of a horse from a long ride.” He spoke slowly and eyed the prisoners as they walked through the drab buildings and shadeless yards of the secluded federal lockup in Aliceville, Alabama. By the fall of 2024, some of the women there had begun to notice him hovering over a soft-spoken immigrant from Mexico who’d been in prison for only a few years. Ela, as she asked to be called, had dark hair, dark eyes and children to get home to back in Utah. Wilder was just a little too close, a little too familiar. Ela’s cellmate, who asked to be identified as Ana, watched it all with unease. At 40, she knew exactly what that kind of attention from an officer could mean in a women’s prison. For 15 years, Ana had served her time at Federal Correctional Institution Dublin, a low-security prison in California, where officers had preyed on the women in their care. Sexual misconduct became so rampant that staff and prisoners alike called it a “rape club.” Eventually, the FBI intervened, and prosecutors charged the warden, the chaplain and nine other officers with sexually abusing female prisoners. Hundreds of women — including Ana — came forward to tell what happened to them, not just to investigators, but also to outside lawyers who sued the system to demand change at the Bay Area prison.    Ana had hoped to leave that all behind when she was transferred out of Dublin. But tucked between the pine trees and low-slung churches of rural Alabama, the Aliceville prison had its own brand of menace. The facility had newer buildings but fewer freedoms. The roofs leaked, and sometimes the air smelled faintly of mold. The shorthanded staff often locked the women in their cells for days at a time. And then there were officers like Wilder, who seemed to be choosing their targets. Thousands of miles from families they couldn’t call during yet another lockdown, Ana and Ela became allies. They paced. They picked at the lukewarm meals delivered on Styrofoam trays. They stared out the narrow slit of a window.  And then Ela broke down, sobbing as her words tumbled out into the stale prison air.  Two years earlier, an officer had pulled her into a closet and raped her, she told Ana, her voice quavering. Now, she said, it was happening all over again — but this time it was the stylish officer in jeans: Felix Wilder. Ela said she’d reported the first assault and nothing happened. Now, she didn’t know what to do. If the prison didn’t care about one rape, why would it care about two? As she listened, Ana felt a dull rage churning in her stomach. She thought of all the things she’d seen and survived at Dublin: the rapes, the harassment, the uncertainty of a life subject to the whims of lascivious men with badges. As she tried to comfort her sobbing cellmate, she wondered whether Aliceville was any better. Maybe, she thought, no place was.  Sitting on her metal bunk, she opened the little address book she’d bought from the prison commissary and flipped to the phone numbers for the lead attorneys in the class action lawsuit against Dublin. “Here,” she told Ela, “you can talk to them.” The arrests and subsequent convictions of Dublin staff — 10 in all — marked the largest sex abuse scandal in the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ history and a rare moment of accountability in a troubled system where many women had learned to stop expecting it. Suddenly, every branch of government stepped in. A federal judge appointed an outside monitor. A slew of agencies issued reports, and the Justice Department dispatched attorneys to visit and evaluate women’s facilities. Congress passed a law to create a new, independent office to oversee the prison system. But after the judge made that unprecedented move to appoint outside oversight, in early 2024 the bureau abruptly announced it would shut down Dublin and transfer its more than 600 women — including Ana — to lockups across the country. Ana had hoped to leave the abuse behind when she was transferred out of Dublin federal prison. Then, quietly, the window of accountability shut. Little appeared to have come of the promised reforms, the site visits and the reports, and Congress never appropriated funding for the new oversight office. More than a dozen current and former federal prison employees told ProPublica and The Marshall Project they’d seen few or no meaningful improvements. One Justice Department official said the only obvious sign of progress was new sexual assault prevention posters. “Nothing has really changed,” said Alix McLearen, a top Bureau of Prisons official who retired in 2024 after serving as the agency’s first administrator overseeing the women and special populations branch. “We had a horrible crisis, and crisis leads to opportunity, and this is an opportunity that has been completely squandered.” An official with the federal prison workers union who — like nearly every current employee interviewed for this story — asked not to be named for fear of retaliation, put it even more bluntly: “Nothing has been done to effectively change sexual abuse of inmates within the BOP. Not on a large scale or small scale.” For the last five years, the culture that spawned a rape club at Dublin has persisted across the system. Reporters at ProPublica and The Marshall Project set out to determine how pervasive the problem of staff sexual abuse inside federal women’s prisons is — and what, if anything, officials have done to solve it. What we found was sexual assault, misconduct or harassment at most of the 27 facilities that currently hold women. We identified more than 185 cases in which prison employees have been accused of sexually abusing people in women’s prisons since 2021, the year the Dublin scandal broke. The cases implicate more than 96 officers at 16 prisons. Of those, just 19 officers have been arrested or convicted. In some cases, officers withheld food or medical care, or threatened to put women in solitary confinement if they refused to comply with sexual demands, court records allege. In others, officers locked them in windowless closets or bathrooms, choked them, or forced them to use sex toys or have sex with each other. In more than a dozen instances, the assaults were so brutal that the women were left bruised and bleeding. Though some abusers have been prosecuted or removed, insiders say the culture of impunity that allows officers to prey on women remains. Officials have repeatedly refused to acknowledge or failed to act on signs of sexual abuse, we found. More than 25 women said that they were abused by officers who had been reported or investigated before, according to lawsuits we reviewed. Palmer invites some of the biggest names in entertainment and culture to share the experiences that have shaped them. From exploring self-worth with Oprah Winfrey to discussing creativity, reinvention, and fatherhood with Anderson .Paak, she moves effortlessly between laugh-out-loud exchanges and thoughtful reflections on life, relationships, and success. Baby, this is Keke Palmer consistently ranks among the top video and top comedy shows on Apple Podcasts. “I’m so honored that Baby, this is Keke Palmer has been named Apple Podcasts’ Show of the Year,” said Palmer. “I love how a conversation about entertainment can open up a bigger conversation about life. events.title: Investor Keith Rabois lost $250,000 betting against Democrats and San Francisco
events.summary: Khosla Ventures' Keith Rabois paid $250,000 after losing three bets tied to San Francisco and the midterms. Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images Khosla Ventures' Keith Rabois is making good on some bets he lost against X users. He paid $200,000 to Sheel Mohnot and $50,000 to Geiger Capital after betting on politics and startups. "The beauty about venture is you can be wrong a lot of the time and still make a lot of money," Mohnot told Business Insider. Keith Rabois rolled the dice. Now he's paying the price. The managing director of Khosla Ventures made a handful of sizable bets on X. In 2023, Rabois bet against fellow investor Sheel Mohnot that no venture-capital-backed startup based in San Francisco would exit for more than $10 billion. They put $100,000 on the line. In April, Rabois added another $100,000 to the pot with a new bet against Mohnot: that Republicans would win the House of Representatives in the midterms. Both turned out to be bad bets. SpaceX acquired Cursor for $60 billion, and Anthropic is heading toward a blockbuster IPO . Then there's the "blunami" that swept the House. On Saturday, Mohnot posted on X that Rabois had paid him the full $200,000. "It's easy to criticize Keith, the bets look lopsided in hindsight but at the time many people were on his side and thought SF was never going to be the same," Mohnot texted Business Insider. Mohnot said he planned to donate $100,000 of the prize pot to the nonprofit Inclusive Abundance. The other half will go to people working to eradicate a disease that runs in Mohnot's family, he said. Rabois also bet Geiger Capital , a popular investing account on X and Substack. In April, Rabois bet $50,000 that Republicans would keep control of the House in the midterms. Earlier in November, Geiger Capital posted a screenshot of the transaction on X. "Wager has been settled," they wrote. "Man of honor." Rabois replied in the thread with a stock-buying suggestion. Rabois and Geiger Capital did not respond to requests for comment from Business Insider. Venture capital is full of (mostly friendly) betting. Poker is big , when investors and founders alike gather around the table to place wagers. In 2023, Andreessen Horowitz alum Balaji Srinivasan said he paid out $1.5 million after betting that bitcoin would reach $1 million in 90 days. Mohnot told Business Insider that some bad bets don't define Rabois, whom he called an "amazing investor." "The beauty about venture is you can be wrong a lot of the time and still make a lot of money," he wrote. "Keith has done that." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Nvidia forms board committee to oversee national security, export controls
events.summary: The committee is tasked with providing oversight for Nvidia’s national security and global trade compliance programmes. Nvidia formed a new board committee to oversee national security, export controls and global trade risk. Suzanne Nora Johnson will chair it, with Stephen Neal and John Dabiri. The move follows Jensen Huang’s resignation and questions over chip export oversight after revelations about his affairs, including with a suspected Chinese spy. The company wants tighter control. The committee will meet at least quarterly and work with outside experts. It comes as the Trump administration plans tougher limits on China’s access to advanced AI chips, including Nvidia’s. BENGALURU – Nvidia said on Nov 17 it has established a new board-level committee to oversee its national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management. The move comes days after the resignation of chief executive officer Jensen Huang amid revelations of his affairs, including with a suspected Chinese spy, raised questions about potential national security risks and the oversight of the artificial intelligence chip designer’s chip exports. Nvidia said that the National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and will include directors Stephen Neal and John Dabiri. The committee is tasked with providing oversight for Nvidia’s national security and global trade compliance programs and will work with independent legal, national security and trade compliance experts. Nvidia’s existing National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team will report to this new committee and interim chief executive officer Colette Kress for day-to-day operations. The committee plans to meet at least quarterly, including sessions with management and in executive session. Formation of the panel also comes a day after the Trump administration said it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips from companies like ​Nvidia, tightening controls as US President Donald Trump headed to the country for talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping. US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has faced criticism for his oversight of export controls on chips to China in the wake of the Nvidia scandal, is among the officials joining Trump on his Asia trip, a White House official said. The company is due to report third-quarter earnings after the market closes on Nov 17. By some estimates, Nvidia has more than half a trillion dollars of commitments in the form of various supply and capacity backstops for chip purchases, data centre leases and equity investments, which nonetheless are a fraction of firm’s market capitalisation. events.title: Who is behind Habibi UK, an X account that targeted critics of Israel?
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? A former US Foreign Service officer ran a company that funded election adverts attacking Jeremy Corbyn’s Labour. The anonymous X account Habibi UK branded opponents of Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza “racists”, “hate marchers” and “anti-Semites”, singling out politicians, broadcasters and campaigners for online attacks. A six-month investigation by the British publication Byline Times has now identified the person behind the account as Benjamin Tait, a 61-year-old former United States Foreign Service officer who went on to run a British energy research company. list 1 of 4 Ukraine drone attack kills two in Crimea as Kyiv targets bridge to Russia list 2 of 4 South Korea cheating scandal: Are AI smart glasses a threat to exams? list 3 of 4 Vance calls out ‘neoconservatives’ over Iran war list 4 of 4 Irish ‌‌‌‌boxer Lee Reeves, 31, dies three months after sustaining injuries The news website and newspaper said that since the initial part of its investigation was published on Thursday, the account has stopped posting. The account, which joined what was then Twitter in April 2015, used a coronation portrait of Queen Elizabeth I as its profile picture, gave its location as “The Realm” and quoted a line attributed to the monarch in its bio: “If thy heart fails thee, climb not at all.” An analysis of nearly 300,000 X posts placed @habibi_uk at the centre of a network of 13 anonymous accounts. It found that Habibi UK had posted more than 42,000 times. The investigation also documented campaigns against 12 public figures in Britain over 10 months. Among those targeted were former BBC presenter and professional footballer Gary Lineker, photographer and outgoing chairman of London’s Southbank Centre arts centre Misan Harriman, documentary filmmaker Louis Theroux, actor and television panellist Nadia Sawalha and Green Party leader Zack Polanski. All of them had spoken out against Israel’s actions against Palestinians. Tait, a British-American grandson of philosopher Bertrand Russell, graduated from Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service in Washington, DC. According to his LinkedIn profile, which has now been taken down, Tait spent two years as a US Department of State officer overseas with experience in political-military diplomacy and “counterterrorism research”. Tait and his wife ran Prospex Research for about three decades. It was a firm that produced energy market reports for clients, including banks, consultancies, government officials and law firms. Reuters, The Wall Street Journal and Dow Jones quoted Tait on energy markets. The company entered voluntary liquidation in September. Tait was writing under the name Habibi by at least 2008 on Harry’s Place, a British political blog that began as a centre-left forum. His early posts focused on alleged “Islamist extremism”, including pieces about campaigner Ismail Patel and the Palestinian aid charity Interpal, according to the investigation. What was Tait’s role in campaign against Jeremy Corbyn? Before the United Kingdom’s 2019 general election, Tait was the sole director and controlling owner of MTCAE Ltd, according to Companies House records cited by the Byline Times. The company ran Mainstream, a campaign registered to spend money during the elections independently of a political party. Mainstream was founded and chaired by Ian Austin, a former Labour MP who quit the party under Jeremy Corbyn and has served as Britain’s trade envoy to Israel under five prime ministers. Austin said the group was set up to oppose “extremism” on the far left and hard right. But the Byline Times found that the Facebook advertisements it examined all attacked the Labour Party, including one that portrayed Corbyn as a national security threat. Electoral Commission returns showed the company spent £134,457 pounds ($171,715) on the campaign, including 6,880 pounds ($8,786) paid to Tait for overhead costs and administration. The returns listed no donor. In March 2021, a High Court official ordered Twitter to disclose details behind the account to Professor David Miller, who had brought a legal claim. The operator’s name remained out of the public record. Despite this, the account went on to gain influence, particularly after Elon Musk took over Twitter in October 2022. Links between the account and the Labour Party establishment run deep, according to the investigation. Austin, who is connected to Tait via Mainstream, shared posts from Habibi UK at least 34 times. John Woodcock, a former Labour MP who sits in the House of Lords, amplified the account 32 times, according to the investigation. It also found that David Toube, general counsel at the Jewish Leadership Council, amplified its posts hundreds of times. The Henry Jackson Society, a British foreign policy think tank, cited Habibi UK nine times in a 2022 report on Hindu-Muslim unrest in Leicester.

events.title: South Korea will suspend all aircraft operation for 35 minutes and markets will open late. Here’s why
events.summary: South Korea will suspend aircraft takeoffs and landings nationwide for 35 minutes on Thursday to minimize noise during the English listening portion of its college entrance exam. The restrictions will be in place from 1:05 p.m. local time, affecting 130 flights, including 81 international and 49 domestic services. The country's stock market will also open an hour later than usual at 10 a.m. local time. South Korea will suspend all aircraft takeoffs and landings nationwide for 35 minutes on Thursday to minimize noise during the English listening portion of the country's highly competitive college entrance exam, the government said Tuesday. The restrictions will be in place from 1:05 p.m. to 1:40 p.m. local time, affecting 130 flights, including 81 international and 49 domestic services, according to the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport. Planes already in the air will be required to remain at least 3 kilometers above the ground during the exam, while emergency flights will be exempt from the restrictions. The measures will also apply to helicopters, light aircraft and drones, with all drone flights prohibited nationwide during the 35 minutes. Violators could face criminal penalties, the ministry said. The government will adjust the departure and arrival times of affected flights, while airlines will notify passengers of the revised schedules in advance. The Korea Transportation Safety Authority will also send text messages to licensed drone operators, including those who have already received flight approvals, warning that drone flights will be prohibited during period regardless of prior authorization. "We will thoroughly implement the necessary measures, including restrictions on aircraft operations, to ensure students can concentrate ton the English listening test in a table environment," said Jeong Chae-gyo, director general of aviation policy at the ministry. Jeong also urged airlines and relevant authorities to cooperate in adjusting flight schedules and notifying passengers in advance, and to advise travelers to check their revised departure and arrival times with their airlines. South Korea's college entrance exam, known as Suneung, is a high stakes annual test that plays a major role in determining students' university admissions. The country's stock market will also open an hour later than usual on Thursday, at 10 a.m. local time, and close at 4:30 pm, as announced by the Korea Exchange.

events.title: AI Told These Ex-Google Guys How to Build a Billion-Dollar Weapons Business
events.summary: When Silicon Valley entrepreneur Chad Steelberg decided he wanted to get involved in the war in Ukraine, he had no idea where to start. So the then CEO of enterprise AI company Veritone did what he knew best: built an artificial intelligence model to help him figure it out. Today, he has proprietary munition and missile designs, several government partnerships, and a defense-as-a-service business valued at more than $1 billion. Steelberg, alongside fellow Google alumnus and former Apple executive Andy Baynes, says they are trying to break the Russia-Ukraine war “stalemate,” Silicon Valley–style. They believe their experience building and iterating technology quickly can help bring Western weapon manufacturing in line with the rapid innovation cycles seen on the battlefield and beat the “attritional cat-and-mouse technology game” that the war, as Baynes describes it, has become. Steelberg, originally from Newport Beach, California, started itching to “make a difference” on the battlefield after he took in a couple hundred Ukrainian refugees into his French chateau in early 2022. He says he was regularly “heartbroken” by the outpouring of grief whenever bad news arrived about a husband, father, or son back home. “I believe I could really change the outcome of this and every war,” Steelberg tells WIRED. "I'm not saying this is purely altruistic,” he adds. “Of course we're going to be making money doing it." This week, their firm, Tiberius Aerospace, said it had secured $85 million in Series A financing, led by European technology investment firm Lakestar and Rochefort Asset Management, a national-security-focused investment firm licensed under the US Defense Department. Ukrainian venture capital firm UA1 is also an investor. Tiberius began as Steelberg’s private research lab, incorporated in 2021, which employed people across France, the UK, and US to experiment on left-field ideas across a range of technologies, from drones and electric vertical takeoff aircraft to quantum computing. After the invasion, he pivoted the lab’s AI and aerospace engineers into writing code and building spreadsheets to objectively analyze the war’s many factors and calculate what could move the needle. The AI model they created quickly ruled out building better defensive technology because that would just harden the stalemate. With his aim narrowed to building an offensive weapon, Steelberg developed several metrics to numerically analyze the lethality of different systems, including cost-effectiveness, and used the AI engine to simulate weapons under different conditions and identify what would disrupt the market. Don’t build another drone, it suggested, build longer-range artillery munitions. The resulting system, called Sceptre, can be fired from a 155-millimeter howitzer—the most common artillery weapon donated to Ukraine. As well as traveling farther than currently available rounds, they claim they can reach supersonic speeds and altitudes beyond jamming range. Giving Ukraine’s guns extra range is important, Sam Cranny-Evans, an associate fellow at UK defense think tank the Royal United Services Institute, tells WIRED, because it would allow Ukrainian gunners to operate beyond the reach of Russian drone attacks. 155-mm shells “can cause massive damage to a group of vehicles or infantry,” he says. “Any technology that can help Ukraine extend the reach of its howitzers and return them to combat would be valuable.” With a prototype he’d designed with the help of AI, Steelberg also started to expand the Tiberius team, including bringing on board Baynes as chief strategy officer in 2023. Baynes had first traveled to Ukraine around a decade ago to investigate how local startup Ring , now owned by Amazon, had outdone Nest , which he’d been working on and eventually sold to Google. He fell in love with Kyiv’s ambitious software engineers and booming tech scene–responsible for globally successful tech tools like Grammarly and Snapchat’s face filters. In 2016, he bought a local life-science tech company with the aim of accelerating next-generation medicines through automating clinical trials and improving protein modeling. “What drew me into Kyiv was the hunger and ambition in the engineering community,” he tells WIRED. “It was difficult to not be enormously attracted to that and to see if it's something that could be put into really critical-mission problem sets like cancer drugs or speeding up clinical trials for life-science companies.” After the Russian invasion, Baynes set himself up in Budapest for around six months to help with the logistics of evacuating women and children and moving equipment into the country. He asked his global network for help finding medical equipment, vehicles, and accommodation for refugees—bringing him back in touch with Steelberg. Baynes believes the West’s response to the invasion has been “inadequate” and that Ukraine needs better offensive capabilities to push Russia’s army back.

events.title: Behind the Curtain: If competence were cool
events.summary: So many government problems, like last week's nationwide aviation meltdown , are foreseeable ... and foreseen. Why it matters: Again and again, we choose to do nothing until a crisis hits. A big reason: These are huge, tedious, complex, unsexy, antiquated systems that require persistence and competence to fix. A big new problem: These systems are deeply intertwined with our daily lives, and highly susceptible to malfunctions, mishaps and AI-enhanced cyberattacks. They're boring until they're vital. The big picture: We have federal agencies and congressional committees designed explicitly to monitor, protect and improve these complex systems. But they've atrophied as power has been centralized in the presidency and congressional leadership, where daily political warfare rarely includes sober discussion of competence and essential interconnected systems. Here are a few of the foreseeable (and foreseen) crises that have been staring at us, many for literally decades: The skies: We've known for years that the air-traffic system relies on copper wire and floppy disks . We've seen and known the vulnerabilities through Democratic and Republican administrations. We've known the fix is expensive: $31.5 billion, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told lawmakers last year. At Friday night's briefing at the White House, Duffy said: "I want $50 billion ." The grid: We've known for a long time that our electricity is delivered through an aging patchwork system vulnerable to accidents or attacks. The nonprofit power authority NERC (North American Electric Reliability Corp.) warned this spring that the system is so strained by rising energy needs from AI and humans that it could jam up or break. The water: Drinking and wastewater systems are old and in dangerous disrepair — a huge risk to hospitals, in particular. In July , cyberattacks hit over 30 municipal water systems in Minnesota, with Iran as a likely culprit . The government's computers: Washington spends over $100 billion a year on information technology. Roughly 80% goes to keeping old systems alive. Eight of the 11 systems most in need of replacement run on dying languages like COBOL . The people who can read, write and fix them are retiring. The debt: We paid $1.052 trillion in interest last fiscal year. That's more than we spent on defense. The Congressional Budget Office sees the interest doubling to $2.1 trillion in 2036 . Every dollar of interest is a dollar that can't fix another crisis on this list. The retirement cliff: Social Security's retirement fund runs dry in 2032. Current law then cuts benefits by 22%, automatically. Medicare's hospital fund follows in 2033 . We have known those dates for decades, and they've been creeping up. Now they're just a few years away. The shriveled arsenal: Rebuilding the advanced weapons we've burned through in the Iran war will take years . Back in May, a paper from the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that replacing some interceptors used heavily in the war, including Patriot and THAAD anti-missile systems, would take three years. The minerals: China controls 91% of the world's rare-earth refining capacity, giving the other superpower a chokehold on vital ingredients of AI. We're one trade war away from slowing AI and the entire economy. The bottom line: When choosing and rating leaders in harrowing times, put a premium on competence. We'll need it. Go deeper : The chain-reaction era.

events.title: Fomula One champion Fernando Alonso to race at Dakar Rally 2027
events.summary: Fernando Alonso will make his return to the Dakar Rally 2027 in Morocco with the Leob and Aston Martin team. Double Formula One champion Fernando Alonso says he will compete at the upcoming Dakar Rally, making his return to the race after seven years. The 45-year-old Spaniard, a 32-time Grand Prix winner and two-time Le Mans 24 Hours winner, announced his intention to race in the annual on Tuesday and said he will work with an Aston ⁠Martin Dreadnought entry run by engineering partner Prodrive. He competed at the Dakar Rally in 2020 with Toyota and finished 13th. “In the end, the decision became simple. I wanted to embrace the challenge completely and take on both Formula One and the Dakar Rally in the same year,” he explained in a statement. “In 2020, Dakar was one of the most challenging and enjoyable experiences of my career. I have enormous ⁠respect for this race and the specialists who have mastered it.” The 49th edition of the Dakar Rally will be held in Morocco from January 9 to 23, with a prologue and first stage in Portugal, after being moved from Saudi Arabia due to security concerns. The 24-round Formula One season is due to start in Bahrain ‌in March after testing in late February. Alonso, who will again have compatriot and five-time motorcycle Dakar winner Marc Coma as co-driver, is racing in the Las Vegas Grand Prix this weekend. He said he had turned his thoughts to Dakar after deciding to continue in Formula One with Aston Martin. “Formula One remains my priority. ⁠But I am a racing driver, and challenges like this are why I love competing. I’m looking forward to seeing what we can achieve.” France’s ⁠nine-time world rally champion Sebastien Loeb and Brazil’s reigning world rally-raid champion Lucas Moraes will be his teammates in a three-car entry. The Dakar will be ‌Aston Martin Racing’s debut in the world rally-raid championship.

events.title: JD Vance says he'll decide 'sometime next year' about 2028 presidential run
events.summary: Vice President JD Vance was pressed about a potential 2028 run in an interview with Fox News on Monday. He said he would decide on running for the Republican nomination "sometime next year." The next U.S. presidential election is scheduled for November 7, 2028. U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Monday he will make a decision next year about whether to run for president in 2028. "We'll figure it out sometime next year," he told Fox News host Laura Ingraham in an interview that aired Monday evening. "I'm not an expert in this but my understanding with a presidential campaign is there's a lot of infrastructure that you have to set up, fundraising, all that stuff and so you can't declare a month before the Iowa caucus that you're going to run for president," he said. "So, you know, I haven't made a decision." Vance has yet to openly declare any ambition to succeed President Donald Trump when his current term ends, but speculation that the vice president has his sights set on the White House has been mounting for some time. In the wake of the GOP's crushing defeat in the U.S. midterm election on Nov. 3, anonymous sources involved in campaigns told Reuters Vance was among the high-profile Republicans who had begun early preparations for a 2028 run. Candidates typically announce their intentions to run in the election in the spring of 2027, with parties holding nominating conventions to formally select their presidential candidates between July and September. Polymarket currently slates Vance as the frontrunner to win the Republican presidential nomination for the 2028 election, with the prediction market giving him a 37% chance of becoming the nominee. Kalshi currently gives a 73% chance that Vance will run for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination. Odds and gambling platforms do not use methodologies used by traditional political polling, and therefore are not substitutes for political polls Pressed on 2028 in Monday's interview, Vance said: "When I make a decision, I will be all in on whatever that decision is." Candidates vying for the Republican nomination face the challenge of convincing voters the party can veer away from unpopular Trump-era policies without alienating its MAGA base. Vance himself has blamed the Iran war for the midterm election outcome. "I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, "I told you so": you're right, you did tell us so," he said in a lengthy X post as the results were coming in. "Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let's take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country." In his interview with Fox News on Monday, Vance said the Republicans got "shellacked" in the midterms. "We have to take messages from that, but the message that we have to take is that the American people want prosperity, they want freedom, they want sovereignty within their own country and they want us to do more of the good things that we've done," he said. He added that lawmakers needed to double down on "economic nationalism" and bring "prosperity to the homeland" to deal with "economic pain" in the United States. events.title: Welcome to New York City's Tech Bro-hemia
events.summary: Whop's Hunter Dickinson says Williamsburg has "San Fran transplant" energy. Amy Lombard for BI At work, 24-year-old Hunter Dickinson lives on the frontier of technology. He's the head of growth for Whop, an e-commerce startup backed by Peter Thiel and Sequoia Capital. In his spare time, Dickinson lives a more bohemian lifestyle in Brooklyn's Williamsburg neighborhood. He buys his meat from a local butcher, ice skates at the neighborhood rink, and once tried salsa dancing at a local club. He's very proud of a rug that he purchased from a local Azerbaijani merchant. "I literally have not left this four-block radius in four years," Dickinson says. One of America's artsiest neighborhoods is attracting a new generation of tech workers . Dickinson calls it "San Fran transplant" energy. Between 2020 and 2024, Census data says nearly 9% of Williamsburg's employed residents worked in computer and mathematical occupations, more than twice the citywide share of about 4%. Walk down Bedford Avenue, and you'll hear debates over coding agents. Take the Manhattan-bound L train, and you'll see commuters texting Instinct. These aren't the scrawny, shut-in, hoodie-clad engineers of a time when Meta was still Facebook. This generation wears chore coats and Japanese basics, their muscles bulging beneath tight-fitting tees. They talk about "taste" and techno. Whop gives its employees a $9,000 annual rent stipend if they live within half a mile of the Williamsburg office. Amy Lombard for BI It's an unlikely hub for an industry that has historically clustered around universities, seeking talent and research. In the age of artificial intelligence, tech companies have a new interest in the language their models imitate, the society they reshape, and the larger meaning of life they may be bringing to an end. You see it in the AI companies hiring ethicists and philosophers and hosting intellectual salons. Williamsburg, with its galleries, street art, and concert halls, offers that. We spent months studying the signs of Silicon Valley in Williamsburg to see what they could tell us about life in the neighborhood. We worked out of cafés, drank at local bars, saunaed at the Bedford Equinox, attended an AI demo night, and spoke with over two dozen people in and around New York's tech scene . Daniel Chesley, a 31-year-old principal at the venture capital firm Workbench, lives in Park Slope and often travels to Williamsburg for meetings. He says he can spot tech workers by their thrifted clothes, Salomon sneakers, and Patagonia backpacks. You can hear their chatter walking up and down Bedford, he says: "AI, Anthropic, compute credits, Nvidia. Things like that." Daniel Chesley hears talk of "AI, Anthropic, compute credits, Nvidia" walking down Bedford Ave. Amy Lombard for BI While Manhattan still employs the most tech workers in New York, Brooklyn's rise has been fast and concentrated in Williamsburg. Real estate developers, especially along the East River waterfront, coaxed startups with post-pandemic office deals and city tax benefits. It helped that the neighborhood had long been gentrifying, slurping up all that disposable income with $8 lattes. Between 2020 and 2024, the neighborhood's median household income was roughly $149,000, compared with $80,500 citywide. Paul Butler, a 36-year-old engineer at Modal Labs, left San Francisco for New York in 2010 after thinking, "I can't even go for a coffee without hearing about JavaScript." He moved to Williamsburg after rents dropped in 2020 and worries it's Silicon Valley all over again. "I'm not saying 'I want all the techies out of Williamsburg,'" he says. "I am one. I just wish that we would take the weekend off and not talk about work at coffee shops." If human creativity is the last bastion for AI to conquer, then part of Williamsburg's appeal lies in its rich artistic legacy. The neighborhood has long been home to Polish, Jewish, Puerto Rican, and Dominican communities, and it still contains one of the largest Hasidic hubs in America. In the 1990s, it earned the title of " new Bohemia ," and gave rise to a new school of art called Immersionism. Dickinson says he loves Williamsburg's "nooks and crannies." Amy Lombard for BI In the aughts, indie rockers took refuge from skyrocketing Manhattan rents. The edgy digital media brand Vice established its headquarters. Music venues took over the warehouses that lined the East River. Twee hipsters shopped at American Apparel's brick-and-mortar on 6th St. By the mid-2010s, the hipster haven had grown up. Vice took over out-of-business music venues. LCD Soundsystem's James Murphy opened up an upscale wine bar. Luxury condos moved in. Ronen Givony, who documented the era of indie music in Brooklyn in his book "Us v. Them," often finds himself back in the neighborhood. "I try not to be the grumpy old man who's like, 'this is how it used to be,'" Givony said. But the difference is "night and day." By the 2020s, Williamsburg's tech scene was starting to sprout. Web3 bros moved into the neighborhood's coworking spaces . The crypto startup Rainbow threw late-night parties — like "tweetups" — at its office; a fresh-out-of-prison Martin Shkreli showed up to its loud, dark basement one night in 2022. Some of Williamsburg's artists are still in the neighborhood, attempting to marry art and tech. Williamsburg-based VC firm Asylum Ventures' website proclaims "the best founders are artists." A few blocks away, the AI design startup Flora hosts digital art shows in the Domino building. Come next spring, a new music venue from a member of the hipster soundtrack band Mumford & Sons will open downstairs at the Domino development. Many of the techy Williamsburgians say they moved to the neighborhood because they thought it was less corporatized than Tribeca or SoHo. And yet, the gritty bars and artists' lofts have been replaced by luxury condos and private equity-owned retail. Today, shoppers can ping-pong between athleisure brands Vuori and Lululemon. Around the corner is Hermès; down the road is a smattering of slop bowl stops . Inside the Domino Sugar refinery, 75% of occupants are tech companies. Amy Lombard for BI The transformation centered on real-estate attractions like the former Domino Sugar refinery, a once-crumbling shell that Two Trees Management converted into a luxe office space. Alyssa Zahler, the developer's managing director of commercial leasing, says 75% of occupants are tech companies; half are in AI. Startups have good reason to move in: Two Trees advertises the city's tax incentives for tech companies crossing the river, as does 25 Kent , an office complex that conveniently houses a sauna downstairs. Specifically, this "stretch of Williamsburg" — along Kent Avenue and north of the Williamsburg Bridge — has radically evolved from its music-and-counterculture past, said Givony.
