events.title: CapitaLand, Far East, Sing Holdings team up in $1.8 billion bid for Jurong Lake District site
events.summary: The top bid of $1.82 billion was from a consortium comprising CapitaLand Development, Far East Organization and Sing Holdings. CapitaLand Development, Far East Organization and Sing Holdings led a $1.82 billion bid for the Jurong Lake District Town Hall Link site, the first plot split from a larger master plan. The site can hold offices, up to 1,200 homes and other uses. Analysts said homes and retail are attractive, helped by strong MRT links and nearby schools. A key risk is office demand. Experts warned suburban office space may struggle in a hybrid work market, and the high land cost could strain financing. SINGAPORE - A mixed-use site in Jurong Lake District (JLD), where a massive business district is being planned, drew two bids at a state tender on Nov 17. The top bid of $1.82 billion, which works out to about $910 per square foot per plot ratio (psf ppr), was from a consortium comprising CapitaLand Development, Far East Organization and Sing Holdings. The second highest bid, of $1.31 billion or about $655 ppr, came from Sim Lian Land and Sim Lian Development. The 3.72ha site, zoned “white”, can be developed into a maximum gross floor area (GFA) of slightly more than 2 million square feet (sq ft). This will comprise a minimum of 430,556 sq ft of offices, up to 1,200 private housing units and about 473,612 sq ft for complementary uses (such as retail, serviced apartments, hotel, sports, recreational and community spaces, medical clinics and attractions). Analysts polled by The Business Times had predicted up to four bids for the site, with the top bid forecast to be anywhere from S$900 psf ppr to S$1,400 psf ppr. The site in Town Hall Link is the first plot carved out of an earlier tendered 6.5ha master developer site, which was to be progressively developed over 10 to 15 years to a maximum GFA of 3.93 million sq ft. This was to comprise at least 1.57 million sq ft of offices, up to 1,700 private homes and close to 800,000 sq ft of space for other uses such as retail, and food and beverage. The master developer site was intended to be a catalyst for the next phase of development in JLD as Singapore’s largest mixed-use business district outside the city centre. The tender was launched in June 2023 and closed in March 2024, with only one bidder – a five-member consortium comprising CapitaLand Development, City Developments, Frasers Property, Mitsubishi Estate and Mitsui Fudosan (Asia). In September 2024, the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) announced it would not award the tender as the shortlisted concept, at the tendered price of around $640 psf ppr, was assessed to be “too low”. The master developer site was put on the reserve list, where sites are triggered for sale only when there is an indication of interest at a minimum acceptable bid price, before the government decided to sell the massive white site in three smaller parcels, starting with the Town Hall Link site. Initially it was put on the first-half 2026 reserve list, before being moved to the H2 2026 confirmed list. When the tender for the carved-out plot was launched in July 2026, URA emphasised that JLD is a key pillar of Singapore’s decentralisation strategy. The Town Hall Link is intended to kickstart the next phase of JLD’s development, which will focus on the 120-hectare new Jurong Lake Central precinct, as well as support medium-term growth in demand for housing and offices. The government has invested significantly in key infrastructure to drive the transformation of JLD, including the revitalised Jurong Lake Gardens and the addition of two new MRT lines: Jurong Region Line (JRL) and Cross Island Line (CRL). The JE5 station on the JRL will be located at the Jurong East MRT station, which is currently the interchange station for the East-West and North-South MRT lines. The JE6 station, also on the JRL, will serve the International Business Park. Both stations are scheduled to open in 2028. The Town Hall Link plot will also be a stone’s throw from the CR19 MRT station, on the CRL; the station is planned to open in 2032. To reduce development complexity and make the Town Hall Link site more attractive to developers, the government is undertaking a greater share of the surrounding infrastructure and land preparation works, including pedestrian links to MRT stations. Property veteran Desmond Sim said: “Confidence, if not a sense of assurance, in JLD has been established. The master planning and infrastructural investments will be a testament to that.” Wong Xian Yang, head of research for Singapore and South-east Asia at Cushman & Wakefield (C&W), said the Town Hall Link site’s residential component is a key draw for developers, given the strong sales achieved by close-to-MRT station launches such as J’den and Lucerne Grand. In November 2023, CapitaLand Development’s J’den sold 88 per cent of its 368 units on launch day at an average price of $2,451 psf.

events.title: Former WH Smith chain TG Jones put up for sale after closing 130 stores
events.summary: Modella Capital plans auction of high street retailer, which employs about 3,500 people, next year The owner of TG Jones is exploring a potential sale less than 18 months after completing a deal to buy the high street chain formerly known as WH Smith. Modella Capital, which also owns businesses including Hobbycraft, completed a deal to buy the 233-year-old business for £42m in June last year. The company, which pushed through a swingeing restructure to close more than 100 stores after receiving high court approval in July, has moved to appoint advisers after receiving unsolicited expressions of interest for the business. Modella, which has closed about 150 of the 480 WH Smith stores since taking control, has appointed the corporate finance arm of Teneo, according to Sky News which first reported the news. “High-street retailer TG Jones has received unsolicited offers for the business,” said Modella and TG Jones in a joint statement. “Management and owner Modella Capital have jointly agreed to instruct Teneo Corporate Finance to review these offers and undertake a market-testing exercise.” An auction of the business, which employs about 3,500 staff, is planned for next year to avoid disruption through the key Christmas trading period. “As ever, our focus is on providing a great experience for customers, especially with the critical Christmas period coming up,” said the TG Jones chief executive, Alex Wilson. “We continue to execute our turnaround plan, which is improving our performance month by month.” WH Smith retained its almost 1,300 stores in train stations and airports, as well as its website and the right to its name, promoting the rebrand of the high street stores to TG Jones . The potential sale comes as the future of Poundland, which employs approximately 12,000 people and operates 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, remains uncertain. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Last week the chain’s owner, Gordon Brothers, won approval from the high court for an extension of legal protection from creditors as it assesses three potential bids . Last month its US owners filed a notice of intention to call in administrators, but has come under pressure to accept a bid for the company that would save retail jobs and protect thousands of suppliers.

events.title: Push to reinstate Jensen Huang tests superstar tech CEO accountability
events.summary: The push to reinstate Jensen Huang is set to test whether America's most powerful CEOs can still be held accountable — or if extraordinary success and political alliances have made them untouchable. Why it matters: Silicon Valley has long treated its most successful founders as indispensable. But a new class of tech billionaires, led by figures like Elon Musk, has amplified that culture while swatting away efforts to curtail their power. Their immense wealth and growing political clout raise a fundamental question: Can corporate boards, regulators, Congress or the courts actually rein in a superstar CEO anymore? Huang's potential return — or the Nvidia board's refusal to entertain it — could signal whether that balance of power is changing. "Power corrupts, and people start to think they are invincible," Anne Wojcicki, the founder of 23andMe and ex-wife of Google co-founder Sergei Brin, told Bloomberg . "We are all complicit in making these people think they are gods. And people do stupid things when they think they are untouchable." Driving the news: A growing campaign to reinstate Huang has attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees, following his departure after revelations of intimate relationships involving subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy. President Trump said Monday he wouldn't mind seeing Huang return. Elon Musk has also backed the effort. Other supporters include Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan , Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney , Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke. Prominent investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker have separately urged the board not to rule out Huang's return. Some pushing for a reexamination of the issue have focused on what they see as a lack of proof that Alice Huang, the executive with whom he had an affair, was a Chinese intelligence asset. That claim has been attributed in media reports to U.S. intelligence officials, although other stories have called it into question. Yes, but: Others have pointed to the fact that Alice Huang worked on behalf of Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer that took steps to help Chinese AI companies access cutting-edge chips. The company has been linked to more than $4 billion in Nvidia chip purchases also arranged nearly $12 billion in orders of top-end Nvidia chips destined for Chinese companies, according to The Wall Street Journal. In addition to the relationships, Huang also faces questions about whether he misled Nvidia executives . Nvidia's board isn't currently considering reinstating Huang, CNBC and Reuters reported Monday. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has urged Nvidia to look outside the company for new leadership, while tech analyst Dan Ives has dismissed the idea of a comeback as unrealistic. Zoom out: Musk has become perhaps the most prominent embodiment of the superstar CEO, repeatedly defying corporate conventions and weathering controversies that might have ended other executives' careers. In 2018, Musk settled SEC fraud charges over tweets about taking Tesla private, stepping down as chairman but remaining CEO. After a Delaware judge invalidated his enormous Tesla compensation package , shareholders voted to ratify it, and the state's Supreme Court eventually restored the award. Last year, Tesla shareholders approved another potentially massive compensation package, underscoring their willingness to grant extraordinary rewards to a leader they consider indispensable. The Trump factor: Trump's return to the White House added another layer to the power of tech executives, many of whom cultivated close ties to a president whose decisions can affect their businesses through government contracts, regulation and trade policy. But this month's midterm elections demonstrated limits to Trump's political power, raising questions about whether his backing will carry the same weight going forward. Huang's fate will offer an early test, though any decision to reinstate him might reflect investor pressure as much as political influence. The intrigue: The campaign to restore Huang has echoes of Sam Altman's dramatic 2023 ouster and reinstatement at OpenAI, when employees, investors and powerful tech figures rallied to force a reversal. OpenAI's board cited vague concerns about Altman's candor and its ability to trust him. A subsequent review found that his conduct did not mandate removal. Charles Elson, corporate governance expert and founding director of the Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware, said Altman's departure was fundamentally a dispute with his board, whereas Huang's case involves specific allegations of misconduct. "What if they were to do nothing? Then you have no code of conduct," Elson said. Altman himself acknowledged the parallels Monday, telling a Semafor conference he has "personal strong empathy to a situation like this," but declined to endorse Huang's return. "Jensen has long been a hero of mine; heroes have flaws," he said, per Bloomberg. The bottom line: Huang's fate could help establish whether the era of the seemingly untouchable CEO is continuing — or beginning to encounter meaningful limits.

events.title: Democrats' squishy definition of Medicare expansion
events.summary: Democrats marching into a debate over expanding Medicare are about to confront difficult questions about how far to go — including for seniors who are already in the program. Why it matters: Holes in traditional Medicare leave seniors exposed to out-of-pocket costs and affordability struggles, but making the program's benefits more generous may be prohibitively expensive. The big picture: Democrats scored overwhelming gains in the midterms after making health care affordability a major priority for the next Congress. Though the election results reinvigorated progressives' push for Medicare for All, there are also less sweeping options for what expanded coverage should look like. How far to go — and what to call the plan — will become critical heading into the 2028 presidential cycle and likely determine whether Democrats can attract any Republican support. Driving the news: Lowering the Medicare eligibility age is emerging as an early front-runner for what Democrats may try to pass and defy President Trump to veto. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) called on Democrats to lower the eligibility age to 55 soon after the election, framing it as an "immediate first step" toward his long-sought goal of Medicare for All. Sanders also wants to add vision, dental and hearing benefits and strengthen children's coverage. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York on Friday threw his support behind that kind of package, as well as strengthening children's coverage, Stat reported . And groups of Democrats in both chambers have recently introduced legislation lowering the Medicare eligibility age to 50. What they're saying: " Medicare for All is unlikely to be enacted in the near future, but the political push for it could prompt a debate about the services Medicare itself does not cover and the high costs current Medicare beneficiaries can incur," KFF executive vice president Larry Levitt wrote last month in JAMA Forum . State of play: Some Democrats are looking at other changes beyond changing the eligibility age. More than a dozen Senate Democrats have introduced legislation capping Medicare out-of-pocket spending at $5,000 a year. House Democrats' health care working group called for both a $5,000 out-of-pocket cap and adding dental, vision and hearing benefits within the first 100 hours of taking the House majority. Between the lines: More sweeping proposals for a single-payer system would result in a Medicare program without premiums or patient cost-sharing. It would instead fund care with taxpayer dollars. Traditional Medicare now requires seniors to pay premiums, copays and other out-of-pocket costs. It doesn't include dental, vision or hearing coverage, and there are no caps on how much seniors pay out of pocket. This lack of an out-of-pocket limit leaves Medicare enrollees more exposed to high costs than they would be in an employer-sponsored plan, on an Affordable Care Act marketplace or in a Medicare Advantage plan. That's why nearly half of seniors in traditional Medicare — around 13 million — buy Medigap policies to fill the holes. What we're watching: Combining expanded Medicare access with more generous benefits only drives up the price tag, creating even more pressure to find ways to pay for it all. Democrats who ran campaigns promising to crack down on corporate bad behavior will undoubtedly look to the health care industry to ultimately pay for the changes. They'd still face GOP criticism for adding financial pressure to Medicare's trust funds and speeding up the date of the program's projected insolvency. Incoming Senate health committee Ranking Member Rand Paul (R-Ky.) "is likely to play spoiler" to Sanders' Medicare for All ambitions, Capital Alpha analyst Kim Monk said in a note on Monday.

events.title: Democrats in Washington Move to Ban Data Centers on Public Lands
events.summary: Demonstrators take part in a protest in May at the Utah Capitol to oppose the construction of a data center in Box Elder County. Natalie Behring/Getty Images A dozen Democrats in Congress are calling for limiting or banning the construction of data centers on public lands. The moves follow reporting from ProPublica that revealed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who leads the White House’s artificial intelligence push, has tens of millions of dollars invested in AI companies. “Our public lands aren’t a piggy bank for Trump’s powerful friends,” Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said in a social media post that pointed to ProPublica’s reporting. Her office told the news organization that the senator, who serves on the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, is working on legislation to regulate data centers on public lands and will use the panel’s oversight authority to address concerns about transparency surrounding them. Burgum was asked about ProPublica’s reporting at a recent event hosted by the conservative website Daily Caller. He said that his financial reporting and ethics were “clean as a whistle,” and that he invested in software companies before they turned to AI. “I don’t even know all the names of the companies that are in the portfolio,” he said of his vast wealth. ProPublica found that hundreds of President Donald Trump’s political appointees in the executive branch, or their spouses, held stocks, owned equity or had other financial ties to AI companies and data center developers. Other offices, including the Environmental Protection Agency and the U.S. Department of Agriculture, defended their political leadership, saying the appointees followed lawyers’ guidance and had not violated ethics rules. Our reporting also found that a U.S. Geological Survey study released earlier this year identified an area of U.S. Department of the Interior land nearly the size of Montana that might be suitable for data centers. Several members of Congress pledged to float legislation to ban data center development on this land. “These lands are treasured and must be protected for future generations to benefit from and enjoy,” Rep. Maxine Dexter of Oregon said in a statement. In mid-November, she filed the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act , which would ban data center construction on land managed by the Interior Department and the Forest Service. Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan in July filed the No AI Data Centers on Federal Lands Act , which would also prohibit their build-out on federally managed land. The measure was dead on arrival in the Republican-controlled House of Representatives. “I’m going to continue building the coalition for our bill, and at the same time, I’m going to push the Oversight Committee to investigate the outrageous corruption of the Trump Administration,” she told ProPublica in a statement. Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan is one of a dozen Democratic members of Congress who have called for limiting data center construction on public lands following recent reporting by ProPublica. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images The White House did not respond to a request for comment on the pushback from Democrats in Congress. Also speaking up were Rep. Jared Huffman of California and Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, who serve as the ranking members of the natural resources committees in their respective chambers. Huffman and Heinrich are in line to take up the gavel in those committees in January when Democrats retake the majority. “These lands belong to the American people, not private interests looking to cash in,” Heinrich said in a statement. “Public lands belong in public hands.” Heinrich is pushing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a generational overhaul of the legislation governing how federal agencies permit major developments. Republicans in Congress and the White House support the swift passage of the bill, as do some Democrats. The more environmentally minded members of the Democratic caucus, however, are calling on Heinrich to slow down and force a better deal once Congress reconvenes next year with Democratic majorities. Environmental policy experts agree that permitting reform is desperately needed to address climate change by allowing the faster build-out of renewable electricity generation and transmission lines. But green groups including the Sierra Club, Natural Resources Defense Council and League of Conservation Voters oppose the bill because it would likely also lead to more fossil fuel projects while limiting input on projects from Native American tribes. The legislation presents a mixed bag for data centers. A spokesperson for Heinrich defended the permitting reform bill, pointing out that it would require data center companies to bear their own costs for connecting to and upgrading the electrical grid. But the legislation would also streamline approval of natural gas-fired power plants , which power many data centers. The bill would make it more difficult to take away a permit after it’s issued. Meanwhile, the Interior Department released a five-year strategic plan last week that includes a proposal to sell off public lands or pursue “strategic rights-of-way agreements, land exchanges and direct transfer of lands.” It is unclear whether the department intends to offer to sell to companies or only to local, state and tribal governments. Researchers who study natural resources policy told ProPublica that the country’s foundational land management law lays out steps that must be followed to dispose of federal land, steps that will be difficult for the Trump administration to legally navigate. Still, with permits for data centers pending before the Interior Department, the release of the strategic plan sparked fear that developers might try to buy federal land. Jayson O’Neill, spokesperson for conservation group Save Our Parks, said the plan was another attempt by Burgum to “sell off what’s left to AI data center developers and his extractive resource buddies.” The Interior Department did not respond to a request for comment on its proposal to sell federal land. The post Democrats in Washington Move to Ban Data Centers on Public Lands appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: JPMorgan upgrades MSCI UAE index on 'impressive' resilience amid conflict
events.summary: JPMorgan has boosted the ​MSCI UAE equity index from neutral to overweight, citing the Emirates' "impressive" economic resilience ⁠amid the months-long conflict in the Middle East. The UAE was embroiled in the US-Iran war that started in late February, and its key crude oil industry was hit by the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The government, however, responded quickly with measures to maintain economic activity in the Arab world's second biggest economy. JPMorgan was "impressed by [the UAE's] economic resilience. Earnings revisions have swung positive, valuations have upside and foreign inflows have returned", the Wall Street ⁠brokerage said in a client note on Tuesday. "We think the current state of no war/no peace in the Gulf is good enough for the UAE economy to keep growing and for the stock market to outperform CEEMEA," the brokerage added, referring to the Central and Eastern Europe, the Middle East and Africa bloc. The UAE economy has fared relatively well despite geopolitical headwinds. GDP grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion in the first half of 2026, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the impact of the Iran war . The non-oil sector's contribution to GDP during the first six-month period increased by 1.8 per cent to 79.2 per cent, the Federal Competitiveness and Statistics Centre revealed last month. Earlier this month, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, said the UAE’s foreign trade rose close to a record Dh3 trillion in the first nine months of the year, despite the challenges. Last week, Fitch Ratings said it expects the UAE's economy to expand in 2026 and has maintained the country's high-grade credit rating, citing resilient fiscal buffers. Additionally, UAE Minister of Investment Mohamed Alsuwaidi said last week that the nation came out of the war “exceptionally well” and the continued economic momentum despite uncertainty is driving the government to open new sectors for foreign investment. Also on Tuesday, JPMorgan upgraded the MSCI Turkey ​equity index from neutral to overweight, citing the ‌investment fund crisis that has shaken ⁠the region's financial markets as over ​and expects equities to rebound. Turkey's investment fund sector ​was hit ‌by a crisis after regulators in September ordered the liquidation of 131 funds managed ⁠by seven asset managers, following warnings that some could not meet redemption ⁠payments. "We think the fund crisis is over and the stock market should bounce back," the brokerage said. "Investors are too worried about the threat of MSCI demotion in our view; we think the chances are 10 per cent ​or lower." With inputs from Reuters

events.title: Trump's biggest project is running out of time
events.summary: Look past the White House renovations , the proposed arch and the golf course : President Trump's border wall project is hundreds of miles behind pace. Why it matters: " Build that wall " helped build MAGA. But with two years to go, tough terrain and mounting political resistance threaten to leave Trump's signature promise unfinished. State of play: At the current pace, the main wall won't be finished until late 2029, while Trump will leave office in January 2029. There are about 619 miles of primary wall left to build, according to data from Customs and Border Protection as of November 10. The Trump administration has picked up the pace — from 2.6 miles a week earlier this year to 3.9 miles a week between mid-June and earlier this month — according to an Axios review of the agency data. But much of the remaining mileage is in Texas, where local landowners are fighting back and Trump's biggest allies were swept out of power in the midterms. Zoom in: The Big Bend sector — home to the state and national parks, multi-generational family ranches and numerous ecotourism businesses — has become a hot spot of resistance to construction, galvanizing political leaders across the spectrum to speak out against any physical intervention. "Just about every Democrat running statewide came to the Big Bend," said Susan Hays, who was just elected to be a Presidio County Commissioner. "all of them care about the border, the Big Bend, and they're going to fight for our public lands." Friction point: Texas Land Commissioner-elect Benjamin Flores, who opposes wall construction plans in West Texas and Big Bend, says his office could leverage state-owned land to advocate for surveillance technology to monitor for illegal crossings, which would be less invasive on the land, instead of a physical border wall there. The state owns 31 linear miles of land along the border. "The federal government is gonna need cooperation from us to get other areas that they may want done [and] that would make more sense to have the wall in," Flores said. The General Land Office already reprimanded CBP and one of the border wall contractors for unauthorized construction in a cease-and-desist letter this July. Between the lines: Trump faces two main fronts of legal fights. Injunctions: More than a half dozen lawsuits are challenging the border wall in West Texas alone, building on legal fights elsewhere on the border and in Washington. Eminent domain: If local private landowner resistance continues, the federal government will also have to file individual eminent domain cases for each plot of land across the border. It has already filed some of these cases, including one against a church in New Mexico. Zoom out: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said at a press conference this summer that he was planning for a physical wall from "the Pacific to the Gulf of America this time next year." CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott gave an extended deadline to the end of 2027. Based on data shared by CBP, there would need to be a rapid increase in construction tempo to make this possible. What they're saying: Flores plans to tell administration officials to ease their aggressive timeline. "Let's be a little bit more careful because you know this is gonna stand there for a long time. Let's understand those ramifications a little bit more. But that is not to say that I'm not willing to explore all legal options at my disposal to make sure I am defending the best interests of Texas," he said. The other side: Art Del Cueto, a former Border Patrol agent and adviser at the immigration restriction group FAIR, argues that the border wall needs to stick to the original plan. "Now you've heard other individuals saying, 'Well, maybe we don't need it where you have natural barriers,' and that's understandable. But when you don't build in those areas, what it's going to do is it's going to create a funnel," Del Cueto said.

events.title: Malaysia Airlines parent says focus is on own growth, sidesteps AirAsia questions
events.summary: There had been no official discussions with the Malaysian government about absorbing AirAsia’s domestic market share or taking over its aircraft. Malaysia Airlines parent MAG says its priority is its own growth, not AirAsia, and it has not held official talks about absorbing AirAsia’s domestic market or aircraft. MAG plans about 8% capacity growth in 2027 after cutting about 6% in 2026, as it manages high fuel costs and aims to improve route profitability. Fuel now makes up more than 50% of MAG’s operating costs, but cargo is a strong area, driven by AI-related semiconductor shipments and e-commerce demand. KUALA LUMPUR – Malaysia Airlines’ parent is focused on its own growth plan, including an expected 8% capacity increase in 2027, its chief executive said, as the government weighs possible support for rival AirAsia . Malaysia Aviation Group (MAG) chief executive officer Nasaruddin Bakar last week told local media there had been no official discussions with the Malaysian government about absorbing AirAsia’s domestic market share or taking over its aircraft. In an interview with Reuters on Nov 14 , Nasaruddin was asked whether he was ruling out that informal or preliminary talks had taken place. “You need to ask other stake holders on that one,” he said. “But I can say that the focus of MAG today is to focus on the business for Malaysia Aviation Group.” The Malaysian government asked Malaysia Airlines and Batik Air whether they could absorb AirAsia’s domestic share as part of scenario planning, Reuters reported in September, citing people with knowledge of the matter. AirAsia is South-east Asia’s largest low-cost carrier and controls about 60% of Malaysia’s domestic market, but the government has been monitoring its financial health and weighing potential support as the privately owned carrier grapples with high fuel prices and foreign exchange losses. Asked whether any aircraft lessors had approached MAG about offering planes currently leased to AirAsia, Nasaruddin said discussions with lessors and financial institutions were centred on MAG’s own needs and existing orders. “We have not discussed anything outside of the scope,” he said. MAG, which is owned by the Malaysian government’s sovereign wealth fund, cut about 6% of its capacity in 2026, roughly 8,000 to 9,000 flights, to manage costs amid high fuel prices. It is planning capacity growth of about 8% in 2027, Nasaruddin said, and could restore more capacity if that was justified by its financial performance and route profitability. “The 2026 capacity adjustment is a tactical response to current market conditions and does not change our longer-term growth plans,” he said. “The projected growth in 2027 comes off a lower base following the capacity reductions implemented in 2026, so part of that growth reflects the normalisation of capacity.” Nasaruddin said fuel now accounts for more than 50% of operating costs, up from the usual 35% to 40%, adding that MAG has raised average fares by 20%, including fuel surcharges. Air cargo remained a bright spot, Nasaruddin said, driven by AI-related semiconductor and component shipments on top of traditional e-commerce volumes. “People are really transporting goods, especially with regards to the small boxes and the semiconductor boxes,” he said, adding that he expected demand to stay strong into 2027 and beyond. MAG operates three Airbus A330-200 freighters and carries belly cargo on its passenger planes. REUTERS

Last week, Trump directed Vice President JD Vance to turn away from negotiations with Iran. Earlier reports that Vance was considering face-to-face talks with an Iranian security official were incorrect, a source familiar with the situation told Semafor. Trump’s post aimed to make clear that the administration doesn’t need a meeting or a deal, the source said. events.title: Florida stayed red in a blue wave. But look at what happened in Hispanic precincts.
events.summary: Some Democrats see Angie Nixon's Senate loss in Florida as a warning about running too far left. But her results with Hispanic voters challenge that idea, an Axios analysis found. Hispanic-majority precincts that some feared would reject her politics swung more than 21 points toward Democrats from 2024 and gave her a slight edge over moderate gubernatorial candidate David Jolly. Why it matters: Democrats gained more ground in Florida than in most states this year despite falling short in the two biggest races. Whether they can finish climbing out of their hole will shape the party's 2028 chances in a state seen as a Republican stronghold. " There definitely was a broad blue shift, it just wasn't deep enough," Daniel Smith, a University of Florida political science professor, tells Axios. "But you don't get to these close numbers without non-party affiliates and Republicans voting Democrat." The big picture: Florida swung further toward Democrats than Georgia's gubernatorial race or Ohio's Senate race, yet Florida Democrats had a bigger hole to climb out of. Governor: Democratic nominee David Jolly improved on the 2022 margin by more than 18 points, nearly 6 points above the median gain across 36 states, and 2 points more than neighboring Georgia, where Democrats took the office for the first time in decades. Senate: Nixon improved on the 2022 margin by nearly 14 points, more than a point above the national median, and 2.5 points above Ohio's Democratic gains. State of play: Florida's five statewide Democratic nominees finished within 1.6 points of one another in two-party margin, the least ticket splitting out of the 23 states with both a governor's race and a U.S. Senate race. Nixon's margin improved in Hispanic-majority precincts by 22 points over Val Demings in 2022 and 21 points better than Kamala Harris in 2024. The shift showed up regardless of where Hispanic voters came from, in mostly Cuban precincts (R+34 to R+14), mostly Puerto Rican ones (D+16 to D+35) and Mexican and Central American ones (D+3 to D+44). The intrigue: Outside of Tampa, democratic socialist Ashley Herrmann flipped state House District 69. Zoom in: The swing was particularly noticeable in the Cuban American core of Miami-Dade. In precincts where 75% or more of the voter base is Cuban, voters favored Nixon slightly more than they did Jolly, data show. Nixon lost Hialeah by 31 points. Demings lost it by 59 in 2022, and Mucarsel-Powell by 53 in 2024. She lost Westchester by 34 points and Tamiami by 33, down from 55 and 54 in 2022. Between the lines: Jolly outperformed Nixon statewide, but only because he had stronger support among white voters and in the most Jewish precincts of Miami-Dade, Palm Beach and Broward counties. The left-wing Nixon held her own with Hispanic voters, though the party's Hispanic statewide nominees did better. In Hispanic-majority precincts, Nixon ran slightly ahead of moderate governor nominee Jolly (losing them by 2.8 points to his 3.2) but behind attorney general nominee José Javier Rodríguez, CFO nominee Annette Taddeo and agriculture commissioner nominee Joey Mendoza Atkins. By Axios' estimates, Nixon ran about 3 points ahead of Jolly among Black and Hispanic voters and about 4 points behind him among white voters. The results could mean the anti-communist and anti-socialist attacks against Nixon resonated less this year — the result of Trump's immigration efforts, Smith said. "The sentiments are still there, but it'll be interesting to see if [the results] were a wholesale move away from the Republican Party for those who turned out to vote or a backlash against the overzealous anti-immigration efforts by the Trump administration," he said. Yes, but: The results still don't have "the full picture" of who actually voted on Election Day, Democratic strategist Steve Schale told Axios Monday. They don't show if some Cubans found Nixon or Jolly's comments appealing versus other Cubans simply not showing up to vote, he said. An Axios analysis found ballots cast in Miami-Dade precincts where most voters were born in Cuba fell 3% from 2022, while they rose 7% countywide. The bottom line: For Schale, Democrats must focus on the "gap," or what it will take to lose a Hispanic precinct by 20 points instead of 30.

events.title: MPs ask what the break clause was for as Palantir wins two more years in the NHS
events.summary: Lawmakers and campaign groups have slammed the UK government's decision to extend Palantir's controversial NHS contract by two years. Health minister James Frith told MPs on Monday that the current contract would continue until March 2029 as the government procures a new version of the Federated Data Platform (FDP). The existing Palantir-led deal , awarded in 2023, has a maximum value of £330 million and includes other suppliers. Frith said the new procurement would focus on interoperability, resilience, and trusted common standards in a "new FDP iteration" which would "welcome international and UK capability alike – whether that is UK small and medium-sized enterprises that want a crack at NHS contracts, sovereign AI-backed capability in the UK or any international provider worth merit." Palantir's cornerstone NHS contract win attracted criticism for lack of transparency. The US supplier had already won £60 million in NHS contracts without competition during and following the pandemic. Use cases from this period were carried over to the FDP. Critics have also challenged the evidence used to promote the FDP's claimed benefits . Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons Science and Technology Committee, said she was "extremely disappointed" by the decision. She challenged the government's reliance on continuity of care to justify keeping the contract, given its existing transition provisions. She said Palantir made it clear it would use the next two years to "embed itself even more deeply in our public services." "If a break clause cannot be exercised because of continuity of care, it is not a break clause; it is a lock-in. The Minister assured me that there were already contractual requirements that smooth continuity of care should continue. Were those assurances made in error?" she asked Frith. Frith confirmed that the contracts included exit and transition provisions and that migration was "possible in principle." "However, given the requirement for a new iteration, given performance and the benefits already in play, and given the opportunity to add new capability, including maternity services, to a next generation of FDP, an 18 to 24-month period for commission and procurement is a reasonable assessment," he said. Technology and government priorities had moved on since the original FDP procurement in 2023, he told MPs. "We will begin a new procurement process along different lines from the current contract," he said. The formal process is set to start during the second half of next year and take around 18 months. "Interoperability, resilience, and trusted common standards can and must be baked into the next generation of FDP. We will also start work, alongside the new procurement, with different providers on developing new capabilities and expertise starting with systems used in maternity care. Innovative providers will be invited to help address the data and digital fragmentation in this important area of care, and test how health priorities can create routes to build UK AI capability," Frith said. Former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson, now Palantir's UK senior vice president , welcomed the extension. "This is good news for patients and for the NHS. And it is the right decision to press forward with a programme that, in the words of Ministers, 'is significantly exceeding its benefits forecast and has exceeded every target' since it launched in 2024," he said. "We will now redouble our efforts over the next two years to continue and accelerate that support. As a result of the announcement, we will also deepen our investment in the UK. The FDP is the right vehicle to deliver the change needed in the NHS, and over the next two years Palantir will do everything in its power to drive that change as far as possible, as fast as possible." Nonprofit tech transparency group Foxglove has challenged NHS contracts awarded to Palantir without competition since the pandemic, when the company initially offered its services for £1. Responding to the extension, Foxglove co-executive director Rosa Curling said: "Palantir and its chief lobbyist Lord Tom Watson clearly think the contract extension is in the bag and appear to be already planning to turn that into another extension in two years, or a new procurement that heavily favors Palantir as we saw in 2023. "The government must provide urgent clarity on whether they plan to help Watson embed Palantir in the NHS for the long term – or will kick this Trump-backing spy tech company out of the health service once and for all." ®

events.title: U.S. allies on edge as Trump heads to summit with Xi and Putin
events.summary: President Trump's trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin has the makings of an unpredictable spectacle — and that's exactly what has U.S. allies anxious. Why it matters: Trump's stated goal for the first-ever summit between the nations' three leaders is to start a discussion on nuclear disarmament. But the fear is that he could go off script and take positions on Ukraine or Taiwan that undermine their interests or appear to side with their chief adversaries, according to several European officials and Western diplomats. "We know that every time President Trump talks to or sees Putin, it translates into bad news for Ukraine and for Europe. We brace for anything," a European diplomat told Axios. Substance aside, Western diplomats worry about the optics of Trump appearing alongside two emboldened strongmen. On Monday, Trump also floated a possible meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Driving the news: Before leaving for the Philippines on Monday, Trump reiterated that his goal for the summit is to talk about denuclearization — a "tough subject," he said, "because it's very hard for any of us to say we'll get rid of our nukes, right?" But other topics will get attention, too, Trump went on to say. "We'll talk about Iran. We have Iran in very good shape, but we'll talk about Iran a little bit," he said. The president also said "we'll talk about my favorite subject, Ukraine." His comments came after U.S. officials stressed in a call with reporters on Friday that the summit would not deal with the war in Ukraine. Chinese officials said the same thing. Context: Neither China nor Russia was enthusiastic about discussing denuclearization. But China agreed after Russian lobbying. And Putin saw the summit as a chance to lobby Trump on Ukraine. Behind the scenes: The Trump-Xi-Putin summit was a topic of closed-door talks among European leaders at a meeting in Dublin last week, according to a European diplomat. Some of them raised concerns about what Trump might say about the war in Ukraine, the diplomat said. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was among the more vocal during the private session. He then went out and spoke about it publicly. "Our message to the U.S. before Trump meets Putin is: No surprises, please," Merz said. Ukrainian officials expressed similar worries. Japanese officials also privately relayed concerns to U.S. counterparts about the message the summit might project about Washington's stance on Taiwan or Asia more broadly, according to a source with knowledge of the matter. A potential public meeting between Trump and Kim Jong Un would be even more concerning for Japan. The intrigue: European diplomats said U.S. officials tried to downplay the summit and lower expectations about any substantive results. But many of the U.S. allies are nervous that the meeting will project an image of the three leaders scheming to carve up the earth into spheres of influence. Some of them invoked "Yalta II" — referring to the 1945 summit between the U.S., Great Britain and the Soviet Union that helped shape post-war Europe. State of play: On the same day Trump meets with Xi and Putin, his envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are expected to be in Berlin with senior officials from Ukraine, Germany, France, the UK, Italy, Poland, the EU and NATO, according to two sources. The purpose is to coordinate ahead of the next round of negotiations with Russia in Abu Dhabi the following week. On Monday, Kushner and Witkoff held a virtual meeting with the representatives of the different entities. "We discussed how to facilitate direct engagement between Europe and Russia, which has been largely absent over the past four years. It is important that both sides hear each other's concerns and proposals directly as we work toward a more stable and secure future for Europe," Kushner wrote on X. The other side: Witkoff and Kushner also spoke on Monday with Putin's foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov about the next steps in the peace process. The White House said Putin had agreed to allow European representatives to join the negotiations with Ukraine and to launch a parallel track of talks regarding a Europe-Russia security deal. But Ushakov said no such agreement had been reached.

events.title: Malaysia-France rare earths project to begin operations in early 2027, Macron says
events.summary: A joint rare earths mining and processing venture between Malaysia and France is expected to begin operations in early 2027 KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia -- A joint rare earths mining and processing venture between Malaysia and France is expected to begin operations in early 2027 as the two nations agreed to deepen cooperation and elevate ties to a strategic partnership, French President Emmanuel Macron said Tuesday. The project, which involves French company Carester and Malaysian firm Malaco Mining Sendirian Berhad, would cover the extraction and processing of rare earths in Malaysia, with reserved volumes and the possibility of refining in France, Macron said. “Operations are due to begin in early 2027,” he said at a joint news conference after talks with Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim. “This will allow us to proceed ... involving not only extraction, but also processing here, with reserved volumes and capacity, including the possibility of refining in France, which is crucial for our entire value chain.” The arrangement reflects Malaysia’s move to build domestic processing capabilities, while France seeks to secure and diversify supplies of critical minerals used in a wide range of products from electric vehicles, electronics and renewable energy to defense industries. The two leaders said that they agreed to elevate bilateral ties to a broader strategic partnership, focusing cooperation on defense, energy, semiconductors and digital connectivity, among other areas. Anwar said that Malaysia has made an exception in its policy against exporting rare earth minerals in return for collaboration with France in developing its rare earths industry. He didn’t provide further details. He said that cooperation with France demonstrated how resource-rich countries could work with foreign partners while securing technology transfer, training and industrial expertise. Macron said that the partnership reflected a shared commitment to national sovereignty and greater independence in a world increasingly shaped by competing major powers. Plans for defense cooperation will include a new industrial road map, support for a regional center to counter hybrid threats and Malaysia's procurement of combat search-and-rescue helicopters from Airbus, he said. For semiconductors, Macron said that Malaysian firm SkyeChip and French company SiPearl will collaborate to develop a high-performance computing platform. More than 300 French companies operate in Malaysia, making France its second-largest European investor, he said. Macron's visit was the third by a French president since diplomatic relations were established in 1957. He earlier visited Cambodia to attend a summit of French-speaking nations, before arriving late Monday in Malaysia. events.title: 1.5-hour-long system outage forces United Airlines to delay departing flights
events.summary: A system outage that lasted more than 90 minutes forced United Airlines to delay departing flights A system outage that lasted more than 90 minutes forced United Airlines to delay departing flights Monday, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration's network prompted a nationwide ground stop. Chicago-based United said in a statement that flights that were in the air and flights on its United Express regional network were not affected. The airline also said there was “no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.” United apologized on social media to customers for the inconvenience. It resolved the issue about one hour and 40 minutes after pilots first began reporting problems to air traffic controllers. United did not immediately provide details about which of its systems were affected, but pilots told air traffic controllers that the problem was related to a system that helps them determine a plane's final weight. Before every departure, pilots use performance software, often on a cockpit tablet, to check that the aircraft can safely take off under current weather and runway conditions. The preflight calculations include the aircraft's weight along with information about the fuel, baggage, cargo and passengers the plane is carrying. The information is also used to guide the autopilot system and the decisions pilots make, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said. “It is extremely important to have all of these numbers accurate and precise,” said Arroyo, who flew for United. “Pilots use that information to establish guidance and performance for their flights from takeoff to landing.” Arroyo said he has seen problems with the weight and balance system before in his career, but the airline did the right thing by delaying flights to ensure safety. Years ago, pilots used to do all those weight calculations manually with a pencil and paper and then radio in the numbers, but today it is all calculated electronically and then loaded into the plane’s computers. In August 2025, United grounded planes at major U.S. airports, delaying more than 1,000 flights because of an hourslong outage of a system called Unimatic, which houses flight information that is fed to other systems including those that calculate weight and balance and track flight times. United said in response to a message from The Associated Press that it had no further information to provide about whether the same system was affected by Monday’s outage. The app combines live air traffic control radio feeds with real-time visual aircraft tracking. The flight-tracking website FlightAware showed United with about 600 delayed flights Monday evening, though it was unclear how many were directly related to the system outage. The United computer problem is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown in recent days. Earlier Monday, thousands of people reported being unable to access their online accounts at several major U.S. banks after JPMorgan Chase had a technical problem. On Friday, the FAA ordered every flight grounded because a newly installed router malfunctioned, overwhelming the aging air traffic control system . And one day earlier, Microsoft experienced a major disruption to its Outlook email service. Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored. events.title: Trump’s accounts traded up to $97.5 million in Nvidia as Huang gained White House access
events.summary: President Donald Trump's investment accounts have bought and sold Nvidia stock at least 103 times since he returned to the White House, with transactions worth a combined $27 million to $97.5 million, a CNBC analysis found. Among the trades was a sale of as much as $1 million on May 18, five days after Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly briefed Trump on Jensen Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Trump denies being briefed. The White House says independent advisors manage Trump's investments without his input. His financial disclosures offer no evidence that Trump directed the trades or that his advisors had access to classified intelligence. President Donald Trump has had plenty of reason to cheer the rise of Nvidia . The chipmaker helped propel the stock market that Trump is fond of touting. Its billionaire co-founder, Jensen Huang , became one of the president's favorite businessmen. And by the end of last year, Nvidia had become one of Trump's three largest individual stock holdings, worth between $12.5 million and $58 million, up from between $615,000 and $1.3 million a year earlier. Since returning to the White House, Trump's investment accounts have bought or sold Nvidia shares at least 103 times — transactions worth a combined $27 million to $97.5 million, according to a new CNBC analysis of his annual and periodic financial disclosures, which were most recently updated through August. By midday Monday, Trump's Nvidia stake, based on the value he reported holding in August, would be worth $4.5 million to $57.7 million with stock priced around $157. But the filings give broad dollar ranges for holdings rather than the number of shares, leaving his current stake unclear. Now, Huang's resignation as Nvidia's CEO on Thursday, following revelations about his relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China and reports of affairs with company employees, has put those trades back in the spotlight. Among them was a sale of $500,001 to $1 million on May 18 , the first Monday after Trump returned from a state visit to China with Huang. Five days earlier, before Huang boarded Air Force One during a refueling stop in Alaska, Secretary of State Marco Rubio had briefed Trump on intelligence concerning Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, The New York Times reported . Trump on Monday denied being briefed . Asked about the reported briefing from Rubio, Trump said, "I haven't heard that," adding that he did not know whether the woman, Alice Huang, was a Chinese spy. The president's financial accounts also bought smaller amounts of Nvidia shares in the days immediately before and after the May 18 sale, part of a broader trading blitz . Such flurries have defined his second term: Trump disclosed more than 21,000 trades in 2025 alone , compared with roughly 500 during his entire first term, according to CNBC's analysis. Trump bought up to $25 million in Meta and millions in SpaceX debt in August Trump’s municipal bond portfolio reaches as much as $1 billion as policy overlaps mount Trump disclosure shows 1,100 July trades, Microsoft and Amazon sales Trump’s oil investments have gained millions during Iran war as his accounts keep trading Trump’s foreign licensing business booms to $59.5 million as Gulf developers pay JPMorgan, Schwab and UBS manage millions in Trump’s $858 million investment portfolio Trump bought as much as $5 million in Axon stock before ICE sought $220 million Taser deal Company that bet big on Trump-backed crypto says its fortunes have improved Trump family got about $500M from crypto venture — but investors saw steep losses Trump Jr. calls banking a 'Ponzi scheme' that forced family to create crypto business The Trump family crypto empire looks to Asia: Eric Trump talks Bitcoin in Hong Kong Trump family says U.S. dollar needs an upgrade and they are the ones to do it A White House spokesperson told CNBC independent advisors manage Trump's portfolio without his input. Trump Organization spokesperson Kimberly Benza said the arrangement is designed to "avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest." The disclosures offer no evidence Trump directed the trades or that his advisors had access to classified intelligence. Trump has long used the stock market as a scorecard for the economy, touting its record highs — sometimes when highs have not actually been reached — despite the turbulence caused by his tariffs and the Iran war . "Look, we have the highest stock market we've ever had," Trump told ESPN commentator and political talk show host Stephen A. Smith on Thursday when pressed about Republicans' midterm losses . Nvidia alone accounted for about 13.5% of the S&P 500's 2026 gains through September, according to an analysis by Choate Wealth that looked at how chip stocks have driven the year's performance. Huang's rise in Trump's Washington has been nearly as striking as Nvidia's on Wall Street.

events.title: Turkish authorities carry out a raid on another opposition TV station and appoint trustees
events.summary: Turkish authorities have raided the headquarters of one of the country's last major opposition-aligned television stations, Sozcu TV ANKARA, Turkey -- ANKARA, Turkey (AP) — Turkish authorities raided the headquarters of one of the country's last major opposition-aligned television stations on Tuesday, detaining several executives and appointing trustees to manage operations in a move critics described as the latest step in a crackdown on independent media . The predawn raid against Sozcu TV came just weeks after trustees similarly took control of another opposition-leaning news channel, Halk TV, in an alleged corruption investigation that critics said was politically motivated. Press freedoms in Turkey have steadily eroded during the more than two decades that President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has been in power, and a majority of media outlets are either under government control or aligned with it. The country ranks 163rd out of 180 countries in the Reporters Without Borders’ world press freedom index. A statement from the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s office said the move against Sozcu TV was part of an investigation into the channel’s alleged violation of Turkey’s anti-terror financing laws and suspected links to a network that was led by the late U.S.-based cleric Fethullah Gulen . The cleric, who died in 2024, was accused by Turkey of orchestrating a failed military coup in 2016 and his network of supporters has been branded a terrorist organization. Gulen had denied the accusations. The prosecutors' office cited suspicion that Sozcu TV and other media outlets linked to its owner, Burak Akbay, were being financed by overseas accounts. Tuesday's raid follows a widening crackdown on the opposition, with dozens of mayors from the main opposition party arrested on corruption charges since 2024, including former Istanbul mayor Ekrem Imamoglu. The popular politician was widely regarded as a possible challenger to Erdogan. The government denies any involvement in legal moves against the opposition, insisting that Turkey’s courts operate independently. The action against Sozcu TV drew condemnation from opposition parties and media groups. Some critics linked the decision to impose a trusteeship to the channel devoting extensive coverage to an investment fund scandal that led to the resignation and subsequent arrest of a senior member of Erdogan’s ruling party. Main opposition New Party leader Ozgur Ozel accused Erdogan’s government of intolerance toward “even the smallest criticism or a single inconvenient truth being heard.” He vowed not to “surrender to these would-be dictators.” Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Musavat Dervisoglu, the leader of the center-right opposition Good Party, described the move as “an overt assault on democracy, the rule of law, the sense of justice, and the public’s right to be informed.” “Turkey will speak, and the voice of the truth cannot be silenced!” he wrote on X. In a joint statement, Turkish journalism associations expressed solidarity with Sozcu TV journalists and called for the decision to appoint trustees to be reversed. “Following Halk TV, the appointment of trustees to Sozcu shows that the media climate in Turkey has entered a dark winter,” the statement read. On Tuesday, Sozcu TV’s regular early morning news program was replaced by a recorded discussion about longevity. Other television stations, including HaberTurk and Tele1, have similarly been placed under trusteeship. events.title: I make up to $800 a month completing AI surveys in my free time. My side hustle has helped pay for vacations and Lego sets.
events.summary: Ethan Quinn. Courtesy of Ethan Quinn Project manager Ethan Quinn uses Prolific AI studies to turn his spare hours into travel money. He reviews AI podcasts, songs, and images, using his professional audio and lighting skills. Over five years, he's earned $14,000 on Prolific, funding Lego sets and trips to Sedona and Tokyo. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Ethan Quinn, a 36-year-old project manager based in Deerfield, Illinois, who has a side hustle completing AI surveys on Prolific to fund his vacations. It has been edited for length and clarity. I'm a project manager who's very passionate about live events. I love utilizing my technical skills and leadership abilities to help turn my clients' visions into reality. I typically work on shows for corporations and live concerts throughout Chicago. While working full-time, I went back to school in 2018 to earn my Bachelor's degree in business management. In October 2024, I transitioned to a new company and role as a project manager for live events, focusing on audio, video, and lighting. I also have a lucrative side hustle on Prolific that brings in extra money I mostly use for travel. When I was looking for extra income at the end of 2020, I found Prolific Prolific is a data collection platform that connects researchers, AI developers, and product teams with real people who take part in studies online. To get onboarded, I verified my identity through the platform and connected my PayPal account. After successfully completing my studies, I became eligible for more specialized opportunities, including AI-related work. I thought this could be a fun way to help with research and earn money from the comfort of my home. The goal at first was to build some rainy-day money and see what the earning potential was. The first surveys I completed were mostly from educational institutions seeking academic research In the last few years, there have been surveys to help train and review AI. With my unique background in audio and lighting, I've been able to help assess AI from a more technical background. These AI studies have allowed me to generate a side income. I've completed more than 6,700 surveys. The best part is this was all done in my spare time . Each survey takes about 10 to 15 minutes. The AI tasks run the gamut from analyzing images and AI-generated podcasts to fact-checking AI-generated answers Some of the AI training involves a user asking a question, for instance, the score of a basketball game last night, and I have to verify that the answer given by the AI is factual. I've reviewed AI-generated songs and been asked to determine which sounded more realistic or human-made. I've also listened to AI-generated podcasts and have an easy time hearing audio errors or glitches in speech that might not be as noticeable to someone without my professional experience. I've caught myself getting so caught up in podcasts and songs because they sound so realistic that I momentarily forget they're AI-generated. This is leaps and bounds ahead of the AI studies I did a year or two ago, when they were clearly artificial-sounding. Additionally, my background in lighting helps me judge pictures more critically and notice when sunlight is not accurately reflected off a person's face. I enjoy helping shape the future of this field by drawing on my specialized background. I've made about $14,000 on Prolific over the last 5 years Initially, I'd only do a few surveys a month . As I've learned more about the platform and process, most of my income has come in the last few years. In my experience, AI surveys pay more than traditional academic-research surveys, but they take more time and concentration, requiring about 20 to 40 minutes per survey. The amount I do each month ebbs and flows. During a good month when I can do a lot of surveys, I make between $300 and $800. If I had a month where my job didn't demand so much attention and focus, I believe I could make over $1,000. I recently had the goal of buying an expensive Lord of the Rings Lego set. Rather than tapping into my savings or my job income, I set aside earnings from Prolific and was able to pay for the set. I was able to save for a fall 2025 vacation to Sedona with my wife, paid for by my Prolific earnings. We also recently went to Tokyo, and we were able to pay for a lot of our meals, a couple of nights at one of the hotels, and had extra spending money from my Prolific earnings. I see this as a long-term opportunity for me These studies are unique, and it's fun to see how AI improves over time. This work isn't for everyone, and I know many people in demanding jobs would rather watch a movie or play a video game to decompress at night. Honestly, some days that's what I need for my mental health. The most important part is treating AI reviews and surveys with the same level of effort and detail that you would put into your career. Low-quality effort is noticeable and does a disservice to the companies paying you to help. Careful, high-quality work matters. events.title: I’m Virgin Group's CEO. I wake up without an alarm, talk to Richard Branson weekly, and secretly check into our hotels.
events.summary: Josh Bayliss Harry Kinnaird/VML This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Josh Bayliss, the 53-year-old CEO of Virgin Group, who is based in Switzerland. The following has been edited for length and clarity. When I was a kid, I wanted to be a scientist, mainly because I'd decided that was how you became the Incredible Hulk. When that plan fell apart, I studied law at the University of Auckland instead. After some time at a firm in Barcelona, I landed in London in 1999 as a litigator at Slaughter and May. I liked being a lawyer; I genuinely did. What started to bother me after a while was that I'd give the advice and then watch somebody else make the call. So in 2005, when Virgin was creating a general counsel job, I went to see Richard Branson about it. He had double-booked himself with something across town and was already running late, which is how I ended up doing my interview in the back of a car stuck in London traffic. By the time we got out, I'd pretty much decided I was leaving the firm. Six years later, I became CEO. I oversee everything Virgin is invested in, as well as everything that licenses the brand. While a lot of that work happens in boardrooms, I get far more out of checking in like any other guest or chatting with the cabin crew on a Virgin Atlantic flight. I really love it when I show up at a Virgin hotel, and nobody knows what my job is. Here's how I do my job. I wake up between 5:30 and 6:15 a.m. most mornings Most mornings I wake up without an alarm. Today, I woke up around 5:20 a.m., though on a normal day, I'm a between 5:30 and 6:15 kind of waker. I'm on the road about as much as I'm at home, and I figured out a long time ago that I can't control the amount of sleep I get. The only two things I can control are exercise and what I eat, so I try to stay in good shape and stay active. At home, the first thing I do is make my wife a coffee. In fact, I'll make us both one, and we'll spend half an hour together having it and talking to the dog before I go exercise. I really enjoy cycling, but I've discovered that high-speed walking and yoga play a big role in my life in my 50s. This morning, I did a fast walk of a little more than 4 miles, and over the weekend, I hiked in the snow. After exercise, I catch up on overnight emails, since our businesses operate across time zones pretty much everywhere in the world. Over breakfast, I read the Financial Times and The Wall Street Journal, and I skim the headlines on what's happened with Virgin companies before I get to my desk. The big strategic questions end up with me I'm the chairman of Virgin Atlantic and on the board of Virgin Hotels, and I'm in close contact with the team at Virgin Voyages all the time. We've got very strong leaders in our businesses, and we entrust the day-to-day operations to them. What comes my way are the bigger-picture strategic questions. The Valiant Lady is an adults-only cruise ship operated by Virgin Voyages. Horacio Villalobos/Corbis via Getty Images Virgin Voyages started sailing on the West Coast this past year, and to add new itineraries, we needed more ships. A question about how we grow the fleet would come onto my desk. The other thing that comes my way is new businesses, and right now we're setting up a train company that will operate between the UK and Europe. A couple of weeks ago, I was in Paris meeting with regulators, government officials, and journalists about it. There's no typical answer to how my week splits because it fluctuates through the year depending on what's happening at each company. Lately, a lot of my time has gone to hotels and the airline. Virgin Hotels recently signed a deal in Atlanta, which we're very excited about, and we're opening a new hotel in Marrakesh. At Virgin Atlantic, we're refurbishing all of our 787s and A330s and fitting Starlink, the satellite internet service, to the fleet, and all the issues that come with that kind of overhaul have been very much on my mind. Come the first quarter of 2027, the cycle tells me there will be different issues at different businesses. I check into our hotels like any other guest My team would probably say I'm a little too focused on every little detail. Two weekends ago, I stayed at the Virgin Hotel in Edinburgh. From the moment I walked to the front door, I was paying attention to the welcome and the way check-in was handled. How comfortable the bed was and what the bathroom amenities were like mattered to me just as much. I happen to think Edinburgh is one of the greatest hotels in our portfolio, if not the greatest. Sir Richard Branson in the Rotunda during the Virgin Hotels Groundbreaking event at India Buildings in Edinburgh. Robert Perry/PA Images via Getty Images On our flights, I'm always asking the cabin crew what would make a difference to them doing their job better. The people on the front line are the ones who see where we could erase those little pinch points and create even more moments of joy, and those conversations are way more beneficial to me than sitting in a board meeting. Richard Branson and I talk every week No week goes by without Richard and me discussing what's going on in the Group, and he's always taught me to keep my eyes open for the next big opportunity. Probably the No. 1 characteristic that has helped me is curiosity. I'm always reading stuff I don't understand and listening to things that take me outside my comfort zone. Over the weekend, I listened to Ezra Klein's podcast at The New York Times, and the last book I finished was "The Artist and the Feast" by Lucy Steeds . For the last 18 months, a lot of that listening has been podcasts about AI. I use AI every day, and it's a great tool, but it has its limitations. It's really important that anybody using it, particularly business leaders, doesn't surrender their critical faculties. You need to interrogate what it's giving you and assess whether it's the right tool for the job. Virgin is very much a people-first business, so we see AI as additive, and the human experience will always be front and center for us. I always protect one part of my calendar every year I'm from New Zealand and live in Europe, so every couple of years I go home to see my mum and dad and my brother and his children, though I'm not sure that counts as a vacation. My wife and I hadn't had a holiday all year, so a couple of weeks ago we flew Virgin to Barbados for a week. We did yoga on the beach every day at sunrise, and it was brilliant. Back home, the last series we watched together was "Widow's Bay," which was great. The one thing on my calendar that always stays protected is our wedding anniversary. Next year will be 25 years, and I always make sure I see my wife on that day. If I could talk to the version of me who started this job 15 years ago, I'd tell him to be ready for anything because anything can be around the corner. events.title: The 10 states set to build the least housing in the coming years
events.summary: Alaska, Connecticut, and West Virginia were all ranked among the 10 states with the fewest approved building permits from January to August 2026. Marli Miller/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images A report tracked how many building permits states issue per 1,000 residents. The report found that Alaska, Connecticut, and Illinois had the lowest permits per resident. States lagging behind the US average may see home prices go up, as supply could fall behind demand. Some states across America need to pick up the homebuilding pace — or housing prices could catch up to them. From January to August 2026, the US national average for housing permits — indicating how many housing units are approved to be built — was 2.83 units per 1,000 residents , according to an October research report from the Lied Center for Real Estate at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. The report provides insights into what the housing market could look like in 2028 and 2029, as these approved permits come online as available housing units, said Nicholas Irwin, coauthor of the report and research director at the Lied Center for Real Estate. Across the country, some states lag behind the national average, which could drive up housing prices in the near future as housing supply fails to catch up with demand. "If you don't add supply, and demand keeps growing as more people move in and more households are formed, it just puts upward pressure on prices," Irwin said. Here are the states that are issuing permits at the lowest rate per 1,000 residents. The states lagging in issuing building permits could face growing affordability concerns , especially those falling short of projected household growth, another measure included in the report. "If we are already at a lag in some of these states — your Nevadas, your Connecticut's, Maryland's — when it comes to building, that's just going to exacerbate currently experienced affordability concerns for each of those states' residents," Irwin said. Alaska was the state with the lowest ranking, standing at 0.72 permits per 1,000 residents, after only 528 units were approved from January through August 2026, 75% below the national rate, the report said. Its permit acceptances have also declined year-over-year, down 8.3% from the same period in 2025 and 12.3% from 2023. Connecticut was ranked the second-lowest state in number of permits per resident in the US, as it approved 3,799 permits, 64% below the national rate. This rate is 17.7% less than during January to August of 2025, and 9.3% lower than the same period in 2023. It was the lowest-ranked state in the report's overall housing supply pipeline rankings — performing poorly across four metrics, including the permit rate per 1,000 residents. Regarding the overall ranking, Irwin said some states are struggling on all fronts. "Nevada, Alaska, Connecticut, North Dakota, Maryland are all doing really poorly, and they're doing poorly no matter how much we weigh our different four pillars," Irwin said. West Virginia was ranked the 10th-lowest state in building permits per resident, at 1.55, 45% below the US average. Overall, it ranked 22nd in the report, with mixed performance across metrics. While its overall number of permits per resident lagged behind other states, its pace of permits relative to household growth was the third-highest in the nation — meaning permitting is outpacing its projected household growth by 5.72. This is because the number of households is projected to shrink in West Virginia, according to the report. Irwin said there are some states that "no matter how you weigh" them consistently end up at the top or bottom of the rankings. "No matter how you look at the data, the building permit regime and how housing is being constructed in these areas is falling way behind of what's needed," he said. "Our main thing, if we can give anything, is just build more housing, build all types of housing." Read the original article on Business Insider
