events.title: I Photographed Her Parents as They Were Sentenced for Her Twin’s Death. Years Later, I Photographed Her Life.
events.summary: I read once that photographers have ongoing conversations with one another across space and time. When Evelyn leaned back on the examination table at her doctor appointment, I instantly thought of W. Eugene Smith’s 1948 Life Magazine photo essay, “Country Doctor.” Smith’s photograph of the doctor taking a smoke break and this photograph of Evelyn have, strangely, so much in common. About eight years ago, I was assigned to photograph the sentencing of Travis and Sarah Mitchell, a couple with deep roots in an insular faith-healing sect outside of Portland, Oregon.   The Mitchells, as members of the Followers of Christ, adhere to a doctrine that forbids medical care. Instead, followers rely on healing through faith. So when Sarah Mitchell gave birth prematurely to twins in 2017 — and both gasped for breath in their first hours — the couple didn’t rush them to an emergency room. Instead, they turned to prayer.  One twin, Ginnifer, lived for four hours, each one a struggle. The family eventually sought medical care for her surviving twin sister, Evelyn, but only after the county’s deputy medical examiner arrived at the location of the home birth and learned, though not right away, of Evelyn’s existence. Even then, he had to seek help from police, who arrived at the Oregon City home and told reluctant family members to take the struggling infant to the hospital or they’d do it themselves.  The Mitchells pleaded guilty to criminally negligent homicide in the death of their infant daughter, Ginnifer, and to criminal mistreatment for failing to seek medical care for her surviving twin, Evelyn. The couple’s lawyer told the judge that the Mitchells grieved the loss of Ginnifer and loved Evelyn. “Travis and Sarah are utterly sincere, decent and caring human beings,” he told the judge. (The Mitchells and their lawyer did not respond to ProPublica and The Oregonian’s recent requests to be interviewed.) Today, my memory of the sentencing is more montage than detail. But I remember the crowded gallery, the couple in black-and-white-striped prison clothing, and their prison sentence of more than six years. Evelyn, who within days of her birth had been placed in the custody of Marshall and Jennifer Phillips, another couple in the Followers of Christ, wasn’t present. She remained in the couple’s permanent care. The Mitchells went off to prison, and I went on with my life.  Such is the grinding rhythm of the daily news cycle. So often I see people on their worst day — and then never again. Stories don’t really end, of course, but my role as a photojournalist is limited. I’m an observer rather than a participant, seeing mostly slivers of the human experience that offer only a window into the whole. It’s rare that I get to see what happens next. Never would I have dreamed that the surviving baby in this case, Evelyn, would be someone I’d later come to know and care about through my work. But that’s precisely what happened eight years after that courtroom scene played out, when I began documenting the lives of Evelyn and her parents, the Phillipses. (In a legal filing in an ongoing case relating to Evelyn’s custody, the Mitchells criticized the Phillipses for allowing her to participate in our coverage.) The resulting story , a collaboration between ProPublica and The Oregonian, is one of several recently published about faith healing and the Followers of Christ church. It intimately explores the Phillipses’ journey out of the sect and illustrates how changes in Oregon state law — in contrast to neighboring Idaho, where the Followers have a handful of churches — have led to a reduction in child deaths.  To spend time around 9-year-old Evelyn is to behold a luminous, magnetic force of nature. It’s impossible to imagine this same girl as a premature baby so small that the only items that fit her were doll clothes purchased from the supermarket toy aisle.  For months, as I documented Evelyn’s life — from her baptism to her home life to doctors’ appointments — my journalism colleagues worked on their own pieces of our project. Teresa Mahoney, video editor at The Oregonian, produced a video introduction to the story that included a sequence of footage recorded by body cameras worn by police officers who stood outside Evelyn’s grandparents’ house that night, at first nudging, then ordering, Evelyn’s family to get her to the hospital. Each time I viewed it, as I watched the officers politely letting time slip away, I’d need to regulate my own breathing as I imagined Evelyn on the other side of that door, struggling to breathe herself. I hope that reporter Noelle Crombie’s words, Teresa’s video and my photographs allow readers to see not only the journey of the couple who are raising Evelyn as their own but also the surviving — indeed, thriving — twin I came to know. That Evelyn is alive at all is, depending on your worldview, a miracle.  My work is all about observing and capturing moments, about freezing time. Here, I was witnessing the unfolding of time. I got to see what happened next. Evelyn’s baptism was a highly anticipated day and meaningful for all involved. The stakes were high for me because the immersion lasted only a few seconds. I had one chance to get it right.  Jennifer Phillips is a steadfast presence in Evelyn’s life. This moment of her curling Evelyn’s hair in preparation for the baptism reminded me of daguerreotypes from the 1800s. In some, mothers who wanted photographs of their babies had to hold them behind velvet drapes so as not to be visible in the portraits. I thought of the nature of emotional labor and how much of it is unseen. Evelyn was getting a kick out of giving Marshall a pounding back massage. We were all at McDonald’s — her favorite restaurant — having her birthday meal. Marshall Phillips and Evelyn attended a father-daughter dance at a high school a few towns away. Evelyn had a list of dances she and Marshall practiced. I had recently lost my father and was carrying grief. But seeing Marshall’s love for Evelyn was beautiful and healing. In person, Evelyn sparkles. When she saw herself in a mirror with her face painted, her delight was electric. The night before Evelyn’s ninth birthday party, the family decorated the room where the event would take place. I know firsthand how much parenting involves endless tasks and routines. Mixed into the chaos are moments of pure joy. Yearly pediatric check-ups are an ordinary aspect of childhood, and for Evelyn it’s no different. Knowing her history, however, gives these moments an undeniable poignance. A check on her heart rate becomes a reminder of the miracle of her very existence. Before bed, Marshall reads a chapter book to Evelyn that combines the concept of evolution with lessons from the Bible. Evelyn was excited I was there and sprinkled in knock-knock jokes between the biblical passages. After that, the family prays together. Although Evelyn didn’t know the other kids a

events.title: Data centre REITs, related stocks slide as US imposes new rule on AI chip exports
events.summary: The news followed the disclosure of an extramarital affair between Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and Megaspeed’s former top executive Alice Huang. US rules on AI chip exports pushed Singapore data centre REITs and related stocks lower on Nov 17, as investors feared tighter licensing and weaker regional demand. Authorities are studying the new measure, which may add Singapore and other countries to export restrictions. Singtel said the impact should be minimal for its sovereign AI services. Analysts said the sector still has strong demand from AI and cloud computing, but growth may become more complex. Risks are higher for firms linked to Chinese AI customers. SINGAPORE – Singapore-listed data centre real estate investment trusts (REITs) and related stocks slid on Nov 17 after news that the United States will impose new rules on the export of AI chips. However, analysts said data centre operators here should continue to benefit from underlying demand for artificial intelligence and cloud computing services. This news followed the disclosure of an extramarital affair between Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and Megaspeed’s former top executive, Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who is suspected by the US of being a Chinese spy. Megaspeed is a cloud computing provider based in Singapore. Jensen Huang stepped down as Nvidia chief executive on Nov 12, while Alice Huang is believed to be in China. The new rule announced on Nov 16 in the US aims to ensure that restrictions on access to sensitive US technology are not circumvented through remote computing arrangements, which may involve data centres in third countries. This would add Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil to a list of countries subject to export restrictions. Companies would then need licences from the US Commerce Department to ship to those countries. The effect would be to create a two-tier operating environment in Singapore: strict export licensing on local and non-US operators, while providing exemptions for US cloud hyperscalers like Amazon Web Services, Microsoft and Google. A joint media statement by the Ministry of Digital Development and Information and the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry said the authorities are studying the details of this new measure carefully and engaging affected companies to understand the potential business impact. A Singtel spokesperson told The Straits Times in response to queries: “We are still assessing the implications, but expect the impact to be minimal. “Our graphics processing unit business is a sovereign AI platform that serves Singapore only. Customers are largely public sector and research agencies, and no chips are being re-exported.” Singtel added that of the 6MW capacity of its RE:AI platform, which provides sovereign cloud services, 4MW has already been installed, with the remaining 2MW being contracted. “We will work with the Singapore Government to obtain the necessary clearance and licences,” Singtel said. For its Nxera data centres, Singtel said “an insignificant amount of capacity” is contracted to neoclouds and this is not a material part of contracted revenue. A neocloud is a specialised cloud computing provider built specifically for AI workloads, rather than general purpose enterprise services. “Nonetheless, we will monitor any impact to customers and execute subsequent pipelines in a disciplined and gated manner,” Singtel said. An ST Engineering spokesman said: “Based on our current assessment, our existing operations are not impacted as our data centres have the computing infrastructure required.” Singtel shares were up 1.8% at around 3.30pm on Nov 17. They closed 2.5% higher at $4.10. But shares of ST Engineering, which designs and builds sustainable data centres, fell 2.3% in the day. It closed 1.9% down at $8.86. Data centre REITs also fell. NTT DC REIT, which trades in US dollars, fell 0.5%, while DigiCore REIT fell 2.2% and Keppel DC REIT fell by nearly 1%. Analysts said that although these new US rules pose challenges, the structural demand for data centres in the region remains. Ritesh Ganeriwal, Syfe group head of investment and advisory, said: “Singapore’s data centre REITs own assets well beyond South-east Asia. “The new rules may cool demand from some customers in the region, but the structural demand for cloud computing and AI remains solid and runs deeper than any one group of customers.” He added that the Singapore REIT market as a whole has already adjusted in 2026 with changes in the interest rate environment and that fundamentals such as rents on renewal have remained strong. Saxo Singapore chief investment strategist Charu Chanana said Singapore’s data centre sector is not facing a demand collapse. But the new US restrictions could make the next phase of growth more complicated, she added.

events.title: Nvidia to reveal first earnings since spy scandal
events.summary: The scandal has battered shares of Nvidia, which until recently was the world’s most valuable publicly traded company. Nvidia will report earnings on Nov 17 after a spy scandal, Jensen Huang’s exit, and new US chip export curbs shook shares and raised doubts over AI growth. The US has tightened rules on advanced chips, targeting data centres and countries like Singapore and Malaysia to stop Chinese firms using foreign cloud access. Investors will watch interim CEO Colette Kress for guidance on sales and strategy, while Singapore and Indonesia assess the impact on data centres and investment. WASHINGTON – AI chip giant Nvidia reports its first earnings on Nov 17 since an alleged spy scandal prompted co-founder Jensen Huang to quit and the United States to tighten export curbs on chips. Investors will closely scrutinise the results for indications the artificial intelligence boom can withstand the crisis, which highlighted a loophole allegedly exploited by Chinese companies. Huang, perhaps the tech industry’s most recognised booster of artificial intelligence, stepped down on Nov 12 following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy . The scandal has battered shares of Nvidia – until recently the world’s most valuable publicly traded company – which is at the centre of an AI build-out that has helped propel markets to record highs and boosted economic growth around the globe. Washington announced new restrictions on Nov 16 on AI chip exports, drawing condemnation from Beijing just before the high-profile APEC summit where US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping are set for talks. Beijing’s foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said: “China will take necessary measures to resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.” The new US export curbs and the wider Nvidia scandal risk casting a shadow over Trump and Xi’s talks at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting, which starts on Nov 18 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Under Washington’s new rules, data centres anywhere in the world will need a US licence to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China, Macau or other countries under US arms embargoes. The rules also require licences to ship advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil – countries the US commerce department says present a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” of the chips. The changes are a response to a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to rent AI computing power from data centres in South-east Asia and elsewhere that run on US hardware not available for export to China. While the loophole has been known to authorities, the revelation of Huang’s affair has drawn intense scrutiny to the practice. His affair partner Alice Huang, who is not related to the 63-year-old, is a former executive of Megaspeed – a Singapore-based cloud computing firm under US criminal investigation for allegedly helping Chinese companies procure advanced Nvidia AI chips in circumvention of export controls. The scandal has exposed a rift within the Trump administration, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accusing the commerce department of ignoring reports that Megaspeed was shifting Nvidia technology to China. The US government confirmed on Nov 16 it was investigating Megaspeed, with the commerce department launching a probe in 2024 for potential export control violations. The Nov 17 third-quarter results, which are scheduled for 6am on Nov 18 in Singapore, will be the first presented under Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, who is serving as interim CEO. “If they try to keep a business-as-usual tone in the call, I think that it probably wouldn’t be well received,” said Jacob Bourne of Emarketer. Investors will be watching for signs of whether Kress will slow Huang’s aggressive investment strategy, which saw him commit tens of billions of dollars to AI companies. Analysts said they would also be eyeing Nvidia’s guidance on future sales, along with its chip sales in Asia, particularly Singapore. That could ripple across the AI investments propping up the US economy – with Nvidia backing major labs including Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, which is expected to begin trading on Wall Street on Nov 19 . Tech firms dragged Asian stock markets down again on Nov 17 as the fallout from the Nvidia crisis rattles trading floors, with the new US moves on chip controls adding to uncertainty. On Nov 17 , Singapore said it was engaging with affected companies and talking to US authorities to ascertain the scope and implementation of the new measures. The city-state is also “exploring how to facilitate trusted access (to AI chips) for Singapore companies”, a government statement said.

events.title: PostgreSQL patches 52 security holes, sends version 14 into retirement
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features SC 26 Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Some fixes need more than installation, while the next major release is due November 19 Postgres 19 delayed after AI reviewers find more bugs than humans can fix October 16, 2026 PostgreSQL 19 graph queries fail the 'would you ship this?' test September 15, 2026 PostgreSQL 19 connects the dots with standardized graph queries September 4, 2026 Postgres pioneer credits Oracle with helping his database take over the world August 19, 2026 After rewriting SQLite in Rust, Turso turns its sights on Postgres July 29, 2026 PostgreSQL developers have patched 52 security vulnerabilities and more than 140 bugs in updates spanning versions 14 to 18, alongside a second release candidate for version 19. The batch includes PostgreSQL 14.25, the final release for the now-unsupported version 14. Users are advised to move to a newer major version. Some fixes also require follow-up work, including rebuilding affected indexes or taking a fresh full backup. Administrators should check the release's post-update instructions. Alastair Turner, community technologist at open source consultancy Percona, said the high-severity code execution flaws should be taken seriously, although exploiting them requires database access. "This isn't something just a brute-force scan of the right port is going to find," he said. "They can make compromises through SQL injection or credential theft a lot worse, but don't create the opportunity for remote, anonymous code execution." Among the fixes is CVE-2026-6460 , a type confusion flaw that could let a database user with permission to create objects execute arbitrary code. It carries a CVSS severity score of 8.8 out of 10. Turner attributed the growing number of security discoveries partly to AI-assisted scanning and partly to increased scrutiny as PostgreSQL gains ground in enterprise computing. "It is a record number of CVEs fixed in a quarterly release, and I don't think we've seen the end of that trend. Looking down the list of where these CVEs came from, we see Anthropic and OpenAI open source scanners, so it is clear AI or brute force is playing a role," he said. Turner said the fixes spanned multiple parts of the software. There "isn't one piece of code that was broken" but rather "a wide base that got patched." "It's also worth noting that this is the third quarterly release in a row which sets a new record for the number of CVEs patched," he added. PostgreSQL 14 users now face a major-version upgrade or running without further security and bug fixes. Their destination may depend on internal upgrade policies. Organizations that require the previous major release, known as N-1, would currently target PostgreSQL 17, Turner noted. Version 18 remains the latest generally available release until 19 arrives. PostgreSQL 19 is scheduled for general availability on Thursday, November 19, barring further problems. It is set to include a new REPACK command , whose CONCURRENTLY option allows reads and writes to continue while disk space is reclaimed. VACUUM FULL requires an exclusive table lock, blocking reads and writes while it runs.

events.title: Deutsche Bank shares sink as whistleblowers reveal Epstein payments, Trump tax leak, Russia bets
events.summary: More than 15 million leaked Deutsche Bank files reviewed by an international media consortium detail alleged failures in risk management, compliance and governance over many years. The Financial Times reported $582 million in suspicious payments linked to Jeffrey Epstein and an accidental 2017 disclosure of tax information tied to Donald Trump. Deutsche Bank says the matters are largely historical and cites 7 billion euros invested in its control environment from 2019 through 2025. Deutsche Bank shares fell sharply in early trading on Tuesday after whistleblowers leaked about 15 million files from the German lender, with media reports revealing alleged historic failures across its risk management and financial crime controls. These include suspicious payments linked to late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and accidental leaks of President Donald Trump 's tax statements. The leaks contain board minutes, emails, internal investigations and other material that point to systemic failures across the Frankfurt-listed lender's business functions stretching back two decades. Deutsche Bank processed $582 million in suspicious payments linked to Jeffrey Epstein, far more than previously known, the FT reported . Suspicious payments are not, by themselves, proof that every transaction was criminal. The German lender also mistakenly leaked details of U.S. President Donald Trump's taxes in March 2017, during his first term in office, the FT said. The blunder — described by CEO Christian Sewing, who was then Deutsche's private banking head, as "an awful mistake" — was kept secret from the White House. The wide-ranging investigation — which was led by a consortium of more than 200 journalists worldwide including the FT, Der Spiegel and Le Monde — also said Deutsche Bank had failed to offboard around 28,000 problematic investment bank clients who had been identified for removal by early 2018. It also alleges that the bank concealed information around cost targets in 2021, when external monitors in New York reportedly warned that Deutsche's risk appetite was running ahead of controls. The files also contain details of the bank's relationships with oligarchs and transactions that the investigation links to Russian money-laundering concerns. It was these ties that motivated whistleblowers to send the information to Indian journalist Josy Joseph and South African journalist Khadija Sharife. The reports once again put Deutsche Bank's risk management practices and controls under the spotlight following years of regulatory scrutiny. The bank — which has been raided multiple times by German officials this year — has, since 2012, paid out some 18.6 billion euros ($20.5 billion) in settlements over alleged market manipulation, money laundering, mis-selling and misrepresentation, among other things, the FT said. In a statement, Deutsche Bank said the issues detailed in Tuesday's media reports go back many years. "Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators," the lender said. The bank said it has undergone a "fundamental transformation" under CEO Christian Sewing, pointing to 7 billion euros of investment in its risk controls between 2019 and 2025. "Deutsche Bank is a different bank today and remains focused on executing its strategy which has proven successful, as evidenced by record profits in 2025 as well as in recent quarters." CNBC has reached out to BaFin, Germany's financial regulator, for comment.

events.title: Abu Dhabi to capitalise on humanoid robot boom with new index fund
events.summary: Abu Dhabi-based global investment firm Lunate is to launch a new exchange-traded fund focused on humanoid robots, amid growing investor interest in the technology. The Boreas VettaFi Humanoid Robots UCITS ETF is expected to list on the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange on December 8 under the ticker ROBOTS, Lunate said in a statement on Tuesday. The ETF, which tracks the VettaFi Humanoid Robot Select Markets Net Total Return Index, will initially hold 41 companies from Asia, the US and Europe. They span four parts of the humanoid robot value chain – semiconductors, robot parts, humanoid robot developers and software. “Our fifth thematic offering on the ADX, complemented by 10 Shariah-compliant and 10 conventional ETFs spanning equity and fixed income, underscores our ongoing commitment to expanding our investment suite with an aim to empower investors and enable them to construct balanced, long-term portfolios,” said Sherif Salem, partner and head of public markets at Lunate. The launch comes amid growing interest in humanoid robots that can perform complex tasks and drive automation and productivity in the industrial sector. Annual shipments of humanoid robots are projected to rise 500-fold, from 20,000 in 2025 to 10 million in 2035, while the industry is expected to generate nearly $5 trillion in annual revenue by 2050. Boreas ETFs are listed on the ADX and Germany's Xetra. Alongside humanoid robotics, the ADX-listed range includes ETFs focused on AI data, power and infrastructure, quantum computing and absolute luxury. The Boreas range of ETFs is managed by Lunate, with product development and research support from Northwind, Lunate’s consultant on thematic ETF strategy. "As costs fall and ageing populations create labour shortages, [humanoid robotics] adoption could move from factories and warehouses into hospitals and homes," said Geir Espeskog, chief executive of Northwind. "Rather than try to pick a single winner, the ETF aims to provide exposure to humanoid developers and the global supply chain that enables them." Lunate, which in January appointed Mohamed Alsuweidi, Minister of Investment , as its executive chairman and managing partner, has more than $125 billion in assets under management and aims to more than double that over the next five years. With a core focus on private markets, the company is also active across the broader asset management spectrum, working with clients that include institutions, family offices and corporates. In April, Lunate's private equity unit Axight agreed to buy a minority stake in Australian asset manager La Trobe Financial to expand its portfolio. Lunate also established Alterra, the UAE's $30 billion climate-focused fund.

events.title: Asia races to expand nuclear power as Iran war exposes energy vulnerabilities
events.summary: Asia's biggest energy importers are accelerating their shift towards nuclear power after the Iran war exposed their dependence on Gulf oil and gas. Plans for more nuclear energy raise the prospect of lasting change in one of the world's most important energy trading relationships. The shift gained momentum at the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey last week, where China and five other countries joined a pledge to triple global nuclear capacity. The number of countries backing the target has risen to 39. Asia already accounts for 66 gigawatts of the 91GW of nuclear capacity under construction worldwide, or 73 per cent, according to Global Energy Monitor. That is more than twice the region's share of operating nuclear capacity. The stakes are particularly high for Gulf exporters. Asia bought 84 per cent of the crude and condensate and 83 per cent of the liquefied natural gas shipped through the Strait of Hormuz in 2024, according to the US Energy Information Administration. The war has exposed the risks of that dependence as Japan, which sourced 93 per cent of its crude imports through Hormuz before the conflict, is seeking to restart more reactors. South Korea has accelerated maintenance at five offline units, while Vietnam has agreed with Russia to build two reactors. The Philippines is considering reviving a nuclear plant built during the 1970s and 1980s that has never operated. On Tuesday, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi proposed “an Asian version of the International Energy Agency” to co-ordinate oil stockpiles and emergency releases. She also called for stronger energy ties with Gulf producers. The Gulf is making its own nuclear push. The UAE's 5.6GW Barakah plant, which was targeted in a drone attack in May , already supplies about a quarter of its electricity. Saudi Arabia has invited international companies to bid for its first two reactors and signed a nuclear co-operation agreement with the US in July , which Democrats in the US Senate are seeking to block. The International Energy Agency expects global nuclear generation to rise by an average of 2.8 per cent a year to 2030, more than twice the pace of the previous five years. China is expected to add almost 30GW of capacity, while India's nuclear output is forecast to grow 15 per cent a year. The impact on Gulf exports will take years to emerge. Nuclear power competes directly with gas in electricity generation, but has a much smaller effect on oil demand, which is driven largely by transport and industry. Gas demand is also expected to keep growing. The IEA forecasts gas-fired generation will increase by about 5 per cent a year in China and 9.7 per cent in India this decade.

events.title: Mary Chia’s half-year revenue plunges 88% as it flags uncertainty over ability to stay afloat
events.summary: Mary Chia said it believes it has sufficient resources to operate for at least another 12 months, taking into account financial support from controlling shareholder Suki Sushi. Mary Chia Holdings’ half-year revenue fell 88.3% to $1.18 million, and net profit dropped 94.5% to $23,000, as its direct selling business stopped contributing revenue. The company warned of material uncertainty over its ability to keep operating, with net current liabilities of $12.52 million, but said Suki Sushi will provide financial support for at least 12 months. Mary Chia faces wider problems, including CPF arrears, court disputes with Fullink Capital, and a plan to raise $1 million through new shares, pending approval. SINGAPORE – Beauty and wellness group Mary Chia Holdings’ half-year revenue plunged 88.3 % to $1 .18 mill ion, and it has flagged significant uncertainty over its ability to continue operating. This was disclosed in the financially troubled Catalist-listed group’s unaudited financial results for the six months ended Sept 30, filed with the Singapore Exchange on Nov 14. Revenue fell fro m $10.03 m illion in the corresponding period in 2025, mainly because its direct selling business stopped contributing revenue from the start of the financial year in April 2026. Net profit also fell 94.5% to $23,000, from $422,000 a year earlier. The group’s short-term liabilities exceeded its short-term assets by $ 12.52 mill ion as at Sept 30, compared with net current liabilities of $12.58 million as at March 31. Its cash and bank balances stood at $3 94,000, u p from $312,000 six months earlier. However, $8 5,000 was restricted for use by the Singapore tax authority in relation to outstanding tax matters involving a subsidiary, leaving $ 309,000 in cash and cash equivalents. Enough to keep operating for another 12 months Mary Chia said these financial conditions indicated material uncertainties that could cast significant doubt on the ability of the group and company to continue operating. Management nevertheless believes it has sufficient resources to operate for at least an other 12 mo nths, taking into account financial support from controlling shareholder Suki Sushi. In an undertaking dated Sept 11, Mary Chia’s controlling shareholder, Suki Sushi, pledged to provide financial support for at least 12 months from the authorisation of the group’s audited financial statements for the year ended March 31. It also agreed not to demand immediate repayment of money owed by the group during that period. In its Nov 14 filing, Mary Chia reiterated the undertaking but said it had yet to complete its assessment of Suki Sushi’s finan cial abilit y to provide the promised support. The company aims to complete the assessment by Dec 31. The unaudited results also revealed that Mary Chia had not recognised depreciation of leased assets or finance costs for the July-to-September quarter because its review and reconciliation of accounting records remained incomplete due to limited finance resources. The company said it would make the necessary accounting adjustments after completing its review. Its independent auditor Foo Kon Tan had earlier issued a disclaimer of opinion on the group’s audited financial statements for the year ended March 31, after being unable to obtain sufficient evidence to form an audit opinion on several accounting matters. Mary Chia’s latest financial results come amid wider financial and legal challenges. In October, the group admitted that it had failed to disclose Central Provident Fund arrears and court proceedings involving four of its five subsidiaries facing action over unpaid contributions. The admission followed queries from Singapore Exchange Regulation about why the subsidiaries had been omitted from the company’s Sept 11 announcement. The group attributed the omission to shortcomings in its internal information consolidation and disclosure assessment processes. According to the CPF Board’s updated computation on Oct 9, the five subsidiaries had outstanding contributions totalling $103,727, excluding late-payment interest and composite sums. Mary Chia Holdings and three related parties recently avoided insolvency proceedings brought by lender Fullink Capital, although a dispute remains over default interest, late payment interest and restructuring fees arising from two loans with a combined principal of $350,000. The High Court confirmed the dismissal of the winding-up and bankruptcy applications on Oct 13, after $651,498.97 was transferred into court on Oct 6 as security pending the dispute’s resolution. Separately, Mary Chia is seeking to raise $1 million through a proposed subscription of 100 million new shares at one cent each. The proposed fund raising remains subject to shareholders’ approval at an extraordinary general meeting on Nov 23 and the receipt of the relevant SGX listing approval. No interim dividend was declared, with the company citing its financial position and the need to conserve cash.

events.title: What we’re learning from firms engaging with our innovation services
events.summary: Three themes stand out: the growing use of AI, innovation crossing traditional sector boundaries, and financial inclusion.As firms develop new products, services and business models, many engage with us through our Regulatory Sandbox and Innovation Pathways to understand how regulation applies to their proposition or to test innovative ideas in a controlled environment.Looking across applications lets us observe emerging trends. It helps us understand how technologies are evolving, and identify emerging regulatory questions.In turn, this supports our wider work and helps us keep pace with developments across financial services.Applications at a glance37% involved AI (up from 31% in 2025), making it the most common technology theme.92% of the firms engaging with our services were doing so for the first time, highlighting continued demand from new innovators.64% of proposed solutions included a retail element, showing continued focus on consumer-facing innovation.The growing use of AIFirms are focusing increasingly on how to deploy, oversee and govern AI in their business models.They’re looking at how to use AI to help consumers better understand and manage their finances, support businesses with payment processes, and provide customers with more personalised guidance and support.Regulation and innovation are working in tandem to deploy new technologies safely and build consumer protection into new products from the outset.Innovation is becoming more interconnectedInnovation does not always fit neatly into traditional sector categories. While payments and digital assets represented the largest sector-specific portion of recent applications, cross-sector propositions have also been common, representing around one-third of applications.Many firms are combining technologies, data, payments and consumer-facing services in new ways. As a result, innovative technologies are increasingly crossing traditional sector boundaries and requiring firms to consider how existing governance, accountability, data use and regulatory frameworks apply.A recent example is our stablecoins cohort in the Regulatory Sandbox. Stablecoin business models often cut across traditional sector boundaries, combining elements of payments, digital assets, and financial market activity. The cohort brought together firms intending to issue UK stablecoins to test how proposed requirements could operate in practice and provide evidence to support policy development.Financial inclusionFirms continue to focus on how to improve consumer access to and engagement with financial services. They’re not only exploring new technologies, but also considering how these tools can help address practical consumer challenges.Applications this year have included propositions aimed at improving consumer understanding, accessibility, personalised support, and access to financial services for underserved groups.A large proportion of proposed solutions included a retail element, indicating that most firms remain focused on end consumers.What we’re learning about Sandbox participation over timeWe are looking beyond current application trends to understand the longer-term experience of firms that have participated in the Regulatory Sandbox.Our preliminary research suggests that, as of September 2026, around 71% of them are still active. We are continuing this analysis to better understand the ongoing commercial success of participating firms and whether their original propositions have continued to operate.We have also been looking to understand at which point of their growth firms engage with the Regulatory Sandbox.We’ve found that the service is particularly relevant at an early stage of a firm’s development, with around 70% of applications coming from firms that are 0 to 2 years old.Demand is strongest when firms are still developing their business models, products and approaches to compliance, and seeking to understand how regulation applies as they refine and validate innovative propositions.Looking aheadApplications to our Regulatory Sandbox and Innovation Pathways give us an early view of the technologies, business models and the regulatory questions that firms are exploring.They also provide insight into developments beyond the UK.We’re continuing to engage with international firms seeking to enter the UK market and sharing insights with overseas regulators and innovation initiatives. This helps us to understand global innovation trends.The trends we have seen so far suggest that innovation is scaling up, becoming more sophisticated, and more focused on addressing real-world consumer needs.We’ll continue to engage with firms as technology develops. One way we’re doing this is through thematic cohorts, which explore key areas in greater depth.Following our Regulatory Sandbox stablecoins cohort, applications to a new climate scenarios cohort opened on 1 October 2026. The cohort invites firms and specialists to test innovative approaches to climate scenario analysis and risk assessment, supporting wider work on sustainable finance and climate-related risks.Firms developing new ideas should consider how existing regulation applies to their proposition, how they can test and scale innovation successfully, and what safeguards will deliver good outcomes for consumers and markets.Our innovation services help firms answer these questions. They also let us test policy approaches and gather evidence on how regulation works in practice. This helps inform smarter, more proportionate regulation.We’re here to support innovators across financial services, helping ensure the UK remains one of the best places in the world to develop, test and scale innovative propositions.

events.title: The future of datacenters depends on behind-the-meter energy generation
events.summary: For the last decade, the datacenter industry has been a quiet engine of the digital economy. It was a background utility that just worked. However, datacenters are no longer passive consumers of electricity. They are becoming active participants in energy generation, storage, and grid management through behind-the-meter infrastructure. This is being driven by the explosive rise of AI and a manufacturing renaissance. Power demand is growing again, increasing an average of 2.1 percent annually over the past five years, with datacenters emerging as a dominant driver of long-term growth. Electric Power Research Institute projects that datacenters could consume as much as 17 percent of U.S. electricity by 2030 , more than triple their current 4-5 percent share. This massive spike in demand is clashing directly with a severely constrained power grid. Key regional utility transmission organizations are expected to face critical reserve shortfalls as early as 2028. At the end of 2025, more than 2,060 GW of new generation and storage capacity was represented by projects actively seeking interconnection to the U.S. grid. For the projects that successfully reached commercial operation, the process took a median of more than five years from request to completion. To keep building at the speed of innovation, datacenter operators are fundamentally rethinking their relationship with power , shifting from being passive grid consumers to active, localized energy producers. Grid capacity is no longer the ceiling. Instead, the next chapter of digital infrastructure will be written behind the meter. Behind-the-meter (BTM) refers to energy assets located on the customer side of the utility connection, including battery systems, microgrids, generators, fuel cells, and distributed energy resources that can operate independently of grid constraints. The Role of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) While every datacenter developer faces grid constraints, the industry’s two dominant business models are adopting distinctly different strategies to bypass the power bottleneck. Hyperscale Operators Hyperscale operators (tech giants like Amazon, Google, and Microsoft) utilize their massive balance sheets to secure gigawatt-scale capacity directly. Rather than acting as passive grid customers, hyperscalers are taking direct, active control of their energy supply chains. They negotiate custom, state-level tariffs directly with utilities, co-locate facilities next to large nuclear or baseload assets, and sign massive off-site Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs). Increasingly, hyperscalers are also deploying large-scale, on-site Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) to bypass grid delays and accelerate their projects. Many are also turning to behind-the-meter natural gas generation to provide additional power on-site. With larger, hundreds-of-megawatts turbines facing long backlogs, some operators are instead deploying multiple smaller, roughly 50 MW turbines in parallel, either on-site or adjacent to the campus. Colocation Providers In contrast, colocation (colo) providers lease space, power, and cooling to third-party tenants. Colos operate on a highly competitive, faster-to-market model where speed-to-revenue is the primary metric. Colocation facilities are geographically constrained, as their facilities must be located close to business hubs to minimize latency rather than simply next to remote power plants. Consequently, datacenter and colocation developers are increasingly integrating on-site, behind-the-meter energy solutions. In highly congested markets, BTM generation and battery storage can provide a path to power while developers wait for grid interconnection. In Virginia, for example, LS Power is pursuing a 300 MW datacenter project designed to receive power directly from its adjacent natural gas-fired Doswell power plant, creating a behind-the-meter supply arrangement that can help accelerate access to power. At the same time, the rules for connecting large loads are beginning to change. In some U.S. markets, datacenters that can provide flexible load, on-site generation or storage are gaining new pathways to connect while giving grid operators greater control over demand during periods of constraint. The New Coordinated Energy Stack: UPS + BESS + Generators Historically, a datacenter’s power architecture was passive, consisting of an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) to bridge 5-to-15 minutes of downtime and backup diesel generators to handle prolonged outages. AI has shattered this legacy design. Although many enterprise deployments still operate below 20 kW per rack, next-generation AI clusters are increasingly exceeding 100 kW per rack, with some designs targeting significantly higher densities. Furthermore, AI training runs create highly volatile, synchronized compute loads, causing electricity draw to spike and drop in massive, sub-second waves. To protect both sensitive computing equipment and the local grid from these fluctuations, operators are deploying a layered, grid-interactive energy stack: UPS (Instant Protection): Positioned in series with the servers, the traditional UPS remains essential for providing millisecond-fast power conditioning and preventing data loss during transient voltage sags. BESS (On-site Shock Absorber & Optimizer): Connected in parallel at the facility level, BESS acts as a real-time shock absorber. It smooths out volatile AI compute spikes, stores cost-effective off-peak power for use during peak hours, and participates in grid-balancing services. On-site Generation (Long-Term Firm Power): Customer-sited generation, including natural gas microturbines, provides the ultimate firm baseload capacity, insulating the facility from grid failures for days or weeks. By layering these technologies, operators can stop treating their power systems like a pricey “insurance policy” that sits idle, and start using them as a smart, money-saving asset. In many markets, demand charges (the fees utilities charge based on peak power draw) make up 30-to-70 percent of a datacenter’s monthly electricity bill. By discharging on-site batteries during peak demand periods — a strategy known as peak shaving — operators can reduce the peak loads used to calculate demand charges, potentially lowering electricity costs significantly. Turning Backup Assets into Strategic Grid Partners Historically, backup diesel generators sat untouched, accumulating maintenance costs unless a blackout occurred. Today, utilities and datacenter operators are establishing mutually beneficial partnerships. Through Virtual Power Plants (VPPs), utilities can aggregate a datacenter’s distributed backup generators and BESS capacity into a single, software-controlled resource. Under grid stress, the utility can dispatch these on-site assets, effectively turning the datacenter into a power supplier rather than a power drain. events.title: Trump administration moves to block China from indirect access to American AI technology
events.summary: The Trump administration has issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best artificial intelligence models. Last week, Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following scrutiny of his ties to a Chinese executive who used to lead Singapore-based Megaspeed International , which is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. The company provides computing power to Chinese companies using chips housed in Southeast Asian data centers, including facilities in Malaysia. “The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the Bureau of Industry and Security under the Commerce Department said in issuing the rule that took effect immediately. The rule came on the same day President Donald Trump departed for a trip to Asia , where he expects to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the third time this year amid a fragile truce on trade. Under the new rule, overseas data centers that serve companies in countries including China, Russia, Iran and Cuba are required to identify their end users. There also will be additional licensing requirements for sales of chips for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil — countries that “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" to unauthorized destinations, the rule says. In Beijing, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun accused Washington of arbitrarily interfering with China's trade and technological cooperation with other countries and suppressing the development of China's high-tech industries. “This is a typical example of economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction, runs counter to the common understanding between the two sides,” he told reporter, adding that it infringes upon the rights of Chinese companies and disrupts the stability of global supply chains. He said China would take necessary measures to safeguard its interests. The U.S. bans sales of the country's most advanced AI chips to China, seeking to maintain an edge in its rivalry with China for predominance in artificial intelligence. However, many lawmakers and policymakers believe the country's export control rules are not tough enough and filled with loopholes such as cloud computing that allows China to rent processing power built on American technology. Last year, U.S. Rep. Michael Lawler, a New York Republican, introduced a bill to broaden the U.S. export controls to include remote access. He told Congress “physical export controls” under current rules do not apply to remote access, allowing China to “access our tech through the cloud” and giving it “a real tool to sidestep” U.S. export restrictions. The bill has passed the House. In the Senate, lawmakers also are seeking tougher legislation to prevent China from accessing advanced U.S. chip and AI technologies. Bills include proposals that would let Congress review licenses to sell advanced AI chips to China, ask the Department of Commerce to track AI chips to ensure they are not diverted to unauthorized regions, and compel U.S. allies such as the Netherlands and Japan to match U.S. restrictions on exports to Chinese chipmakers. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Last week, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick came under pressure when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Commerce Department was late to place restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed. On Monday, Trump acknowledged tension between Treasury and Commerce on the matter. He suggested that Lutnick may have delayed placing the export restrictions to avoid a “blow up” in the fragile U.S.-China relationship. “We’re having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, Trump said. In a joint statement late Monday by the Commerce and Justice departments, it said Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed for potential export control violations in 2024, which was followed by requests to Nvidia for records in May 2025 related to sales to Megaspeed. The following month, it said, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list, and agents from the Commerce Department in conjunction with Singapore law enforcement conducted on-site checks of Megaspeed and interviewed Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang. The Justice Department then took the lead role in the criminal probe of Megaspeed, the statement said.

events.title: U.S. companies from Nvidia to Apple face a growing China dilemma
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO has intensified scrutiny of U.S. chip sales to China and their national security risks. Nine countries signed a U.S. declaration on safeguarding sensitive technologies, days before U.S. President Donald Trump meets his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping. Apple’s China ties leave its new CEO weighing diversification against the need to preserve manufacturing capacity. BEIJING — How does the U.S. stay ahead of China in the artificial intelligence race? Keep advanced chips out of Beijing's reach, or sell weaker versions to keep Chinese companies reliant on American technology? The consequences for U.S. businesses came into sharper focus after Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO, ahead of U.S. President Donald Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week. Huang, who resigned last week amid reports he'd had an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence suspects of being a Chinese spy, had argued that keeping U.S. technology available in China could help the U.S. stay ahead in the tech race. Others want tougher restrictions on chip sales: The Trump administration tightened restrictions on Chinese companies' remote access to advanced U.S. chips on Monday, seeking to prevent them from bypassing export controls by using data centers overseas. The question facing Nvidia is part of a broader dilemma for U.S. tech companies: how far to remain invested in China as tensions between the two countries put their access to customers and supply chains at risk. 'Competing pressures' from Washington and Beijing On Sunday, nine countries, including Singapore and the U.K., signed the U.S. State Department's "San Francisco Declaration" to safeguard sensitive technologies. "Companies operating in China face competing pressures from Washington and Beijing," a client brief from New York-based consulting firm Strategy Risks said following the Nvidia scandal. "Actions that satisfy one government can create serious problems with the other, putting market access, investments, and corporate reputation at risk," the brief said. "Executives need to understand and price out these trade-offs before making consequential decisions." China's economic slowdown and escalating bilateral tensions have made it harder for American businesses there. Few expect Trump and XI to significantly expand on a fragile trade truce achieved last fall. Huang was among the tech CEOs at the Xi-Trump summits in September and May, but U.S. officials said Trump does not plan to raise the alleged Nvidia spy case during Thursday's meeting. Elon Musk is travelling with the president, who is otherwise not bringing a business delegation as he did in May. "American tech companies have been diversifying away from China," Kyle Chan, a fellow at The Brookings Institution, told CNBC, but Nvidia and Apple are "in some ways stark outliers against this trend." Analysts are watching how Apple CEO John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in October, navigates bilateral tensions. "Ternus may accelerate a process of diversification away from China that Tim Cook started," Chan said. "But it's hard to imagine that China will not play an essential role in Apple's future under Ternus, given the depth and breadth of China's manufacturing supply chains." Apple still manufactures most of its iPhones in China , and Greater China , which Apple defines as mainland China, Hong Kong and Taiwan, accounts for around 15% of sales . "The most defensible path is managed decoupling—not the rolling deferrals and hedged announcements that defined Cook's tenure—but a genuine strategic commitment to building a company that can absorb the reductions of China access without losing the ability to manufacture at the cutting edge," Strategy Risks CEO Isaac Stone Fish wrote in American Affairs earlier this year. China's economic clout, however, also increases the fallout from any retaliation Beijing decides to enact in response to tighter U.S. policy. Companies, especially U.S. multinationals, pursued the China market after it began re-opening to foreign businesses in the 1980s. Consumer demand boomed, while local factories produced so much they reached 40% of global container exports this summer. The U.S. AI data center buildout relied on China-made parts. China has amassed control of the supply chain for critical minerals. Beijing has used its grip on rare earths as leverage in trade talks with the U.S. and the EU. Despite some buildout of the rare earths supply outside China, "it's just not at the scale that the world needs to continue to build products and for industry to continue to evolve," said Cameron Johnson, a Shanghai-based senior partner at business consultancy Tidalwave Solutions. He cited looming shortages of yttrium, which would limit the production and repair of airplane engines. "There's just no road map. That's really one of the biggest issues," Johnson said.

events.title: Hyundai Motor takes full ownership of Boston Dynamics
events.summary: According to a third-quarter regulatory filing by Hyundai Glovis on Nov 17, all put and call options tied to Boston Dynamics’ common shares were exercised and expired during the period. Hyundai Motor Group now owns 100% of Boston Dynamics after buying SoftBank’s last 9.65% stake, giving it full control of the US robotics unit. Hyundai plans to commercialise the Atlas humanoid robot, aiming for 30,000 units a year by 2028 and first using them at its Georgia plant for simple factory tasks. Boston Dynamics’ revenue rose 29% to 136 billion won in the first nine months of 2026, but losses widened to 626.6 billion won; an IPO could come around 2029 or 2030. SEOUL – Hyundai Motor Group has acquired full ownership of its US robotics subsidiary Boston Dynamics, accelerating its push to commercialise the Atlas humanoid robot. According to a third-quarter regulatory filing by Hyundai Glovis on Nov 17 , all put and call options tied to Boston Dynamics’ common shares were exercised and expired during the period. The transaction concludes the buyout of SoftBank’s remaining 9.65% stake after the Japanese tech conglomerate triggered its put option in July under an earlier shareholder pact. Existing stake holders – including Hyundai Motor group executive chair Chung Euisun, HMG Global and Hyundai Glovis – acquired the remaining shares, giving Chung and group affiliates 100% ownership of Boston Dynamics. As part of the transaction, Hyundai Glovis injected 46.5 billion won (S$44.8 million) to raise its stake by 1.08 percentage points to 12.47% at the end of the third quarter, following a 63.1 billion won investment in the first half of 2026. Industry insiders say the ownership consolidation marks a pivotal turning point for Hyundai’s robotics push. With little need to balance external shareholder demands, the group can execute capital expenditures, R&D and cross-affiliate collaborations with greater speed and autonomy. Central to this strategy is commercialising the humanoid robot Atlas. Hyundai aims to build an annual production capacity of 30,000 Atlas units by 2028 and deploy them directly into industrial operations. The initial roll-out will take place at Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America in Georgia. The robots will first handle relatively low-intensity tasks such as sorting and transporting auto parts before expanding into complex assembly work once the technology is validated. By integrating Boston Dynamics’ AI-powered robotics with its automotive manufacturing and logistics systems, Hyundai seeks to boost factory efficiency while building a new growth engine. After securing full ownership, one key hurdle for Hyundai is to achieve profitability in its robotics unit. While Boston Dynamics’ revenue for the first nine months of 2026 rose 29% year-on-year to 136 billion won, its net loss widened to 626.6 billion won due to heavy R&D and production costs. With governance restructuring now complete, Boston Dynamics is gearing up for a potential initial public offering, which sources suggest could occur around 2029 or 2030 once production ramps up. No official timeline has been set. THE KOREA HERALD/ASIA NEWS NETWORK

events.title: Can this experimental orchard save the UK’s cider industry?
events.summary: Farmers are utilising science and nature to help orchards adapt and thrive in the face of shifting temperatures, rainfall and pests O n Myrtle Farm in Somerset, there are thousands of apple trees laid out in rows of 100. Over the past year, each has endured the same wet winter and long summer drought . Now, the different ways each tree responded to these challenges are being analysed in trials that could shape the future of apple growing – and the taste of cider – for decades to come. Myrtle Farm is the home of Thatchers Cider , which this year had its earliest ever harvest in the company’s 122-year history. Yet the farm’s experimental orchard of 3,800 trees, where each 100-tree row produces a different apple variety, offers hope that – even as the climate emergency deepens – future harvests will become more consistent and predictable. The trials aim to identify robust apple varieties that are resistant to diseases and pests, crop reliably and can withstand the most extreme weather that might affect Somerset . Two apples ripe for harvest, which this year ran from the middle of August to November at Myrtle Farm “Somerset is the best county in the world for making cider. But the climate is changing. It has been changing for a long time. We need to be in a position where we’ve got the experience, the knowledge and the trees in place to deal with those changes,” says Martin Thatcher, the company’s managing director. One of the biggest challenges he faces is the length of time it takes to introduce a new apple variety and change growing methods in orchards. “It doesn’t happen overnight. Each apple tree takes seven years to get to a fruit crop and could last 40 years. So it takes a very long time [for experiments] to come to fruition,” he says. The trials came about because, nearly 30 years ago, his father, John Thatcher, rescued 458 varieties of cider apples grown at the Long Ashton research station, a government-funded horticultural and agricultural research centre founded in 1903. “My father took cuttings of every single variety before the centre was closed down, so we have an orchard with 458 varieties in it.” Nestled by the Mendips, the Shiplate orchard, near Bleadon, has more than 65,000 trees across 57 hectares (140 acres) The collection includes traditional cider apples and newer varieties that cater for modern tastes. “We’re looking at that orchard now and first of all seeing which apples make fabulous cider. And then we’re looking at how the trees are doing under modern orchard conditions – and if they’re good healthy trees and they’re cropping, we will plant them out in rows of 100-tree trials, to future-proof our orchard growing.” He is trying to use fewer pesticides, so is keen to find varieties that are naturally resistant to disease and pests, and will blossom at exactly the moment when spring conditions suit apple tree pollinators such as bumblebees and honeybees. Another priority is to find varieties that need less winter chill in a warming climate: apple trees, he explains, need a sustained cold period in winter to complete their dormancy, which enables their fruit buds to develop properly in spring. “That winter chill is really important – and last year, we probably didn’t have quite enough, and some varieties are more susceptible to a lack of winter chill than others.” An apple shaker grasps the tree to shake off ripe fruit, which is then collected by the harvester and pressed within hours at the Myrtle Farm mill. The orchard is home to older cultivars such as Somerset redstreak and dabinett, as well as newer ones including three counties and red falstaff Thatchers’ orchard manager, Chris Muntz Torres, says jonagold, a cross between golden delicious and a jonathan apple, performed particularly well in trials this year. “They’ve got this vigour, this willingness to grow, whatever the weather.” He thinks this is because the tree’s vigorous growth above ground is matched by a strong root system. “That’s what we want – a variety that, irrespective of the weather, is robust enough to grow.” Myrtle Farm has also begun planting wildflower strips in its orchards, to attract insects that prey on pests such as the rosy apple aphid – a strategy that research has shown could save apple growers up to £3,000 a hectare every year and support native pollinators. Nigel Jenner, head of agronomy for tree fruit at the global fruit producer AM Fresh UK, works with independent apple farmers, who represent about 30% of Britain’s apple-growing industry. He says roughly 70% of these growers – about 220 – have planted wildflower strips in the past five years, and that number is increasing. The exhibition orchard has 458 varieties of apples, many of them rare ones such as these leathercoat russets, which date back to the 16th century “We know this is the way forward,” Jenner says. “It works and it has a meaningful effect on your chemical input and your spray bill.

events.title: HSBC offloads US$300m in troubled data centre loan at steep discount
events.summary: HSBC has sold the slice of an US$18 billion (S$23 billion) financing package for a data centre in New Mexico tied to Oracle. HSBC sold about US$300 million (S$386 million) of a troubled New Mexico data centre loan at a steep discount, showing growing fear over AI-linked debt. The loan was for the Oracle-linked Project Jupiter, an US$18 billion data centre in New Mexico. The sale came after Oracle sent a force majeure notice. The project has faced delays, permit problems and regulatory pushback, raising doubts over the Stargate AI build-out and its future pace. HONG KONG – HSBC Holdings offloaded a roughly US$300 million (S$386 million) piece of a loan to build a troubled New Mexico data centre project at a steep discount, underscoring deepening anxiety surrounding the AI boom. The bank sold the slice of an US$18 billion financing package, which funds construction of the campus in Dona Ana County tied to Oracle, at prices in the mid-80s, according to people familiar with the matter. The sale took place several weeks ago, shortly after Oracle sent a notice to the project’s developer citing force majeure, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private information. HSBC’s move comes as lenders weigh their exposure to AI debt alongside renewed regulatory pushback following a Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections . Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure from Nvidia , a linchpin of AI’s rapid expansion, has also triggered concerns about the pace of AI growth. The massive venture in southern New Mexico, known as Project Jupiter, has been beset by regulatory hurdles and opposition. Oracle sent the force majeure notice to the developer, a unit of Blue Owl Capital, in an attempt to put off payments should the venture get derailed, Bloomberg reported in late September. A group of about 20 banks provided the US$18 billion loan to help fund the data centre’s construction, Bloomberg reported in late 2025. The construction financing is referred to as Project Miner. The loan comprises different tranches tied to various buildings at the site. While lenders in the syndicated loan market are generally free to sell their stakes in the secondary market, banks holding construction project financing loans typically keep them on their balance sheets. In some circumstances, they have to wait for a so-called pooled sell-down agreement to expire before they can sell. Banks looking to exit before the completion of a project’s construction will often have to sell their debt at a discount greater than the upfront fees received. Project Jupiter is a major part of the Stargate AI infrastructure build-out that US President Donald Trump unveiled in early 2025 alongside leaders of Oracle, OpenAI and SoftBank Group. But the campus, designed to handle 2.45 gigawatts, has hit serious setbacks, including delays in acquiring air and pipeline permits key to its plans. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Africa’s coasts are the next frontier for UAE climate finance
events.summary: As Cop31 nears its end in Antalya, Turkey, the race for Africa’s resources is accelerating. Washington has raised the investment ceiling of its International Development Finance Corporation to $205 billion and is aiming much of it at Africa's critical minerals , including a planned stake of about 20 per cent in Balama graphite mine in Mozambique. The UAE is already ahead of that curve. It has committed more than $110 billion to projects throughout Africa in recent years, making it one of the continent’s largest investors. Much of that capital sits in ports, logistics, energy and agriculture. Yet many of these assets share a vulnerability that rarely appears in investment memos: an exposed coastline . For instance, more than 60 per cent of Mozambicans live in low-lying coastal areas. In 2023, Cyclone Freddy displaced more than 184,000 people there. Parts of the country’s central coast lost three quarters of their healthy mangrove forests between 1990 and 2024, stripping away the natural buffer that once absorbed storm surges before they reached towns, roads and ports. That creates a business case for UAE investors. Coastal ecosystems are infrastructure. Researchers at the University of California, Santa Cruz found mangroves prevented $1.5 billion in direct flood damage in Florida during Hurricane Irma in 2017. Mangroves also store three to five times more carbon per hectare than mature tropical forests, which allows restoration to earn revenue from carbon credits. The UAE understands this at home. It has planted about 51 million mangroves towards its target of 100 million by 2030, and it cofounded the Mangrove Alliance for Climate with Indonesia. Through Alterra, the $30 billion climate vehicle launched at Cop28, held in Dubai, it aims to mobilise $250 billion of climate investment by 2030. The question is whether that expertise and capital can be used in Africa in a way that lasts. Experience suggests one factor matters more than any other: the people who live beside the forest. Large carbon concessions negotiated with governments but not with communities have struggled. A high-profile carbon credit deal in Liberia has stalled. Restoration that pays local people, by contrast, tends to hold. A carbon credit is a promise that trees will stand for decades and that promise is only as strong as the incentives of the families who could cut them down. On Idugo Island, on Mozambique’s Zambezia coast, more than 700 families make sea salt. Most used to sell at harvest, when a 50kg bag fetched about 300 meticais ($4.70). With a community warehouse and working capital, financed partly by the UK government’s Coast Facility, they can now hold stock until the lean season, when the same bag can sell for up to 1,800 meticais. Young men who once cut mangroves for income now work in that business. The forest is worth more to them standing than cut. Development agencies are already absorbing much of the early risk. The US Millennium Challenge Corporation’s $500 million Mozambique compact includes $100 million for coastal livelihoods and climate resilience in Zambezia, led by two national institutions, ProAzul and Biofund. That grant-funded groundwork in community consent, land rights and local enterprise is exactly what makes a region investable for the private capital that follows. For UAE businesses, three opportunities stand out. First, infrastructure investors can protect their own assets. A port operator or logistics group that funds the restoration of the coast around its operations is buying insurance against storm damage and disruption, at a fraction of the cost of engineered defences. Second, UAE climate funds can co-invest alongside development finance. Blended structures, in which grants and guarantees absorb the first losses, are the most efficient way to channel Alterra-scale capital into nature-based projects that would otherwise be too small or too risky. Third, UAE companies buying carbon credits to meet their net-zero targets can insist on contracts that share revenue with communities. Credits backed by legally binding benefit-sharing carry lower reversal risk, and therefore deserve a premium. Next year, Addis Ababa hosts Cop32, putting Africa at the centre of the world’s climate talks. The UAE, a bridge between Gulf capital and African growth, is in a strong position to lead a new kind of investment there: one that treats healthy coasts not as a cost of doing business, but as an asset that protects every other investment on the shore. Vahid Fotuhi is founder and chief executive of Blue Forest, a UAE-based developer of mangrove restoration projects in Africa and Asia

events.title: Soros joins family offices selling Nvidia last quarter
events.summary: George Soros, 96, has a net worth of US$9.7 billion (S$12.4 billion), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. Soros Fund Management cut its Nvidia stake by almost a fifth in the quarter to 30 Sept, selling about 206,000 shares worth up to US$47.4 million. Several family offices and firms also trimmed Nvidia, while others bought more. They still held more than US$1 billion in Nvidia shares at quarter end. Nvidia remains a key AI stock, but Jensen Huang’s sudden exit as CEO has hit sentiment. The company is searching for a successor and reports earnings on 17 Nov. LONDON – George Soros’ family office joined investment firms for the world’s ultra-rich in trimming Nvidia bets last quarter, locking in gains ahead of Jensen Huang’s dramatic exit from the vaunted chip designer. The billionaire’s namesake money manager cut its stake in Nvidia by almost a fifth in the period ended Sept 30, the biggest disclosed reduction for its Nvidia holding in 2026 after it had previously added to its position, according to data compiled by Bloomberg from quarterly regulatory filings. Michael Platt’s BlueCrest Capital Management, as well as an investment firm for Abu Dhabi ruler Sheikh Mohamed Bin Zayed Al Nahyan, also cut their Nvidia stakes during the same period. The Santa Clara, California-based company’s shares were up 22% in 2026 through the end of September, roughly double the gain of the US benchmark S&P 500 Index for the same period. The selling family offices – totalling at least a dozen – all kept at least some shares of Nvidia, with their combined holdings totalling more than US$1 billion (S$1.29 billion) at the end of the quarter. For many of those firms, Nvidia remained one of their top US stock positions. Nvidia has ranked among the world’s hottest stocks in recent years as it rapidly became a poster child of the artificial intelligence boom, but Huang’s abrupt departure last week from the company that he has overseen for more than three decades has led to a reckoning. Huang, 63, was ousted as CEO on Nov 12 after revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, including with Nvidia employees and a woman suspected by the US Justice Department of being a Chinese spy. Nvidia’s shares have fallen more than 25% since the New York Times first reported in late October that Huang may have been the target of a Chinese spy plot. Nvidia, which reports third-quarter earnings on Nov 17 , has begun its search for a successor, even as some of Huang’s allies in Silicon Valley – and President Donald Trump – are campaigning for his return to the top job. Nvidia’s dominance in the tech boom has made it an important part of many family offices’ investment portfolios, and some of those firms increased their positions in the stock in the third quarter. Among those buying Nvidia were firms managing fortunes on behalf of duty-free shopping tycoon Alan Parker, Brazil’s Moreira Salles finance dynasty and Missouri’s Van Tuyl family. Soros Fund Management, led by former UBS Group AG executive Dawn Fitzpatrick, sold about 206,000 shares in Nvidia last quarter worth as much as US$47.4 million, filings show. Its remaining Nvidia stake was worth nearly US$200 million as of Sept 30. Soros, 96, has a net worth of US$9.7 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. Money managers overseeing more than US$100 million in US equities have to file a 13F form within 45 days of the end of each quarter to list their holdings in stocks that trade on US exchanges. It offers one of the few glimpses into how hedge funds and some large family offices invest. Other highlights from the latest 13F filings include: Jeffrey Skoll’s Capricorn Investment Group slashed its biggest holding, selling 9.8 million shares of SpaceX worth almost US$1.5 billion as of Sept 30. Alta Advisers, an investment firm for a branch of Sweden’s Rausing dynasty, increased its number of equity holdings by more than a third last quarter, with 114 new positions including stakes in ExxonMobil, Blue Owl Capital and AMC Entertainment. WIT LLC, which manages a portion of the Walton family fortune, is comprised solely of stakes in exchange-traded funds. It sold 2 million shares of the iShares ESG Aware MSCI EM ETF and bought 2.75 million shares of the Vanguard FTSE Developed Markets ETF. BLOOMBERG
