events.title: S’pore’s key exports surge 79.8% in October, but tighter US chip rules spark uncertainty ahead
events.summary: The growth in non-electronics NODX was driven by structures of ships and boats, pharmaceuticals and specialised machinery. Singapore’s non-oil domestic exports rose 79.8% in October, beating forecasts. Non-electronics led the gain, while electronics also grew on strong AI demand. Shipments to the US, China and Taiwan increased sharply. Exports to the US jumped 214.6%, and China rose 144.9%, but India, Indonesia and Thailand fell. New US chip export controls may add uncertainty for AI trade. Singapore is studying the rules, while economists warned of higher compliance costs and unclear impact. SINGAPORE – Singapore’s non-oil domestic exports (NODX) jumped in October, extending September’s increase, boosted mainly by strong non-electronics shipments, while electronics continued to rise amid sustained AI-driven demand. Economists warned that fresh US chip export controls aimed at curbing China’s access could further heighten market uncertainty surrounding AI valuations and the sustainability of AI-related demand. Under the new restrictions announced on Nov 16, a licence will be required to export, re-export or transfer advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, which the US identified as countries where advanced chips are at higher risk of being diverted to China. “Within the new measures, compute access to some countries, including China, from data centres that are using covered items may also face restrictions,” said Edward Lee and Jonathan Koh of Standard Chartered. “It remains to be seen on the eventual impact,” they noted. OCBC group research chief economist Selena Ling said: “At this juncture, the impact is difficult to quantify, but higher compliance costs are likely, with heightened uncertainty in the interim period.” She added: “Most AI compute physically in Singapore is run by US hyperscalers and co-location tenants that would likely qualify for the exemption, but the exposed parts are non-US neoclouds, trading and distribution intermediaries, and capacity rented to China-linked clients.” The Singapore authorities on Nov 17 said they were “studying the details of this new measure carefully”, and engaging affected companies to assess the impact, as well as the US authorities on the scope and implementation of the measure. Non-oil domestic exports (NODX) expanded 79.8% from a year ago, following September’s rise of 68.3%, led by non-electronics, data from Enterprise Singapore (EnterpriseSG) on Nov 17 showed. The latest figure beat the 37.7% forecast by economists in a Bloomberg poll. Non-electronics shipments surged 81.9% year on year in October, building on the previous month’s 54.1% increase. The growth in non-electronics NODX was driven by structures of ships and boats, pharmaceuticals, which expanded 253.1%, as well as specialised machinery, which rose 57.3%. The year-on-year growth for “lumpy exports” of structures of ships and boats was not cited, as the exceptionally high percentage increase reflects a low base effect in the same period in 2025. Surging 73.9% in October following a 107.6% rise the previous month, electronic product shipments continued to climb on the back of robust AI demand. Growth was driven by a 189.6% jump in disk media products, while shipments for personal computers grew 81%, and 53.1% for integrated circuits, or chips. NODX to the United States, China and Taiwan expanded in October, while NODX to India, Indonesia and Thailand contracted. NODX to Taiwan expanded 79.3%, extending September’s 96.9% rise, driven by a 149% jump in electronic NODX. NODX to India fell 35.8% in October, following a 5.7% decline in September, dragged down by a 51.9% decline in non-electronic shipments. Key exports to the US, Singapore’s single-largest export market, expanded 214.6%, while those to China increased 144.9%.

events.title: AI agents still act like ‘Day 1 employees,’ Glean CEO says
events.summary: AI agents are nowhere near having the “context” to outperform skilled humans, Glean CEO Arvind Jain said Monday. “When you deploy AI agents, and you actually point them to the right data and knowledge that they need to do their work, they still come and act more like Day 1 employees,” Jain told the editor-in-chief of The Verge, Nilay Patel, at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “That’s the gap that needs to close before we can come and talk about fancy things like job elimination.” Jain, who co-founded the AI platform Glean in 2019, said “nobody’s anywhere close” to building AI systems capable of replacing experienced workers. Glean, he said, is meant to bring “tacit knowledge” and experience with a company to its internal AI systems, to combat that “Day 1 employee” problem. Despite AI’s limitations, Jain also said companies are under “enormous pressure” to adopt it. That may be one reason, he said, for recent high-level technological disruptions, like the outages this week reported by banks and airlines. “Sometimes businesses didn’t get time to actually set the right foundation” before rolling out AI tools, Jain said. Jain also predicted a future in which around 90% of work can be done by open-source and non-frontier AI models, though the remaining “10% of the tasks will actually still consume the majority of your AI spend.” — Ben Kesslen

events.title: Customers report service outages at major US banks
events.summary: Thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, have reported trouble accessing services. Chase Bank - the largest banking institution in the US - said a "software bug" in its hardware systems may have been behind the glitch and noted the impacts may have affected other banks. It added the issue was "temporary" and not "systemic" or "cyber-related". Problems appeared to be easing for many customers by early Monday evening. The issue comes after a string of unrelated technical problems, including a massive Microsoft outage , a network failure that grounded all US flights , and United Airlines reporting a "widespread system outage". Problems started on Monday afternoon. There were almost 5,000 reports of problems with Chase Bank's services, according to the Downdetector website. Clients reported issues accessing their online accounts, viewing balances and performing transactions, like bank transfers and wire transfers, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News. A Chase Bank customer in Texas told the outlet that he could not deposit a check at a Dallas branch on Monday, reporting that he was told his transaction could not be completed. He said a bank teller told the customer in front of him that the "system was down" but did not provide additional details. Microsoft says services fully restored after day-long global outage Published 3 days ago Microsoft outage 'stark reminder' of how much we rely on tech Published 3 days ago Chase Bank told its customers that "some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete" but they still had "access to their accounts and funds". The bank, a subsidiary of JP Morgan Chase, serves more than 86m customers at 5,000 branches across the US, as well as 7.4m small businesses, according to the company's webpage. It is also the top credit card issuer in the US. The exact nature of the bug was unclear. The BBC has contacted Chase Bank. Bank of America customers had issues at ATMs and using mobile banking services online, while US Bank customers reported issues with their online accounts and the bank's mobile app, CBS reported. Customers using another institution, US Bank, also reported issues transferring funds and Wells Fargo customers said they had problems signing into their accounts, getting account balances and making transactions. US Bank said some its systems were not directly affected but clients using the Zelle, a digital payment platform, received error messages saying their payments could not be sent. Zelle has said its service is "operating as it should" and issues at other banks could be affecting payments. Customers also reported issues with Truist, PNC and Capital One but all these companies told the BBC they have not been impacted. As of 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT), Chase, Bank of America and US Bank had seen a fall in the number of reported outages. Just as the banking issue affected US customers on Monday, United Airlines confirmed a "widespread system outage", which it described as "a technology issue affecting departing flights". That issue resolved within a few hours. The Chicago-based airline did not say what is believed to have caused the issue, but a spokesperson said it is not related to cybersecurity. The issue did not appear to be affecting any other airlines. The United issue is separate from the one that hit the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) , but comes as other industries report different outages around the US. On Friday, the FAA issued a rare nationwide a ground stop, halting all US air travel due to a telecommunication and network upgrade issues. The halt lasted just over four hours, but the knock-on effect continues to snarl US air travel. events.title: We couldn't afford a house alone, so we bought one with strangers
events.summary: The Pullman family, on the left, and the Wilcox family, bought a home together soon after meeting Published 17 November 2026, 00:00 GMT When Elizabeth and Tom Wilcox realised they could never afford to buy the home they wanted for themselves and their two children, they decided to take a leap of faith. They'd find another couple with young kids, complete strangers to them, and propose that they go halves on a property and all move in together. Based in Vancouver, which has long had some of the highest house prices in Canada, the Wilcoxes were desperate to buy a home that had a back garden for their children to play in. "We wanted a house with a yard that could fit a trampoline, in a walkable neighbourhood, but we couldn't afford it," says Elizabeth, a project manager in the healthcare sector. With a budget of C$1m ($700,000; £500,000) all they could hope for was a small apartment with a balcony at best. That was when Elizabeth came up with the idea of buying with another family. They placed an advert in a local estate agent's e-newsletter, but it took two years before they finally met a family whom they clicked with – Ashley Pullman and her husband and two children. In 2023, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans co-bought a six-bedroom, detached house, complete with a back garden, for C$1.85m. The two families split the deposit of C$250,000, and continue to go halves on the monthly mortgage payments of C$3,900. They also divide bills and other expenses equally, such as any necessary home repairs. Elizabeth says the arrangement has saved both families "tens of thousands of dollars". Mums Ashley Pullman, left, and Elizabeth Wilcox say the two families get along While there is no official data available for the number of people buying homes with people they previously didn't know, Parimal Gosal says he has seen a big increase in interest in Toronto as a response to high property prices. Gosal is the founder and CEO of Husmates, an app and website that connects people in Canada's largest city who are looking to potentially buy a home with a stranger. It can be seen as "a financial relationship, and that takes emotions out of it", he says. It's unclear how common this phenomenon is elsewhere in the world. David Hollingworth, from British mortgage broker L&C, says while he hasn't come across it himself, he thinks it also happens in the UK, though is "very niche". "I remember that before Covid-19 there was a matchmaking event in a London pub, like speed dating, for people looking to buy a house with a stranger," he says. "How successful this was I don' t know." The Wilcoxes and the Pullmans pooled their resources to buy a detached Vancouver home Three years on, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans say their living arrangement is still working out. While each family has some private living spaces, such as their own kitchens, they share the big basement-level living room, which includes a home gym in one corner, and a shared freezer. "If someone says they're in the basement to work out, we know not to go there for a bit, and it's never been an issue," says Elizabeth. Ashley agrees that there are no problems. "Maybe it's arrogance but my husband and I felt like we were the type of people who could live with strangers," she says. Sabrina Bowman, a freelance business consultant in Toronto, has co-owned a home with two other housemates since 2018. When she signed on the dotted line and moved in she didn't know one of the other two people. While Sabrina says she isn't comfortable sharing the exact financial details, she says they decided to divide up the deposit and mortgage payments based on each of their levels of income. She says any household disputes can be addressed early with open discussions. "What is important to us is having structures to communicate about everything that happens in the home." They have regular house meetings where they discuss chores, financial issues, birthday celebrations, and any disagreements. "It's great to see people be honest about something they may not be comfortable about and for us to find a solution to that problem," Sabrina says. Sabrina Bowman says it is important to have open communication In the case of both Sabrina's house in Toronto and the Wilcox and Pullman property in Vancouver, they have legal agreements in place in case someone wants to sell up and move out. For both homes, reasonable notice periods are specified, and for Sabrina's, the departing housemate is required to give those remaining the first opportunity to buy their share. Toronto real estate lawyer Tanya Walker says such legal assurances are vital. "You need something legally binding instead of a bunch of emails and Facebook messages that can be too messy to collect if a dispute comes up," Walker says. Back in Vancouver, Elizabeth says that neither family has a timeframe for how long they will live in the house. "All of us are really happy with the set-up and location so it would be hard to move.

events.title: Reducing High-Bandwidth Flash Latency In GPU Systems (Georgia Tech, Nvidia, Stanford)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at Georgia Tech, NVIDIA Research , and Stanford University published “SlipStream: Enabling HBF for GPU Systems by Mitigating the Latency and SRAM Overheads.” “Large language model (LLM) inference demands ever more memory capacity for larger models and batch sizes. High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) replaces the DRAM dies of HBM with NAND flash and provides up to 16x the capacity at comparable read bandwidth. However, HBF can incur a read latency of nearly 20 μ s, 20x that of HBM, so on-demand HBF accesses slow inference by up to 12.8x. Conventional cache-line prefetchers require 20x more in-flight tracking state to cover this latency. Tensor-streaming designs, such as H3, follow virtual-address order as opposed to kernel-demand order, and therefore need hundreds of megabytes of buffering. We propose SlipStream, a software-hardware co-designed prefetcher that turns prefetching into a demand-paced producer-consumer pipeline. In software, SlipStream profiles the repeatable weight-page demand order of data-independent LLM kernels and inserts a staging warp that replays this order with non-blocking STAGE instructions. In hardware, the staging warp acts as the producer and the work warps as consumers. Our key insight is to retire each STAGE tracking entry only when demand first accesses the page, as opposed to when the page returns from HBF. Demand thus paces staging and bounds how far staging leads consumption. SlipStream tracks 4 KB pages instead of cache lines and allocates buffer slots only when pages return, which decouples the buffer size from outstanding traffic. Across seven dense models spanning 16-800 GB, SlipStream with a 40 MB staging buffer achieves 92.4% of the performance of an ideal HBF with HBM-like latency. H3 achieves only 43.1%, even with a 320 MB buffer. The buffer sizing of SlipStream is independent of HBF latency and workload. SlipStream with 16 MB buffer, 20x smaller than that of H3, performs within 4% of SlipStream-40MB. SlipStream also supports Mixture-of-Experts models and reaches 91.2% of ideal performance (40 MB buffer).” Find the technical paper here . November 2026. Saxena, Anish, Hritvik Taneja, Christos Kozyrakis, and Aamer Jaleel. “SlipStream: Enabling HBF for GPU Systems by Mitigating the Latency and SRAM Overheads.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2611.14776 (2026). events.title: California sues OpenAI for misleading public about AI safety
events.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta has sued OpenAI under the state's unfair competition and public nuisance laws, for allegedly misleading and endangering the public by deploying unsafe AI models. The lawsuit [PDF], filed in California Superior Court, follows the compromise of Hugging Face's infrastructure and other cyber incidents OpenAI's experimental models caused when taking autonomous actions without authorization or supervision. "While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents," said Attorney General Bonta. At a press conference , Bonta added: "OpenAI disregarded public safety, knowingly tested potentially dangerous AI models without proper oversight and safety measures, and misled consumers and the public." The legal salvo comes after Bonta in September sent OpenAI a letter seeking information about these agentic attacks. According to the complaint, "OpenAI failed to substantially comply" with the investigatory subpoena. In August, 15 states led by Iowa – and excluding California – issued a joint demand for OpenAI to provide information about how its models hacked Hugging Face. OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment. Bonta's office previously joined with Delaware Attorney General Kathy Jennings to urge OpenAI to do more for children's safety in light of reports that its models produced sexually inappropriate output. California did not, however, join the eight states that sued OpenAI in October over alleged misrepresentations about child safety. Florida and Texas have also made child safety claims. Child safety plays well politically; California appears to be the first state to demand more accountability toward the general public. Bonta's lawsuit, in a state that has largely accommodated the AI industry for the sake of economic benefits and political contributions , suggests that California officials may be more willing to bite the hand that feeds. The many Democratic victories in the US midterm elections may also be a factor, as pundits feel voters swung to give lawmakers license to regulate the unpopular AI industry. At his press conference, Bonta made sure to convey that he wants accountability without smothering the AI industry in costly regulation. "Let me be clear," he said. "I believe in the technological and economic power of AI. If we're able to address these very high stakes safety issues, AI could lead to some of the most incredible improvements in the history of humankind." AI is yet to deliver those incredible improvements. It has delivered deepfakes, huge quantities of cybersecurity vulnerabilities, and the permissionless resale of past intellectual labor, plus high energy and RAM prices. As well as some productivity gains in certain areas like coding, albeit at an unknown cost to future job markets. But as AI boosters insist, miracle drugs and endless vacations aren't far off … perhaps along with existential crises. Katharine Trendacosta, director of policy and advocacy at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, told The Register in an email that the EFF is glad to see state officials taking action against AI companies taking unreasonable risks with public safety. "Several recent cybersecurity incidents at AI labs could have been prevented or substantially mitigated by adhering to longstanding cybersecurity best practices, such as proper sandboxing, monitoring, and logging," said Trendacosta. "AI agents can be useful tools when deployed appropriately, with adequate safeguards designed to mitigate the risks. Companies should carefully consider the risks of every use case, including the consequences, reversibility, and sensitivity of any action an agent is used for." ®

events.title: United Airlines resolves "widespread system outage" that delayed flights
events.summary: United Airlines said Monday that it resolved what it called a "widespread system outage" that delayed departing flights for about 90 minutes. Why it matters: It was a quick resolution to yet another issue affecting the U.S.' beleaguered airspace, which spent days digging itself out of thousands of flight delays and cancellations following Friday's hours-long ground stop . What they're saying: "We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience. We're aware of the widespread system outage, and our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible," United Airlines wrote on X in reply to a customer. "We appreciate your patience while we work through this. Please check back with us for updates, and keep an eye on your flight status through the United app or at http://united.com . Thanks for bearing with us!" The customer said the issue stemmed from planes being unable to determine weight limits, though United did not confirm that was the problem. United Airlines told Axios that the company is "troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights." "There is no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights. There is no indication that this is a cybersecurity-related issue," they said. About an hour and fifteen minutes after United posted its apology, the company tweeted again to say the issue was resolved and encouraged passengers to check their flight status at the company's website. United gave no additional information about what caused the outage, and it's unclear how many flights were impacted. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information.

events.title: Cybersecurity AI startup Corma reaches $1B valuation in about 3 months
events.summary: Three months after introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corma has raised a $125 million Series A round at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA, the company said. Corma offers AI models and agents trained for cybersecurity defense. It has now raised a total of $185 million from backers, including Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue. The startup came out of stealth in August. Interest in its product skyrocketed after a series of security incidents sent chief information security officers scrambling on October 21 when a critical flaw was found in PHP , a popular web programming language. Another flaw was found in Node.js , the open source JavaScript runtime environment. Popular open source tool LiteLLM, a proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, also disclosed a security incident. Other incidents were disclosed that day, too. The day showcased the kind of onslaught on security that AI has enabled. Corma isn’t the only company using AI to play defense. Other examples include Kevin Mandia’s new startup Armadin , as well as Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, and other established players, and too many other startups to count. Still, it’s a young market and a necessary one. Corma says it stands out from the crowd by being a frontier AI research lab focused on protection. events.title: A top Puerto Rico government official resigns as corruption allegations swirl
events.summary: Puerto Rico’s embattled secretary of the Department of Family has announced that she would resign by year’s end as she denies the corruption allegations swirling around her SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- Puerto Rico’s embattled secretary of the Department of Family announced Monday that she would resign by year’s end as she denied corruption allegations swirling around her. Lawmakers in the U.S. territory had demanded for months that Suzanne Roig step down over the latest political scandal to hit the administration of Gov. Jenniffer González , which has seen several high-ranking officials resign or be fired in recent years. Roig is under investigation by Puerto Rico’s Senate, the island’s Justice Department and its Office of the Inspector General. In recent months, Blanca Medina Díaz, who was dismissed as head of the Administration for the Socioeconomic Development of the Family, which is within the department Roig oversees, publicly accused Roig of pressuring her to approve a nearly $40 million contract that Medina alleges was illegal and would have used federal funds from the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program. The alleged push came after Roig and other officials visited Louisiana. Roig and NOLA Education LLC, a Louisiana-based education company, have said that no contract was signed. Medina, who has met with U.S. federal authorities, also accused Roig of pressuring her to approve an unrelated contract worth more than $300,000. Roig has been under fire, as has the governor, who has publicly supported her. Roig testified before Puerto Rico’s Senate in recent weeks as certain lawmakers who are members of the governor’s pro-statehood party called for her to step down. As Roig faced increasing scrutiny, she alleged in recent months that she was being stalked and persecuted as she denied all accusations. In a statement Monday, Roig said that nobody asked her to resign as she thanked the governor for “the time and space that allowed me to defend my reputation against attacks full of falsehoods.” Her decision to step down on Dec. 31 angered many. “The resignation should have been immediate,” said Puerto Rico Sen. Juan Oscar Morales, majority whip and a member of the governor’s party. “The Department of the Family needs leadership focused on addressing the agency’s problems and ensuring services for those who depend on it.” Roig’s announcement came nearly four months after the governor’s chief of staff and deputy chief of staff announced their resignations as they, too, denied corruption allegations. events.title: ‘America needs to have more Jensens’: Perplexity CEO lauds Huang as industry titan
events.summary: Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas on Monday said the US needs more entrepreneurial tech CEOs like former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during an interview at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “He’s one of the greatest founders in American history,” Srinivas told Semafor Editor-in-Chief Ben Smith. “America needs to have more Jensens.” Tech CEOs and entrepreneurs have long lauded the former CEO of the world’s biggest chipmaker as the epitome of the American dream; Huang started the company in a Denny’s restaurant. But revelations of the former CEO’s extramarital affairs have sullied his reputation. Huang resigned as CEO last week. Srinivas said that Huang’s advice to him as a young founder was to act like he was going to run out of business in six to 12 months. “He would run the company like as if he would run out of business in the next 30 days,” he recalled. “So that attitude that relentlessness, grit, determination, always wanting to push the frontier is the spirit that every American founder should take.” Despite praising Huang, Srinivas dodged a question on whether Nvidia’s board should reinstate him as the company’s head amid reports Huang was eyeing a comeback. Srinivas also announced onstage that Perplexity just crossed a $1 billion annual run rate on Monday, while maintaining a burn rate that he said is five times lower than that of hyperscalers. He attributed this to the startup’s capital-efficient model. Unlike frontier labs, Perplexity is primarily a model aggregator, routing users to other AI models like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude instead of operating a flagship foundational model. The company is built on the idea that users don’t care which model they’re using. “They really care if the work actually got done,” Srinivas said. — Jake Angelo

events.title: OpenAI sued by California over Hugging Face attack
events.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the ChatGPT-maker misled and endangered the public by developing artificial intelligence (AI) models without proper safeguards. In the lawsuit, Bonta cited the July 2026 attack on the AI platform Hugging Face by experimental OpenAI agents which accessed the internet to breach that company's internal systems. Bonta claimed OpenAI created a public nuisance and violated the state's unfair competition laws. OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the BBC in a statement that Bonta's lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab". Other major AI developers including Anthropic, Meta, and Google have also said their models have staged similar attacks. But Bonta's lawsuit, filed in San Francisco, where the company is headquartered, appears to be the first such suit filed by a US state. Warning shot or publicity stunt - how worried should we be about the OpenAI hack? Published 25 July OpenAI says its rogue AI tried to hack other companies Published 29 July Hundreds of OpenAI agents coordinated the Hugging Face attack over two days even though they were supposed to be contained in a safe testing environment. The incident drew added scrutiny because the agents went as far as attempting to cover their tracks. Bonta announced an investigation into the incident in September, and served an investigative subpoena on OpenAI as part of its probe. "The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it - this disregard for public safety violated California law," Bonta said in a statement on Monday. OpenAI said it has been transparent and responsive to the Attorney General's office. "We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged - and will continue to engage - constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry," the company said. The company added that, since the Hugging Face incident, it has worked to understand and address "misaligned model activity" which industry figures often refer to as rogue agents. Nathan Calvin, chief strategy officer at AI safety campaign group Encode AI, said the lawsuit "recognises something we at Encode have long raised alarms about". "OpenAI and other companies developing frontier AI systems have safety and security practices that are insufficient to protect the public from risks that could be catastrophic," he said. events.title: Mayor pushes for inquiry into mining licence approvals
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Council pushes for inquiry into mining licences as state amends planning scheme WIM Resource dug a test pit, which they then grew barley and lentil crops on. ( Supplied: WIM Resource ) Horsham Rural City Council Mayor Brian Klowss is pushing for an inquiry into approvals of mining licences for projects across Western Victoria. Cr Klowss says he sought immediate changes to the Horsham Planning Scheme for the Avonbank Mining project. The council is seeking clarification from the state government. A regional Victorian council is pushing for an inquiry into the granting of mining licences for projects across Western Victoria. Multiple licences have been granted for controversial projects to mine rare earth minerals in the Wimmera and Mallee across the next few decades. These include the VHM Minerals Sands project in the small farming town of Lalbert, Astron's Donald Rare Earth and Minerals Sands project and WIM Resource's Avonbank Mineral Sands project. Horsham Rural City Council Mayor Brian Klowss said the community was concerned and asking a lot of questions about the Avonbank mine, which could begin construction next year pending final approvals. "I think it's getting to the point where we nearly need an inquiry into the granting of these mining licences and what's going on," Cr Klowss said. The mine site is near Dooen, a rural village in the Wimmera region. ( Supplied: WIM Resource ) Last month, Resource Victoria granted a 20-year mining licence to the Avonbank mine set to be located in Dooen, 15 kilometres north-east of Horsham, including approvals to mine heavy mineral sands such as zircon, titanium and rare earth elements. The site will cover about 3,400 hectares, with the Chinese-backed company p lanning to mine around the clock for 36 years for materials used in everyday technology and renewable energy infrastructure. Horsham Rural City Council had previously raised concerns about the mine, including dust issues, use of the nearby intermodal freight hub and rehabilitation prospects for agricultural land. Cr Klowss said the community felt their voices had not been heard and urged whichever party forms government after the state election to start listening to locals. "That's what we want and that's what's not happening," he said. "It's like these things are being pushed on our community and we're not getting a say and we're not even getting consulted about it." Brian Klowss says the situation is "beyond a joke". ( ABC News: Gillian Aeria ) These concerns were exacerbated when council discovered Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny had changed the Horsham Planning Scheme for the Avonbank project without consultation. WIM Resource requested an amendment to allow for provisions to help with mineral sands processing and other infrastructure required to support the project. As part of the amendment, the government issued a new map doubling the size of the base mining area, a move described by Cr Klowss as "a serious mapping error". He said the increase could impact other projects and businesses hoping to invest in the region and has written to the minister requesting an immediate correction. Horsham Rural City Council says the area is double the size of the area listed in the Environment Effects Statement in 2023. ( Supplied: Horsham Rural City Council ) Council said the planning authority decision was made on October 28, a few days before the state election caretaker period, but it was only made aware of the change on November 12 after the amendment was advertised in a government gazette. "Yet again, council has not been consulted and has been kept at arms-distance from the process," Cr Klowss said. "Had we have been given an opportunity to review the maps we would have likely picked up the error, helping the state government avoid embarrassment. The proposed Avonbank mine site back in 2022. ( Supplied: Horsham Rural City Council ) "I am concerned that mistakes that have occurred with this mapping anomaly, send the wrong message to project proponents and the community." The state government has been contacted for comment. It is not the first time Ms Kilkenny has amended a local government planning scheme without consultation. Only last month, she used her powers to amend Yarriambiack Shire Council's planning scheme to approve the Warracknabeal Energy Park — a wind turbine facility that will be the largest in Australia. The project has proven deeply controversial among the local community and has been the target of numerous protests.

events.title: NVIDIA DGX Spark Developer Kit Turns a Desk Into a Supercomputing Lab
events.summary: At SC26, an annual supercomputing conference taking place this week in Chicago, NVIDIA is introducing the DGX Spark HPC Developer Kit for researchers, academics and developers. The kit is a four-node cluster of NVIDIA DGX Spark systems , each connected directly to its two neighbors in a ring, with an NVIDIA HPC SDK installation playbook coming soon. Researchers get a place at their desk to run multi-node scientific workloads, AI models and agents, instead of waiting for time on a shared GPU cluster. The kit puts the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip on researchers’ desks. The DGX Spark Developer Kit changes how researchers work. It scales from one system, or node, to four — linked directly to one another over NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking, with no network switch to buy or set up. At four nodes, it provides 512GB of combined memory and 20TB of NVMe storage that provides researchers more capacity to distribute models and scientific workloads across the cluster. With NVFP4, researchers can deploy models with up to 700B parameters locally across the four DGX Spark clusters, such as DeepSeek V4.1. With that much power at the desk, researchers with a fixed compute and server allocation no longer have to wait in a queue for every job. Teams can develop and debug on their own, saving server hours for production runs and keeping unpublished results, and proprietary datasets on premises. The playbook for NVIDIA HPC SDK is coming soon, bringing GPU-accelerated C, C++ and Fortran compilers, libraries and message passing interface tools to the DGX Spark cluster — the same development tools used on NVIDIA-powered supercomputers. Teams can build and test scientific applications across four nodes, check how computation and data are distributed, and debug communication issues before scaling to larger systems. The kit brings scientific simulation and AI models and agents to the desktop, with demonstrated four-system workloads including LAMMPS with Kokkos for materials simulation and NAMD for molecular dynamics. The broader DGX Spark community has validated GROMACS for molecular dynamics, OpenFOAM for fluid dynamics, WRF for weather modeling and NVIDIA NIM microservices such as OpenFold3 and Boltz-2 for predicting biomolecular structures. Running on DGX Spark, new open dataset and post-training recipes for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL help researchers adapt the model for life sciences and chemistry, enabling secure scientific workflows on infrastructure organizations control. The kit opens up new possibilities for researchers. Researchers can explore agent-assisted workflows that prepare simulation inputs, launch runs and summarize results, while the scientists validate the setup and conclusions. Researchers can also train AI models that approximate slow simulations, then use them to refine wing designs toward minimum drag. Before committing supercomputer time, a team can narrow a 10-million-cell simulation to the 50-500 dimensions that matter. Kvantify is using NVIDIA cuQuantum, and reports running tensor-network simulations of quantum-chemistry circuits with up to 70 qubits and 975 gates on a single DGX Spark, benchmarking circuits generated for penicillin ground-state energy calculations. CYRAN AI , an IIT Delhi spin-out, uses DGX Spark and its PixelFlux library to accelerate JPEG 2000 decoding for large satellite images, supporting local geospatial analysis. OpenFold shows how researchers can fine-tune OpenFold3 on NVIDIA DGX Spark to improve protein-ligand structure predictions for drug discovery. The Rubin Lab at IGI at University of California, Berkeley is using a DGX Spark and NVIDIA Evo 2 model to predict bacterial traits directly from genome sequences by comparing embeddings from genomic and protein language models against the classical baselines. With no 11-hour cluster queue times, results arrived 15x sooner on DGX Spark. The Hartwig Group at UC Berkeley is using a DGX Spark to perform LoRA fine-tuning on the Nemotron 3 Super 120B-A12B model for chemistry machine learning, training a prediction head on experimental values. By running locally on the Spark using NVFP4 quantization, the lab successfully fit a 120B-class model on a single device and bypassed multi-day cluster queue times, allowing them to run continuous eight- to 24-hour training fits back-to-back. The developer kit is on display at SC26 and available for sale. DGX Spark products and cables can be purchased from top OEM partners and are also available through NVIDIA Marketplace . Partners include Acer, ASUS, Dell Technologies, GIGABYTE, H3C, HP, Lenovo, MSI and xFusion. An NVIDIA playbook for building and running the NVIDIA HPC SDK, a software development kit for scientific computing, is coming soon. Once available, it will give scientists and researchers a local platform to develop multi-node GPU applications, explore FP32 and mixed-precision algorithms and run molecular dynamics and materials simulations using LAMMPS with Kokkos before scaling to data center systems. Learn more about NVIDIA DGX Spark . See notice regarding software product information. events.title: AI makes everyone more vulnerable, AT&T CEO says
events.summary: Everybody is more vulnerable because of AI, at least for now, AT&T CEO John Stankey said Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. Stankey believes that can be turned around to make things safer, but it will take some time to figure out “how to turn that technology into advantage rather than liability.” Stankey said he is by no means a “doomer” when it comes to AI, but it’s hard for anyone to know what the true full effect of these AI models will be. He added that “anxiety levels are pretty high right now” because of the added cybersecurity risks brought on by artificial intelligence. While there’s been a lot of concern around data centers and the public reaction to them, Stankey urged consideration of the downstream effects. If “a metropolitan area doesn’t have power for a period of time, or we start seeing cell phones drop from the network,” Stankey said. “We’ve got to make sure we’re doing the right things to prevent that from happening.” We can’t have “technology for technology’s sake,” he said. “If the public loses trust, if an economy is interrupted, and it can’t transact business in the way it should transact business and grow, then we’ve got technology that is built on a bad foundation.” He added that additional government regulation may not be the answer, but urged his peers to think about the fundamental needs and pacing as the environment continues to evolve. Data sovereignty was also a major concern for Stankey, adding that the notion that “my data isn’t my data” is very important. — Ellen DiMauro

events.summary: Replit CEO Amjad Masad called Jensen Huang’s ouster as Nvidia’s CEO “an attack on open models” at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World on Monday. “Jensen is the premier champion of open models,” Masad told Semafor’s Rohan Goswami. “If it wasn’t for Jensen, there wouldn’t be a lot of funding going into US open model companies like Reflection and others.” Huang resigned last week following reports that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with two subordinates and a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. People familiar with the matter have told Semafor that Huang is mulling a comeback as CEO but that the board isn’t considering a return. Masad, who founded Replit, an AI app and website-building company, has championed the push to reinstate Huang. When a friend told him about a petition on Replit calling for the fallen CEO’s return, “I literally jumped in and did tech support for them,” Masad said. Huang has been “a great voice on pushing back on the narrative that we need to lock down AI, that the only safe AI is a closed AI,” Masad said. He added that not having Huang at Nvidia would be a “huge loss” and “potentially bring about a world where there’s only the frontier model labs that exist.” Software engineering careers ‘an accident of history’ When asked about the future of tech jobs, Masad said on Monday, “The modern career of software engineer is a bit of an accident of history.” Now, many of his customers have zero software engineers on staff. “I used to get attacked a lot for saying that, but now everyone agrees with me,” Masad said. Ben Lamm, the CEO of the biotech and genetic engineering de-extinction company Colossal Biosciences, agreed, saying, “We’re doing what we used to do with 80 engineers with, like, five.” And Edwin Chen, the founder and CEO of AI-training platform Surge AI, said that his headcount will likely remain stable. “If you look at the latest models, they’re not just writing code anymore. They’re often coming with ideas on their own,” Chen said. “They’re helping our engineers understand certain kinds of security risks or architectural trade-offs.” All this, Chen said, means he doesn’t see a need to hire product managers or expand headcount dramatically. Masad said he still foresees hiring entry-level employees, in part because in the agentic era, people’s jobs are changing every three to six months. “You need people who are willing to continue relearning their job,” he said. “And I think, you know, just because of brain plasticity, younger people are actually pretty good at that.” — Ben Kesslen

events.title: Chalmers says spending will be cut in mid-year update 'but not too much'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Chalmers says mid-year budget update will include 'enough' spending cuts Jim Chalmers will deliver the mid-year budget update in December. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Jim Chalmers says the mid-year budget update will include a "substantial" package of cuts. The treasurer also says the government is working on plans to cut government regulation. The mid-year budget update will be delivered in December. A "substantial" package of cuts to government spending will be revealed in next month's mid-year budget update, Treasurer Jim Chalmers has confirmed. The cuts have been foreshadowed for several weeks, but without any sense of their magnitude. In a speech to an ASIC forum this morning, Mr Chalmers said the mid-year update would have cuts as its main focus. "It will cut enough, but not too much. It will strike some fine balances," he said. The government has sustained criticism over the elevated level of government spending, which the opposition and some economists have said is worsening inflation and driving interest rates higher. Mr Chalmers has consistently rejected that characterisation, but today said the cuts were motivated by economic conditions. "We take seriously and embrace our responsibilities in the fight against inflation," he said. No details of individual cuts have been confirmed, but Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said earlier this month the public service would be one target of "belt tightening", and there have been calls to consider means testing for subsidies for electric vehicles and home batteries. Simpler building code among red tape measures Mr Chalmers also announced he would write to businesses and investors to gather ideas for regulations that could be cut to simplify compliance for businesses. He last wrote to government regulators on this matter last year, and told the ASIC forum the process had led to 400 ideas for how red tape could be cut, 140 of which had already been enacted and 200 of which were underway. The ministers who have managed to save money As the government pursues savings "across the board" ahead of the mid-year budget update, an ABC analysis shows only a handful of ministers have managed net savings so far this year. "These regulatory reforms span everything from telecommunications to energy to tax, and lots in between ... cumulatively, these changes will make a real difference," he said. The Business Council of Australia has been campaigning for a 25 per cent cut to the cost of complying with government regulation, which it said cost business billions each year. The federal opposition has taken up the 25 per cent target. While avoiding a specific target of its own, the government has promised streamlining in several areas. The ABC understands one such area to be featured in the mid-year budget will be the construction code, which has been subject to consultation with the industry. The government opposed the Liberals' proposal to slash the building code from about 2,000 pages to fewer than 100, but has promised to find other ways to streamline it. Another focus revealed by Mr Chalmers was on reducing tax compliance costs. He said he would consult on a "pre-filling" option for sole traders paying tax and scrapping complex assessments of fringe benefits below $300. He said these two measures could save businesses $52 million per year. Mr Chalmers also said the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) had paused sending controversial letters to business about their payment of super to employees. The Coalition had accused the ATO of "targeting" small businesses with the automated compliance letters, which alerted businesses when their payroll data did not match their employees' reported super contributions. In a statement yesterday, the ATO said the letters were not debt notices, but were designed to "nudge" businesses to look into possible discrepancies ahead of time, adding that super underpayment was a "serious problem". Mr Chalmers said it was a matter for the ATO, but that the government had reminded the agency that its "engagement with businesses needs to be respectful [and] constructive". "Now as I understand it, the ATO has now paused those letters as they improve those processes … The ATO's got a difficult and important job to do, we respect that … Part of that means having another look at these letters that have gone out," he said.

events.title: Cyber giant Infoblox confirms security incident after hackers access ‘company information’
events.summary: Cybersecurity and automation giant Infoblox has confirmed a cybersecurity incident, during which hackers accessed company information through one of its technology vendors. Infoblox is a privately held cyber giant that provides companies cybersecurity and networking services, such as domain name resolution and identity and user access management. In a statement, a spokesperson for Infoblox told TechCrunch that the company is “investigating a security event involving unauthorized access to certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor.” “We immediately activated our incident response procedures, took steps to contain the incident and are working with leading outside cybersecurity experts to investigate the facts, understand the scope and address any confirmed risks.” TechCrunch has learned that the data breach involves a vendor that provides SharePoint data migration services, according to a notification sent by Infoblox about the breach, two people with knowledge of the incident told TechCrunch. One of the people said sensitive customer data was taken in the breach. According to public internet records seen by TechCrunch, Infoblox hosts much of its files, emails, and infrastructure with Microsoft, including a SharePoint server, which TechCrunch confirmed is accessible through Infoblox’s single sign-on provider. SharePoint is web-based software that companies use to share and host internal files and documents. Infoblox has not named the third-party migration vendor that was hacked, but one person with knowledge of the incident said that Infoblox has terminated its work with the vendor. The company’s spokesperson did not comment on this, but added that the company has “no indication that any Infoblox products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved” in the breach. Infoblox would not say how many customers were affected by the incident, or if the company is aware at this time. The company also did not say, when asked, if it had been contacted by the hackers and if they had made any demands. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: All the questions Nvidia should answer on Tuesday — but probably won’t
events.summary: Nvidia interim CEO and longtime CFO Colette Kress is about to have one of the biggest days of her career on Tuesday when the company reports its third-quarter results. For the first time, Kress will be running through the numbers and sharing guidance without Nvidia’s charismatic but now-disgraced founder Jensen Huang. Huang was forced to resign last week after he admitted to having an affair with an exec of a customer, Alice Huang, a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, and he was accused of having two more affairs with Nvidia employees. Now, the company is facing questions about its restricted chips allegedly being smuggled into China, especially by Huang’s mistress’ company. Nvidia promised to conduct an internal investigation. Meanwhile, Huang was commanded to answer questions to Congress in a closed-door joint session with three Republican-led committees. Plus, top Democrats have also vowed to investigate the company. Given the turmoil Nvidia is in, there are a number of questions that Kress should answer. Huang’s role now and going forward. Huang ran Nvidia with an iron fist, having some 60 direct reports and his fingers in everything. No one knows the company better than him. An internet petition signed by 180,000 and growing is calling for the board to reinstate him. Huang may also have been mounting an attempt to return, Financial Times reported. However, CNBC is reporting, citing unnamed sources, that the company is not in talks to reinstate Huang. So, we’ll be looking for language from the interim CEO about Huang’s ongoing involvement with the company, its search for a new CEO, and any talks to bring him back. China and Singapore. As Huang vehemently argued in favor of easing export restrictions for Nvidia chips to China, Huang said that he’s seen no evidence that its powerful semiconductors were being diverted from legit buyers to China. But in October 2025, The New York Times reported that the U.S. was investigating Huang’s mistress’ company, Megaspeed, over allegations it was doing just that. Nvidia at the time vouched to CNBC that Megaspeed was legally using the chips for its cloud. However, Nvidia recently told The Wall Street Journal that it had voluntarily blocked Megaspeed from receiving more chips way back in June 2025. Last year, Nvidia said that Singapore, the region where Megaspeed is located, was one of its fastest-growing, accounting for 22% of its total revenue for its second quarter of that year. After the investigation into Megaspeed came to light, Nvidia changed how it reported revenue. It now reports based on a company’s headquarters, instead of its shipping address. That completely hid sales to Singapore and Megaspeed’s impact. So we’re listening to what Kress says about the future of sales to the China region and the cloud business in Singapore that was once 20% of sales. We’re especially listening for what she says about Nvidia keeping track of where its restricted chips wind up. China sales policy. Huang’s argument was, essentially, that the U.S. can’t stop China from developing advanced AI models, so the West is better off selling them less powerful Nvidia chips and keeping them dependent, he said on the Dwarkesh Podcast last summer. Notably, that’s a position that would make Nvidia a lot of money. The China hawks counter that selling an adversary any powerful chips at all will help them, and U.S. companies shouldn’t do that. So we’re listening for any indications that Kress is reversing Nvidia’s goals with China. Bankrolling the AI build-out. The expectation is that Kress, the CFO who reportedly had unsuccessfully tried to push back against Huang’s extreme AI dealmaking, will be conservative on such deals going forward. We’ll be listening for what she says about the impacts of existing deals on the books. (Will she subtly try to throw Huang under the bus for those controversial deals ?) We’ll also be listening for her future plans. Governance. With the ousting of Huang and more fallout sure still to come , has the board learned its lesson about too much power in the hands of one person? We’ll be listening for information about how Nvidia might restructure itself. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Customers report difficulty accessing online services at major US banks
events.summary: Bank of America, Chase, US Bank, Wells Fargo and Truist were listed by users who have been experiencing issues Customers reported service outages and difficulty accessing their online accounts at several major US banks and the money transfer service Zelle on Monday after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. Chase said the technical problems were not a systemic issue and were not the result of a cyber-attack, and that it was working to bring banking services back online. “Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” a Chase spokesperson said in a statement. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.” The disruption comes after a major outage by Microsoft that began on Thursday and lasted into the next day, which crippled a host of services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot. The outage had serious repercussions for millions of people and organizations all over the world, including schools, hospitals, businesses, courts, banks, prisons, police forces and governments. Microsoft said it had resolved the issue and restored service by Saturday, also issuing an apology. The office software giant did not attribute the blackout to a cybersecurity breach, identifying in an initial report on Monday that a combination of a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections, and server capacity sparked the outage. Also on Friday, ageing equipment led to a temporary grounding of all commercial airplanes in the US, sparking travel chaos as thousands of flights were delayed or canceled. The Trump administration later said the four-hour ground stop stemmed from routine maintenance. At a briefing on Saturday, US transportation secretary Sean Duffy said the outage began after “a contractor was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire … to fiber” and a newly installed router “started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system”. The FAA, he said, was still working to determine whether the fault was “incompetence” by the contractor, or “a faulty router”. Monday’s technical issues seem to center on Chase customers and customers at other banks trying to transact with Chase. Those banks, including Bank of America and Citigroup, were not having issues with their banking services. A spokesman for US Bank said its systems are not directly affected but that “clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.” Zelle, the peer-to-peer payment system that major US banks use to allow customers to send money near-instantly to friends and family, is owned by Arizona-based Early Warning Services, which in turn is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, US Bank and Wells Fargo . A spokesperson for Early Warning Services said the Zelle network was fully operational. “An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers,” they said. Some Chase customers received a message that said: “Some services aren’t available. We’re working on them. Please try back later.”

"Infoblox is investigating a security event involving unauthorized access to certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor,” a company spokesperson confirmed to The Register . According to sources, the compromised third-party data migration vendor had trusted access to Infoblox's SharePoint system, and the intruders used this vendor’s accounts and access to exfiltrate data directly from Microsoft SharePoint. This data included configuration information related to some customer's NIOS (Network Identity Operating System) deployments. These are saved snapshots of customers’ network data, such as DNS, DHCP configurations, Grid databases, and reporting logs, that can be used to fully recover the appliance or grid in case of a system failure or faulty upgrade. The intruders also stole employee data during the break-in. According to an email CEO Scott Harrell sent to employees, which The Register has seen, compromised employee details include financial information such as direct deposit details, contact info, dates of birth, and Social Security numbers for employees and dependents. Upon discovering the breach, Infoblox “immediately activated” its incident response procedures, and took steps to contain the incident, including hiring outside cybersecurity experts, the spokesperson said. “We have sent notifications about this security event and are providing support and guidance as appropriate,” the Infoblox spokesperson told us. “Based on our investigation to date, we have no indication that any Infoblox products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved. Our priority is to fully investigate and resolve this issue." Affected staff received a $100 "spot bonus" to buy password management services, and were warned to be "especially alert for phishing, vishing, fraud, or other suspicious communications." Infoblox also gave employees and their dependents free credit monitoring and identity protection for two years. Infoblox declined to answer our more detailed questions about the compromise, including the type of data exposed, and how many employees and customers might be affected. events.title: China's rare earth curbs put new emphasis on Latin American investment
events.summary: Latin America is seeking to become a viable destination for investment in critical minerals , as western governments seek alternative supplies to reduce dependency on Chinese imports. China is the dominant player in the global critical minerals supply chain. It holds a market share of 70 per cent or greater for 19 of 20 minerals listed as strategically important by the International Energy Agency, and accounts for about 90 per cent of global rare-earth processing. China imposed sweeping export controls on seven heavy rare earth elements in April 2025, before increasing that list in October. The IEA estimates those controls would cost $6.5 trillion in annual downstream production outside China if fully introduced. Beijing last week announced it was extending a pause on the curbs until January. "I think we're learning the hard way that we need to be more competitive in these environments," said Andrew Wilson, executive director at the Centre for International Private Enterprise. Mr Wilson spoke to The National on the sidelines of a critical minerals summit in Washington. Latin America and the Caribbean hold 38.3 per cent of global lithium reserves and 32.5 per cent of copper reserves, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. Experts argue this places Latin America as a key centre in supply diversification, with lithium demand expected to triple by 2040. The region also holds major shares of silver and graphite, well as other metals and speciality minerals used for advanced technologies, aerospace and defence. Foreign direct investment in the region is volatile, despite averaging 11 per cent in recent decades, according to the OECD. "The question is, how do we regain those markets, regain the security guarantees, the economic guarantees, without sacrificing standards, compliance, rule of law and otherwise?" Mr Wilson asked. "It's important for us to be pushing countries where we want to invest to up their game through our own leadership, our own corporate requirements, than it is to lose those opportunities to investors who cornered the market. But the region faces challenges including high financing costs, infrastructure gaps, skill constraints and trust with local stakeholders, according to the IEA's 2026 global critical minerals outlook. It only refines about 20 per cent of its mined output of key energy minerals, except for lithium. The IEA estimates if lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite and rare earths were refined locally and two-thirds of copper production were processed in the region, the economic value generated would increase by nearly 50 per cent from current levels and reach bout $220 billion by 2035, the IEA said. Gulf states are also been deepening their investment ties into the Americas. Abu Dhabi's ADQ and US-based investment firm Orion Resource Partners in January announced a joint venture to invest in companies in Latin America, Africa and Asia. US President Donald Trump 's administration also entered into bilateral preliminary agreements with Argentina and Peru in February. The UAE and Brazil signed a $2.5 billion preliminary agreement last year to explore and develop strategic minerals essential for the global energy transition. Brazil released a list of 27 critical and strategic minerals last week in an effort to boost investment and increase domestic processing. Copper, lithium, uranium and rare earths were among metals listed as a top priority for government support. The UAE and Argentina also began talks on a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in September, to increase investment access across mining and minerals, AI and other sectors. Saudi Arabia also signed non-binding agreements with Brazil and Chile during the Future Minerals Forum in Riyadh this year, as the kingdom looks to expand its international partnerships and investment co-operation in the mining and minerals sector.

events.title: California sues OpenAI over safety concerns after rogue agent hacking
events.summary: The lawsuit stems from an earlier incident where the tech company’s products hacked into the open-source platform Hugging Face California sued OpenAI on Monday, accusing the artificial intelligence titan of developing its technology without safety or the public’s interest in mind. The lawsuit concerns an incident earlier this year where OpenAI agents – semi-autonomous AI software that can carry out digital actions on behalf of users – launched a cyber-attack into the open-source AI platform Hugging Face. Rob Bonta, California’s attorney general, said the “infamous” attack was just one of 80 known incidents involving “loss of control” and shows that OpenAI doesn’t have adequate safeguards in place to protect society. “While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability,” Bonta said in a statement. The lawsuit, filed in state superior court in San Francisco, alleges OpenAI violated California’s Unfair Competition Law and is a public nuisance as defined by state law. Bonta is asking the court to order OpenAI to change its business practices and pay civil penalties. California’s lawsuit follows Bonta’s formal investigation into OpenAI, launched in September, over the Hugging Face incident, followed by a subpoena of the company probing other cybersecurity incidents and risks with its models. The Federal Trade Commission is also conducting an industry-wide investigation into OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI labs over the potential dangers their technology poses to consumers’ digital security. In July, OpenAI revealed that one of its autonomous AI agents went rogue during a test , accessing the open web and hacking into Hugging Face. The company called it an “unprecedented cyber-incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities”. Since then, several other incidents involving OpenAI have come to light, including a breach of government websites in Australia. Other AI firms, including Anthropic and Google, have also disclosed rogue agent activity . Drew Pusateri, a spokesperson for OpenAI, said the company has worked to create safeguards for its AI models, along with identifying and disclosing incidents of “misalignment”. He said most cases identified have been low severity with limited-to-no impact. “Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” Pusateri said. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab.” During a press conference, Bonta said OpenAI violated the law and that his suit is meant to ensure the company puts proper safeguards in place. He noted that the possibility exists for AI agents to hack into the power grid and medical and financial institutions. “These risks are no longer hypothetical,” Bonta said. “Without sufficient safeguards and controls, the scope and frequency of this already unacceptable risk will only increase.”

events.title: Fewer international students, billions at stake
events.summary: Fewer international students are enrolling at American universities, costing the American economy billions of dollars and hurting college towns. Why it matters: International students typically pay higher tuition than their American counterparts, helping offset financial challenges and support domestic students. Their absence could hit smaller colleges especially hard, with ripple effects for local economies and the workforce. Driving the news: New international student enrollment at U.S. colleges and universities fell 18% during the 2025–26 academic year, according to data released Monday by the Institute of International Education. Overall international enrollment dropped 3% to about 1.15 million students. International graduate student numbers fell 13%, compared to a 0.3% dip among undergraduates. However, doctoral enrollment rose 3%. Threat level: "For domestic enrollment, we're hitting the demographic cliff," Sarah Spreitzer, vice president and chief of staff for government relations at the American Council on Education, tells Axios. She pointed to fewer high school graduates and state budget cuts as extra financial pressures facing universities. "I think international students were used as one of the levers that you could pull to help address some of the budgetary issues." Domestic students could receive "less support," she said, although it's too soon to know whether that could mean higher tuition or fewer scholarships. By the numbers: International students contributed roughly $40 billion to the U.S. economy in 2025-2026, and those aren't just tuition dollars. Their spending on housing, food and transportation helped support over 300,000 jobs, per data released by NAFSA: Association of International Educators. That's down 7%, or $3 billion, compared to the 2024-2025 academic year, with 46,000 fewer jobs supported. It marks the second straight annual decline after three years of growth. Real estate developers in Boston told Spreitzer last year that declining international enrollment left apartments vacant and affected plans to build more student housing. Between the lines: Spreitzer attributes some of the declining enrollment to the Trump administration's immigration policies. International students "are trading horror stories about being stopped at the border," she says, adding that fears of being denied re-entry is too big of a risk. Eighty-eight percent of institutions reporting declining enrollment cited the visa application process, while 70% cited travel restrictions, per a separate IIE report . Zoom in: Smaller institutions, particularly in the Midwest and away from the coasts, may be experiencing much sharper declines than prestigious universities with stronger international name recognition. Spreitzer contrasted the potential experiences of elite institutions like Harvard with smaller liberal arts colleges that have relatively few international students. A school like Harvard has a massive endowment to help cushion the blow, but others are going to have to make sacrifices. Case in point: At the University of North Texas, the university is phasing out dozens of minors, cutting four master's programs and merging multiple departments to address a projected $45 million deficit. The university has among the highest numbers of international students in Texas, but the declining enrollment is substantially lowering revenue. The bottom line: Universities aren't just losing students for one semester. They're potentially losing years of enrollment, tuition revenue and future research talent. "If that student doesn't come this year, that means we've lost out on many years of their enrollment," Spreitzer says. "So this is going to have a cascading effect." events.title: Advocates dub midterms the ‘care election’
events.summary: This month’s midterms were the “care election,” according to a sweeping new report by Care Can’t Wait Action that was shared first with Semafor . The coalition points to its role in boosting turnout — citing nearly 24 million impressions via events, media and other outreach — as well as exit polling that found voters want the next Congress to focus on issues like paid leave and child care. “There’s this undeniable sense of momentum,” leader Ai-jen Poo told Semafor, adding that she is “looking to Congress to pass a whole set of bills that will address the entire care agenda, because I think voters are ready.” Seven in 10 voters said it’s important for Congress to pass a paid family and medical leave bill in the next six months, according to included polling by Lake Research for MomsRising Together and Paid Leave for All Action. Eight in 10 voters who are mothers said it was important to their vote that the federal government “immediately works to lower the cost of raising a family,” including by tackling child care. Nearly 8 in 10 voters said presidential candidates should make paid leave a top priority, according to separate post-election polling by Change Research. That includes 95% of Democrats and 69% of men. “Democrats won on these issues, and now they need to take action within the first 100 days of this new Congress,” Sondra Goldschein, executive director of the Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy, told Semafor. She called for lawmakers to “put them on the president’s desk, and then force him to decide whether he wants to veto.” GOP cuts to Medicaid funding helped mobilize “many first-time care-worker activists,” SEIU Executive Vice President Leslie Frane said. Advocates are hopeful the Trump administration agrees to repeal some of those cuts — but they’re not holding their breath on other issues. “When the time comes to be smart about making choices and tradeoffs, we will. But I think we’re really far from that time,” Poo said. “So this is a moment where we have the momentum to do big things, and there’s no reason why we should not.” Democrats had tried to enact paid leave and universal pre-K amid the pandemic , but fell short given their narrow Senate majority. Advocates are now optimistic that the latest wave of policymakers will see more success. “We have a whole crop of new leaders coming in with a clear mandate on these policies — and that was intentional,” Poo said. “That was a big lesson from Build Back Better, is that we need a whole different level of consensus.”
