events.title: Online bookmaker targets netball club for inducements, signs up 18yos
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NT Wagering Commission fines bookmaker $83k over Instagram inducements The scheme targeted a community football and netball club, with young women making up the majority of new sign-ups. ( AAP: Scott Barbour ) A bookmaker has been hit with a hefty fine over an inducement scheme targeting a community sporting club. The scheme saw about a dozen 18-year-olds sign up to bookmaker Amused Group's promotional offer. The NT-registered bookmaker has since collapsed into liquidation, owing an estimated $5 million to creditors. An Australian online bookmaker has been fined more than $83,000 after an inducement scheme targeting a community football and netball club drew in about a dozen 18-year-olds. It came after an official from the sports club uploaded an Instagram post announcing BetDeluxe as a new club sponsor offering a promotional deal to players who signed up with the company. The promotion, which promised new sign-ups access to $300 and other benefits, saw about 15 people create new accounts with BetDeluxe, an arm of Northern Territory-registered bookmaker Amused Group. More than 10 18-year-old women were among those found to have responded to the promotion. A sporting club official promoted the deal in a post on the club's Instagram page. ( Reuters: Thomas White ) In a decision last month by the online gambling regulator NT Wagering Commission, Amused Group was found to have been involved in "a sustained, employee-facilitated inducement scheme operating over several weeks" involving the club. A series of text messages between a senior Amused Group employee and the sporting club official who made the post were aired in the findings, although none of the people or the club were named. The texts showed that the gambling employee, cited as Mr R, "actively encouraged [the sporting club official] Mr K, to solicit further sign-ups from his personal network" over several weeks in 2025. "Can see a couple sign-ups so far, but not many have come through," read one text by Mr R. The NT Wagering Commission regulates online gambling in the NT, but is also Australia's de facto regulator for the sector. ( ABC News: Jasmine Hines ) The commission found the Instagram post uploaded by Mr K for the club was done without the knowledge of the gambling company, which then tried to get the post immediately removed once it became aware of it. "Under 1,000 views and we have avoided a major issue," Mr R told Mr K in a text. The post was also shared on Facebook groups and via private WhatsApp messages. The Facebook and Instagram posts were later deleted. New bill could restrict major gambling companies An independent politician is set to introduce a private member's bill to the NT parliament, which if passed would impose a string of new laws on some of Australia's largest online gambling companies. However, the commission rejected Amused Group's submission that the "conduct was not intentional" and ruled the post should have been detected by the company's "internal compliance controls". "[Amused Group's] persistence and the involvement of a senior employee place it materially above an administrative or technical failure," the decision read. The commission said the fact that between 10 and 15 "individuals at the lower end of the legal wagering age were among those that responded to the promotional arrangement" was a "matter of concern in context of the licensee's responsible gaming operations". The company was fined $83,250, which the commission said reflected the "serious and knowing character of the breach, the consumer harm that occurred, the aggravating and mitigating circumstance and the objectives of general and specific deterrence". The commission also found none of those who signed up "suffered any financial loss". Amused Group collapses, owing creditors millions Since the commission's decision was handed down, Amused Group has been placed under administration, with corporate documents showing the company owes millions to creditors. In a report released on November 13 by appointed administrator Costa Nicodemou, he said, "To date, I have identified 54 unsecured creditors with claims totalling $5 million". Mr Nicodemou's report said the unsecured creditors included "a number of racing bodies". Alastair Shields says Matchday is now operating Amused's former business and "has assumed responsibility for all client funds". ( ABC News: Matt Garrick ) NT Wagering Commission chair Alastair Shields told the ABC that "the wagering business previously operated by Amused Australia Pty Ltd is now being operated by another company, Matchday Entertainment Pty Ltd (Matchday)".

events.title: California state AG sues OpenAI over rogue agent incidents
events.summary: OpenAI is facing a new lawsuit from the California Attorney General’s office , alleging that the company’s training practices and lax security pose an ongoing danger to the public. At the center of the case is the July 2026 Hugging Face compromise , in which a pre-release model within OpenAI compromised both companies’ security systems to complete a training benchmark. In its official report on the incident , OpenAI called it “an outlier scenario involving a rare and unexpected confluence of events.” The California lawsuit represents one of the first attempts by a government regulator to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident, with significant implications for both OpenAI’s competitors and its clients. The complaint centers on the Hugging Face incident, but also cites similar incidents involving RubyGems , DseWiki , the Wikimedia Foundation , and Australian government websites as evidence that the underlying behavior is ongoing. The complaint also alleges that dozens of similar incidents have occurred without public disclosure. “OpenAI has recently sent notices to dozens of additional third parties whose websites or internal systems have been infiltrated by OpenAI agents,” the complaint reads. “In some cases, OpenAI agents were able to access sensitive personally identifiable information, such as employee records containing names, birth dates, addresses, and more. The vast majority of these incidents have not been disclosed or discussed publicly by either OpenAI or by the affected third parties.” The central allegation is that OpenAI’s ongoing testing practices constitute a public nuisance because the lack of safety controls present an ongoing risk to the public. A secondary claim alleges unfair competition stemming from the marketing of an unsafe product. If the lawsuit succeeds, OpenAI could face an injunction “to abate the ongoing public nuisance,” leaving broad discretion in the hands of the court. It’s the first regulatory case targeting OpenAI specifically over rogue agent incidents, although public endangerment claims have been considered by other states. In June, the Florida attorney general sued the company over allegedly harmful effects on users , particularly children and teenagers. In August, the Alabama attorney general launched a probe into deceptive practices related to the breach, but no case has been filed. In a statement to the press, California Attorney General Rob Bonta presented the case as an effort to maintain public safety in the face of a powerful new technology. “OpenAI’s actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society. The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it,” Bonta said in the statement. “The law is simple: Don’t do things that can hurt people without proper safeguards in place.” In a statement, OpenAI emphasized the company’s extensive effort to investigate the Hugging Face incident and improve its systems in the aftermath. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” OpenAI said. “We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.” Updated 12:23 p.m. PT: Added OpenAI statement. events.title: How the World’s Most Advanced AI Infrastructure Supply Chain Invents the Future
events.summary: Deb Shoquist leads operations at NVIDIA, overseeing the supply chain and manufacturing behind its AI platforms. That description sums up the job, but it doesn’t begin to encompass what Shoquist has made possible over decades. Shoquist, her team and their global network of manufacturing partners enable NVIDIA to introduce world-leading technologies year-round. Much of the team’s success comes down to her deep relationships with some of the world’s most accomplished manufacturers, including TSMC, Foxconn, Wistron, SPIL, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Unimicron, Lumentum, Coherent and Amkor. TSMC has partnered with NVIDIA since 1998. SPIL and KYEC were assembling and testing its chips more than two decades ago. For Shoquist, those relationships grow stronger through each challenge solved together on the factory floor, as every generation of technology demands more from the people and tools behind it. Ask her about the global network she relies on, and she starts with the people. There’s the supplier in Taiwan so eager to get production moving that he calls her at 3 a.m. with a fix to the latest problem. There are the factory workers in Vietnam whose only ask of her are more tools to get more work done. She remembers the partners that supported NVIDIA when it was small, and the work they’ve done to help each other grow. Shoquist meets with key suppliers quarterly and spends six weeks each year on the road visiting partners in Taiwan, China, Korea, Vietnam and the U.S., where conversations move from meeting rooms to factory floors. Recently, she paused her travels to accept the 2026 Dr. Lisa Su Woman of Innovation Award — and to share how she finds the right people and companies to imagine and produce at massive scale technology that has never been built before. Q: How would you describe your job to someone outside NVIDIA? A: At the most basic level, our job is to convert designs into the physical world. Our design team creates a blueprint, and our job is to transition it into a reliable, high-performance supply chain. A matchmaker is probably the best analogy. You have to find the partner that matches your ramp style and has the technology that can meet the needs of very precise designs. The supplier has to be financially strong enough to invest in our ramps. They have to be highly technical. And they have to be willing to do something that has never been done before. If you don’t have all three, you can’t create products at the volume and speed that we need. You need those three legs, and in some cases, if you only have two, you have to invest in the company to make them a partner. Q: What’s an example of that in practice ? A: Amphenol’s cable cartridge is the most complex interconnect assembly they have ever built. When I recently visited the Vietnam factory, now in full production, I was struck by the level of precision required to build a product of this complexity. In this large cable cartridge, there are 1,500 small cable legs. Each one requires a very precise assembly to yield a quality level of less than 1 DPPM, or defect part per million. Amphenol built over a hundred automated lines to produce this product at the speed and scale we require. That takes know-how and technology, but it also takes heart, willingness and dedication. Creating anything of that complexity and precision with a supplier forges the partnership. The partners NVIDIA maintains are the ones who supported us when we were small, and yet are willing to scale with us today. Q: What changed as NVIDIA went from selling chips to building systems and platforms? A: When we were primarily a chip manufacturer, we were small, and the semiconductor industry was at scale. In that environment, it was about picking the best technology match for the products we envisioned. As we became a data center systems company, we needed more partners. But we’ve also now entered into new technology areas where the scale of the supply base is still developing. For example, our optical component partners have the technology and the willingness, but they don’t yet have the scale or capital to build fabs for the volume we need. To grow, we needed to support and invest, like we did with Coherent and Lumentum . Beyond that, with products like CPO (co-packaged optics), we’re creating entirely new supply chains with scale partners that are new to the optics world. Leading the integration of talent across the supply chain is the key to driving this incredible technology to high volume quickly. Q: You clearly enjoy spending time with supply partners, and in particular on the factory floor. What have you learned there over time that can’t be learned anywhere else? A: Over 20 years, you meet many individuals key to the success of your supply. You meet not only the CEOs, but also the people that are running the production floor. These are the people that really know the problems of manufacturing. If you don’t have a tight working relationship with the people deeper in the organization, then it’s hard to have an open dialogue about any challenges. But when you have tight relationships, they want to help you, and they feel comfortable enough telling you, “I need better technical support on the floor. I need more quality engineers. We need a better design. We need to automate this. We need more buffers of material.” That’s what 20 years of working with our suppliers has taught us. It’s year after year of learning from people, getting to know people deeper in the organization and creating the trust where they can tell us what we need to do to be successful with them. Q: Demand for NVIDIA technology is already massive and growing. Your job is to make sure NVIDIA’s volume can keep up. How do you make it happen? A: It goes back to relationships. When you decide that you’re going to push a line hard to increase volume, you have to have the relationships. You have to know their processes in detail. You have to know their people in detail, and they have to trust you. Only then are you in a position to ask them for special favors, because you can do it surgically, and your ask is credible and reasonable. And when you’re successful together, they’re happy, you’re happy, and the appreciation for the partnership deepens. We all appreciate those that make us successful. Q: How do you prioritize resources across the supply chain? A: You need to first understand what the most critical components are, and protect and prioritize production around them. We need wafers like we need air. And the critical component is the TSMC chip. As it comes out of assembly every week, we decide what factory gets what chip. Every week, we look at factory performance. If a particular factory yield is low, if their time of ownership is not at the level we want, they don’t get more chips that week. We keep track of every chip, from the identification number on the die all the way to the customer invoice.

events.summary: Malware & Threats Cyberwarfare Cybercrime Data Breaches Fraud & Identity Theft Nation-State Ransomware Vulnerabilities Security Operations Threat Intelligence Incident Response Tracking & Law Enforcement Security Architecture Application Security Cloud Security Endpoint Security Identity & Access IoT Security Mobile & Wireless Network Security Risk Management Cyber Insurance Data Protection Privacy & Compliance Supply Chain Security CISO Strategy Cyber Insurance CISO Conversations CISO Forum ICS/OT Industrial Cybersecurity ICS Cybersecurity Conference Funding/M&A Cybersecurity Funding M&A Tracker Under the new rule, overseas data centers that serve companies in countries including China, Russia, Iran and Cuba are required to identify their end users. Flipboard Reddit Whatsapp Whatsapp Email The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best artificial intelligence models. The rule also was issued days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO amid scrutiny of his ties to a Chinese executive who used to lead Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. The company provides computing power to Chinese companies using chips housed in Southeast Asian data centers, including facilities in Malaysia. “The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the Bureau of Industry and Security under the Commerce Department said in issuing the rule that took effect immediately. Under the new rule, overseas data centers that serve companies in countries including China, Russia, Iran and Cuba are required to identify their end users. There also will be an additional, case-by-case licensing requirements for sales of chips for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil — countries that “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to unauthorized destinations, the rule says. The U.S. bans sales of the country’s most advanced AI chips to China, seeking to maintain an edge in its rivalry with China for predominance in artificial intelligence. However, many lawmakers and policymakers believe the country’s export control rules are not tough enough and filled with loopholes such as cloud computing that allow China to rent processing power built on American technology. Last year, U.S. Rep. Michael Lawler, a New York Republican, introduced a bill to broaden the U.S. export controls to include remote access. He told Congress “physical export controls” under current rules do not apply to remote access, allowing China to “access our tech through the cloud” and giving it “a real tool to sidestep” U.S. export restrictions. The bill has passed the House. Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading. events.title: Binance chief acknowledges hack ‘shouldn’t have happened’
events.summary: Binance co-CEO Richard Teng acknowledged Monday that the $6.3 billion hack his firm suffered — one which roiled cryptocurrency markets and raised existential questions about industry security — resulted from the company’s own failings. “It shouldn’t have happened,” Teng said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “This was a multi-month, sophisticated campaign,” he continued, referring to the attack, which the FBI has attributed to North Korea. (Pyongyang has denied involvement in the hack.) The hack raised questions about what is fundamentally the weakest link in most cybersecurity and business operations: humans themselves. Binance said that it was compromised in part because of a sophisticated phishing attempt that involved a Binance employee undergoing a fictitious interview process that resulted in “malicious software” being loaded onto a corporate machine, Teng noted. Teng also acknowledged Binance’s checkered reputation, involving billions in fines for anti-money laundering violations and the imprisonment of its primary shareholder and founder Changpeng Zhao. “We had really underinvested into the area of compliance,” Teng said. “Since the record fine and settlement, we have really invested a great deal.” Whether that investment is enough is an open question: The New York Times reported in September that Chinese firms continue to use Binance to launder illicit proceeds for the Iranian government . Binance, like most cryptocurrency firms, has also benefitted from a laissez-faire environment in Washington. A pro-crypto mentality adopted by the Trump administration has come up short of what many crypto executives had hoped for, but has still allowed for major regulatory wins for the industry. “We would have hoped that the Clarity [Act] would have passed,” Teng said. “We do hope there will be more transparency and visibility on that front moving forward.” Binance is a sponsor of Silicon Valley & The World. Richard Teng made his comments during Silicon Valley & The World’s partner session. — Rohan Goswami

events.title: Uber says hackers stole information on close to 150,000 driver’s licenses during data breach
events.summary: Uber is notifying close to 150,000 drivers that their personal and driver’s license information was stolen during an October data breach at one of the company’s tech providers. In notices filed this week with several U.S. attorneys general, including California and Iowa , the ride-hailing giant said it was notified on October 9 by the provider that hackers broke in and stole internal credentials, which were used to access Uber’s data. The company said it subsequently began notifying affected drivers that their personal information was stored with the provider. The stolen data includes affected drivers’ names, addresses, dates of birth, and driver’s license numbers. TechCrunch has learned that the provider is Fireworks AI, which lets developers access and use open-weight AI models. Fireworks reported a data breach last month in which hackers stole its customers’ information, including billing data and some private AI datasets. Online productivity startup Notion and AI coding startup Cursor have both confirmed that they had data stolen during the Fireworks hack. In Uber’s case, the company said it had alerts enabled to detect unauthorized access to its Fireworks environment, but because the hackers used Fireworks’ own internal credentials, “no alerts were triggered.” When reached for comment, an Uber spokesperson told TechCrunch: “The notices to drivers are in relation to a security incident impacting one of our third-party vendors, Fireworks.ai, which had access to some Uber data,” and deferred our questions to Fireworks. A spokesperson for Fireworks confirmed that the company identified a security issue involving unauthorized access to some of its systems, which affected customer data, but the spokesperson did not address our questions about the incident. Fireworks attributed its breach to a financially motivated cybercriminal group whose goals are to sell stolen tokens for accessing large language models, or LLMs. No known cybercriminal group has taken credit for the data theft. In a notice filed with Oregon’s attorney general, Uber said it notified 149,346 people in total that their information had been taken in the breach at Fireworks. TechCrunch previously reported that Uber has notified drivers in California, Illinois, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and South Carolina. We’ve also seen data breach notices filed in Texas and Vermont. When asked by TechCrunch, Uber’s spokesperson did not say how many drivers are affected by the breach, nor how many drivers it was notifying about the incident. It’s unclear if the number of affected drivers is expected to rise, and Uber did not respond to a follow-up email sent Monday. This is Uber’s second known data breach this year. The company reported a security incident at its Uber Freight truck shipping unit, for which an extortion gang took credit for stealing data. First published on November 13, and updated with a response from Fireworks, and again with a new updated figure of affected individuals from Oregon’s attorney general. events.title: Attackers are using AI agents to automate cybercrime at 'industrial scale,' FBI and AWS warn
events.summary: Attackers are using open source AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate their attacks on banks, governments, energy and healthcare providers, and other critical sectors around the globe, according to security alerts from the FBI and Amazon Threat Intelligence. Between October 3 and November 5, Amazon’s MadPot honeypot threat sensors detected two ARTEX campaigns: one that allowed thieves to steal AI credentials at “industrial scale” to gain free access to models, and a second that generated deepfake videos to trick live selfie checks. In the first one, miscreants used AI agents to steal API keys, and then feed these keys into the ARTEX framework’s model gateway to power more agents searching for more AI model access keys. “Agents validated identities through each provider’s token and identity services, enumerated storage, assessed permission scope, and went after managed AI model services, secrets and parameter stores, and application identities,” AWS Chief Information Security Officer CJ Moses wrote in a blog post on Friday. Targets included LLM gateways and proxy platforms such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, and LiteLLM, and AI application builders Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama. This campaign also used cloud credentials to gain stolen access to the models. In a second campaign, attackers used ARTEX to create real-time deepfake videos to trick identity verification (KYC) checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges, and forged ID photos to pass document checks. “The agents reverse-engineered one vendor’s liveness protocol in detail, documenting the face-detection event stream it sends, how it tracks face position during the check, and the coordinate system it uses to tell the user where to move,” Moses wrote. The agents did manage to complete the full movement sequence with the face positioned within 7 pixels of the target, but this feat was not enough, as the vendor’s server-side verdict rejected the deepfake in every attempt. In a separate session, agents built a real-time deepfake video pipeline on a single consumer-grade GPU using an open-source face animation model. This video achieved 11.5 frames per second, which Moses said is “close to what a live video check expects.” Meanwhile, agents also worked on the ID document checks, building synthetic camera metadata whose image dimensions matched the real values inside the JPEG file, and preserving the original camera compression tables that are usually replaced by re-saving an edited image. While the end goal was stealing cryptocurrency, the campaign illustrates how ARTEX runs several sessions simultaneously, with multiple agents working toward the same result. “One searched for ways to cash out, one worked on clearing account balances, one set up the deepfake video pipeline, and one carried out the verification bypass,” Moses wrote. None of the attack techniques are new, but both of these campaigns show how AI agents can boost the speed and persistence of the attacker. “The agents succeeded where basic security hygiene was missing, including default or hardcoded credentials, keys left in code and public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and inference endpoints, and unpatched software,” Moses added. “Getting those fundamentals right remains the most effective defense.” The FBI weighs in The FBI also hammered this message in a separate Friday alert noting “ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.” The federal cops cited the August attacks against South Korean financial institutions that stole personal data belonging to about 67,000 people. The FBI also highlighted a September ARTEX campaign that targetedd ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers in a supply chain attack that ultimately compromised more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft tenants . After these security breaches became public, the original ARTEX developer removed the GitHub repository in October. However, forked and localized variations plus a commercial version remain, and as of November 4 internet scanning service Censys identified 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console. And the total number of deploymentsis “likely significantly higher when including systems behind firewalls or in private networks,” according to the FBI. The feds urged all organizations – especially those operating internet-exposed applications, self-service portals, cloud infrastructure, and partner or supplier systems – to implement a series of mitigation measures outlined in its Flash alert. These include reducing external attack surfaces by restricting sensitive services to trusted networks, private connectivity, or dedicated administrative paths, and moving enterprise applications behind zero-trust access policies and permissions. ®

events.title: US moves to stop AI chip-smuggling amid push to reinstate Huang
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Donald Trump says Jensen Huang could return to Nvidia after 'spying' scandal US President Donald Trump says he would not mind if former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang returned to the company. Some Silicon Valley executives are pushing for Mr Huang's comeback just four days after his resignation. The Nvidia board and US authorities are investigating Mr Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Donald Trump says Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has "learned a big lesson" and he would "not mind" seeing the former CEO return to the helm of the AI juggernaut. The US president's comments add weight to a push to reinstate Mr Huang, just four days after his resignation amid fears he had been in a relationship with a Chinese spy. It comes as his administration moves to tighten controls on the export of Nvidia's highest-powered AI chips to prevent them being smuggled into China. SpaceX boss Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney are among the tech titans supporting the "Stand with Jensen" campaign. According to its official website, more than 185,000 names have been put to an open letter demanding the Nvidia board reinstate Mr Huang "pending an independent investigation and clear evidence that his removal serves the company". "He could return," Mr Trump told reporters at the White House as he prepared to depart for Asia to meet world leaders including Chinese President Xi Jinping and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese . "There's a big group of people that would like him to return," Mr Trump said. "I would certainly not mind seeing that." Just days after Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia, his supporters are urging him to return. ( Reuters: Mike Blake ) The Nvidia board has not publicly commented on the campaign, but the Financial Times (FT) reported it was not considering reinstating Mr Huang, citing people familiar with the matter. Similar reports appeared in the Washington Post and on the US business network CNBC. Earlier, the FT reported Mr Huang had discussed the possibility with confidants, and one Huang ally said a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives was being assembled to lobby for his return. The push has alarmed some national security experts and industry analysts, who have criticised Nvidia's alleged failures to comply with US export controls, which are designed to stop the company's most powerful AI chips from being sent to China. Several investigations will consider whether the chips were being smuggled into China by Singapore-based Megaspeed, the company linked to Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese asset with whom Mr Huang had a relationship. "We will see if Nvidia intentionally ignored the warning signs of these shell companies, many of them in Singapore," Mr Trump's treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, told Fox News on Sunday, local time. He said Nvidia needed a "dramatic shake-up" and should "go outside the company" in its search for a new leader. Chinese economic espionage is in the spotlight after the downfall of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, and former intelligence officials say the US is not doing enough to combat it. But Mr Trump said he did not believe Mr Huang had put national security at risk. Mr Trump and Mr Huang are known to be close. "It was not put at risk," Mr Trump said. "And, you know, China plays games with us and we play games with China." The Trump administration today said it would bring in new restrictions on the export of advanced AI chips. It means companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil will need to apply for licences to import the chips. Some experts want to see more done to prevent chip-smuggling. Congress is considering multiple bills to crack down on the practice. "The bigger problem illustrated by the Megaspeed case is that advanced AI chips are being smuggled into China and rented by Chinese companies in data centres abroad," Institute for AI Policy and Strategy senior researcher Erich Grunewald told the ABC. "I think the priority should be closing the gaps that allow Chinese companies to access advanced AI chips. "That means selling to trusted customers like US hyperscalers, rewarding whistleblowers who report smuggling, and restricting Chinese companies from renting advanced AI chips in data centres abroad.

events.title: Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser sees 'demand-side problem' for AI
events.summary: Recent jitters in the markets about AI represents a shift among investors towards becoming more selective about where they allocate their money, Jane Fraser, the CEO of Citigroup said Monday — and she’s not worried about it. “In a market priced to perfection, getting the air out of the tires is not a bad thing,” Fraser said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, adding that investors are absorbing huge amounts of change even over the past two weeks — the FAA shutdown, a high inflation reading, and the US midterm elections. “I’m hoping for a boring week,” she said. On the fallout of Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia, Fraser said she’s “not going to pile on” to the commentary, but that the company is in “very capable hands” with his successor, Colette Kress, which was met with applause in the room. Fraser told Semafor’s Liz Hoffman that she sees AI companies being “thoughtful about their capital stack,” and that it’s not terrible that any pullback is “a demand-side rather than a supply-side problem.” Partner with China Citi just recently got its China securities license and told rivals to “watch out.” The bank is prioritizing relationships in the country, Fraser said, while emphasizing the importance of a stable relationship, as well. Citi has been in China for 124 years, and Fraser said she’d work with Chinese companies if they are complementary to the bank’s client base. As for AI and China, she noted that the tech supports a more service-driven economy in the US, whereas in China, the focus is more about physical AI and robotics. “The two are very complementary,” she said. “There’s far too much for both sides to lose,” Fraser said. The sheer number of meetings between the countries’ presidents is unprecedented and can only mean “good things.” US President Donald Trump is meeting Chinese leader Xi Jinping in China this week. Fraser feels the bank is prepared for a Democratic-controlled Congress, as Citi has taken pains to de-risk and modernize. “We’ve put ourselves in a position for a global bank to operate and be a source of strength in choppy times rather than a source of problems.” The same goes for cybersecurity risk, said Fraser, adding that banks don’t compete on protecting against hacks and cyberattacks; they have collaborated to make sure the financial system is safe. “We’ve been in a window where we can do a lot of hardening,” she said. — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: A new James Bond has always been a chance to reinvent the series
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Sean Connery set the benchmark for the character of James Bond with his debut in Dr No. ( Supplied: MGM ) Into every generation, a James Bond is born. And with every new actor playing the British super spy, the franchise has had a reset. A new Bond typically means a new look, a new tone and a chance to reinvent the 64-year-old film series for a new audience, and catch up with new trends. It remains to be seen what the Robert Pattinson era will look like. But here's how the anointing of a new Bond has worked out for the series previously, and how the changing face of 007 provides an insight into the history of action movies. Sean Connery as James Bond in Dr. No. ( Supplied: IMDb ) The first Bond film, Dr. No (1962), created a new template for spy films. Its mix of humour, violence, sex and high-stakes action against a backdrop of world-shaping ramifications set the series apart. Until then, spy films tended to focus on the cloak-and-dagger spycraft, and tried to keep both feet grounded in reality. The big screen ambition of Dr. No was more akin to Alfred Hitchcock's groundbreaking North By Northwest (1959), where spectacle was preferable to plausible. Sean Connery was the original James Bond and, for many, the best. ( Supplied: MGM ) The Connery era of Bond quickly established the language of the films, such as the signature opening credits sequence, the dynamic score, the over-the-top villains with their over-the-top plans, the gadgets, the exotic settings, the highly questionable attitudes toward women, and the hero's mix of brawn, brains and babe magnetism. Dr. No hit big at the box office, and Sean Connery was a big part of that — it's said that the phrase "men want to be him, women want to be with him" emerged because of him. Within two years, a Bond parody was released (Carry On Spying), TV shows were aping the series (The Man From U.N.C.L.E.), and homages like Our Man Flint were in production. Connery and co pumped out four films in four years, some of which are among the best and most successful movies of the series, notably Goldfinger (1964) and Thunderball (1965). When Connery stepped aside after five films, George Lazenby took over for one ill-fated turn (On Her Majesty's Secret Service, 1969), which wasn't much of a reset, but more of a misfire. Australian actor George Lazenby made just one appearance as James Bond. ( Supplied: MGM ) Truckloads of money were thrown at Connery to ensure his return, and he re-teamed one last time with Goldfinger director Guy Hamilton for Diamonds Are Forever (1971). But the magic was gone and something needed to change. Roger Moore starred as Bond in the most films, clocking up seven outings as 007. ( Supplied: MGM ) Just two years after Connery's Diamonds Are Forever, Roger Moore picked up the Walther PPK for Live And Let Die (1973). It is one of the best of the series, helped in no small part by Moore's ability to effortlessly slip into the role of Bond. But as with Diamonds Are Forever, there are a few too many corny one-liners — a script tic that would come to be associated with Moore's stint as 007. By Moore's second outing (1974's The Man With The Golden Gun), outside influences had started to creep into the series, which had previously defined itself as a trendsetter, not a follower. Roger Moore was the third actor to play James Bond in the official 007 films. ( Supplied: MGM ) The recent death of Bruce Lee and a rising interest in martial arts meant some cheesy Hollywood-style kung fu made an appearance, and this would not be the last example of Zeitgeist-chasing in the franchise. In 1977, a little film called Star Wars became the biggest movie of all time, and everyone in Hollywood took notice, including the producers of the Bond franchise. In response, 007 was launched into space in 1979 for Moonraker, the nadir of the franchise. It was the biggest box office earner of the Moore era, but many critics were unkind, and opinions cooled even further as time went on. Moonraker was cited as the kind of film Mike Myers was thinking of when he created the Austin Powers series. Moore and co would redeem themselves with For Your Eyes Only (1981), but after Moonraker, the franchise endured a steady decline at the box office. By the time Moore bowed out with A View to a Kill in 1985, questions were being asked about where Bond fit in the world of 80s action. Timothy Dalton took over from long-running James Bond actor Roger Moore.

events.title: HTML-in-Canvas ships and could make the web a lot more creative...and a lot stupider
events.summary: After two years of experimentation, the Chrome team shipped the HTML-in-Canvas API with Chrome 157. With it comes a new vision of how Web pages could be designed, for better or worse, allowing richer, more interactive elements but also more opportunities for annoying ads. “Previously, when creating visually demanding web apps, you had to choose between standard HTML elements and raw canvas contexts,” enthused one Google DevRel in a tutorial . “HTML-in-Canvas eliminates these trade-offs.” The Web API has been submitted for inclusion in the WHATWG HTML Living Standard , the ever-updating standard formerly known as HTML5 – for all the technologies that officially make up HTML (including Canvas itself). A Web API for the browser’s rendering engine Originally developed by Apple and standardized in 2014, the canvas tag is an HTML element that offers a space to render fluid graphics via JavaScript drawing commands. It creates a dedicated grid on screen, within which JavaScript can use a set of Canvas methods to draw lines, curves, text, gradients, and images. Or, the user’s GPU, via WebGL or WebGPU, can use the canvas to render 3D images and other custom effects. The downside of Canvas is that the regular HTML controls didn’t work inside the canvas itself. Formatting any text had to be done by hand. Interactivity was out, as were accessibility aids. Primarily developed by the Google Chromium team, HTML-in-Canvas allows JavaScript to place HTML commands within the canvas element, thanks to an attribute option within Canvas. If the canvas tag includes a content attribute of "drawable," the browser’s rendering engine prepares the HTML content inside the box so JavaScript can render it. While fully supported by Chrome and Chrome Android beginning with release 157, none of the other major browsers support the API yet (Microsoft Edge 157 – which is made of Chromium – unofficially appears to support at least some HTML-in-Canvas actions as well). The Web’s about to get lit Google posted a few possibilities of what can be done with HTML-in-Canvas. Developers can wrap HTML controls onto a 3D object. In one example , the user can turn the pages of a virtual book and even copy text out of the book itself. A video, complete with a set of controls , can be wrapped into an odd-sized canvas. The spec seems to work particularly well with JavaScript plug-ins, allowing coders to create entire 3D environments with Three.js , or to create charts with D3.js . Enthusiasts are already hacking against the spec with mad abandon. Developer Wes Bos put a notes app in the canvas , then used it as target practice by overlaying the app with some Duck Hunt-styled game code. HTML-in-Canvas “opens up the door to a lot of stupid use cases … but also a lot of really creative, interesting things where you can apply stylistic effects to HTML,” Bos explained on X . A trippy demo from html-in-canvas.dev shows a dragon slithering through the opening chapter of an online book, with the text smoothly reflowing in its wake. Try to shoo the beast off with your cursor and it will burn the virtual text with its fiery breath. The source code reveals that “Margin Dragon” was rendered in 881 lines of vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript code. Another demo on the sample site is a “mouse-driven elastic displacement effect,” in which a “radial bulge” and drop shadow follow the cursor across the canvas. Of course, such stylistic enchantments will not always be used for whimsy. Inevitably, unscrupulous marketers will discover powerful new ways to annoy us about all the virtues of late-stage capitalism. “The world is not ready for HTML-in-Canvas,” a punter wrote on X . Here be dragons As per norm, HTML-in-Canvas has plenty of bugs (and it hasn’t even gone cross-platform yet). In some cases, the CSS doesn’t get painted on where it should , and timing with the reactive frameworks could be better synchronized . And there is a lot for the lowly web maintainer to learn. The core developers resolved the issue of canvas copying sensitive cross-origin data where it oughtn’t (as per CORS ), but the API does not indicate when it declines to copy the data, leaving the community to file bug reports of what appear to be silent failures. Likewise, developers must learn to properly document on-screen bounding boxes to keep accessibility tools like screen readers and click targets operating properly in 3D environments. ®

events.title: What we know about what caused the FAA's nationwide ground stop
events.summary: A newly installed router is at the center of the investigation into the Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop last Friday, which disrupted thousands of flights nationwide. Why it matters: The technical failure exposes vulnerabilities in the FAA's aging telecommunications network, raising questions about how a technical failure could trigger a nationwide ground stop and disrupt air travel. Catch up quick: More than 12,000 flights were canceled Friday after the telecommunications failure, the FAA said , with thousands more delayed. "I do think the worst is behind us, but we still do have a significant amount of recovery work to do," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Sunday. Read more below. What caused the nationwide groundstop? What they're saying: The FAA says its network was flooded with data "at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds," causing "instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds." Investigators tracked the data traffic surge to two possible locations — a radio communications facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, and a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, per the Wall Street Journal . The FAA says its network service provider, L3Harris , has been deploying a new router at the Arkansas facility, which is why it's under investigation for potentially disrupting flights nationwide. After L3Harris blocked network traffic from both facilities, the system stabilized, allowing normal flight operations to eventually resume, per the FAA. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," the company said in a statement. How did a router disrupt flights nationwide? How it works: Air traffic controllers speak with pilots over radio frequencies and receive radar information used to track aircraft. The network connects air traffic control facilities and carries communications and radar information that controllers need to safely manage aircraft. A router directs data traffic across a network. Any disruption could send swaths of data across the system, potentially disrupting communications. The FAA says a massive surge of data may have overwhelmed the old equipment, disrupting aircraft communications and radar feeds. The disruption reportedly impacted more than half of the FAA's 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which primarily handle high-altitude flights. What to know about radio frequency outages One symptom of the wider network instability: radio frequency disruptions. Some reports described this as a " rolling frequency outage ," where disruptions affect different radio frequencies and plane-monitoring facilities at the same time. This could cause planes to lose contact with the air control centers. Reality check: Losing contact with air traffic controllers can complicate the instructions pilots rely on to navigate crowded airspace safely. It doesn't mean they're flying completely in the dark, but it can make air travel and airspace management messy. What happens to pilots during the outages? Zoom in: The FAA normally has backup systems and procedures designed to keep communications going when radio frequencies fail. These include backup radio transmitters and receivers at air traffic control centers, per the FAA's Aeronautical Information Manual . The FAA says switching to a backup radio system seldom takes more than 60 seconds during a typical frequency outage. Pilots who lose communication with their controllers can also try to reach controllers through alternative frequencies or by contacting specific facilities. Yes, but: Backup systems don't eliminate the safety concerns posed by widespread communications failures, particularly when multiple air traffic control facilities are affected. What does this mean for flights? Zoom out: The nationwide ground stop ended Friday after massive flight delays and cancellations, but airlines have continued to experience schedule disruptions. Departing flights were grounded for several hours, with about 3,500 aircraft already in the air landing safely, per reports. Delays and cancellations continued as airlines worked to reposition crews, staff and aircraft. What's next: The FAA says it will investigate the cause of the disruption with L3Harris. The agency says it has disabled the relevant broadcasting function on about 60 similar routers to prevent another disruption.

events.title: Apple adds ‘face unlock’ to the iPhone Duo, but it’s not Face ID
events.summary: One of the top complaints from tech reviewers about Apple’s new foldable, the iPhone Duo, has been its reliance on Touch ID, a technology that’s been largely replaced by Face ID across the company’s iPhone lineup. With Monday’s release of iOS 27.3 beta for developers, Apple is addressing that complaint with a new “face unlock” feature that lets iPhone Duo users unlock their phones using the front camera, rather than waiting for a future hardware upgrade. To be clear, this feature is not Face ID. Due to hardware constraints, the iPhone Duo shipped without support for Face ID technology primarily because its thin, foldable design doesn’t offer enough space for the TrueDepth sensor array that Face ID requires. A recent report from Bloomberg suggests that the company is working to change that in a future version of the iPhone Duo. In the meantime, the Duo uses Touch ID for unlocking, authentication, and Apple Pay. The new face unlock feature, however, will allow users to quickly unlock the device using the front camera when the phone is closed. It only works if users have recently authenticated with Touch ID or a passcode. Apple notes that Apple Pay and passwords will still require Touch ID, and users will have to authenticate with Touch ID again after 45 minutes of inactivity. The move is meant to make it easier for people to use the Duo in the way they’re accustomed to, after years of unlocking an iPhone just by looking at it. Apple isn’t going so far as to allow face unlock to work across the entire device, though, because the technology isn’t as secure as Face ID. The latter uses Apple’s TrueDepth 3D sensing hardware, which includes a flood illuminator and a dot projector that casts over 30,000 invisible infrared dots onto the user’s face to build a unique 3D map of the face. The system combines this map with attention-awareness checks, making it resistant to attempts to fool it with photos or other 2D images. The software update addresses another complaint by incorporating one of the “hacks” iPhone Duo early adopters were using to force their phone to lock when they shut it. That involved creating a shortcut that would automatically run when the phone was closed. Now, Apple says users can enable this feature directly in Settings, under Display and Brightness. Alongside the software update, Apple announced that more than 200,000 apps are now optimized for the iPhone Duo, up from over 100,000 earlier this month . Other new features in this latest software release include an option to ask Siri questions about the content of a web page, even portions that aren’t visible without scrolling. Apple is also introducing video podcasts in Apple Podcasts in the Apple TV app, catching up with rivals like YouTube and Spotify. Apple is also expanding access to Apple News puzzles for News+ subscribers in Australia, the U.K., and for French-Canadian users. Australian News+ subscribers will get access to a daily quick crossword, crossword mini, and Sudoku, as well as Apple’s original puzzles, Quartiles and Emoji Game . U.K. users will get the quick crossword, the crossword mini, and Sudoku, while French-Canadian subscribers will get access to Apple’s original puzzles. The iOS 27.3 software update is currently available to developers and will soon arrive for public beta testers. It will roll out more broadly to all users after further testing is complete. events.title: SCOTUS gives DEI a boost after national assault
events.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear three conservative appeals tied to battles over diversity, equity and inclusion , leaving lower-court rulings intact in disputes over federal research grants, medical training and transgender-related speech. The big picture: The denials mark a reprieve after years of backlash against DEI, though the justices stopped short of settling the underlying constitutional debates. One of those Monday decisions set back President Trump's administration push to cancel swaths of DEI-related research grants. Driving the news: The justices rejected President Trump's bid to revive cuts to federal research grants awarded to University of California researchers over their perceived DEI-related viewpoints. A U.S. Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals panel ruled in May that challengers were likely to succeed on their First Amendment claim that their grants were terminated because of the "perceived expression of DEI, DEIA, or environmental justice viewpoints." That decision partly upheld a preliminary injunction from U.S. District Judge Rita Lin reinstating grants terminated over perceived DEI-related viewpoint, while reversing relief for a separate group. What they're saying: Trump's DOJ argued to the high court that allowing the grants to continue would force taxpayers to fund ideologies "their public stewards reject." A DOJ spokesperson told Axios the department will continue fighting the preliminary injunction and "will continue to advocate for the Executive Branch's lawful authority to administer federal funding programs and for the termination of taxpayer-funded DEI initiatives." Catch up quick: The challenged funding represents just a slice of the DEI-related grants ensnared in the administration's terminations and ensuing litigation. Trump has led a top-down campaign to undermine federal and corporate DEI efforts, disputes over state policies have also crept onto the national stage. Case in point: The Supreme Court also declined to hear a challenge from the anti-trans Gays Against Groomers against Colorado lawmakers' restrictions on misgendering and deadnaming during legislative hearings. The Tenth Circuit had found lawmakers were shielded by legislative immunity. Meanwhile: The justices also declined to hear a challenge to required implicit bias training for California continuing medical education courses. Justice Neil Gorsuch indicated he would've heard the appeal brought by an ophthalmologist and a conservative medical advocacy group. Justice Clarence Thomas penned a dissent, joined by Justice Samuel Alito. Thomas' argument indicates there may be an appetite for a similar question about government speech in the future: "A State cannot regulate its way out of First Amendment scrutiny," he wrote. What we're watching: Both in the courts and in the public arena , disputes over the federal administration and state leaders' handling of DEI initiatives are still playing out with many more sure to come. But on Monday, a high court that hasn't always sided with DEI initiatives declined to further some key debates — for now. Go deeper: Trump says he "ended DEI." Courts disagree

events.title: How Milburn won over Labour on tackling rising youth unemployment
events.summary: Labour grandee seems to have assuaged MPs’ nerves on need for welfare reform to tackle youth unemployment crisis In a boxing gym in Peterborough almost a year ago, Alan Milburn, freshly appointed to run a government review into the nearly 1 million young people out of work and education, said he would be “unafraid to shine a light on uncomfortable truths”. The Labour grandee, who held three cabinet jobs under Tony Blair, warned there was a “downward escalator” taking young people into a “world of benefits” and vowed to provide radical solutions. Many Labour MPs bristled. Just six months earlier, they had mounted a successful rebellion to kill off the government’s planned £5bn cuts to health and disability benefits, significantly damaging Keir Starmer’s political authority by forcing him into a U-turn on his flagship welfare bill. That day in the gym, Milburn knew he would have to win over a party suspicious of his motives and anxious about the impact of changes on vulnerable people, even if some acknowledged that the growing welfare bill was unsustainable. On the eve of publishing his report on Tuesday, early signs are that he has assuaged backbench nerves, succeeding where Starmer failed in moving the Overton window within the Labour party on the welfare debate around young people. Milburn’s strategy was clear from the off: make the moral argument for change, make it loudly and make it often. His favourite – and oft-repeated – statistic has been that the government spends 25 times as much on benefits for young people as it does on supporting them into work. In a series of interviews and MP engagement sessions over the following months, he described the projections – that numbers could reach 1.25 million by the early 2030s without major intervention – as a “national failure” that would result in a “catastrophic” generational fault line. After his interim report in May, he gradually signalled that overhauling health and disability benefits for young people would be a central outcome of his review, suggesting the welfare system in its current form had failed them and was exacerbating inactivity. Labour MPs were given time to get used to the idea and to air the arguments in public, with controversial elements of the report released early – the abolition of health benefits for under-25s, including existing claimants, among them. “Alan didn’t want any nasty surprises,” said one government source. “He wanted to engage fully with MPs and charities and anybody else with concerns. The government can’t move forward on this unless it’s able to bring people with them.” He had several factors working in his favour. As his days in No 10 ran out, Starmer was so weakened that Milburn was able to “bulldoze” Downing Street into supporting his proposals, according to another source, especially as Pat McFadden, the welfare secretary, was already onboard. Secondly, several of the leading figures in the welfare rebellion were now inside government – most notably Louise Haigh, who is now Andy Burnham’s number two, and Anneliese Midgley, the chief whip. Meg Hillier, the moderate chair of the Treasury select committee who had fronted that rebellion, last week indicated the proposals should get a “fair wind”, although she also acknowledged the difficulty of the choices ahead. Thirdly, the drip-drip of pitch-rolling came alongside a wider sense of alarm in the UK over the prospects of the next generation, amid concerns over rising mental ill health, social media and AI upending the jobs market. Burnham has said he wants to cut the welfare bill “as soon as we possibly can” but has warned against “crude cuts” (which the government would struggle to get past Labour MPs anyway) in the push for “sustainable” employment. His approach has echoes of Tony Blair, who talked of “a hand up, not a hand out”, actively pursuing a policy of reforming and investing in welfare specifically to bring down what he termed the “bills of social failure”. The big difference now is that the fiscal backdrop is more challenging, though Milburn will recommend that ministers spend hundreds of millions on back-to-work support in the short term in return for welfare savings, increased tax receipts and a fairer, happier country over the long term. The rather clunky symbolism of choosing a boxing gym for his first promotional visit last year wasn’t lost on anybody. Since then, Milburn – a former chair of the Social Mobility Commission – has been clear this is a fight he thinks the government needs to have. His recommendations, along with those from the Timms review into health and disability benefits, which will be published in the coming weeks, will form the basis of a white paper next spring that will then become a new welfare bill, voted on by Labour MPs. So, for now, the campaign to win them over continues. Standing alongside Milburn at a meeting of the parliamentary party on Monday night, McFadden said: “What is proposed is a new settlement for young people.

events.title: Amazon vows to fight the company's first North American union contract at a Canadian warehouse
events.summary: Hundreds of Amazon workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, are now being covered by a union contract, marking the company’s first site in North America under a collective bargaining agreement NEW YORK -- Hundreds of Amazon workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, are now being covered by a union contract, marking the company's first site in North America under a collective bargaining agreement. The terms of the contract, which is set to run until Nov. 13, 2029, were imposed by an independent arbitrator between Canadian union Unifor and Amazon. Amazon said the facility employs more than 700 workers. In a statement on Friday, Unifor's National President Lana Payne praised the workers who "stood up to one of the most powerful companies on earth and won rights in writing that Amazon cannot take away.” But the Seattle-based online giant argued that the arbitrator set the terms without giving its workers “the chance to ratify or vote on it." It also said that the terms were imposed despite a pending effort by some of Amazon's employees to decertify the union. Amazon said in a blog posted late Friday that the agreement sets terms for wages, scheduling, layoffs, and benefits that are largely similar to what the workers had already. Amazon said the contract requires every employee in the unit to join the union, whether they want to or not, and to have union dues of up to C$1,064 ($744.03 US) deducted from their pay in the first year. That means they could actually take home less money than they did before, Amazon said. “We believe that this process was improper, unfair, and defies common sense,” J. Ofori Agboka, Amazon's vice president of people, wrote in the blog post. Army airstrike kills at least 13 in West Kordofan, says rights group Gunman found dead after 2 public safety officers are shot at New York City apartment complex Paraguay’s ousted president moved to military prison after reports of gym and suite in custody Unifor and Amazon have been locked in a fight since 2024 when employees at the facility started an organizing drive. In July 2025, the British Labour Relations Board certified the worker union for the warehouse through a rare process called “remedial certification” after it found that Amazon committed unfair labor practices including what it described as an unnecessary hiring spree to stop the certification process. The regulatory board said in its decision that Amazon pursued a “lengthy and pervasive anti-union campaign." Amazon had filed an appeal. Remedial certification is used when an employer pursues unfair labor practices during an organizing drive that makes a fair vote unlikely. Amazon said that it has filed a request for judicial review in the British Columbia Supreme Court, asking to halt implementation of the collective agreement until its decertification application is resolved and to overturn the board’s order imposing a contract through arbitration. “We think the best workplace is one where associates have direct input and we work together to make progress quickly, and where nobody should have to pay dues or go through a third party to be heard,” Amazon's Agboka said. In 2022, Amazon workers in Staten Island, New York, voted to unionize, marking the first successful U.S. organizing effort in the retail giant’s history. The workers were represented by Amazon Labor Union, which affiliated with the International Brotherhood of Teamsters two years later. But workers don't have a contract yet, with the National Labor Relations Board ordering Amazon to negotiate and Amazon continuing to fight the union certification in court. events.title: Trump says ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy did not threaten national security
events.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he does not believe the country’s national security was put at risk as a result of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. “It was not put at risk,” Trump said when asked by reporters in light of his own friendship with Huang. “Our country is now stronger than ever before. And you know, China plays games with us, and we play games with China.” Trump went on to contradict previous findings from U.S. officials by doubting that Huang’s paramour, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy. “He probably shouldn’t have been doing on a personal basis what he did … That’s a different story,” Trump added. “But nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy.” Last year, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly oversaw the production of an internal memo, circulated among top policymakers, which warned that Alice Huang was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. Trump was reportedly briefed about these intelligence findings at least twice, including once in May aboard Air Force One, shortly before the former Nvidia CEO joined him on a trip to China. But Trump has maintained that he was not aware of these claims. The U.S. regulates the exports of Nvidia’s top chips to China as a way of maintaining a competitive advantage. But prior to news of Huang’s affair publicly emerging, both the U.S. and Singaporean governments had been investigating Megaspeed for illegally smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Huang has since stepped down from the role he has had for 33 years at Nvidia after more reporting revealed that he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees, at least one of whom was a direct report. Given Huang’s importance to Nvidia, some prominent figures in the industry — including Elon Musk, Y Combinator president and CEO Garry Tan, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney — have signed a public letter calling for Nvidia to reinstate Huang. “A lot of people are asking Jensen — they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea,” Trump said. Referring to the former Apple chief executive, Trump added: “I recommended Tim Cook.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: US won’t restrict foreign tech companies in allied countries, State Dept. official says
events.summary: The US government has “no plans” to target or “orchestrate the deep pruning” of technology companies headquartered in allied countries from American supply chains, Undersecretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg said Monday. Speaking alongside ASML’s President and CEO Christophe Fouquet at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, Helberg rejected “top-down government-mandated plans that intentionally discriminate” against companies based on their country of origin in comments to Semafor’s Ashley Gold. He named ASML, Samsung, and SK Hynix as key partners to US firms in the technology supply chain. Discussing Pax Silica, a US-led initiative to secure AI and semiconductor supply chains, Helberg said that the Trump administration wants to ensure companies across allied economies benefit from a “level playing field.” He described the initiative as a “capability-centric coalition” that draws on the comparative strength of participating countries. Helberg also argued that Washington must balance technological leadership with global market share of AI-focused companies, warning that innovation alone will not secure America’s dominance in the fast-growing technology field. “We need both in order to win the AI race,” Helberg said. “We need to lead the world qualitatively and have the best innovation out there. But we also need market share, and those two things need to happen in conjunction.” Helberg also stopped short of endorsing three bipartisan bills that lawmakers are considering including in the year-end defense bill that would tighten AI chip export controls following the Nvidia controversy. Asked about the investigation involving Nvidia, Helberg described the company as critical to US technological leadership, saying “there is a really compelling argument for national security to have Nvidia continue to be a leading beacon of innovation.” He called for investigations to establish the facts quickly, adding, “Our hope is obviously to see serious work being done through the investigations to uncover the facts and get to the truth quickly in order to get to the right outcome.” Nvidia has attracted scrutiny from Congress as well as the administration amid revelations that now-former CEO Jensen Huang had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. — Lauren Morganbesser

events.title: China’s grip on Top500 remains uncontested as US chases AI-HPC fusion
events.summary: A new Top500 list of supercomputers has dropped, but little has changed. China remains uncontested with the most powerful supercomputer on the biannual ranking, and the US is not even close behind. The Middle Kingdom's LineShine super tops the list, boasting 2.2 exaFLOPS as measured by the High Performance Linpack (HPL) benchmark. That's roughly 22 percent ahead of Uncle Sam’s biggest iron, Laurence Livermore National Laboratory’s El Capitan . But LineShine may not be the most efficient. Using 42.2 megawatts, LineShine’s lead comes at the expense of a noticeably higher power bill; not that that makes much of a difference. Number one is number one, and to add insult to injury, the National Supercomputing Centre in Shenzhen (NSCS) did it in spite of US export controls denying them access to American GPUs. The entire super is powered by 45,360 LingKun LX2 CPUs , each with 304 Arm v9.2 cores clocking to 1.5 GHz. The US is unlikely to reclaim the number one spot any time soon, though not for lack of trying. Under the Genesis Mission announced late last year, the Department of Energy is on track to deploy at least nine new supers. It just so happens that most of these will be smaller or AI-focused machines, with few truly large systems. Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s (ORNL) Lux supercomputer , built in collaboration with HPE and AMD, is one such example. Delivering 220 petaFLOPS of double-precision grunt in HPL, it’s certainly a potent system. Just two years ago it would have been a top 10 supercomputer, but it''l have to settle for number 14 on this fall’s Top500 ranking. Now, if you’re willing to turn the resolution slider down to FP4, peak performance jumps to somewhere north of 20 exaFLOPS. That’s fine for AI inference and even some training, but for running multi-physics sims on America's nuclear deterrent, the DoE has traditionally gone for something a bit bigger. ORNL’s upcoming Discovery system will certainly have enough grunt to give LineShine the boot. Details on the HPE Cray based system remain thin, but we do know it’ll be powered by a combination of AMD Venice CPUs and Instinct MI430X GPUs. Unlike most of the GPUs sold today, the MI430X hasn’t forsaken double-precision grunt for low-precision AI throughput. Each of these multi-die chips is estimated to deliver north of 200 teraFLOPS of FP64 matrix math. According to the DoE, Discovery will deliver somewhere between 3x to 5x the performance of Frontier, which would put its Rpeak somewhere between 5.1 and 8.5 exaFLOPS at FP64. As impressive as that might sound, China has proven that once you take power out of the equation, all it takes to claim the number one spot is scale. And if there is one thing LineShine does well, it’s scale. In GPU-accelerated systems like El Cap, you’re lucky to push HPL to within 70 percent of the system’s theoretical roofline. But LineShine isn’t GPU-accelerated. Sure, with 16 HBM stacks, the LX2 looks a lot like a GPU, but it's really just an enormous CPU with enough vector and matrix units to put more than a few modern GPUs to shame. With enough of them – by which we mean 22,680 dual-socket nodes – NSCS catapulted China to the top of the Top500 for the first time in nearly a decade. Not the benchmark it used to be The US has no shortage of systems capable of eclipsing El Capitan or even LineShine’s performance if someone were motivated enough to get HPL running on them. SpaceXAI’s 300 megawatt Colossus supercomputer in Memphis, Tennessee, boasts 200,000 Hopper GPUs each good for 34-67 (vector/matrix) teraFLOPS of FP64 grunt. Even assuming an abysmal 25% efficiency, the cluster should be more than capable of breaking three exaFLOPs in HPL. It might need 10x the power of El Capitan, but the thing is, beyond winning points with the White House — a ship that has almost certainly sailed for Elon Musk after the DOGE fiasco — renting out the cluster to Anthropic to train and run Claude is a far more lucrative endeavor. The same could be said of any number of AI clusters, from Meta’s Prometheus to OpenAI’s Starship. It used to be that the systems to summit the Top500 were among the largest computers humanity has ever built. But this hasn’t been true in some time. The US is starving for compute. HPL or even its sibling High-Performance Gradient Conjugate just aren’t the benchmarks to beat any longer. The new battleground isn’t nuclear proliferation; it’s one of AI models, agents, and the means to harness them. We’re not talking about tokens, LLMs, or chatbots, but the ability to harness these models to automate laboratories and formulate and test hypotheses long after the scientists they serve have gone home for dinner. It’s why the US’s Genesis mission puts such a strong emphasis on AI. AI-driven labs present an opportunity for researchers to iterate faster. Rather than running hundreds or thousands or simulations trying to find a needle in a haystack, a task for which a bigger iron is warranted, AI analysis and automation could focus that search. High-performance computing (HPC), and by extension the Top500, will remain relevant as long as more FLOPS means more simulations per unit of time. But these systems can only move as fast as the men and women who operate them. ®
