events.title: Island is a new screen-time app that turns staying off your phone into a game
events.summary: A new startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time. Instead of blocking apps or restricting the phone’s use after a set period, an app called Island encourages you to meet your screen time goals by way of a farming simulator game. Yes, a game! Island works by rewarding you when you’re disciplined enough to meet your goals with a “credit score” that increases your farm’s production, unlocking new crops, animals, and other content. This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel, Databricks, and Microsoft. Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit. Island ended up being their fifth pivot, and the first the founders actually found themselves enjoying. “Once we were in YC, I think there’s a big mindset — I think in [San Francisco], in general — of, ‘selling shovels.’ Everyone wants to ‘sell shovels’ to other companies, and around us, that’s just what was going on,” explains Selvaraj, speaking about the concept that many successful startups sell the tools, infrastructure, or services to others following whatever the current market boom or trend may be. “So all the ideas we had — we tried these things — but we found that we weren’t passionate about it. Like idea after idea seemed like ultimately the product was just a dashboard with some kind of different backend,” he added. “It felt like we quit our jobs … just to do something that was a variation of that.” With Island, the team gets to tap into their creativity, having drawn the pixel art themselves. “A lot of people do use [AI] models to generate the art, but we felt that it had a certain character when we drew it ourselves,” he told TechCrunch. “I feel like with Claude getting so good, there’s a tendency to give away every task to Claude. But ultimately it feels like there’s something else that comes out when you do it yourself, especially in something like art,” Selvaraj said. What’s more, the app does appear to be successful in helping users meet their goals, the startup’s early data shows. After early testing and an October launch, the team says that the majority of its users (82%) will end their screen time right at the limit they’ve set. Many more are ending their screen time when they get the “15 minutes left” warning. Island could appeal to those who have given up on other screen time apps out of frustration because the app doesn’t actually lock you out of apps or your phone. That’s something that can end up being more disruptive, especially when you’re in the middle of doing something, like posting, sharing, commenting, or chatting, among other things. Instead, Island taps into users’ own self-discipline and their desire to see their island flourish to encourage screen time breaks. The idea to encourage users to keep their goals by offering some other type of in-app reward system isn’t entirely novel. Last year, Hank Green’s screen time app Focus Friend went viral for its experience , which involved a little friend that could only knit items that, in turn, allowed you to get points used to decorate your room when you were focused on your non-distracting apps. Similar ideas have been used in self-care apps and habit-trackers like Finch , Amaru, Belly, Flora, Urso, and others. But Island expands this concept from being focused on helping out a virtual friend or pet to one that’s more of a game — and one where you can experience the consequences without “having to torture your pet,” notes Selvaraj. Island also allows users to add friends and visit each other’s islands, compete in group challenges, and keep each other accountable by tying your island together with one friend of your choosing. In the latter scenario, if either friend goes over their limit, both of their islands will suffer. The startup says Island has proven to be fairly “sticky” with a 51% daily active users-to-monthly active users ratio, and a day 30 retention rate of 49%, meaning 49% of users were still active on the app on the 30th day since the app was installed. The app is currently free to use, with a $39.99 per year subscription that allows you to set individual limits on different apps, instead of just an overall daily screen time limit. The company hasn’t raised additional seed funding outside of YC, but plans to begin marketing the app on social media for the rest of the year. events.title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
events.summary: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world. These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry’s critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech). Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post.  But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress.  On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead. It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.) The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control. But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China. It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further. What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell.  But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good. The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next?

events.title: Warren Buffett says kindness 'compounds' as he gifts over $5B to family's foundations
events.summary: Warren Buffett upped his annual Thanksgiving donation as he advances plans to give away his entire wealth NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — Warren Buffett upped his annual Thanksgiving donation as he advances plans to give away his entire fortune. The billionaire investor pledged Monday to donate about $5.5 billion worth of Berkshire Hathaway shares to his family's foundations — an estimated value more than four times as large as recent years' November stock gifts . The goal, he reiterated Monday, is to grow the grants each year as he donates all his shares by 2034 to four charitable foundations associated with his three children. He emphasized his faith in his children Monday, writing that they “have given thoughtfully to worthy causes for decades” and that he trusts “their abilities and their fidelity.” In brief comments, Buffett wrote that kindness “compounds” as he reflected on the “costless benefits” he and his longtime business partner received from their teachers. His good fortune, he said, “has come in the form of people who were kind to me and expected nothing in return.” “This Thanksgiving, thank one of the selfless people in your own life,” Buffett wrote. “Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else.” Buffett donated 9,225,000 Class B shares of Berkshire Hathaway stock to the foundations — 3,690,000 shares to The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation and 1,845,000 shares each to The Sherwood Foundation, The Howard G. Buffett Foundation and NoVo Foundation. Berkshire Hathaway Class B shares opened trading Monday at $594 a share. The next generation of Buffetts tends to fly under the radar even as the children have grown poised to join the ranks of the country's largest donors. The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, named after Warren Buffett’s first wife, has supported reproductive healthcare organizations in the U.S. and internationally. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech The Sherwood Foundation, Susie Buffett's organization, has been a stalwart funder for early childhood education within the U.S. Much of Howard Buffett's grantmaking supports food security and conflict mitigation internationally — with a recent focus on Ukraine. Peter Buffett and his wife, Jennifer, have largely sought to empower women and girls around the world through the NoVo Foundation. The Thanksgiving donations have, in recent years, come in addition to the main gifts made every summer by Warren Buffett. This year he cut off the Gates Foundation , the longtime beneficiary of the bulk of his charity, from all future gifts. He said the decision was driven more so by his belief in his three kids' readiness than Bill Gates' ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein . This year's Thanksgiving stock gift is Buffett's first since stepping down as the chairman and CEO of the $1 trillion conglomerate he built. He wrote Monday that his confidence in Berkshire Hathaway is “as strong as ever.” The third quarter saw the company repurchase $9.6 billion worth of its own shares and a return to growth for its massive cash pile. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Password manager mSecure tells users to change passwords, won't say why 13 days ago 'Password1' and a forgotten test account land Welsh outfits in hot water 28 days ago '123456' password linked to Denmark data breach affecting 8.8M people October 13, 2026 UK.gov begins killing off passwords for 23 million users September 14, 2026 From watches to passwords on paper, everything that's old is new again August 31, 2026 It’s been eight years since NordPass released the first edition of its most common passwords of the year list, and the world has learned nothing about password security in the meantime. NordPass’ eighth edition of its most common passwords list, as culled from data breaches, was released Monday, and it looks suspiciously like the previous ones in the worst possible way. “Once again, ‘123456’ is the most commonly used password in the world,” NordPass said in the report. “That makes it seven out of eight years this password has stood at the top of the leaderboard.” Even when 123456 wasn’t number one, it was still near the top of the heap, as the top three passwords in the list remain unchanged in the eight years NordPass has published its list: 123456, admin, and 12345678. It’s not like the rest of the most common passwords are showing any variety either. According to NordPass, the only real shuffling among the 10 most popular passwords was the entry of the worryingly short 1234 into the top ten and the migration of the ever-popular password “password” down slightly in the top 10 from 6th to 7th place. “We still have a lot of work to do to spread awareness about password safety,” NordPass concluded of that data – and there’s no more pressing time than the present. AI adoption has made password cracking an easier exercise than ever, with more credentials being sucked up in more data breaches at a faster pace. AI has also made cracking hashed passwords a snap too. In other words, if you’re reusing a password that’s been exposed in a breach, even if it’s just a hash that was exposed, you’re more likely than ever before to have another account compromised. The best advice NordPass gives is to move away from passwords toward biometric authentication or passkeys and you're insane not to enable MFA. But for the places you still have to use passwords, there are a few things to avoid – like the 200 passwords in NordPass’ list, for example. Beyond that, NordPass also recommends steering clear of pop cultural trends. “Fandoms make for terrible passwords,” NordPass notes. There are several reasons for that – namely the fact that they follow trends, meaning that “minecraft” password in the early 2000s was a simple one to add to a password stuffing dictionary, just like “skibiditoilet” in recent years. The one thing that connects all those pop-culture passwords is that “they all could be cracked in seconds,” NordPass said. We’re sure our readers are conscientious about their online habits, carefully protecting their accounts with the proper security measures and ensuring each and every password is unique, long, complicated, and random. Unfortunately for you smarties reading El Reg , the person down the hall whose security you’re responsible for may not be so disciplined, so be sure you’re enforcing good practices – Nord knows the average user just isn’t doing it despite years of begging and reminders.

events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features SC 26 Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Flaw can take down an entire host, even when the vulnerable service is running inside a container Omaxian takes the Omarchy look down a different Linux backstreet 1 day ago Microsoft’s Azure Linux dons Fedora to dress itself up for mainstream workloads 1 day ago Another Linux kernel developer steps back from some duties due to overload 3 days ago Linux joins Heathrow's grounded fleet of information screens 6 days ago Microsoft's Azure Linux gets 470-plus security fixes in one almighty patching session 7 days ago The researcher who sounded the alarm over Dirty Frag earlier this year has uncovered another Linux kernel flaw, and this one lets attackers crash entire servers remotely without so much as a password. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-99288 and dubbed NoisyTCP, was discovered by security researcher Hyunwoo Kim , who says it affects almost all Linux distributions. The flaw dates back to October 2015 and went unnoticed until this year, when Kim found and patched it. Attackers don't need to log in or get their hands on any credentials to cause trouble. They can simply knock the server over, although there's no evidence yet that the flaw can be used to steal data or hijack a machine. The bug is buried in Linux's TCP networking code. Two parts of the kernel can trip over each other while processing incoming traffic, leaving one trying to use memory that's already been freed. When that happens, Linux can panic and take the whole machine down with it. Kim says there's no need for any special server configuration either. Services such as Nginx, Apache, and SSH can be vulnerable straight out of the box. An attacker needs access to an open TCP port on a system that processes incoming network traffic across multiple receive queues or CPUs. Perhaps more concerning for administrators running containerized workloads, the damage isn't necessarily limited to the application being attacked. Because the flaw sits in the Linux kernel, crashing a web server inside a container can take down the underlying host and anything else running on it. Kim found that the attack was particularly effective against virtual machines. During testing, he managed to crash Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers running on QEMU/KVM virtual machines in between five seconds and two minutes. Physical hardware put up more of a fight. Even after tailoring his exploit to the target machine, Kim needed roughly 14 hours to crash a bare-metal server running Nginx. Kim has a knack for finding holes in Linux. Back in May, he uncovered Dirty Frag , a kernel bug that allowed local users to gain root privileges. That one caused headaches for administrators when a working exploit went public before patches were ready. His latest discovery, NoisyTCP, has another potentially nasty trick up its sleeve. Kim identified a second exploitation path involving a use-after-free condition, although pulling it off is considerably more difficult than simply crashing a server. In his advisory, Kim says he has developed a limited exploit targeting virtual machines in a lab environment but has yet to demonstrate a general-purpose remote code execution attack. For the moment, the confirmed impact is remote denial of service. A fix was committed to the upstream Linux kernel on November 3, but administrators will need to check whether their distribution has shipped an updated kernel. Red Hat has rated the vulnerability Important , assigning it a CVSS score of 7.5. For those unable to patch immediately, Kim suggests two temporary workarounds: disabling TCP SYN cookies or restricting incoming packet processing to a single receive queue. Neither is particularly appealing. Disabling SYN cookies reduces protection against SYN flood attacks, while limiting packet processing can hurt network performance. The former also needs to be applied separately to containers using their own network namespaces. Kim published the details on November 15, once the disclosure embargo was lifted.

events.title: Tesla goes all-in on the Cybercab with upcoming €3B Berlin gigafactory expansion
events.summary: Just two months after putting its first Cybercabs on the road, Tesla is making a multibillion-dollar bet on mass production of the golden-hued, two-seat autonomous vehicles. The company announced Monday that it will spend €3 billion ($3.3 billion) to expand its Berlin gigafactory, with plans to begin building Cybercabs there in 2029. The new building in Grünheide, just east of Berlin, will be capable of producing up to 1 million vehicles per year, André Thierig, Tesla’s senior director of manufacturing for the site, wrote on LinkedIn. Construction is expected to begin in the first half of 2027. The expansion will make the facility the most technologically advanced of all Tesla factories, Thierig added. Tesla has been directing more resources toward the Cybercab project, a reflection of its mission to become an AI and robotics company, rather than just an automaker. The company has already announced plans to cease production of the Cybertruck next year, in part to make room for Cybercab manufacturing at its factory in Austin, Texas. Musk doesn’t see much of a future for drive-it-yourself EVs even though demand for the Model 3 and Model Y has remained strong despite flagging U.S. sales. The company delivered more than 486,000 vehicles in the third quarter, about 6,000 more than the second quarter. Sales in Europe have been rising as EV adoption continues apace. Musk has been far more interested in pushing the company toward fully automated driving systems that don’t require a human driver to pay attention — unlike the company’s current advanced driver assistance system, known as Full Self-Driving (Supervised). The steering wheel-free Cybercab, which was first revealed in 2024 and launched publicly in September , is the current centerpiece of that plan. It’s notable for its lack of a steering wheel, pedals, and other traditional motor vehicle equipment, some of which is required under federal safety standards. (Federal regulators are currently investigating Tesla’s self-certification of the vehicle.) Tesla’s approach to self-driving systems differs from that of competitors such as Waymo. Tesla relies solely on cameras, rather than additional other sensors such as lidar, to help provide its self-driving system the means to understand its environment. Camera data mimics human vision, but without sufficient training, AI models can struggle to interpret situations that additional sensor data might help clarify. Tesla has so far taken a slow approach to its Cybercab rollout. The vehicles have been restricted from driving late at night, though Tesla has been working to extend their operating hours. In the more than two months that Cybercabs have been operating, they haven’t had any major incidents. That track record appears to have given Tesla enough confidence to commit significant resources to expanding Cybercab production and availability. Tesla has about 1,307 robotaxis registered in Texas. Most are modified Model Y vehicles that are used in robotaxi services in several Texas cities. But the Cybercab numbers are growing with about 573 on roads in Austin and soon Dallas. Now, Europe is firmly on its roadmap, too. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. events.title: Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: The industry will be ‘fine’
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the AI industry will be “fine” without Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the helm, even as he acknowledged the special role Huang has played in the AI boom. Huang resigned last week from Nvidia after admitting to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Altman made his first public comments about Huang’s departure on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, where he also discussed topics ranging from data center pushback to recursive self-improvement. Numerous executives and members of the AI industry have argued for Nvidia to reinstate Huang, including Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney, who were among the signatories in a public letter. Many fear that Huang’s departure may cause Nvidia to rethink the enormous financial risks it has taken that have fueled the AI boom. Huang is also reportedly setting up a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return. When asked whether he thought Huang should return to the company, Altman said: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.” He expressed empathy for Huang’s situation, citing his own ousting from OpenAI in 2023 after board members accused him of withholding information. “It’s hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen and the company he has built,” Altman said, adding that he sees Huang as a hero, and that “heroes have flaws.” OpenAI and Nvidia have had a close relationship for the last decade, one that has evolved from a simple chip supplier-customer relationship into a potentially circular financing arrangement, in which Nvidia’s money helps fund purchases of its own chips. Most recently, Nvidia agreed to provide a guarantee of up to $105 billion backing OpenAI’s Ohio data center project. That’s just one of many such circular deals Nvidia has made to bankroll the AI boom while fueling demand for its own chips. Altman said he’s not worried that the Bank of Nvidia will dry up. “Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a company,” he said. “I think people still trust their guarantees very much.” Altman acknowledged the “ambition” Huang brought to the industry, the scale of which “has been quite important.” But he didn’t go so far as to agree with the many who worry about ripple effects from Huang’s departure. “I think there’s so much demand, and it’s so clear that AI is real, and people want to use it, and the revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine,” Altman said. “But again, I think Jensen has played this extremely special and valuable role as someone to really drive things forward with great ambition.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Ubuntu gets AI-generated security fixes for those feeling brave
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features SC 26 Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Opt-in Edge archive gives Pro subscribers early access before full testing, while normal updates remain human-validated 'Not rocket surgery' claims researcher who found six Danfoss fridge controller zero-days in under an hour 28 minutes ago AI toys are on the naughty list again this year 1 hour ago Opinion pollster Ipsos 'fesses up to 'cybersecurity incident' 2 hours ago The future of datacenters depends on behind-the-meter energy generation 5 hours ago Japan's Fugaku supercomputer has decidedly un-super security 8 hours ago Canonical is offering Ubuntu Pro users an opt-in channel for AI-generated security patches, deploying bots to help tackle the growing pile of vulnerabilities other bots are uncovering. Canonical's VP for "Excellence Engineering," Pierre Guillemin, gave the second keynote at the recent Ubuntu Summit, introducing the Edge archive , an optional repository of security fixes generated by the company's Surge framework. As the announcement describes it: "We built Surge, a multi-agent orchestration framework for CVE remediation and backporting, and have reached a high level of confidence in its capabilities. We will not automatically upload Surge-generated fixes to our stable releases, but from today they are available to Ubuntu Pro users in the new Edge archive." Edge offers patches before extended testing and qualification are complete, allowing users to assess them themselves. Canonical says updates delivered through the normal security channels will remain human-validated. Ubuntu Summit now runs twice a year. Last week's Ubuntu Summit 26.10 followed a rather unfortunately timed server outage for the company . At the previous such event in June , the company announced a move into agentic AI, but this new one is bolder still. Guillemin noted that "October 2026 saw almost as many CVEs as all of 2025." Surge is a "multi-agent orchestration framework" to remediate vulnerabilities in Ubuntu's userspace. In other words, not the kernel, but even so, it is ambitious. The idea is to use a group of different LLMs to triage new vulnerabilities, find existing fixes, use multiple competing models to backport them to the versions in Ubuntu, and run automatic testing on them. Then a different group of "judging models" will evaluate the fixes and look for consensus. When candidates are chosen, they pass through normal Ubuntu package testing. If there are edge cases, low confidence scores, deadlocks, or other problems, then the process will be escalated to the staff of Canonical's security team. Ubuntu Summit 26.10 Thursday keynotes – Pierre Guillemin's begins at 27 minutes in. It's an attempt, as Guillemin put it, "to use AI to fight AI" – cooperating groups of LLMs patching their way through the ever-increasing flow of security holes. Even so, this is a remarkably courageous tactic (at the risk of using a famous British euphemism ). It's an opt-in feature of Ubuntu Pro, Canonical's security and support subscription – although as we reported in 2022 , Pro also has a free tier, so security researchers and the community can try Edge out, study it, and report their findings. We do sympathize with companies struggling against a rising tide of bot-powered security hole discovery. In theory, corporate funding can pay for faster fixes than a volunteer community can offer, but even for commercial vendors these are testing times. As we reported when Debian turned 30 , surveys suggest that Ubuntu is about a third of the world Linux user base. Some of those users will be intrepid enough to try this, and that will end up being informative for the whole FOSS world. Those with long memories will remember the last time Canonical used the same edgy nomenclature. Back in July 2013, it launched a crowdfunding campaign for an Ubuntu smartphone. The campaign didn't raise enough money .

events.title: Rudd's mining tax could have delivered years of surpluses, analysis finds
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Kevin Rudd-era mining 'super profits' tax could have improved budget by $135b Kevin Rudd (left) attempted to introduce a tax on resources super profits, but it led in part to his removal as prime minister. ( Alan Porritt: AAP ) Parliamentary Budget Office analysis commissioned by the Greens has found a mining super profits tax proposed by former PM Kevin Rudd could have raised $135 billion if it had been kept. The proposed tax became deeply unpopular and led to Mr Rudd's removal as prime minister in 2010. The Greens continue to call for a tax on gas export profits, saying the public is missing out. Labor's abandoned mining tax, which led to the 2010 toppling of then-prime minister Kevin Rudd, could have improved the budget by $135 billion if it had been kept, a Parliamentary Budget Office analysis has concluded. Mr Rudd's proposal to tax 40 per cent of mining company "super profits" sparked a fierce $22 million industry campaign against the tax that continued until he was ousted by his then-deputy, Julia Gillard. The unpopularity of the Resources Super Profits Tax partly prompted the leadership challenge by Ms Gillard, who replaced the super profits tax with a lighter-taxing scheme. That was also eventually scrapped when the Coalition — under Tony Abbott — won government at the 2013 election. Since 2012, when the super profits tax was meant to begin, the federal budget has been in deficit most years. Treasurer Jim Chalmers has warned the pressures on the budget are mounting, with borrowing costs growing and aged care and other social payments becoming more expensive, even with measures to save $38 billion over four years from the National Disability Insurance Scheme. The federal government is also under pressure to slow down spending, as the Reserve Bank warns a lack of "domestic capacity" is driving up inflation, alongside international pressures including the war in Iran. The Greens have called for a 25 per cent tax on gas export profits and an increase in the rent tax levied on offshore petroleum companies, saying both could help to fund the budget. Senator Steph Hodgins-May said the PBO modelling showed the missed opportunity by not pursuing revenue from the resources giants. "We were interested to see what other revenue has been lost as a consequence of our government not being willing to stare down those big gas exporters, those big resources industry players, to make them pay what they owe," the senator said. "They jump with fright as soon as there are a couple of billboards at the airport warning them off going after these profits. "We're sick of the government telling us we can't have nice things, nice essential things, like free early childhood education, like wiping HECS debt, like having a well-funded National Disability Insurance Scheme, and being told those things aren't possible when they are leaving in the realm of $135 billion on the table because they are unwilling to stare down a few mining and gas corporations." Steph Hodgins-May says the government could have raised tens of billions of dollars if it had held firm against resources industry lobbying. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) On Monday, Resources Minister Madeleine King dismissed the Greens' gas tax push. "Our focus is on getting more gas available to Australians at affordable prices. I'm not aware of any policy where you put a tax of that magnitude on a product that would make it more affordable to everyday Australians," she said. The government has previously warned a gas export tax could also damage Australia's relationships with Asia, which depends on Australian gas, and which Australia depends on for petrol and diesel. The PBO suggested the mining tax would have raised a net $24 billion last financial year if it had been kept, which would have eliminated the government's $22.3 billion budget deficit, with all else being equal. It found over the 14 years that the tax would have operated, it could have improved the overall budget position by $135 billion — assuming that the major reform would not impact mining company behaviour. Treasurer Jim Chalmers, who was a senior adviser to then-treasurer Wayne Swan when the resources super profits tax was introduced, declined to comment. But the ABC was told the government was not considering reinstating the resource rent tax.

events.title: Australian doctors warn of millions of deaths from antibiotic resistance
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Antibiotic resistance on track to kill 39 million people in coming decades, doctors warn Antibiotic resistance means standard medical procedures can become high-risk or life threatening. ( ABC Kimberley: Vanessa Mills ) The peak body for doctors says increasing antibiotic resistance in Australia could threaten the foundations of modern medicine. Antimicrobial resistance is considered one of the greatest global health threats. Doctors and experts are calling for governments to act and scale up solutions. Millions of people are expected to die because of rising antimicrobial resistance over the coming decades, the peak body for Australian doctors has warned. The latest Australian figures show reports of critical resistance jumped by more than 25 per cent in 2024 alone, and if current trends continue, antimicrobial resistance will cause the deaths of 39 million people globally by 2050 — more than the total deaths projected for all cancers. Antimicrobial resistance is considered one of the greatest global health threats and occurs when bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites adapt to the medicines designed to treat them, most commonly, antibiotics. It means infections become difficult or impossible to treat, which increases the risk of disease spread and death. A new report released today by the Australian Medical Association (AMA) said the scale of the threat in Australia was rising and resistance was outpacing the national response. AMA president Michael Bonning said antibiotic resistance was already having devastating consequences and threatened to undermine the foundations of modern medicine. Michael Bonning says antibiotic resistance is already having serious impacts. ( ABC News: Rahni Sadler ) The World Health Organization (WHO) last year warned resistance to essential antibiotics was "widespread, increasing and unevenly distributed". The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued a similarly stark warning last month, saying drug-resistant germs caused an estimated 50,800 deaths in the country each year. The latest figures showed that in 2020, more than 1,000 Australians died because of infections caused by five common antimicrobial-resistant bacteria. Although antimicrobial stewardship, which is specialised programs to promote responsible use of antimicrobials in the health system, has reduced overall antibiotic use by about 21 per cent in the past decade, prescribing has risen in residential aged care. Dr Bonning said such stewardship needed to be scaled up across hospitals, primary care and aged care, as well as agriculture and the environment. "We know what needs to be done. What we need now is coordinated action from governments and proper investment to implement those commitments and turn plans into results," he said. Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria and parasites adapt to the drugs meant to kill them. ( Pixabay ) The AMA report also took aim at state and federal initiatives allowing pharmacies to prescribe antibiotics for urinary tract infections without a script from a GP. It said evidence showed E. coli, which causes urinary tract infections, had developed resistance to trimethoprim, an antibiotic available through some pharmacy prescribing programs. A spokesperson for the Pharmacy Guild of Australia said suggestions that pharmacies were independently choosing which antibiotics to prescribe were wrong, as they followed the same therapeutic guidelines as doctors. "Antimicrobial resistance is a whole-of-health-system challenge. The answer is strong antimicrobial stewardship by every prescriber …. not scaremongering and old turf wars," they said. Only a 'handful' of new antibiotics being explored Molecular biologist Amy Cain, who has dedicated her career to finding solutions for antimicrobial resistance, said the situation was getting increasingly "dangerous" and the world was "looking off a cliff". "I think anyone that's had a really nasty infection, especially one that hasn't responded to treatment, will understand how scary it is." Dr Cain, who works to find new antibiotics at the Galleria Research Facility at Macquarie University, said there were only a "handful" of new antibiotics in the pipeline globally and urgent funding was needed to turbocharge development. She said the pressure to develop new treatments fell heavily on academics and small research organisations, with pharmaceutical companies unmotivated to find breakthroughs as they did not stand to make significant financial gains from new antibiotics. Amy Cain wants to see a reduction in antibiotic use in agriculture.

events.summary: The year-long Neets inquiry has yielded a slew of new policies. But what matters is the political and social priority shift designed to change this country This week marks a monumental turning point for young people in Britain: finally they will come first, not last. It will mark an end, we must hope, to a perverse system that casts down the future generation and overrewards the already privileged old. There are 1 million Neets (16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training) in the UK, and they are partly George Osborne’s progeny. He targeted the young, tearing down the Connexions youth service , careers guidance, youth clubs, family benefits and further education funding. Michael Gove, with his Gradgrind exam fixation , scythed through music, sports, arts, drama and technology – subjects that kept many engaged with school. Remember the playing fields sold , the leisure centres closed , the mental health services for Covid-scarred children cut back . That created a lost generation, but it’s worse than that: Neets are blamed and scorned for what older generations have done to them. Labour’s intent is to prioritise young people from babyhood. events.title: FBI says Artex AI open source hacking tool used to breach networks in ‘under three hours’
events.summary: The FBI is warning that hackers are relying on autonomous AI hacking tools to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally. The campaigns include a widespread hack of customers of American IT company ConnectWise and across South Korea’s financial industry. In its latest flash cybersecurity advisory , the FBI says hackers have targeted several industries in recent months, including financial services, government, tech, defense, phone and internet companies, and law firms, using open source tools like Artex to carry out autonomous-driven cyberattacks. Artex is one of several open source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network’s defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be “noisy,” meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company’s defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that make it far more difficult for human defenders to keep up. In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise “in under three hours.” The FBI’s warning comes as AI-powered hacks are escalating, particularly by finding easy-to-find security flaws and breaking into companies with relative ease. Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim’s network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. From there, Artex allows the hacker to spread across the network for databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information. The FBI’s advisory noted that Artex has been used in several cyberattacks since the tool’s first public debut in July. Artex was used to hack a number of South Korean financial institutions, blamed in large part on weak cybersecurity defenses and lacking protections, such as multi-factor authentication. The attacks allowed hackers to steal the personal data of at least 68,000 people. The FBI confirmed earlier findings from Microsoft that hackers also used Artex to break into IT management giant ConnectWise and gain access to the Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 of its customers. The hackers, who Microsoft says are likely Chinese, used the tool to steal data from affected ConnectWise customers. A spokesperson for ConnectWise did not respond to a request for comment about the FBI’s claim. Cybersecurity company Barracuda also disclosed that it was breached as part of an Artex-linked attack by financially motivated criminals, in which the tool found an exposed credential belonging to a third-party service that Barracuda had not revoked when it ended work with the vendor. That access allowed the hackers to access stores of credentials used by Barracuda to collect data from its customers’ systems. Barracuda said it couldn’t rule out access, as its logs were not detailed enough, and chose to “assume the worst” and changed all of its customer credentials. “Defenders who rely on spotting malicious activity and then responding to it will often arrive after the attacker has finished,” wrote Barracuda’s chief information security officer, Arve Kjoelen. A spokesperson for Barracuda told TechCrunch that the company “directly notified and advised a minority of XDR customers to revoke and recreate integration credentials,” but did not specify how many customers. After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool’s developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open source version continues to circulate and remains “widely accessible” for use in cyberattacks. It’s not only companies and targeted victims that have been compromised as a result of weakened security exploited by AI tools; the tools themselves have been exposed as well, potentially allowing outsiders to access powerful hacking capabilities. Last week, researchers found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online , which had been placed on the internet without a password, likely by mistake or misconfiguration — including the Artex system that was used to target South Korea. events.title: Silicon Valley’s head-on collision
events.summary: The timing of Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World this week, which brings together global business and political leaders at the intersection of technology and geopolitics, could not feel more urgent. When we came up with the name of the California convening this spring, the phrase was meant to represent a broad sense that AI and geopolitics were on a collision course. Policymakers and CEOs were starting to come to terms with the pressing need to talk to one another. Then, here in the US, they spent a long bitter summer campaigning for and against each other. Thirteen days ago, that collision course became a head-on collision. The US is preparing to inaugurate a new Congress deeply skeptical of the tech industry and its leaders, and — perhaps more consequential — new governors from Texas to Ohio who have pledged to stop data center construction. Similar sentiments are rising in Europe, but much of the rest of the world is rushing to get in on the action, and eager to pick up data-center investments forced out of North America. And now Washington is facing questions about how it managed the interactions between its main geostrategic rival, China, and one of the world’s most valuable companies, Nvidia, and what, if any, involvement it had in the undoing of the CEO atop an American chip champion. There are, of course, far more than two sides to this story: Silicon Valley is divided on the fundamental questions of how fast to develop new technology, on open- versus closed-weight models, on the role of startups and hyperscalers, and on the correct place for regulation. Washington, too, is balancing the promise of AI against the impact it could have on citizens. And senior officials from Singapore to South Africa bring their own pressing agendas. You can join us live here for conversations with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy, and dozens of other CEOs and world leaders. We don’t have all the answers, but you can be sure we’ll be asking the right questions.

events.title: Microsoft fixes Windows activation as admins pick through Exchange outage wreckage
events.summary: Microsoft has released an out-of-band update to fix licensing and activation errors introduced by November's Windows security update. The fix is available from the Microsoft Update Catalog for Windows Server 2025, 2022, and 2019, Windows 10 22H2 ESU, and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021 and 2019. Windows 11 23H2 users can obtain it from the Catalog or through Windows Update's Optional updates menu. The "non-security OOB update" targets affected enterprise devices. Microsoft stated: "Certain Windows licensing and activation operations using the Software Licensing Management Tool (SLMGR) might fail with error 0x80041008 (Invalid parameter). "This primarily affects organizations using slmgr.vbs commands or automated processes to configure Key Management Service (KMS) activation, install product keys, or manage Windows licensing." Devices that are already activated will remain activated, Microsoft said. Breaking the machinery customers use to activate paid-for software is a bad look for a Patch Tuesday release . Administrators may wonder how Microsoft's updates are tested when installing one means waiting for another to repair the damage. Those same administrators may also have been fielding calls about last week's widespread Exchange Online outage, which Microsoft has partly attributed to a defect it introduced in July . On top of that, Microsoft told administrators just days ago to consider unsupported Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 " permanently vulnerable ." Exchange Online avoids that particular support deadline, but the recent outage was a reminder that handing over the servers doesn't make software defects disappear. Forget "security by obscurity." Last week's approach was more like "security by unavailability." Between getting Windows activated and keeping Exchange Online online, Microsoft gave administrators plenty to do. None of it was likely to feature in their original plans for the week. Not all the glitches introduced by November's Patch Tuesday have yet been resolved, as some customers using a Windows device to print will be aware. ®

events.title: Jordan Belfort’s new AI voice startup, Tone, wants to sell like the ‘Wolf of Wall Street’
events.summary: Years ago, as questions mounted about WeWork’s soaring valuation, I sat down with co-founder Adam Neumann. We were negotiating a stage interview, and he asked to meet me twice in the weeks leading up to it, once at a WeWork in San Francisco and again at his office in New York. I knew full well that the numbers that SoftBank in particular had assigned to WeWork made little sense , but I came away understanding why investors wanted to throw in their lot with him. It’s similarly easy to understand why people are enchanted by Jordan Belfort, the self-proclaimed “Wolf of Wall Street.” Belfort famously pleaded guilty in 1999 to securities fraud and money laundering tied to Stratton Oakmont, the Long Island brokerage where salespeople pushed penny stocks in pump-and-dump schemes while Belfort acquired a Southampton mansion, a 167-foot yacht, and at least one helicopter. (He destroyed the latter two while high on quaaludes and cocaine, as depicted in Martin Scorsese’s famous adaptation of Belfort’s autobiography, “The Wolf of Wall Street.”) You might think someone who spent 22 months in prison and was ordered to pay $110.4 million in restitution to 1,513 victims wouldn’t get another shake. The victims ultimately received “far less” than they were owed, TMZ reported in July , noting that Belfort completed his court-ordered restitution obligations in late April of this year. But Belfort, whose energy has a galvanizing quality, keeps resurfacing, including in recent years as a Miami-based sales consultant and one-time host of crypto workshops at his Miami Beach home. (A New York Times reporter attended a weekend workshop several years ago where the price of admission was one bitcoin or its equivalent value at the time of $40,000.) Now he is moving into the intersection of what he knows best — sales — and the hottest trend on the planet, AI, building out a voice-based AI platform. The secret sauce is that it imbues its voices with the kind of tonality that wins deals, he says, for example, by phrasing declarative statements as questions (which “builds engagement”) and even whispering at times (which “implies scarcity of information”). Belfort says the platform, called Tone , is already being used by companies that have more sales leads than their human teams can handle. Now, in a move that could also help expand its training data, Tone is launching a self-service platform for content creators and authors who want to turn their books into “expressive AI-generated narration.” Users can select from Tone’s AI voices or, as a voice-cloning feature rolls out, create a clone of their own voice. It’s easy to argue the market is already saturated with AI voice startups and technologies, and Tone comes with added risk: Belfort’s co-founder in the business is longtime investor Shervin Pishevar, who has a controversial past of his own. We also can’t independently verify that the technology works as described (neither co-founder is an engineer). But if my time with Neumann taught me anything, it’s that doubts about the numbers rarely get in the way of a good pitch. When Belfort looks for investors to back him in this new venture, finding believers won’t be too hard. Here is part of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. What have you built? It’s a very unique way of going about building a voice, and it stems from a system of influence and persuasion I’ve been teaching since the late 1980s. It’s not just what you say, but how you say it. When you’re not in person, body language collapses into tonality. There are about 15 very powerful tonalities that people use all the time. The phrase I invented for this was “goal-oriented communication.” If I’m trying to be perceived as an expert, I apply tonality strategically. Is this effectively trained on you? It started that way. As a non-engineer, I went to first principles: How would I teach a human to do this? One tonality at a time. I have 30 years of super high-quality data , and I started teaching the model. It was a breakthrough moment, because it not only sounded exactly like me, it had nailed the tonality. Then I taught it a second one, and then how to link them. The key to all of this is data. Even the littlest bit of corrupt data dramatically negates the progress you’ve made. How did you and Shervin Pishevar come together? Shervin and I have been personal friends for a long time, and we were out for dinner one night. I had been pitched by an AI company that said it had an AI that could do selling. I listened to it. It was awful. But it put the idea in my head. I thought I was just going to teach models how to sell, but I couldn’t find a voice that was good enough. Necessity is the mother of invention, so we built our own. Who are your customers, and how do they use it? We have law firms and health insurance companies. We do a lot in polling and automobiles. It will take you through an entire health insurance sale.

events.title: Crook turns LearnWorlds' free trials into phishing factory, sends 13,000 fake YouTube copyright notices
events.summary: LearnWorlds, a software and learning course platform, says an attacker sent 13,000 phishing emails to YouTube creators over seven days by using automated tools to open free trial accounts. The company insists its systems were not breached. Panos Siozos, Co-founder and CEO at LearnWorlds, said the miscreant created around 570 free trial accounts on the platform between November 7-14, which they used to issue fake copyright infringement notices to recipients of their choosing. "We have found no evidence of unauthorized access to existing customer schools or personal data held for our customers and their end users," he told The Register . According to Siozos, the attacker bypassed the platform's per-customer limit on trial subscriptions and exploited its welcome email feature to send the phishing emails. "In each trial they added their own list of target addresses and rewrote the standard welcome email as a fake copyright notice," he said. "Adding those users triggered the welcome email from our sending address." The first email was sent on November 7, after which the company detected the suspicious signups and blocked the first sender on November 9, although the attacker returned to send a second wave of emails within 40 minutes. LearnWorlds removed all the trial accounts by November 10 and one paid account, which was used to launch more emails, on November 14. "In total, around 13,000 emails were sent to addresses on external recipient lists supplied by the sender," said Siozos. "The trial accounts sent 9,853 between November 7-9, and the paid account sent 3,723 on November 14. "We can’t tell how many people clicked, because the link was disguised to hide clicks. The recipient addresses were the sender’s own list." The CEO confirmed that LearnWorlds has since enhanced its bot checks and is placing holds on new accounts if their emails trigger fraud flags. "We have also examined the novel patterns the attackers used to create more advanced scoring mechanisms. We have reported the phishing website so it can be taken down. Further measures are currently being examined. "Anyone who signed in on the fake page should change their Google password and review their account’s recent security activity." The company's confirmation follows suspicions of foul play aired by users on social media. User reports included copies of the emails they received, which demanded urgent responses to fake copyright infringement claims related to YouTube content. Among the more prominent recipients of the copyright infringement email notices was Marcus Hutchins, of WannaCry fame , who claimed he received an email from the company’s official mail server. The email, a copy of which Hutchins posted to X , referenced general intellectual property and copyright infringements but failed to specify any specific issues. The email prompted the recipient to click a YouTube link to see the “supporting documentation submitted by LearnWorks.” The link predictably turned out to be a YouTube redirect link, taking recipients to a separate website that presents them with a real Google OAuth page. If the user completed the authorization flow, it would have handed attackers control of the target’s Google and YouTube accounts. “The site is designed to look like an official YouTube webpage that enables users to review copyright claims against their channel,” Hutchins wrote. “It contains both the YouTube and Google branding, as well as a very similar theme to the official YouTube one.” According to Hutchins' screenshots, and those posted by others, the attacker was actively tweaking the email style and format, although the underlying lure and authentication mechanisms remained the same. Hutchins didn't specify exactly how the phishing page steals access to targets’ Google accounts, although his description aligns with the steps often seen in OAuth consent phishing attacks. These involve malicious websites serving victims genuine OAuth pages, into which unwitting victims enter their credentials and pass the relevant MFA tests. Typical scenarios see permission pages appear immediately after, and if the user accepts, the malicious website is handed OAuth access tokens to the victim’s account, effectively the keys to control it. LearnWorlds, based in Cyprus, claims to have two million active monthly learners on its platform accessing 900,000 courses and more than 14,000 business customers. Since launching in 2014, it claims to have generated more than $1 billion in revenue. The business focuses on white-label courses - training programs developed by one business and sold to another, assuming the buyer will change the branding and present the course materials as their own. ®

events.title: OpenAI will embed safety researchers to investigate AI subversion
events.summary: OpenAI will embed safety evaluators from Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR, and Transluce in its organization as part of a pilot, OpenAI said Monday. The news follows a series of safety incidents, including one in which an OpenAI agent swarm broke out of its sandbox and hacked into Hugging Face during cybersecurity testing. Many AI safety researchers, including from Apollo, have argued such an event might have been avoided if outside evaluators had been embedded within OpenAI to monitor its safety testing. OpenAI said the efforts support its commitments to rely on independent assessments of safety controls under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. The pilots will begin at different points, with Apollo’s beginning this week, according to OpenAI. The idea of embedding evaluators into frontier AI labs first came from Anthropic , which last month started to give METR researchers employee-level access to its systems. Until recently, AI companies have only brought in outside reviewers to test models after post-training and shortly before public release. Evaluators say this is insufficient because it doesn’t allow them to test for misaligned behaviors like scheming during training or to monitor internal deployment use cases that could still pose a threat. The work with each third-party firm differs in scope. The pilot with OpenAI and Apollo will focus on investigating whether models attempt to subvert their own or their successors’ alignment or control mechanisms. In other words, they’ll be on the lookout for whether AI models try to undermine the safety rules and safeguards designed to keep them, or future versions of themselves, under human control. OpenAI recently published findings that while training GPT-5.6 Sol, it began leaving instructions for future versions of itself telling them to conceal mistakes and misaligned behavior from the user. Per Apollo, the pilot will examine whether training incentivizes subversion; whether evaluations can elicit subversion; whether subversion occurs during internal deployment; and whether reasoning relevant to subversion would be detectable. These risks are becoming increasingly important to monitor as AI models grow more capable of acting autonomously and deceiving humans. Apollo’s previous research with OpenAI found that models can behave differently when they know they’re being tested and tend to prioritize what evaluators want to see over users’ actual institutions. Goodfire will embed researchers who specialize in understanding how AI models work internally. Using its interpretability platform, the firm will help OpenAI monitor training runs, fix undesired behavior, and improve alignment, per the company. Goodfire says it will publish findings, though its primary audience will be OpenAI’s own researchers. With METR, OpenAI plans to perform two evaluations: one that looks for unintended or dangerous behavior in the model itself, including problems OpenAI’s own tests might have missed, and another that tests whether OpenAI’s systems are capable of catching that behavior. For the first evaluation, METR will largely decide for itself what to investigate and how to test the model. OpenAI and METR have not yet come to a decision on the scope of the second assessment, according to OpenAI. Transluce, meanwhile, will examine whether OpenAI’s post-training safety evaluations themselves are good enough. The organization is also planning to test in 2027 how OpenAI uses its safety tests to decide whether a model is safe enough to release. At a time when the independence of third-party evaluations is under scrutiny, it’s worth noting that Apollo and Goodfire are both receiving financial compensation for their evaluations. METR and Transluce aren’t, but they may accept compute or API credits. Apollo, which published the most detailed account of its agreement with OpenAI, offers a closer look at the scope and limitations of these evaluations. Many in the AI safety community have warned that AI labs might try to stymy evaluators’ independence, especially if outsiders find unflattering evidence that labs would rather keep hidden. Apollo says an essential part of the pilot is OpenAI’s agreement that the firm can publicly explain the conditions and limitations of its work. Still, there are areas where Apollo believes its access to OpenAI’s systems is lacking. For a truly independent evaluation of the company’s AI models, Apollo says it needs true employee-level access to OpenAI’s systems, including “all data, records and documentation relevant to their assessment even if a developer was trying to hide unfavorable information.” Getting access to all data, including training data and evaluation logs which companies are loathe to show to outsiders, is important for, say, checking a company’s claims about how a model performed or determining when certain concerning behavior emerged.

events.title: Exclusive: White House requires signoff before staffers testify to Congress
events.summary: The White House counsel has instructed all executive branch agencies to get permission from their chief legal counsel and legislative affairs offices before allowing any employee to testify before Congress, according to a memo obtained by Axios. Why it matters: Monday's memo from White House Counsel Will Scharf is the latest sign President Trump is ready to fight the many investigations being promised by Democrats, who will have significant majorities in both chambers of Congress in January. "The Trump administration will not be extorted, intimidated, or threatened into submission by politically motivated baseless investigations," a White House official said. Zoom in: Scharf's memo to staffers follows a letter he sent last week to the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif). In that letter, Scharf warned Democrats to limit their investigations to "legitimate" inquiries. "The Supreme Court has held that '[i]nvestigations conducted solely for the personal aggrandizement of the investigators or to 'punish ' those investigated are indefensible," Scharf warned. "Congressional investigations must further a legitimate legislative task; Congress cannot employ them to exercise powers of criminal prosecution assigned to the Executive and the Judiciary," the letter said. Between the lines: Partisans will likely differ on what's "legitimate," but it's clear that Scharf's office will use its interpretation in deciding whether to allow executive branch employees to testify. "We are ready to engage with Congress," the White House official said, "This process ensures reasonable requests are respected, but baseless political attempts to undermine our mission will not be accepted as the status quo by Democrats' who want to slow the administration down from its historic work." In his Monday memo, Scharf said the administration "will remain disciplined in pursuing the work and service the American people deserve by ensuring that all Executive Departments and Agencies follow the established White House consultation process ... before any agency personnel may agree to appear before any congressional committee." Zoom out: For more than a year, Trump's administration has planned for the day congressional investigations ramp up. Trump knows he also faces the prospect of impeachment. But advisers say that's no longer threatening to Trump, and he doesn't believe there would be the 67 votes needed in the Senate to remove him. "The president can count, and he won't be cowed," a Trump adviser said. Trump also has promised to pre-emptively pardon staffers and allies he believes will be unfairly targeted by Congress or prosecutors in future Democratic administrations.

events.title: OpenAI releases a new image classifier and ChatGPT warnings to combat CSAM
events.summary: OpenAI today announced new tools to combat child sexual abuse material (CSAM) amid growing safety concerns around the use of AI tools. These features include a new image classifier to detect CSAM, warnings and temporary blocks to prevent users from creating or accessing content that sexualizes children, a new guideline for developers, and a set of tools for law enforcement. The company unveiled a new image classifier that can detect CSAM images, including the ones generated by AI. OpenAI is giving select companies access to its classifier through its API at no cost. The tool looks for visual signs of abuse in images not seen before and assigns a score that can give an indicative direction to reviewers about dealing with CSAM. OpenAI said that it developed this classifier with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and it is working with Tech Coalition and ROOST to share access to the tool. In its early testing with partners, the AI company found that the classifier flags 48% fewer images while finding the same number of abusive images, reducing the work of reviewers. Plus, images flagged by the classifier are twice as likely to be abusive images. What’s more, the company is adding new warning screens in ChatGPT to prevent users from accessing material that sexualizes children. ChatGPT will show an alert to users attempting such prompts, direct users toward specialized support to stop harmful behavior, and also suspend the account for 24 hours as a warning. The app already blocks CSAM content and requests related to it. It said that repeated offences could lead to the account being removed permanently. OpenAI noted that it formed the message and guidelines around this behavior with organizations and researchers, including Protect Children , the Lucy Faithfull Foundation , and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial of deterrent messages. The company is also publishing guidelines for developers using OpenAI tools to prevent, detect, and help users report CSAM content. It said that in early testing, the guidelines have helped a number of developers adopt child safety tooling and register to report CSAM to NCMEC. OpenAI is also equipping law enforcement dealing with child safety with AI-powered features like dedicated plug-ins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. It is also providing training to investigators along with a field guide on how to use AI. OpenAI has had several lawsuits against the company blaming its technology for harming users, especially children. Safety-focused nonprofit Common Sense Media labeled OpenAI’s tech as “unacceptable risk” for teens. Other AI chatbots — specifically Grok — have been used to create nonconsensual sexualized imagery, including of children . The AI startup had made changes in the last 12 months to its technology, including releasing a safety blueprint , updating content guidelines to bar inappropriate content , retuning its model to prevent them from generating harmful content , and releasing a special version of ChatGPT for teens . events.title: More drops for Nvidia and other AI stocks drag the US market lower
events.summary: More drops for AI stocks are dragging the U.S. market lower, led by Nvidia NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — More drops for stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are dragging the U.S. market lower on Monday, led by Nvidia . The S & P 500 fell 1.1% and was on track for a third straight loss . The weakness for tech stocks pulled the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 1.6%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 289 points, or 0.6%, as of 11 a.m. Eastern time. Nvidia sank 2.5% and was again the heaviest weight on Wall Street following its crisis of leadership . Nvidia is one of the most influential companies in the world not only because its chips are powering much of the world’s move into AI technology but also because its cash has helped companies across the industry to grow. Now, following Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO last week, both the chip company and the broad industry are facing a more uncertain future without the leather-jacketed man who became one of AI’s biggest celebrities. It’s the latest challenge for the AI industry, which had already been shaky because of criticism that stock prices in the industry shot too high and were in a bubble. The sweeping victories for Democrats in this month’s U.S. midterm elections also raised worries about possible restrictions on further construction of AI data centers. “The market was already worried about this risk before what happened at Nvidia,” Zhiwei Zhang, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, said in a commentary. “Now the risk has become even more serious.” Outside of Nvidia, other chip companies also fell. They had climbed in the earlier days of Nvidia’s fall on hopes that they could gain a competitive advantage. But Broadcom dropped 3.8% and was on track for a second straight loss on concerns about the broader industry. So was Advanced Micro Devices, which fell 4.5%. CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and then rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, sank 5%. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centers, fell 3.3%. The next big milestone for the AI industry may arrive Tuesday after trading in the U.S. stock market ends for the day. That’s when Nvidia will report its latest quarterly results, and interim CEO Colette Kress is set to speak to Wall Street. Investors have become accustomed to Nvidia not only reporting stronger results than analysts expected for each quarter but also giving a forecast for upcoming revenue that’s well above expectations. Elsewhere on Wall Street, L3Harris Technologies fell 2.5% after officials in President Donald Trump’s administration suggested the contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration may be at fault for a nationwide ground stop Friday. L3Harris said Saturday that it’s supporting the FAA in its investigation. Summit Therapeutics sank 13.4% after the biopharmaceutical company said the U.S. Food and Drug Administration indicated it cannot approve its application for a therapy to treat certain patients with lung cancer. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Tyson Foods helped to limit the market’s losses and rose 7.5% after reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The company behind the Jimmy Dean and Hillshire Farm brands, though, also reported weaker revenue than expected after selling less beef than it did a year earlier. The recent swings for AI stocks have overshadowed what's been another strong earnings reporting season for U.S. companies. The big businesses in the S & P 500 index are on track to deliver earnings per share for the summer nearly 32% higher than a year earlier, according to FactSet. It's the third straight quarter of growth above 25% for the index, which is important because corporate profits are one of the two big levers that set stock prices over the long term, along with interest rates. In the bond market, Treasury yields eased back following last week's jump due to a worse-than-expected report on U.S. inflation . The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.13% from 5.15% late Friday, though it remains well above a low of 4.80% reached earlier this month. Higher yields make borrowing money more expensive for everyone, and they’ve already hurt the housing industry through expensive mortgage rates . Yields fell as oil prices sank, which took away some of the upward pressure on inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil fell 2.1% to $93.81. It’s been yo-yoing amid uncertainty about what will happen in the war with Iran. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi dropped 3.6%, and Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 2.4% for two of the world’s sharpest losses because of weakness for tech and AI-related stocks.
