events.title: We don't need no education platform evolution. Hey, Redmond, leave those kids alone
events.summary: "Give me the child until he is seven, and I will give you the man." This saying about the importance of influence in early education is variously attributed either to St Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Jesuits, or Aristotle, depending on whether you wanted to entrust your very young son to Catholic priests or ancient Greeks. Fortunately for both groups, perhaps, neither of them ever said that, even though both certainly believed it. Another group that certainly believes it is the cadre of tech company policy makers, which goes a long way to explain the cultural and legislative backlash to what happens to young people online. The least pernicious and longest established example of the catch 'em young principle is the educational discount for hardware and software. Apple has been the highest profile company to do this, with hardware discounts and aggressively positioned complete service packages for educational institutions, often integrated with funding authorities. If you grow up using a package or platform, it becomes your first tech language and you're likely to become a lifetime customer. Microsoft has also played this long game, seasoned where it can with curriculum integration. Its latest wheeze, described by the company as educational platform evolution is a response to institutions' changing needs, with clearer pathways to adopting and enabling new technologies. Yada, as we say, yada. The evolved platform removes email and Teams from the free student tier, while imposing the requirement for Windows hardware to qualify, along with comprehensive restructuring of higher tiers and storage not necessarily to the advantage of the educators. This is the same sort of evolution to evolving needs as the British Empire brought to natives of other lands. Hello, India. Greetings, Africa. Whassup, America! These warships packed with gun-toting Brits are here to evolve your changing needs in local resource management. Microsoft has realized what Imperial Great Britain adopted as its primary principle. If you can get your future, ahem, customers over a barrel, then not only can you imprint your brand on their minds, you can take their money. You have to come up with some balderdash to cover it, whether it's about civilization and progress or enabling educators to… oh God, these poor fingers can't even type this stuff. Missing completely is the idea that educators' evolving needs may not include spending even more money on basic necessary services when budgets are stretched tight. Moreover, while existing uses of the old tier can stay on it until the end of next year, new sign-ups have to be on the Enhanced Speedy plans. Keen students of history, especially those in the former colonial lands of Eastern North America, may care to refresh their memories of events some 250 years ago. It is quite natural, when being bent over a barrel ceases to be an amusing pastime, to seek a less barrel-shaped position. In this case, the pressure to find alternatives has many elements. As well as the cost, support for Macs and Chromebooks becomes problematic. Both platforms are heavily represented in education at various levels, with the Macbook Neo thundering onto the battlefield with colors flying. Add to that the pressure towards digital sovereignty in Microsoft's own colonial outposts, the accelerants for an Old World version of the Boston Tea Party are only building. We even have a Boston of our very own . It's very nice. Microsoft isn't threatening anyone with guns and rapine, not yet anyway, and the whipping away of free student access to email and Teams only feels like extortion because of the misery it is causing across the sector. It is perfectly legal for Microsoft to cause as much suffering coated in balderdash as it likes. It is also perfectly legal to return the favor by actively seeking a sector-wide migration strategy. There are pioneers to learn from, especially huge multi-state, multi-supply chain organizations like Airbus and the various European governmental entities that are some way down that path already. This growing pool of expertise may be the most important factor in being able to react to Microsoft's efforts to turn education into a science fair experiment in high velocity frog boiling — one where the frog most definitely feels the heat — that and the growing distaste for the antics of American big tech. It's not just the forcing of unwanted technology that makes the barrel increasingly unbearable, nor using that as an excuse to charge more, it's what the companies are actually trying to do in Europe. Google Chromebooks are nice. Google wolves invading your villages because the company illegally erased their ecosystem are not nice. You thought those Wi-Fi snooping Maps cars were bad? The Microsoft educational platform "evolution" is foolhardy, counterproductive, and hugely tone deaf. It will not make it new lifetime customers, it will increase the speed at which its already hostile constituency grows resentment and appetite for radical action. Colonies revolt when the time is right, and empires are lost when arrogance and under-estimation of the situation combine with mismanagement and strategic blindness. The US midterms showed how that storm is blowing in. To choose this time to provoke an entire global sector is functional illiteracy writ large. Perhaps Microsoft should get an education. ®

events.title: Mubadala and Centerbridge to acquire UK's Canaccord Wealth
events.summary: Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund Mubadala Investment Company and US-based Centerbridge Partners have agreed to acquire UK-based Canaccord Wealth in an all-cash transaction. The transaction , which involves Canaccord Genuity’s wealth management business in the UK and Crown Dependencies, gives the business an enterprise value of approximately £1.17 billion ($1.54 billion), Mubadala said in a statement on Monday. Canaccord Wealth provides investment management and financial planning services to private clients, with £43.4 billion in assets under management and administration as of June 30. “We see significant opportunity in a market where growing wealth and increasing financial complexity are driving demand for expert advice,” said Yasir Badri, executive director of financial services at Mubadala. The transaction is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to closing conditions and regulatory approvals. Once completed, Mubadala and Centerbridge will jointly own Canaccord Wealth, with the existing management team retaining a “meaningful” ownership interest. “The UK wealth management sector continues to benefit from powerful structural tailwinds, as demand for high quality, personalised financial advice grows alongside increasing complexity in clients’ financial needs,” said Ben Langworthy, senior managing director and head of Europe at Centerbridge. Canaccord Wealth's assets under management and revenue have nearly tripled over the past decade, the statement said. The investment by Mubadala and Centerbridge will support the business’s next phase of growth, it added. Mubadala, which invests on behalf of the Abu Dhabi government, has been steadily expanding its global investment portfolio with a focus on sectors including renewables, mobility, advanced technology, artificial intelligence and life science. Last year, it reported a 17 per cent annual rise in assets to $385 billion, with its portfolio spanning six continents across asset classes. Last month, Mubadala's chief financial officer said it planned to maintain its annual investment with a focus on Asia. “Last year, we invested about $39 billion, which is roughly 10 per cent of our portfolio, and our aim is to continue doing that through all cycles. Every year, we want to deploy that same amount,” Carlos Obeid told the Milken Institute Asia Summit in Singapore. In September, Mubadala announced a significant minority investment in Chinese coffee chain Luckin Coffee alongside its controlling shareholder, Centurium Capital, in a deal worth about $1 billion.

events.title: The next customer brands need to win over isn’t human—and it doesn’t care how big your company is
events.summary: Tati Lindenberg has a challenge on her hands. As global CMO of Unilever’s homecare division, she’s made her name by marketing to humans—often by playing on senses and emotions. But soon, she’ll need to market to a different kind of customer—one that doesn’t feel, sense, or care how big your company is. That is the AI agent.   “The store, online or offline, has always been where the decision is made. The AI answer is becoming a new kind of shelf,” says Lindenberg. “In that world, a brand needs to be recognised, trusted and preferred by people and by machines.” In the U.K., 52% of shoppers have used AI for at least one shopping task in the past three months, according to McKinsey research. In China—where adoption of AI is more advanced—that figure rises to 80%. The power of agents in decision-making is growing. Currently, most consumers use AI to conduct research and will make the ultimate decision on what to buy themselves. But soon, a substantial number could trust agents to handle the entire process. Mastercard forecasts that one in 10 people will routinely use AI agents to shop and pay by 2030. Meta’s personal AI agent Muse, which is capable of researching products and making purchases, is expected to launch in the U.K. “within weeks.” Purchases of Unilever’s beauty, wellbeing, and home care products are more likely to be delegated to AI, according to Nick Carroll, Mintel’s retail principal strategist. “In general, consumers are most interested in automating those less emotive and most regularly purchased categories,” he says. Mintel data shows household products are most ripe for disruption; 41% of consumers would feel comfortable automating these purchases. Unilever isn’t the only company harnessing AI in the purchasing process. At the start of the year, JD Sports unveiled new tech that allows U.S. shoppers to make purchases using platforms such as Microsoft Copilot, Google’s Gemini, and ChatGPT in a single click. Similarly, John Lewis announced “a significant investment”in AI-powered shopping in March to ensure its products appear on those same platforms.  When AI becomes a customer The increased use of AI agents by consumers has quickly become a topic of boardroom discussion. Nearly half (47%) of consumer products executives  surveyed by EY  believe the ability to influence AI recommendations will be essential to remain competitive over the next five years. But only 20% believe they can deliver on that objective today.  If companies don’t bridge that capability gap, there will be swift and material consequences. As EY points out, only 10% of consumers need to shift their behavior to make a significant impact on revenue and profits. The lack of confidence in this area reflects the complexity of the task at hand. AI agents work in a fundamentally different way to search engines, and little is known about their algorithms, with many  viewing them as a ‘black box.’ What’s more, consumers are asking far more detailed queries than they would have asked traditional search. “A normal Google search is 3.2 words on average,” says Fredrik Kridahl, founder of AI search consultancy Hyper Agency. “An average query on an average prompt is 91 words.” Perhaps most importantly, major brands don’t have the same automatic advantage as they do with Google. Kridahl points to research showing only 38% of URLs cited by AI rank in the top 10 for regular search engines and 31% rank outside the top 100. “AI doesn’t care about how big your company is,” he says. “It cares about the facts and giving the right advice.” Marketing to machines Consumer adoption of AI is contributing to a major shift in marketing strategy. Very Group digital director Sarah Hanna says AI search currently accounts for less than 2% of all traffic to its site. But she’s aware that figure will soon grow.  “Getting in front of AI agents is set to become just as important as traditional SEO,” she says. “Retailers need to ensure their product information is accurate, detailed and structured so AI can understand, recommend and compare their products effectively.” JD Sports is doing similar work behind the scenes. Chief technology and transformation officer Jetan Chowk says the brand is working to ensure its offer is “visible, accessible and accurately represented” online. “We’ve been investing in our digital infrastructure to support this, making it easier for AI platforms to access up-to-date product information, pricing, and availability,” he says. “Getting in front of AI agents is set to become just as important as traditional SEO.” Sarah Hanna, digital director, Very Group This is all part of what Steven Bailey, EY Americas commercial excellence leader, terms the “unglamorous” work of marketing to bots. “You need to be clear on price, promotion, product, persona, who is this for, and then differentiation and characteristics,” he says. “That has to be encoded and machine-readable in a way that maybe it didn’t before.” Positive reviews on retailer sites and on social media are another vital component. If an agent sees a product is well rated, it will feel more confident recommending that option to a user. “We optimize metadata, product pages, and community platforms such as Reddit, so our brands surface correctly when people ask natural questions,” says Lindenberg. “If someone asks, ‘I need a quick clean up, what detergent should I use?’, we want Persil Wonder Wash to be in that answer, for the right reasons.” Human connection still matters All this back-end activity could be interpreted as a death knell for the more emotional marketing campaign. After all, an AI agent won’t be moved by initiatives such as the latest Dirt is Good campaign by Unilever, which focuses on ending period stigma in sport. Nor will it feel motivated by the ‘create the new’ call to action in this year’s JD Sports Christmas ad. Yet experts believe this activity is, if anything, more important than before. EY’s Bailey still sees a clear place for “romance copy” in the agentic commerce era. “AI is rewarding things that are machine-readable, but it’s also a shining light on where you have gaps,” he says. “What this also means is that trust and humanness now become worth even more, because they are differentiators.” Consumers still value brands that forge an emotional connection, Bailey adds. Not only does that inform their choices when they use AI for research, but shoppers are also far more likely to allow AI to automate purchases from these trusted brands.  “The danger is optimizing so hard for algorithms that we lose the distinctiveness that makes a brand worth choosing.” Tati Lindenberg, Global CMO, Unilever home care Even outside of creative campaigns, that distinctive voice and human element remains vital. Online descriptions need to “make the emotional and experiential dimensions more understandable to AI”, says Kathryn Gramling,

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Travellers face delays and cancellations at Sydney Airport due to cloud and wind activity Airlines are working to minimise disruptions to passengers. ( ABC News: Billy Cooper ) Airline travellers have experienced major delays at Sydney Airport due to severe weather conditions, with 104 flight cancellations recorded on Monday night Wind and cloud activity had impacted flights to and from Sydney Airport, with the bulk of cancellations affecting domestic routes. In a statement, an Airservices Australia spokesperson confirmed the delays, recommending passengers check with their airline for flight updates. "Aircraft delays are being experienced in Sydney today with factors including cloud and wind affecting air traffic operations," they said. "Airservices is working with industry to safely manage air traffic demand throughout the day." Wind and cloud activity had impacted flights to and from Sydney Airport. ( ABC News: Billy Cooper ) There was also Virgin Australia ground crew industrial action related to pay and working conditions that took place on Monday. A Virgin Australia spokesperson said there were a number of "contingencies in place" to ensure the industrial action did not impact operations or passengers' travel. The airline was working to minimise the weather-related disruption to guests. Qantas has also experienced disruptions and cancellations across their network. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) A Qantas spokesperson said the adverse weather had resulted in a ground delay program being put in place by Airservices Australia, affecting all airlines. "[This] has caused disruptions and cancellations across our network. A small number of services were cancelled overnight in preparation for the ground delay program," the spokesperson said. "Customers were contacted directly and re-accommodated on alternate flights within 24 hours of their original booking." The airline was working to up-gauge some aircraft to increase capacity and recover cancelled flights. Toula Vorinos's Virgin flight to Melbourne was due to depart Sydney at 10am this morning before it was cancelled. At 8pm she was still waiting at the airport, and had managed to secure a seat on a Jetstar flight leaving at 9:15pm. "We got a notification when we got off the boat on the way to the airport ... and we've been waiting since literally 7:20 this morning," she said. Toula Vorinos's flight was due to leave Sydney at 10am but was cancelled. ( ABC News: Nabil Al-Nashar ) Brownwyn Jackson from the Sunshine Coast was struggling to get accommodation near the airport after the cancellation of her connecting flight to Hobart. "So, have been trying for the past two hours to get another flight that didn't happen, so now trying to get accommodation and an alternative flight tomorrow [Tuesday] hopefully," she said. "I've got accommodation in Hobart booked for a week, so it's quite a waste of money as well, plus the extra night tonight, so very frustrating." Ms Jackson said she received no notice about the disruption, and found out from another passenger when she went to check-in. Barbara Evans is staying in Sydney until she gets a flight home to Launceston. ( ABC News: Nabil Al-Nashar ) Barbara Evans got notified that her evening flight to Launceston was not going ahead while at the airport. She had arrived three hours prior to departure, and has since been trying to work on alternatives to get home. "I can't get down there even via Melbourne tonight. I can't do it on Jetstar tomorrow, I can't do it direct on Virgin tomorrow," she said. "I could do it by going to the Gold Coast and then the Gold Coast to Adelaide … it's totally crazy. Aidan Osmani told the ABC it was "frustrating" after his flight to Brisbane for a work trip was cancelled, and his rescheduled flight was going to the Gold Coast. He had been waiting at the airport for more than an hour-and-a-half. "It is what it is, and just have to be patient and wait," he said.

events.title: What Is Acoustic Micro Imaging? A Quick Guide To This Inspection Process
events.summary: We all know how important inspection is for advanced packaging. Not only are these processes critical for ensuring higher yield, but they’re also integral for maintaining device reliability. As the industry pushes for smaller features and tighter spacing, even the smallest defects can pose major challenges. For instance, delaminations and air gaps can be detrimental in a market that demands increasingly complex devices. Such defects will lead to electrical or mechanical failures down the road. One technology that’s mitigating these issues is acoustic micro imaging (AMI). AMI is a high-frequency ultrasound technology, and it’s being used by the industry as an inspection method. How AMI works At the core of AMI technology is a transducer, or a device that turns energy from one form to another. It starts with a pulse of electrical energy, then converts it to mechanical energy, or a high-frequency ultrasound wave. Because ultrasound doesn’t travel through air, this allows inspectors to obtain clear images of gaps and delaminations in the device that could otherwise be difficult to see. However, the transducers used for AMI are not all the same. Each transducer handles a specific frequency, and they’re chosen based on the sample that needs to be inspected. By moving the transducer across the sample, the inspector can generate multiple images that can then be analyzed by the AMI software. Through this analysis, the inspector can choose to accept or reject parts based on the number of defects the package is found to have. So, how do these defects typically present themselves? The biggest difference between ideal and defective samples is that some defective samples will have very clear air gaps. However, another common defect is thinning of the attach material on solder pads. When this material is too thin, any stress that would be put on the device could lead to delamination. An uneven solder or thermal interface material (TIM) layer may also indicate a larger problem with the build process. When to use AMI – inspection, destructive testing, and X-rays With the ability to gather so much information without damaging the device, why would anyone choose to perform a destructive test to identify a defect, rather than simply use AMI inspection to check for them? One reason is for R&D purposes. Oftentimes, companies want to ensure that a process is fully developed before integrating it into their production cycle, and a destructive test can confirm proof of concept for AMI. An example of this in action is a standard capacitor inspection. New capacitor companies will often require a destructive test to confirm the presence of voids or delaminations found by the AMI software. Once the destructive proof of concept has been completed, the company can then integrate the software into their inspection process. There are some key differences between AMI and its transmission technology counterpart, which is more comparable to X-ray. Whereas AMI is an ultrasound technology, transmission scanning uses both a sending and receiving transducer positioned above and below the sample. Both transmission technology and X-ray create composite images, unlike AMI, which inspects layer-by-layer. Ultrasound and X-ray are complementary technologies. There are some things AMI can do that X-ray can’t, and vice versa. For certain applications, both technologies may be recommended. For example, composite images are preferable for inspecting spherical objects like ball grid arrays. The challenges and future of AMI Although AMI technology has tangible benefits, keeping up with the industry’s rapid pace is a hurdle that AMI must continually overcome. As applications become more complex, AMI software needs to quickly adapt to changing components. For instance, instead of scanning a single flip chip, AMI software could now be required to inspect multi-die stacks. One way this mounting complexity is being addressed is through machine learning algorithms. For example, some wafers have via patterns that look similar or identical to delamination, and humans have typically been responsible for distinguishing them. However, through advancements in machine learning, AMI software can now identify via patterns and exclude those from the defect count. As machine learning becomes more robust, it will open new doors for inspecting increasingly complicated devices. In addition, customer requirements for higher resolution and better throughput are also driving new developments for AMI software. To meet these rising demands, Nordson Test & Inspection developed its automated SpinSAM tool that can inspect four 300mm wafers at a time. Traditionally, acoustic microscopy systems move the transducer in a raster pattern, which is a small grid made up of individual pixels. This approach allows inspectors to collect data at every XY point, but it also requires decelerating to turn the transducer at the end of each line, thereby reducing throughput. Some acoustic microscopes address the need for better throughput by skipping lines and interpolating data points, or by using multiple transducers and stitching images together – both of which have their own drawbacks. In contrast, SpinSAM spins the wafer to move the transducer and the wafer continuously, allowing inspectors to scan each pixel faster, allowing for better throughput without image stitching distortion. The post What Is Acoustic Micro Imaging? A Quick Guide To This Inspection Process appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering .

events.title: Are AI Agents The New Semiconductor IP?
events.summary: Key Takeaways: AI agents could make customized design workflows faster and less expensive to develop. Multi-agent systems introduce new challenges for orchestration, verification, and tool integration. Consumption-based pricing could reshape EDA business models, but trust and proprietary data remain obstacles. AI agents are emerging as a new category of reusable design capability, but with a twist. Rather than providing tightly defined design blocks, agents can be used to explore different options, integrate them, and use those changes to improve designs. At the leading edge, soft IP developers have been customizing their code for large customers for more than a decade to boost performance and/or reduce power. But that customization is typically narrow and costly, and optimizations for one design may not directly transfer to derivative chips — especially multi-die assemblies at the leading edge. Agents, in contrast, can be used to customize different functions with little or no human intervention, and they can self-optimize for different workloads and use cases, and some agents can even adjust for aging hardware. And they can do all of this much faster than a human, even though an experienced engineering team is needed to verify those results and recommendations. “We have in-house specialized AI agents to do different things, to do spec analysis, RTL generation for design, for formal and functional verification, and then CDC linking, and place-and-route,” said William Wang, CEO of ChipAgents . “We provide our optimized agents to a customer, and sometimes a customer builds their own AI agent. But there are some similarities with the IP business. Sometimes we’re specifically building an agent for one customer for a particular flow, which is similar to what happens in the IP business. What’s different is that we can do it in a very short amount of time. With IP, you need 10 months. Our cycle is much shorter because AI agents are very easy to customize. In some cases we can give solutions to the customer the same day.” Those solutions still need to be verified and debugged. But the ability to sort through many different options quickly is an attractive formula, especially with rapid evolution of AI. “I draw parallels to the early 2000s gigahertz wars, where all of a sudden everything was multicore,” said Mo Faisal, CEO of Movellus . “Now we’ve gone from,’ Everything is going to be a GPU,’ to ‘Oh, no, it’s CPUs and GPUs, and this is a one-to-one ratio.’ So effectively we’re going through the same architectural churn that we go through every 10 to 15 years.” The business of agents Business models still need to solidify around agents. but they also need to be flexible enough to evolve at the same pace as the technology. “If you look at how the EDA industry has evolved, we’re not selling perpetual licenses anymore,” said Rob Knoth, senior group director of Strategy & New Ventures at Cadence . “We moved to time-based licenses many years ago. Now we see similar things as agents roll around. They’re hitting up the tool usage even more because they want to find answers quickly, and they’re trying lots of experiments. So putting together more of a consumption-based model is really good because customers know how to use that.” This isn’t a simple transition, though. While the promise of agents is significant, their adoption in chip design will take time. In addition, security and permissions aren’t always well-defined. “There are some things where you’d really rather sell an agent than sell the software,” said Wally Rhines, CEO of Silvaco . “People are trying to figure out if anybody in EDA is actually pricing based upon tokens rather than traditional pricing models. It doesn’t seem like anyone is, but their customers are all talking about it. I’m very much open to selling an agent that will automate [manufacturing equipment] calibration, then jump back to my store of synthetic simulated data against the physical data. We don’t get to see the physical data, but we do know how many tokens our agents consumed. It’s a way that EDA can sell a product, get the benefit, and no one ever sees the underlying data that companies want to keep proprietary.” Divide and conquer, but with caveats One of the big changes with the shift from generative AI to agentic AI is the need for orchestration, and this has broad business implications. Orchestration is basically a blueprint that defines how tasks are assigned, how agents access tools and data, and how that work is coordinated. But it’s especially challenging if multiple agents execute at the same time and their actions overlap. “What’s different about traditional AI and agentic AI is the coordination of multiple agents that are working in parallel, but doing different types of work,” said Robbie Williamson, vice president of customer engineering for cloud AI at Arm . “It’s not like there’s a unique workload that we haven’t seen before. It’s more about how do you coordinate all of these at the CPU level, and have enough bandwidth, memory, etc., to do all of this at scale. Instead of an individual making a request and driving AI, we have computers that can do it much faster. The transition that we see when we talk to hyperscalers is now about what they need from the CPU. With training, that wasn’t as important because you’re just batching the job and waiting for it to come back.” That creates a new hierarchy in the design flow. “What has happened with this multi-agent workflow is that, in an organization, you’re trying to design a chip,” said Prith Banerjee, senior vice president of innovation at Synopsys . “When they’re having a problem with the PPA, some engineers say they know exactly what changes to make to lower the power. They’ll do clock gating. But when you clock gate power, then it changes something else. It increases the area. So some area will come in — and this is exactly what happens in the real world with coordination when multiple people come together to design a system. events.title: The resignation of Jensen Huang marks the end of an era. And not the one you think
events.summary: Just days after the American electorate delivered a sweeping midterm rebuke that materially curtailed Donald Trump’s presidential power, the independent board of Nvidia— the world’s most valuable firm for much of the year—launched an investigation into its own CEO, Jensen Huang. The board’s focus was Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. His resignation swiftly followed. In less than a week, we witnessed the core machinery of accountability brought to bear on two of the most powerful men in the world. But while the midterm outcome is being heralded as a resounding revival of healthy democracy, the Nvidia example should not be mistaken for a corporate oversight renaissance. Instead, Nvidia’s boardroom intervention may mark the end of a governance era, especially when it comes to frontier AI firms. Nvidia has a single-class share structure, meaning the CEO—who has a minority of votes at under 4% —remains accountable to an independent board. Elsewhere however, the governance guardrails for other powerful tech executives are rapidly eroding—a dismantling revealed in IPO filings—just as these companies amass unprecedented global influence. SpaceX and Anthropic’s recent filings disclose that post IPO, their founders have a majority of shareholder votes via multi-class share structures , dual-class for SpaceX, and a novel five-class system for Anthropic. Popularized by Alphabet and Meta , this shields them from short-term market pressures, and the appeal is clear: in the U.S., a record 36% of new listings in the first half of 2026 had dual-class shares. Yet by insulating the founders, ordinary shareholders lose any real say over major decisions, leaving traditional corporate accountability resting in the hands of insiders. Both companies also took advantage of stock exchange rules for ‘controlled companies.’ This allowed SpaceX to skip requirements for an independent board and gave Anthropic leeway to bypass standard rules for how its board members are chosen. Musk can only be removed from the board or his executive positions by the vote of Class B holders, of which he personally holds approximately 91.6%. To be fired, he would have to vote to fire himself. Anthropic’s novel approach features a Long-Term Benefit Trust—whose members appoint their own successors—that chooses a majority of the board. The co-founders hold 50.1% of the votes on all other matters, including appointing the rest of the board. Anthropic argues that the structure is designed to prioritize AI safety. But is also cements the power of the founders and the trust, leaving everyday public investors with no voting leverage to hold the board accountable to either the profit motive or the public benefit mandate. SpaceX has gone a step further by relocating its corporate domicile to Texas, where the law sets a much higher bar for minority shareholders to legally challenge the board in court. The state imposes a 3% shareholding requirement, which equates to over $50 billion in SpaceX stock. Taken together, these mechanisms represent a dismantling of the corporate governance levers meant to protect shareholders and society when things go wrong. And while OpenAI has yet to file, the swift 2023 reinstatement of its CEO—and the subsequent departure of several independent directors—demonstrates the sheer leverage already wielded by those at the helm. In recent months, advanced AI agents from frontier labs have broken past security controls, accessed external systems and carried out unauthorized cyber actions. As these early AI risks begin to materialize, questions about which corporate structures are best equipped to ensure AI safety and security, along with whether and how to regulate AI, are fast becoming matters of pressing public concern. This is a pivotal moment. At the industry level, current and forthcoming IPOs look set to ‘bake in’ higher-risk corporate governance arrangements, while state jurisdictions are actively exploring legal frameworks for agentic AI organizations that legitimize the complete absence of human oversight altogether. The rapid advance of frontier AI may feel inevitable, bringing boundless potential alongside incomprehensible risks. Yet in the race to build our automated future, these firms are strategically layering available federal, state, and market levers to consolidate control. Regulatory exemptions that might be appropriate in isolation to help startups scale are being combined by AI giants to escape oversight at the exact moment we need it most. No individual is infallible—whether vulnerable to error, hubris, or compromise—which is precisely why corporate guardrails are needed to mitigate the hazards of concentrated power. Politically, there is great impetus for action. American voters have just demonstrated the power of institutions that allow people to hold their leaders to account. The lawmakers they have elected must ensure that frontier AI companies cannot engineer that accountability away. Investors may choose to accept founders’ terms. The rest of us have not agreed to accept the risks. events.title: Abu Dhabi’s Al Ain Asset Management and Emaar team up for Dh8 billion projects
events.summary: Abu Dhabi’s Al Ain Asset Management is teaming up with Emaar Hospitality to launch five property projects worth Dh8 billion ($2.17 billion) in Abu Dhabi amid continued demand for property in the emirate. The first project, consisting of 452 apartment units and some penthouses, will be built on Al Maryah Island , according to its group chief executive. Timelines and locations of other projects were not disclosed. The five projects will be built in an area spanning 4.7 million square feet, with Al Maryah Island project to be built in one million square feet. The starting price for a one-bedroom home will be Dh3.7 million and “sales will begin very soon,” Rabih Karam told The National. “It’s a standalone project in one of the most strategic areas of Al Maryah Island, directly connected to the mall, ADGM and Cleveland Clinic,” he said. The launch of the new projects comes as demand for property remains strong in the emirate, despite Iran-war-driven uncertainty. A total of 38,483 property transactions worth Dh171.26 billion were registered in Abu Dhabi in the first nine months of 2026, marking a 76.1 per cent increase in value and a 32.8 per cent rise in volume on an annual basis, according to data from the Abu Dhabi Real Estate Centre. A growing number of companies are setting up their base at the ADGM, boosting demand for property in and around the international financial centre, including Reem Island. Reem Island recorded the highest transaction value at Dh29.86 billion during the period, followed by Al Hudayriyat Island (Dh28.62 billion), Al Saadiyat Island (Dh18.69 billion), Yas Island (Dh13.4 billion) and Zayed City (Dh5.36 billion), ADREC data shows. Assets under management at ADGM grew 54 per cent annually in the first six months of 2026, with 49,027 professionals now based at Al Maryah Island and Reem Island, an increase of 34 per cent on the same period last year. “Demand has been amazing in Abu Dhabi. We are witnessing it in our other projects that we are selling currently," Mr Karam said. The company sold two mansions for Dh350 million each in one of its developments on Saadiyat Island this summer, he added. He, however, did not say who bought these villas, but he said, “these are profile of people that they can choose to be any place in the world, and they are choosing to be in UAE and in Abu Dhabi”. The privately owned company is chaired by Sheikh Hamdan bin Zayed. The latest partnership with Emaar follows the launch of Address Beach Resort and Residences in Dubai in JBR by the two companies in 2016, Mr Karam said. The collaboration has since expanded with the launch of Vida Residences Saadiyat Island, which introduced the Vida brand to Abu Dhabi for the first time. The company did not disclose how it planned to fund the new developments. Emaar is looking forward to introducing more of its hospitality brands to Abu Dhabi, Mohamed Alabbar, founder and managing director of Emaar, said in a statement on Monday.

events.title: AIX investors urged to register claims before creditors' meeting in December
events.summary: Investors in AIX Investment Group's liquidated unit have been urged to register their claims by December 4, as its liquidators plan to hold the first creditors' meeting four days later. AIX Secure SPV, the Cayman-registered issuer of fixed-income notes linked to Dubai-based AIX Investment Group, was placed into liquidation on October 30 by the Grand Court of the Cayman Islands. The court appointed Angela Barkhouse of Kroll (Cayman) and Michael Byrne of Kroll Middle East Consultancy in the Dubai International Financial Centre as joint official liquidators. Claims must be filed online through the liquidation website, said law firm ALBM Excello Law, whose clients were among the creditors who supported the winding-up petition, in a statement on Monday. The firm is helping AIX investors file claims, appoint proxies and put forward members for the liquidation committee. “Many AIX investors are based in the UAE, and the liquidators have been authorised by the Cayman Islands Court to pursue proceedings before the DIFC Courts and the Dubai courts,” said Sujith Mathew, partner at ALBM Excello Law. “We will continue to monitor developments and keep investors informed as the liquidation progresses.” What went wrong AIX Secure SPV, which was registered in the Cayman Islands on December 9, 2022, was established to issue debt notes to raise funds for investment activities, either directly or through affiliated entities. However, investors alleged that AIX Secure SPV failed to make interest payments when due and filed claims against them. According to the Financial Times , investors have filed claims seeking to recover about $10 million, including two individual claims for almost $2 million and $8 million. The company reportedly suspended payments to thousands of investors after promising annual returns of up to 30 per cent. AIX on its website said that “a period of exceptional geopolitical uncertainty and significant volatility across global financial markets has affected valuations and investment realisation cycles within a limited part of AIX’s product offering”. Last month, the UAE's Capital Market Authority said it was reviewing AIX Financial Consultations' activities after receiving information that the company had delayed or even missed payouts. Without disclosing the details of the information it received or the nature of the review, the CMA said it would keep the matter confidential to ensure a thorough, fair and impartial assessment. Following the Cayman Islands ruling, AIX said it had written to its investors directly, explaining why it was proposing a restructuring rather than a forced sale of assets in the current market conditions. “AIX intends to apply to the court for a stay of the order within the period permitted, and will ask the court to consider in full the alternative to liquidation presented to investors in October,” it said on November 4. Steps for investors The liquidators have “determined that AIX Secure SPV should be treated as insolvent, so the liquidation committee must have between three and five creditors”, the latest statement said. While late claims will still be accepted, those creditors may be shut out of the meeting. “A claim admitted for voting is not yet admitted for payment; the liquidators will assess claims for distribution later,” it added. The liquidators have also asked investors not to visit their offices. According to the letter to creditors, nominations for the liquidation committee close on November 26. Submission of claim information for voting, notice of attendance and proxy forms are due by December 4. The creditors’ meeting will be held virtually on December 8. The committee will advise the liquidators on strategy and approve the basis of their fees.

events.title: Techie rigged off-spec fan near flammable liquid and an exposed motherboard, then left it to run for days
events.summary: If you've made mistakes at work that threatened to torch your career, The Register has just the column for you. We call it Who, Me? , we print one every Monday, and you're reading this week's instalment! Today, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Axl" who once worked at a petrol station (aka a gas station for US readers). One Friday afternoon, in the shadow of a holiday weekend, the PC that drove the station's pumps and point of sale stopped working, leaving it unable to operate. Axl called the manufacturer and got the very unwelcome news that a technician could visit on Tuesday at the earliest. As the petrol station was in a spot that would attract a few weekend tourists, the potential losses were substantial, and Axl felt he needed to act. He knew the main computer lived inside a large metal box affixed to a wall, an arrangement that meant electronics and flammable vapors were always kept well apart. The machine's power switch was accessible, so Axl turned it off and on again – and watched the machine come back to life, before shutting itself down five minutes later. That behavior was a strong hint that something was overheating but confirming that theory was not easy because the metal case included a lock (see previous remarks about preventing fires) and Axl didn't have they key. Axl inspected the hinges on the box, found they were held on with screws and was able to remove the lid and access the PC. "Aside from the considerable amount of dust and hair inside, I could see that the CPU fan was not turning," he wrote. "Either it had failed or was not receiving the control signal to cool." The service station had an office out the back. Axl liberated a desk fan, pointed it at the PC, and watched it come alive again. An hour later, the PC was still working, so Axl decided he needed a fix that would last the weekend. "I drove to a local electrical shop and purchased a high speed bathroom extraction fan which I rigged up inside the case, then closed it up best I could with tape and cardboard," he told The Register . That rickety rig kept fuel flowing for three days. "On Tuesday afternoon, the support engineer arrived and I explained how I kept us in business over the weekend," Axl wrote. "He just shrugged his shoulders, smiled and changed the failed fan. I didn't even get the 'It's our kit, leave it alone' lecture." He did get the satisfaction of a job well done. "No one died from an exploding petrol station and the tourists were happy they could go home," he wrote. Have you made a risky fix in a dangerous place? If so, the safe option is to click here and send your story to Who, Me? We promise to handle it with care and hopefully share it on some future Monday. ®

events.title: Gas starts flowing from Jackdaw after government green light
events.summary: The Jackdaw platform is located 150 miles east of Aberdeen Gas has begun flowing from the Jackdaw gas field, with the UK energy secretary saying it will help to heat millions of homes and businesses this winter. Ministers last month announced the Jackdaw field, which lies 150 miles east of Aberdeen, had been approved after years of uncertainty and a court case. It has now been announced that it has begun producing gas which will start flowing into Britain, according to its operator Adura. The UK government approved production from the gas field in the North Sea last month, amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact. Miliband says he won't resign if government approves Rosebank oil field Published 22 hours ago Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences Published 21 October Jackdaw is operated by Adura under a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor. A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: "Last month, I gave Jackdaw the green light and today its gas will start flowing into Britain, thanks to the hard work of the skilled North Sea workers. "It means homegrown gas from this project will help to heat millions of British homes and businesses this winter and beyond, in a boost for our energy security. "It also will help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission gas as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear." Claire Mueller, Jackdaw project director at Adura, said the gas field was "now helping to power Britain". She added: "At a time of considerable uncertainty around the world, Jackdaw will provide secure energy from our own waters to heat British homes and power our economy, while reducing our reliance on imports with higher emissions. "Jackdaw also demonstrates what can be achieved when Britain makes pragmatic, evidence-led decisions about the energy it needs, while properly accounting for our climate responsibilities." Mueller said the decision was a "positive step towards restoring confidence in the North Sea". She added that Adura was "proud to be producing the oil and gas our country will continue to need for decades". Why is the Jackdaw gas field approval so controversial? Adura has said Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand. The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing – known as a tie-back in industry terms – before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire. The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy. The timeline of Jackdaw and Rosebank The decision to green-light Jackdaw drew criticism from some Labour backbenchers and environmentalists, while Conservatives called on the government to also approve the Rosebank oil field. Both projects were approved for development by the previous Tory government in 2022 and 2023 respectively but these decisions were struck down by the Scottish courts after a challenge from environmental campaigners. This followed a Supreme Court ruling that developers had to account for the climate impact caused by burning fossil fuels in their planning applications. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to stick to the UK's net zero target despite giving the green light to Jackdaw. He previously said the decision would "significantly strengthen our energy security by increasing domestic gas production by about 6% and support the UK's energy supply for more than a decade". A decision on the larger Rosebank oil project is yet to be made. Protesters gathered outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero in Westminster on Wednesday morning The co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the Jackdaw approval as "climate vandalism". He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now." Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank. Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change. Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify". The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.

events.title: India feels less threatened by AI than the US, official says
events.summary: Indians see AI as less of a threat than people in the US because fewer workers hold the “cognitive and office-oriented jobs” that the technology could replace, one of the country’s top tech officials said. Young Indians are drawn to technology and see AI as a way to raise productivity, reduce poverty, and help India become a developed country within two decades, S Krishnan, secretary of India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. The gains, he predicts, could touch sectors such as agriculture, education, healthcare, and government. Krishnan told Semafor Deputy Editor-in-Chief Shelly Banjo that AI tools could help advise farmers with the expertise that’s only available to the largest companies, or screen chest X-rays for tuberculosis to enhance the productivity of the stressed healthcare sector. With around 6 million people in IT and related services, Krishnan said India has the workforce that can diffuse the technology throughout the economy. But the constraint, shared in many countries, is that “AI compute is still in short supply and expensive.” Krishnan said India and the US were “pretty close” to a trade deal, with one or two issues left to resolve. “We’d prefer to have it by yesterday, but, yes, as quickly as we can,” he said. Asked about a potential bilateral visit between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and US President Donald Trump, which hasn’t happened in Trump’s second term, he said: “Well, I think they still share a very good relationship.” — J.D. events.title: Microsoft’s Azure Linux dons Fedora to dress itself up for mainstream workloads
events.summary: Microsoft has issued version 4.0 of its very own Azure Linux, which it built atop Fedora for the first time and now suggests is ready to run mainstream workloads. Redmond’s history with Linux is long and tangled. Former CEO Steve Ballmer infamously labelled the project a cancer but by 2015 Microsoft had quietly adapted the OS to power some switches in its Azure Cloud. Microsoft then built some of its own Azure services on containers and created a lightweight Linux for them to run in. In 2020, Microsoft released that Linux as CBL-Mariner, largely so that developers who used services like Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) that relied on the OS could access the platform they were building for. In 2022, CBL-Mariner became Azure Linux 2.0, another container-centric lightweight release. Version 3.0 followed in 2024, now billed as ready for “broad Azure usage” with Azure Kubernetes Service. In June 2026, Microsoft announced version 4.0 and billed it as suitable for Azure Virtual Machines, VM Scale Sets, and container images. The big change that made that repositioning possible was basing the OS on Fedora rather than Microsoft’s own Common Base Linux. Microsoft also tuned the Linux kernel – version 6.18 LTS – by adding Hyper-V guest drivers and other features that make it behave well in Azure. It also natively supports tools like Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Azure Monitor, and the Azure CLI, which Microsoft reckons committed Azure users already employ and therefore want to apply to their cloudy Linux workloads. Or as Redmond puts it: “the familiarity of [the] RPM package ecosystem, while adding Azure-native security, compliance, and operational capabilities.” All of those changes add up to an OS that Microsoft says is worth a look “Whether you're running web applications, databases, or GPU-accelerated AI/ML workloads.” Redmond makes that recommendation in part because Azure Linux comes with “no additional OS licensing cost.” Other commercial Linux distributions will cost users money, meaning Microsoft can now make an argument that SUSE and RHEL subscriptions might be superfluous for both AKS users and those who use Azure to host other applications on Linux. Azure Linux 4.0 debuted last Thursday and is available here . Redmond’s latest Linux debuted just days after Microsoft issued a monster upgrade to version 3.0. ®

events.title: Thrift shop asks shoppers to nominate a charity
events.summary: Julie Rindam (front) and Jeanette Worthington (back) plan to be transparent with donors by having a book in the shop which will evidence where money is going. Shoppers and donors at a new charity shop will be able to help decide which organisations benefit from the money it raises. Twisted Sisters Thrift Store, in Tunstall opened last week, and is inviting customers to nominate causes they would like to support, with a different charity set to receive donations each month. Owner Julie Rindam said the idea came after the closure of a charity shop; she had run for eight years. "The pastor is retiring and it was either another empty shop or I took it on." Rindam said many of the shop's regular donors wanted to continue supporting charitable causes, leading to the idea of allowing the community to decide where the money goes. "All my donators still wanted to drop off to us, so we thought, well, how about a different charity every month?" she said. "We ask all the donators who they'd like us to donate to, so every month it will be a different charity benefiting." Rather than supporting a single organisation, the shop plans to keep a record of suggestions, being completely transparent with customers and donors before selecting a charity at the end of each month. "Everyone who drops off, we ask and we keep a book and every month we'll pick a different charity to benefit from, whether that's City Dogs Home, Cancer Research, Diabetes or other charities," Rindam said. The owner hopes that the store will also be a centre for the community. Shop manager Jeanette Worthington said the approach was designed to ensure local people remained involved in how the money was distributed. As well as raising money for charity, the store also aims to act as a community hub, offering free food, sanitary products, contraception and school uniforms when available. Worthington said supporting local people was just as important as supporting charities. "People know they can come here, it's a safe space," she said. "We will help anybody if we have the time and if we can't do it, we'll say come back at such and such a time." Janet Smart had been a regular donater to the shop before it was taken over by the new team. Regular customer and donor Janet Smart said the shop had become a valuable part of the community. "When I'm decluttering everything, it comes to here because I know they don't charge a lot. People haven't got much money today," she said. "You meet such nice people in here as well." She added that the social side of the shop was equally important. "I think for people on their own, it's nice to be able to come in somewhere and people chat with them." Jack Spencer is managing to find clothes and items that he wouldn't be able to find in more mainstream stores. Shopper Jack Spencer said the store offered affordable options for people who might otherwise struggle to buy certain items. "It feels a lot more personal, a lot more out there. You go in, you don't know what you're going to walk into, it changes constantly," he said. "You might find something that you could have been looking for, but you just couldn't afford it." For Rindam and Worthington, the hope is that both the charities and the local community will benefit. events.title: 'Break-in and rising costs could kill my business'
events.summary: Gordon Kidd says he is struggling with business-related costs and a recent break-in has not helped The owner of a cycle shop says he is considering closing the business after a break-in and soaring costs. Gordon Kidd, who runs Shifnal Cycles, estimates that a burglary last month cost him about £20,000 after three customer bikes and a frame were stolen and the subsequent repairs to his shop. Along with rising bills and a "lack of government support", the former armed forces veteran said the business in Shifnal may not be viable if financial pressures continue. A government spokesperson said that, from next year, businesses such as cycle shops would see their business rates either frozen, reduced or cut to zero, with half of the high-street retailers paying no rates. West Mercia Police said it had received a report of a burglary on 31 October, and an investigation was ongoing. "They stole customers' bikes, which, for me, as a shop owner, is my biggest fear," said Kidd, who was concerned the burglary could affect his reputation. "That might put them [customers] off from using my shop, and that kills a shop." He added: "I've got to do what's financially viable for the business. "I've got to look at another avenue now, and I've got to look at a more cost-effective way of doing it." Burglars stole three cycles and a frame and damaged the shop in the raid Alongside coping with the impact of the burglary, Kidd called on the government to do more to help small businesses. "I don't know how the government expects small businesses to operate and make a living," he said. "We just break even with the repairs side of things, and it's tough." He said the break-in "had not helped whatsoever". "A lot of people probably think that bike shops make a lot of money when we really don't," he said. Kidd, who not only sells cycles but also repairs and services them, told the BBC that the break-in had made him feel angry that his safe space had been invaded. He suffers post-traumatic stress disorder and said the business was "like therapy". "Working on bikes calms me down; it helps me keep in control of my PTSD and my mental health in general." A government spokesperson said: "Corporation tax remains capped, and there are generous tax reliefs offered for hiring young people. "We are also making the business environment work better through our £4.3bn business rates support package, small business plan and action on late payments. events.title: Taiwan deputy minister on Jensen Huang scandal: ‘We feel sad’
events.summary: The scandal surrounding former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has sparked a wave of sadness in his native Taiwan, the island’s deputy digital minister said Sunday. Huang had a close relationship with Taiwanese tech companies, meeting with them every year, Isabel Hou said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & the World. “The relationship is very personal,” she told Semafor Editor-in-Chief Ben Smith. “The supply chain leaders, I think, were concerned about how this kind of trust can be replaced. It will be tough.” Those ties went beyond business: Hou referenced a New York Times article in which Huang’s longtime hairstylist admitted he was too upset to sleep , drank a bottle of red wine, and prayed for the former chip CEO after his resignation. “We feel sad,” she added. The Nvidia ordeal has fueled calls in Washington for tighter chip export controls, given Huang’s years of lobbying to sell chips to China, and the revelation that he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman whom US officials suspect spying for Beijing. US authorities are probing whether Megaspeed, the company the woman formerly led, smuggled Nvidia chips to China. Singapore-based Megaspeed has denied the allegations. US lawmakers from both parties have pushed for tougher export restrictions, and Democrats have opened an inquiry into the Trump administration’s approval of Nvidia’s H200 chip sales to China. Taipei has been aligning its export control policy with the US. Hou said Taiwanese don’t want frontier chips going to China, where they could end up in military equipment aimed at the island. Reading a line prepared by her staff, she called for a policy that’s “precise, predictable, and coordinated with partners.” China, once the destination for the vast majority of Taiwan’s outbound investment, now draws less than 1%, Hou said, as companies expand elsewhere, many in the US. In AI especially, Taiwan needs “trusted partners.” — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: US official says government needs to make a better case for AI
events.summary: The US government has a responsibility to explain AI’s benefits to the public after the midterm elections showed widespread antagonism to the technology, a top State Department official said Sunday. Jacob Helberg, the undersecretary for economic affairs, said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & the World that the election, in which many voters were opposed to AI and data centers, should be seen as an “opportunity.” “The onus really is on everyone serving in government at all levels, local, state, and federal, to do a better job of communicating to the public the opportunity and the upside of this great technology,” Helberg told Semafor Editor-in-Chief Ben Smith. Helberg pointed to data showing that AI has helped prop up the US economy through investment and productivity gains. He said AI hasn’t caused mass job losses, and “we haven’t seen any evidence at all that super intelligence has had an inflationary effect,” using the Trump administration’s preferred alternative term for AI. Competitor obsession Helberg, who has spearheaded the Pax Silica effort with US allies to secure global supply chains for critical industries, also said US global tech policy shouldn’t “obsess” over China. “Great companies don’t try to succeed by obsessing over their competitors,” he said. “One of the temptations in policy roles is you spend so much time studying what competitors do that it almost becomes easy to over-obsess on them.” While Pax Silica is building a bloc of US-allied nations to reduce their dependence on China, Helberg said the effort is intended to be “an America-centric initiative, not a China-centric initiative.” — J.D. events.title: Czechs gather in big numbers to reject government's plan to overhaul funding of public media
events.summary: Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague against the Czech government's plan to overhaul funding for public broadcasters PRAGUE -- Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague on Sunday against a plan by the government of Czech billionaire Andrej Babiš to overhaul funding for public broadcasters that many say will erode media independence and democracy. The massive protest took place at the capital's Letná Park, where huge crowds gathered during the 1989 Velvet Revolution, which ended more than 40 years of communist rule in the country. The rally, just two days before the anniversary of the 1989 protests, drew an estimated 350,000 people, said Mikuláš Minář, the lead organizer from the Million Moments for Democracy group. They demanded that the government withdraw its plan and expressed concern that Babiš and his coalition partners pose a threat to democracy. “We do witness here something extraordinary today,” Minář said. “It's just a beginning.” Under the plan, the country’s public radio and television broadcasters would be financed from the state budget, replacing the existing system of regular fees paid by individuals, households and businesses. The broadcasters would receive about 15% less money than they do now, which could lead to layoffs, limited production and program cancellations. Critics say the overhaul would give the three-party coalition the means to take control of the media, similar to what populist governments did in Slovakia under Prime Minister Robert Fico and in Hungary, before former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was ousted from power in April. “We refuse the Slovak scenario,” one protest banner read. “Hands off the media,” said another. One of the protesters, singer Šarka Dumišincová, said that for her “the media represent freedom. And the fact that someone here is trying to control that freedom is unacceptable to me. That’s why I’m here today.” The ruling coalition unexpectedly moved ahead with the plan in the lower house of Parliament on Oct. 24. Its lawmakers limited the opposition's speaking time before voting at 4:36 a.m. to advance the bill through the first of three parliamentary readings. Thousands took to the streets the following day to protest the rushed process, and public media employees went on strike on Nov. 3. The strike was backed by labor unions, universities, students, churches, artists, athletes and international media organizations, among others. “We are here to stand up against the rule by force in the style of 4:36,” Minář said Sunday, referring to the time the bill cleared its first reading. Whipped cream sold at Costco in 12 states voluntarily recalled Authorities investigate 'credible' unknown device threat at Illinois plant Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Media freedom and the rule of law in the Czech Republic were debated Wednesday in the European Parliament. EU Justice Commissioner Michael McGrath said national legislation must ensure that funding for public service iis based on transparent and objective criteria and guarantees "adequate, sustainable and predictable financial resources.” Babiš vowed to press ahead with the plan despite the protests and denied that it would affect media freedom. He returned to power in the Czech Republic after his ANO, or YES, movement, won the country’s election last year and formed a coalition with two small political groups — the anti-migrant and pro-Russian party Freedom and Direct Democracy, and the right-wing Motorists for Themselves. Babiš has opposed some key European Union policies on environment and migration and rejected financial aid for Ukraine and guarantees for EU loans to help it fight the Russian invasion . His government has been under fire from NATO allies for failing to spend enough on defense. Protesters also condemned its defense policy and demanded the resignation of the Freedom party leader, parliamentary Speaker Tomio Okamura, and Defense Minister Jaromír Zůna. The party is in charge of the ministry. "While (Russia's President Vladimir) Putin threatens Europe, the pro-Russian (party) is systematically undermining the state’s defensive capability and endangering national security,” Minář, the main protest organizer, said. Associated Press video journalist Stanislav Hodina contributed to this report. events.title: A new generation of media will shape the 2028 Democratic primary
events.summary: The Scoop Last week, while shouting out supporters at the Muslim Public Affairs Council gala in Washington, DC, Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed singled out a figure in the crowd for special thanks: the founder of Zeteo, Mehdi Hasan, whose posts and videos pushed back against claims that progressives had underperformed more moderate candidates. Three days later, Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom told the anti-Trump digital outlet MeidasTouch that the network had given him a key boost at a moment when few people believed Mississippi would be in play for a Democratic candidate. “Thank you for giving me the opportunity very early on, when nobody thought Mississippi would be on the radar, to tell my story, tell my message,” Colom said. The first two years of President Donald Trump’s return to power were a waking nightmare for the Democratic Party. But in Trump’s shadow, oppositional media on the left has seen a period of extraordinary growth. Creators like Aaron Parnas, Keith Edwards, and Jack Cocchiarella gained millions of followers railing against Trump on YouTube. Independent media companies like The Bulwark, Crooked Media, and Zeteo gained millions of combined subscriptions on Substack, which grew from a platform largely favored by right-leaning or “heterodox” publishers to one dominated by left-leaning new media outlets and voices. Scarred by Trump’s 2024 podcast tours, Democratic donors are pouring money into the independent media space, and Democratic candidates have new media figures on speed dial. And now this ascendant new media ecosystem is positioning itself to help pick the next Democratic presidential nominee — or at least weed out a few of the duds. Progressive outlets are aiming to serve as a check on traditional media that they feel wants to knock out left-wing candidates, while moderate forces are starting up their own media to try and counter a zealous left flank that has shouted down moderates online. “That’s going to be the war more than anything: the attention fight… How can I, with the least amount of friction, get these people to start sharing clips?” Cocchiarella told Semafor. The Left While many legacy outlets that had experienced ratings and subscriptions growth during Trump’s first term have seen little to no meaningful gains in his second go-around, independent media outlets critical of Trump, the mainstream media, and Democratic Party leadership saw huge gains. Since the beginning of Trump’s presidency, Zeteo has added almost 2 million YouTube subscribers. The Bernie Sanders-ite outlet More Perfect Union has added 3 million. Hasan Piker, the leftist Twitch streamer who became a midterm campaign fixation, has gained millions of followers on YouTube and increased viewership of his stream. Now, both MPU and Zeteo are hoping to bring different issues — or candidates — to the front of the Democratic presidential primary debate. Over the last two years, Zeteo has provided early coverage and political air cover for left-wing and socialist candidates, particularly those that have expressed aggressive criticism of Israel. In an interview on Thursday, Hasan pointed to the company’s early interviews with then-New York City mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani and El-Sayed as examples; both were able to gain exposure to like-minded voters while other outlets were skeptical of their candidacies. “From Zohran Mamdani’s race, to AOC’s rise, to Abdul El-Sayed’s victory, I think it’s been very clear — I’m not saying they wouldn’t have happened without us; that’s a little bit too arrogant and not accurate — but certainly they were aided and abetted and strengthened and bolstered by the fact that we exist,” he said. Hasan said potential 2028 candidates clearly have taken notice. Before the midterm elections, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., said in a candid rare interview on Zeteo that he was considering running in 2028 , an admission he hadn’t made on-camera anywhere else. Hasan said although his political views are clear, multiple likely candidates who do not necessarily share Zeteo’s progressive, Israel-critical stance had nonetheless been in touch in recent days about appearing on the outlet’s show. “Democratic presidential [hopefuls] and their teams have reached out to us, not the other way around, even people we’ve criticized,” Hasan said, noting that he’s angling for an interview with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a pro-Israel Democrat. Other outlets are more interested in highlighting specific issues, but could end up tipping the conversation in favor of certain candidates that they choose to spotlight. More Perfect Union, the viral video channel founded by Sanders advisor Faiz Shakir, has not outright endorsed candidates in races, but its story selection and tone have bolstered candidates on the left. During the midterms, the organization published a video on then-Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner titled It was less investigatory (the piece did not uncover the various scandals that later led to Platner’s decision to drop out), and more complimentary; it gave space for Platner to explain his view on various media controversies, and showed working class Platner supporters who were unbothered by the unfolding scandals. Over the last few months, More Perfect Union has interviewed Sanders and Reps. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. In an email, More Perfect Union Editor-in-Chief Josh Miller-Lewis told Semafor that although the organization had not finalized its 2028 plans yet, it was hoping to host multiple events with candidates. The organization also hopes to grow its More Perfect University program, which hosted town halls where candidates faced college student questioners. But primarily, Miller-Lewis said, it plans to create content that would “put candidates in conversation with working class audiences and force substantive policy discussions that are often lacking in election coverage,” citing videos the organization made with Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz during the 2024 election and El-Sayed during the 2026 Senate race. “Our goal will be to create spaces where our working class audience has the opportunity to challenge candidates in substantive, solutions driven conversations, candidates can outline the big ideas they’ll prioritize if elected and show viewers how candidates engage with the voters they need to persuade to win,” Miller-Lewis wrote. Beyond highlighting more ideologically aligned candidates, left-wing outlets also plan to highlight shortcomings of centrist and moderate candidates. Ryan Grim, a founder of the foreign policy-centric Drop Site News, noted that the investigative outlet will be expanding its domestic coverage to focus on spotlighting how three powerful interest groups hope to influence the Democratic presidential primary. “Crypto and AI, and to some extent AIPAC, are gonna wanna participate, which is wonderful, and we’re a big democracy, but we’re gonna make sure that the public knows who they’re support

events.title: Intel sued by investors after PC sales slump hits share price
events.summary: Intel, the US chip giant, is being sued by its shareholders who accuse the firm of hiding the severity of a slump in its personal computer (PC) sales that caused its share price to plunge almost 29% in one day. Billions of dollars was knocked off the value of the company after it forecast disappointing revenues ahead of its latest earnings report. The BBC has contacted Intel for comment. In October, Intel firm announced its computer hardware sales had dropped sharply in the three months that ended in September. That report undermined earlier suggestions from the chipmaker that demand had been improving, sending Intel shares plunging, according to the lawsuit. The lawsuit, filed by legal firm Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd on behalf of owners of Intel common shares between 23 July and 29 October this year, was filed against the chipmaker, its chief executive Tan Lip-Bu and other company leaders. Intel has poured huge investments into manufacturing to meet the enormous demand for AI computing power. As more semiconductors are channelled towards data centres, chips for PCs and other electronics have become more expensive. Intel boss Tan had told analysts that the industry was facing an "unprecedented memory crunch", resulting in a shortage of chip supplies for PCs. "We need to address these challenges with urgency," Tan said in October. Intel shares have fallen sharply in the past month by 37.5%, though its share price is still up by 51% overall this year.
